notice: These are expanded, original revision guides organized around learning areas in the app's Kenya CBC catalogue and grouped into level bands (PP1-PP2, Grade 1-3, Grade 4-6, Grade 7-9, Grade 10-12). They provide broad topic coverage, explanations, worked examples, practice activities, and self-check questions, but are not official KICD curriculum designs or a complete syllabus. Topic selection, depth, and sequence vary by grade, school, and pathway; confirm coverage with the current KICD design and the school's approved programme.

grade_focus.PP1: Explore through play, conversation, movement, and familiar objects with adult guidance.
grade_focus.PP2: Build confidence through play, observation, conversation, and short guided activities.
grade_focus.Grade 1: Use familiar examples, simple language, concrete materials, and short guided practice.
grade_focus.Grade 2: Practise core ideas with familiar examples, clear steps, and growing independence.
grade_focus.Grade 3: Connect familiar ideas, explain simple choices, and practise skills with less prompting.
grade_focus.Grade 4: Build understanding through examples, classification, discussion, and guided investigation.
grade_focus.Grade 5: Apply skills to familiar situations, compare examples, and record observations clearly.
grade_focus.Grade 6: Combine related skills, explain methods, and prepare for more independent learning.
grade_focus.Grade 7: Build foundational understanding with guided examples and familiar local contexts.
grade_focus.Grade 8: Apply ideas independently, compare examples, and explain reasoning.
grade_focus.Grade 9: Integrate learning in extended tasks, justify conclusions, and transfer skills.
grade_focus.Grade 10: Analyse concepts, apply evidence, and connect learning to pathway and community contexts.
grade_focus.Grade 11: Evaluate evidence, strengthen independent inquiry, and apply concepts to unfamiliar contexts.
grade_focus.Grade 12: Synthesize learning, justify decisions, and communicate well-supported conclusions.

Language Activities.overview: A playful guide that helps young children listen carefully, speak clearly, sing rhymes and enjoy stories. All activities are oral and use everyday things found at home and at school.

units.title: Listening and paying attention
units.notes: We listen with our ears and our eyes, and we look at the person who is talking. When we sit still and keep quiet, we understand the words being said to us. Listening well helps us hear many sounds around us, such as birds, cars and drums. A good listener waits for a turn and then answers in a clear voice.
units.worked_example: The teacher claps three times and asks the children to clap the same number. A child who listened well claps three times and smiles.
units.activity: Play a listening game where an adult makes a sound behind a cloth and the child says what made it.
units.check: Can you tell me one thing a good listener does?

quiz.prompt: What do we use to listen to a person talking?
What does a good listener do when someone else is talking?
options: Waits for a turn, then answers

quiz.prompt: A good listener sits still and keeps quiet?
We listen to sounds with our nose?
Which of these is a sound we can hear around us?

units.title: Greetings and polite words
units.notes: We greet people when we meet them and when we leave them. In the morning we say good morning, and in the evening we say good evening. We also use kind words like please, thank you and sorry. Greeting shows respect and makes other people happy, so we greet everyone with a smile. Children can greet their parents, teachers, friends and visitors every day.
units.worked_example: A child walks into the classroom, looks at the teacher and says, good morning teacher, and the teacher says good morning back.
units.activity: Practise greeting three people at home today using their names and a kind word.
units.check: What do you say when someone gives you a gift?

quiz.prompt: What do you say when someone gives you a gift?
What do we say in the morning when we meet someone?
We say good evening when we meet someone in the morning?
Why do we greet people with a smile?
options: To show respect and make them happy

quiz.prompt: We can greet our teacher and our friends?

units.title: Naming people and things around me
units.notes: Everything around us has a name. We name people like mother, father, teacher and friend, and we name things like cup, chair, ball, plate and shoe. When we know names, we can ask for what we want easily. Children learn new names by pointing, touching and saying the word aloud. Naming games make learning new words fun, quick and easy for children.
units.worked_example: An adult holds up a spoon and asks, what is this? The child says, it is a spoon, and then points to another spoon in the kitchen.
units.activity: Walk around the house together and name ten things you can see or touch.
units.check: Can you name three things in your classroom?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a name for a person?
Which of these is a name for a thing?
Everything around us has a name?
How can children learn new names?
options: By pointing, touching and saying the word

quiz.prompt: Knowing names makes it hard to ask for what we want?

units.title: Talking about my family
units.notes: A family is a group of people who love and care for one another. In my family I may have a father, a mother, brothers, sisters and grandparents. We eat together, play together and help one another at home. Children can talk about the people in their family using simple words. Every family is special and good in its own way.
units.worked_example: A child says, this is my mother, she cooks food for us, and this is my small brother, he likes to play with a ball.
units.activity: Draw your family on paper and tell an adult the name of each person you drew.
units.check: Who are the people in your family?

quiz.prompt: What is a family?
options: A group of people who love and care for one another
A place where we buy food

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a member of a family?
In a family, people help one another at home?
What do families do together?
Only one kind of family is good?

units.title: Rhymes and songs
units.notes: Rhymes and songs have rhythm and repeated words, which make them easy to remember. We sing songs about animals, numbers, colours and our daily life. Singing helps children hear the sounds of words clearly and learn new words. We also clap, stamp and sway as we sing together. Children enjoy songs and will happily sing them many times together, again and again.
units.worked_example: The children sing a short rhyme about a little bird, clapping the beat with their hands and saying the last word of each line loudly.
units.activity: Sing a favourite rhyme with an adult and add hand actions to each line.
units.check: Which song do you like to sing the most?

quiz.prompt: Why are rhymes and songs easy to remember?
options: They have rhythm and repeated words

quiz.prompt: What do we do with our bodies as we sing?
Singing helps children learn new words?
What can songs be about?
options: Animals, numbers, colours and daily life

quiz.prompt: Children should sing a song only one time and never again?

units.title: Listening to and telling stories
units.notes: Stories take us to interesting places and teach us good behaviour. When we listen to a story, we find out about the characters and what they do. We can then tell the same story in our own words to a friend. Stories help children build many new words and ideas. A story told with actions and funny voices is even more fun to hear.
units.worked_example: After hearing a story about a clever hare, a child retells it and says, the hare ran away from the lion because he was clever.
units.activity: Ask an adult to tell you a short story, then tell it back to a friend in your own words.
units.check: What happened at the end of the last story you heard?

quiz.prompt: What do stories teach us?
After listening to a story, what can we do?
options: Tell the same story in our own words

quiz.prompt: Stories can help children learn new words and ideas?
What makes a story even more fun to hear?
Characters in a story do nothing?

units.title: Sounds around us
units.notes: Our ears help us hear many sounds every day, and some sounds are loud while others are soft. We hear sounds from animals, vehicles, people and things in the home. We can often tell what made a sound even when we cannot see it. Listening carefully to sounds helps children notice small differences between words, which prepares them for learning letters.
units.worked_example: An adult shakes a tin with stones, then a bottle with water, and the child guesses which one made the loud sound.
units.activity: Close your eyes for one minute and count how many different sounds you can hear.
units.check: Which sound did you hear today that was very loud?

quiz.prompt: Which body part helps us hear sounds?
Some sounds are loud. What are other sounds like?
We can often tell what made a sound even when we cannot see it?
Listening carefully to sounds helps children get ready for what?
Are all sounds around us the same?

units.title: Speaking in short sentences
units.notes: We speak to share what we think and feel. A short sentence has a naming word and an action word. For example, we say the baby is crying or father has come home. Children learn to speak clearly by saying one full sentence at a time. Speaking politely in a calm voice helps others to listen, and a child can talk about home using two or three short sentences.
units.worked_example: A child looks at a picture of a girl eating and says, the girl is eating her food.
units.activity: Tell an adult three short sentences about what you did this morning.
units.check: Can you say one full sentence about your best friend?

quiz.prompt: A short sentence has a naming word and what else?
Which of these is a short sentence?
We speak to share what we think and feel?
How should we speak so others listen?
We should speak in a loud rude voice?

units.title: Describing words for colours and sizes
units.notes: Describing words tell us more about people, animals and things. We use colour words like red, blue, yellow and green, and we use size words like big, small, long and short. When we describe something well, other people can picture it in their minds. Children can describe real objects they can see and touch, such as a big red ball. Playing simple games with coloured blocks makes these words easy to learn.
units.worked_example: An adult shows two cups and asks which one is bigger; the child points and says, the blue cup is big and the yellow cup is small.
units.activity: Pick five things in the room and describe each one using a colour word and a size word.
units.check: Can you describe your favourite toy to me?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a colour word?
Which of these is a size word?
We use describing words to tell more about things?
Which words describe a ball best?
Green and red are size words?

units.title: Naming action words
units.notes: Action words tell us what people and animals are doing. We run, jump, eat, sleep, wash and play every day. We can show an action with our bodies or say it in a sentence. Children learn action words quickly when they move their bodies as they speak. Saying the word while doing the action helps a child remember it for a long time.
units.worked_example: The adult says the word jump and the child jumps; then the child says swim and moves both arms as if swimming.
units.activity: Play a game where an adult calls out an action word like skip or clap and you do it.
units.check: What are you doing right now?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is an action word?
What do action words tell us?
options: What people and animals are doing

quiz.prompt: We can show an action with our bodies?
Which of these shows an action?
Moving our bodies makes action words harder to learn?

units.title: Asking and answering questions
units.notes: We ask questions when we want to know or find out something new. We use question words like who, what, where, when and why. We also answer questions that other people ask us. Answering with a full sentence is better than answering with only one word. Children learn to ask and answer by having short talks with an adult every day.
units.worked_example: An adult asks, where is your bag? The child answers, my bag is under the chair.
units.activity: Ask an adult three questions about their day and listen carefully to each answer.
units.check: What question would you ask a visitor to your class?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a question word?
What is better than answering with only one word?
We ask questions when we want to find out something new?
Which of these words is also a question word?
We should never answer questions other people ask us?

units.title: Pre-writing patterns and marks
units.notes: Before children write letters, they practise making simple marks and patterns. We draw lines from left to right, from top to bottom, and round and round. We can use a finger in sand, a stick in mud or a crayon on paper. These patterns train the fingers and the eyes for writing later. Scribbling and tracing are good, not wrong, at this age.
units.worked_example: A child draws a row of straight lines in a tray of sand, then draws a big round circle without lifting the finger.
units.activity: Trace big round shapes and straight lines with your finger in sand or flour.
units.check: Can you show me how to draw a straight line from left to right?

quiz.prompt: Before writing letters, what should children practise?
How can we draw patterns?
options: With a finger in sand, a stick in mud or a crayon

quiz.prompt: We draw lines from left to right and from top to bottom?
Are scribbling and tracing good at this age?
Practising patterns is bad for young children?

units.title: Sounds of letters in my name
units.notes: Every letter has a sound, and letters join together to make words. We start with the sounds in our own names, such as the first sound we hear. We say the sound slowly and listen carefully for it in other words. Children can clap the sounds or parts they hear in a word. Knowing letter sounds helps children read simple words later on.
units.worked_example: For the name Mwikali, the adult and child say the first sound mmm and then find other words that begin with the same sound.
units.activity: Say your name slowly and clap once for each part you hear.
units.check: What is the first sound you hear in your name?

quiz.prompt: What does every letter have?
Where do we start when learning letter sounds?
options: With the sounds in our own names

quiz.prompt: Letters join together to make words?
What can children clap when they hear a word?
Letter sounds have nothing to do with reading?

Mathematical Activities.overview: A hands-on guide where young children sort, count, compare and play with real objects to build early number ideas. Every activity uses everyday things and short spoken games with an adult.

units.title: Sorting and matching objects
units.notes: We sort things when we put them into groups that are alike. We can sort by colour, shape, size or what the thing is used for. We can also match things that go together, like a cup and a saucer. Children sort using real objects such as bottle tops, stones, spoons and clothes. Sorting helps children see how things are the same or different.
units.worked_example: A child sorts a pile of bottle tops into two groups, one group of red tops and one group of blue tops.
units.activity: Collect stones and leaves outside and put them into two separate groups.
units.check: Can you tell me how you sorted your stones?

quiz.prompt: What do we do when we sort things?
options: We put them into groups that are alike

quiz.prompt: Which of these can we sort things by?
A cup and a saucer are things that go together?
Which objects can children use for sorting?
Sorting helps children see how things are the same or different?

units.title: Comparing big and small things
units.notes: Things around us come in different sizes, and we can compare two things at a time. We say which thing is big and which thing is small. We also use words like long, short, tall, heavy and light. Children compare real objects they can hold, such as shoes, spoons and balls. We can also line up three things from the smallest to the biggest.
units.worked_example: A child puts a father's shoe and a baby's shoe side by side and says, the father's shoe is big and the baby's shoe is small.
units.activity: Find three shoes at home and line them up from the smallest to the biggest.
units.check: Which is bigger, an orange or a mango?

quiz.prompt: When we compare two things, what do we say?
options: Which is big and which is small

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a size word?
We can line up three things from the smallest to the biggest?
Which is bigger, an orange or a mango?
We cannot compare things by their size?

units.title: Making patterns
units.notes: A pattern is a line of things that repeat again and again. We can make patterns with colours, shapes, sounds or body movements. For example, we can clap, stamp, clap and stamp in a steady beat. Children can copy a pattern shown by an adult and then make a new one of their own. Patterns help children notice order, which prepares them for number work later.
units.worked_example: A child threads beads in the order red, blue, red, blue and then continues the same pattern to the end of the string.
units.activity: Make a pattern with stones and leaves on the ground by taking turns with a friend.
units.check: What comes next in this pattern: clap, stamp, clap, stamp?

quiz.prompt: What is a pattern?
options: A line of things that repeat again and again

quiz.prompt: In the pattern clap, stamp, clap, stamp, what comes next?
We can make patterns with colours, shapes and sounds?
What does copying a pattern help children notice?
Patterns have nothing to do with number work later?

units.title: Counting things one to five
units.notes: We count things to find out how many of them there are. When we count, we touch each thing once and say one number for it. The numbers one, two, three, four and five come in that order. The last number we say tells us how many things are in the group. Children count real things like fingers, cups, stones and chairs, and counting songs help them remember the order.
units.worked_example: A child counts five spoons, touching each spoon and saying one, two, three, four, five, then says there are five spoons.
units.activity: Count five of your toys out loud and then count five steps as you walk.
units.check: How many fingers are on one hand?

quiz.prompt: When we count, how many times do we touch each thing?
Which number comes after three?
The last number we say tells us how many things are in the group?
How many fingers are on one hand?
We can say the numbers one to five in any order we like?

units.title: Counting things six to ten
units.notes: After five, we go on to the numbers six, seven, eight, nine and ten. We count bigger groups by touching each thing once and saying one number for it. We can count our ten fingers and ten toes, or ten small stones. We can also build a group of ten by joining two groups of five. Counting up to ten many times helps children say the numbers in the right order.
units.worked_example: A child picks up ten stones one by one and counts out loud until reaching ten.
units.activity: Count ten items in the house, such as cups or shoes, and say how many you counted.
units.check: Can you count from six to ten without missing a number?

quiz.prompt: Which number comes just after five?
After six, which number comes next?
We can count ten fingers and ten toes?
Two groups of five make how many?
The number ten comes before the number six?

units.title: Recognising numbers
units.notes: Numbers have names and also shapes that we can learn to see. The number three looks like three, and the number five looks like five. We can point to a number card and say its name out loud. Children match a number to a group with the same number of objects. Seeing numbers in the home, such as on a clock or a door, helps children remember them.
units.worked_example: The adult shows the number four, and the child says four and then picks up four bottle tops to match.
units.activity: Look for numbers on a phone, a clock or a calendar and name each one you find.
units.check: Can you point to the number two on this card?

quiz.prompt: Numbers have names and also what?
What do we do with a number card?
options: Point to it and say its name

quiz.prompt: We can match a number to a group with the same number of objects?
Where can we see numbers at home?
options: On a clock or a door

quiz.prompt: Numbers have no name at all?

units.title: Position and direction words
units.notes: We use position words to say where things are. We say in, out, on, under, inside, outside, in front and behind. These words help us follow instructions and find what we need. Children learn best when they move their own bodies to show each position. We can also say what is near to us and what is far away from us in the room.
units.worked_example: An adult says, put the ball under the chair, and the child does it and then says, the ball is under the chair.
units.activity: Play a game where you go in the box, out of the box and behind the door.
units.check: Where is your bag right now?

quiz.prompt: Which word tells us where something is?
If your bag is below the table, where is it?
Position words help us follow instructions?
Which of these is a position word?
Near and far do not tell us anything about place?

units.title: More, fewer and the same
units.notes: We can compare two groups of things and see which group has more. We can also see which group has fewer, or if both groups have the same number. To find out, we can match one thing in the first group with one thing in the second group. If some things are left over, that group has more. Children use real objects like stones and bottle tops to compare groups every day.
units.worked_example: A child lines up four stones and three leaves, matches them one by one, and says, the stones are more than the leaves.
units.activity: Make two groups of stones outside and say which group has more.
units.check: Which group has fewer, a group of two sweets or a group of five sweets?

quiz.prompt: When both groups have the same number, what can we say?
How can we find out which group has more?
options: Match one thing with one thing

quiz.prompt: If some things are left over, that group has more?
Which group has fewer, a group of two sweets or a group of five sweets?
A group of five has fewer things than a group of two?

units.title: Shapes around us
units.notes: Shapes are all around us in the things we see and use. A ball is round, a book is a rectangle and a window can be a square. We can also see circles, triangles and ovals in the home and outside. Children learn shapes by touching them, tracing them and finding them in real things. We can sort objects by their shape, such as putting all the round things together.
units.worked_example: A child holds a round plate, traces its edge with a finger and says, this shape is a circle.
units.activity: Walk around and find one round thing, one square thing and one long thing.
units.check: What shape is the face of a ball?

quiz.prompt: What shape is a ball?
What shape is the face of a book?
We can see circles, triangles and ovals in the home and outside?
How do children learn shapes best?
options: By touching, tracing and finding them

quiz.prompt: A book has the shape of a circle?

units.title: Joining and taking away
units.notes: We can join two groups of things to find out how many there are altogether. For example, two stones joined with three stones make five stones. We can also take some things away from a group and count what is left. Children do this best with real objects they can move with their hands. Talking about the action while doing it, such as adding one more, helps children understand.
units.worked_example: A child has three oranges, gets two more from a basket, and counts five oranges altogether.
units.activity: Put five stones in a tin, take away two, and count how many stones remain.
units.check: If you have one sweet and I give you one more, how many sweets do you have?

quiz.prompt: If you have two stones and add three more, how many altogether?
What happens when we take some things away from a group?
We can join two groups of things to find how many there are altogether?
If you have one sweet and I give you one more, how many sweets do you have?
Taking things away makes a group bigger?

units.title: Day, night and the days of the week
units.notes: We do different things at different times of the day. In the morning we wake up, wash and go to school. In the evening it becomes dark and we get ready to sleep. The sun gives us light in the day, and the moon and stars come out at night. Children learn the days of the week by saying them in order each morning.
units.worked_example: The children say the days of the week in order, starting with Monday and ending with Sunday.
units.activity: Talk about what you do in the morning, at midday and at night.
units.check: What do you do when it becomes dark at night?

quiz.prompt: What do we do in the morning?
options: Wake up, wash and go to school

quiz.prompt: What gives us light in the day?
The moon and stars come out at night?
What do we do when it becomes dark at night?
The sun gives us light at night?

units.title: Measuring with our hands and feet
units.notes: We can measure things using parts of our own bodies. We can measure a table by counting how many hand spans cover it. We can measure the floor by putting one foot in front of the other and counting the steps. We can also pour water or sand from one cup to another to see which holds more. Children enjoy measuring things in the home, the classroom and the playground.
units.worked_example: A child measures the length of a mat by walking heel to toe and counting six steps.
units.activity: Measure how many hand spans wide your table is, and then measure a chair.
units.check: How many foot steps long is your mat at home?

quiz.prompt: How can we measure a table?
How can we measure the floor?
We can measure things using parts of our own bodies?
What can we pour from one cup to another to see which holds more?
Measuring things is only done in school?

units.title: Money in play and shopping
units.notes: We use money to buy the things that we need and want. In Kenya we use coins and notes, such as one shilling, five shillings and ten shillings. Children can play shop and pretend to buy and sell simple things like fruit. In the game they learn to give money, take change and count coins. Playing shop also teaches children to greet, ask and say thank you politely.
units.worked_example: In a pretend shop a child buys a banana for five shillings, gives a ten shilling coin and takes five shillings change.
units.activity: Set up a small pretend shop with an adult and buy and sell things using coins.
units.check: What do we use to buy things at the shop?

quiz.prompt: What do we use to buy things at the shop?
Which of these is money used in Kenya?
In the shop game we can learn to give money and take change?
What do children learn while playing shop?
options: To greet, ask and say thank you

quiz.prompt: Money is used only for playing and never for buying things?

Environmental Activities.overview: A discovery guide that helps young children learn about their bodies, homes, families, plants, animals and weather through play. Children explore the world around them using their senses and simple talks with an adult.

units.title: My body parts
units.notes: My body has many parts that work together. I have a head, two eyes, two ears, a nose, a mouth, two arms and two legs. Each part helps me to do something, like seeing, hearing, smelling and walking. Children can touch and name the parts of their own bodies during songs and games. Naming body parts helps children say what hurts when they do not feel well.
units.worked_example: The children sing a song and touch each named part, such as head, shoulders, knees and toes.
units.activity: Play a game where an adult names a body part and you touch it on your own body.
units.check: Which body part do you use to smell a flower?

quiz.prompt: How many eyes do you have?
Which body part do you use to smell a flower?
We have two arms and two legs?
Which body part helps us to walk?
We use our ears to see?

units.title: My five senses
units.notes: We learn about the world around us by using our five senses. We see with our eyes and hear with our ears. We smell with our nose, taste with our tongue and touch with our skin. Children can explore safe things from the home, such as soap, fruit and soft cloth. Talking about what we see, hear and feel builds new words and ideas.
units.worked_example: With eyes closed, a child smells a piece of orange and says that it smells sweet.
units.activity: Touch a soft cloth, a rough stone and a smooth leaf and say how each one feels.
units.check: Which sense do you use to hear a drum?

quiz.prompt: Which sense do you use to hear a drum?
What do we use to see?
We taste with our tongue?
Which sense do we use to touch a soft cloth?
We smell with our ears?

units.title: Keeping my body clean
units.notes: Keeping our bodies clean helps us stay healthy and strong. We wash our hands with soap and water before we eat and after using the toilet. We bathe, brush our teeth, comb our hair and cut our nails often. We also put on clean clothes and wear shoes to protect our feet. Children learn these habits best when a grown-up does them together with them every day.
units.worked_example: A child shows how to rub soap on both hands, wash between the fingers and rinse with clean water.
units.activity: Sing a hand-washing song while you wash your hands with soap before a meal.
units.check: When should you wash your hands?

quiz.prompt: When should you wash your hands?
options: Before we eat and after using the toilet

quiz.prompt: What do we use to wash our hands?
We should brush our teeth and comb our hair?
Why do we wear shoes?
We should never wash our hands?

units.title: My home and its surroundings
units.notes: My home is where I live with the people who care for me. At home we have rooms like a kitchen, a sitting room and bedrooms. Around the home we may see a garden, trees, animals and a road. Children can name the different places in and around their home. We take care of our home by keeping it clean and keeping things in their right places.
units.worked_example: A child draws a simple house and names the door, the window, the roof and the path outside.
units.activity: Walk around your home with an adult and name the different places you see.
units.check: Which room in your home do you sleep in?

quiz.prompt: Which room do we sleep in?
What might we see around the home?
We take care of our home by keeping it clean?
Which of these is a room in the home?
We should throw things anywhere in the home?

units.title: My family and relatives
units.notes: A family is made up of people who are related to one another. My family may have a father, a mother, brothers, sisters, grandparents, uncles and aunts. In my family we share food, work together and help one another. Children can talk about the people who live with them and those who visit them. Families are important because they give love, care and a safe place to live.
units.worked_example: A child says, my grandmother lives in the village, and she tells us stories when we visit her.
units.activity: Name the people in your family, starting with those you live with.
units.check: Who looks after you at home?

quiz.prompt: Who are relatives?
Which of these is a relative?
Families share food and help one another?
Why are families important?
options: They give love, care and a safe place

quiz.prompt: Only a father and a mother can ever be in a family?

units.title: My school and the people in it
units.notes: School is a place where children go to learn and play with others. At school we meet the teacher, the head teacher, other children and the workers. We learn letters, numbers, songs and good manners at school. Children follow simple rules, share, wait for their turn and keep the school clean. Going to school happily every day helps children grow and make new friends.
units.worked_example: A child names the teacher, the classroom and the play area, and says what people do in each place.
units.activity: Point to and name three places in your school, such as the classroom, the toilet and the play field.
units.check: What do you like doing most at school?

quiz.prompt: What do we do at school?
Who do we meet at school?

What should children do at school?
options: Share and wait for their turn

units.title: Weather and what we wear
units.notes: The weather changes from day to day and from season to season. Some days are sunny, some are rainy, and some are cold and cloudy. We wear different clothes for different kinds of weather. When it rains we may wear a raincoat or carry an umbrella, and when it is hot we wear light clothes. Children can watch the sky in the morning and say what the day will be like.
units.worked_example: A child looks outside, sees dark clouds and rain, and says that it is going to rain, so an umbrella is needed.
units.activity: Look outside in the morning and tell an adult what the weather is like today.
units.check: What do you wear when it is raining?

quiz.prompt: What do you wear when it is raining?
options: A raincoat or use an umbrella

units.title: Plants around us
units.notes: Plants grow all around us in gardens, fields and forests. A plant may have roots, a stem, leaves, flowers and sometimes fruit. Plants need water, sunlight and soil to grow well. We get food, shade, medicine and wood from different plants. Children can plant a seed in a tin, water it every day and watch it grow taller each week.
units.worked_example: A child puts a bean seed in wet cotton wool, keeps it in the light, and after some days sees a small green shoot.
units.activity: Plant a bean or maize seed in a tin and water it each morning.

units.title: Animals around us
units.notes: Many different kinds of animals live around us, both at home and in the wild. Some animals live at home, like cows, goats, sheep, hens, dogs and cats. Other animals live in the wild, like lions, elephants, zebras and monkeys. Animals give us food and skins, help with work and make us happy. Children learn to keep themselves safe near animals and to treat every animal kindly.
units.worked_example: A child sorts pictures or toy animals into two groups, those kept at home and those living in the wild.
units.activity: Name three animals you have seen near your home and tell where each one lives.

units.title: Water and its uses
units.notes: Clean water is very important for people, animals and plants to live. We drink water, cook with it, and wash our bodies, clothes and dishes with it. Plants and animals also need water to live and grow. We should use clean, safe water and keep our water containers covered. Children can help by fetching water, covering it and not wasting a single drop.
units.worked_example: A child shows how to pour water into a covered container and then closes the lid firmly.
units.activity: Count three ways your family uses water at home and say them aloud.

units.title: Food we eat
units.notes: We eat food to grow, to have energy and to stay healthy. We eat foods like ugali, rice, maize, beans, green vegetables, fruits and milk. A good meal has different kinds of food on the plate. We should wash our hands before eating and wash fruits before we eat them. Children should eat food that is well cooked and drink clean water every day.
units.worked_example: A child looks at a plate of ugali, beans and greens and names each of the foods on the plate.
units.activity: Name the food you ate today and say which ones are fruits and which are vegetables.

units.title: Keeping safe at home and on the way
units.notes: Children should stay safe at home, at school, on the road and in the market. We must not play with fire, sharp knives, hot water or electricity. On the road we hold an adult's hand, look both ways and use the crossing. We should not go away with people we do not know. Children should tell a trusted adult at once if something feels wrong or unsafe.
units.worked_example: A child stands at the roadside, holds the adult's hand, looks left and right, and then crosses safely.
units.activity: Practise with an adult how to look both ways before crossing a safe path or road.

options: Hold an adult's hand and look both ways

options: Tell a trusted adult at once

units.title: Caring for our environment
units.notes: We all share the land, water, air and the things that grow around us. We keep our environment clean by putting waste in the right place. We should plant trees, water them and not cut them down carelessly. We also save water, keep our rivers clean and care for the animals around us. Children can help at home and school by picking up litter and keeping the compound tidy.
units.worked_example: A child picks up a plastic bottle on the playground and puts it in the bin instead of throwing it on the ground.
units.activity: Walk around your compound with an adult and collect any rubbish you find into a bin.

What can children do to help the environment?

Psychomotor and Creative Activities.overview: A playful guide for young learners to move, make and explore with their bodies and hands, building control, balance and imagination through songs, games and simple creative tasks.

units.title: Moving my body safely
units.notes: We use our bodies to move and play every day. We can walk, run, jump and stretch. We must always move in safe open places. We look around us before we start to run. We keep a little space between us and our friends. When we move carefully, nobody gets hurt at all. We stop quickly when the adult says stop. Safe moving keeps our play happy and fun.
units.worked_example: Let us play a game called Red Light, Green Light. When the adult says green light, we walk forward slowly. When the adult says red light, we stop and stand still.
units.activity: Mark two lines on the ground outside. Walk slowly from one line to the other and freeze when the adult claps.
units.check: Can you stop your body quickly when you hear the word stop?

quiz.prompt: Where should we move and play?
What should we do before we start to run?

units.title: Knowing my body parts
units.notes: Our body has many parts. We have a head, two hands, two legs and two feet. We can touch our nose, ears, eyes and mouth. We move our arms and legs when we dance. Knowing our body parts helps us follow games and songs. We can name each part as we touch it. We can also bend our knees and turn our heads. Our body helps us play, learn and help at home.
units.worked_example: Sing a song like Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes. Touch each part as you sing its name.
units.activity: Ask a friend to call out a body part. Touch that part quickly and smile.
units.check: Can you point to your ears and your knees?

quiz.prompt: How many hands do you have?

units.title: Walking, running and stopping
units.notes: Walking is slow and calm. Running is fast and needs care. We swing our arms when we walk. We look ahead when we run. When the adult claps, we stop and stand still. Stopping lets us rest and listen. We walk indoors and run only outside. Running too fast may make us fall down. We keep our eyes open and our feet steady. Walking and running help our legs grow strong.
units.worked_example: Play a drum game. Walk when the drum beats slowly. Run on the spot when it beats fast. Freeze when it stops.
units.activity: Walk around a circle with friends. When the adult says stop, everyone stands still and listens.
units.check: What do you do with your body when the adult says stop?

quiz.prompt: Which one is fast?

We run only outside, not indoors?

units.title: Jumping, hopping and skipping
units.notes: Jumping pushes both feet off the ground. Hopping uses one foot only. Skipping is a happy step and hop together. We bend our knees before we jump. We land softly on our feet. These moves make our legs strong and our hearts happy. We can jump over a small line on the ground. We can hop like a rabbit or a frog. We take turns so nobody bumps.
units.worked_example: Count to three and jump up high. Land with soft knees and a big smile.
units.activity: Place five small objects in a row. Hop over each one on one foot, then swap feet.
units.check: Can you hop on one foot and then the other?

quiz.prompt: How many feet do we use to hop?

units.title: Throwing and catching a ball
units.notes: We throw a ball with our hands. We look at the person we throw to. We catch a big ball with both hands. Our hands make a soft nest for the ball. We start with a big soft ball. Big balls are easy to hold and catch. We stand a short distance from our friend. We throw gently and wait our turn. Catching takes practice and patience.
units.worked_example: Stand two steps from a friend. Throw a big soft ball gently. Open both hands to catch it.
units.activity: Throw a soft ball up and catch it yourself. Count how many times you catch it.
units.check: How many hands do you use to catch a big ball?

quiz.prompt: How many hands do you use to catch a big ball?
What should we do before we throw the ball?
options: Look at the person we throw to

quiz.prompt: We catch a big soft ball with both hands?
How should we throw the ball to a friend?
We should throw the ball roughly at our friend's face?

units.title: Balancing on one leg
units.notes: Balancing means holding our body still. We can stand on one leg like a tall tree. We stretch our arms out to help us stay steady. We look at one spot and do not wobble. We count slowly while we balance. Balancing helps us when we walk and climb. We can balance on the left leg and then the right. We can hold a friend's hand at first. When we are ready, we balance all alone.
units.worked_example: Stand tall like a tree on one leg. Stretch your arms out and count to five before you put your foot down.
units.activity: Balance on one leg while singing a short rhyme. Try the other leg next.
units.check: Can you balance on one leg while you count to five?

quiz.prompt: How do we stand when we balance like a tree?

units.title: Climbing and crawling safely
units.notes: Crawling means moving on our hands and knees. Climbing means going up and down carefully. We hold tight with both hands when we climb. We climb only on safe things like low steps. We watch where we put our feet. An adult should always watch us. Crawling under a table is fun and safe. Climbing helps our arms and legs grow strong. We come down slowly, never in a hurry.
units.worked_example: Crawl like a baby cat under a low table. Come out slowly and stand up.
units.activity: Make a safe tunnel with two chairs and a cloth. Crawl through it one at a time.
units.check: Which two body parts do you use when you crawl?

units.title: Rolling and spinning around
units.notes: We can roll a ball on the ground. We can roll our body on a soft mat. We can spin around slowly like a top. When we spin, we stop and stand still. Spinning too fast can make us dizzy. We always roll and spin in safe spaces. Rolling on a mat feels soft and warm. We keep our arms close to our body. Spinning games are more fun with a friend.
units.worked_example: Lie on a soft mat and roll gently from side to side. Stop when the adult claps.
units.activity: Roll a ball to a friend and let them roll it back. Say the friend's name as you roll.

units.title: Finger play and busy hands
units.notes: Our fingers can do many clever things. We can wiggle them, count them and touch our thumbs. Finger songs make our hands strong. We use our fingers to pick up small safe objects. We can open and close our hands slowly. Busy fingers help us draw and button clothes. We can make a tiny ball with soft paper. We can clap our hands to a rhythm. Strong fingers help us hold crayons well.
units.worked_example: Sing a finger rhyme like Where Is Thumbkin. Move each finger as you sing about it.
units.activity: Pick up ten bottle tops one by one and put them in a cup using only your fingers.
units.check: Can you show me your thumbs and wiggle all your fingers?

units.title: Drawing and scribbling
units.notes: Drawing is fun and has no wrong way. We hold a crayon in our hand. We make lines, circles and wiggles on paper. Scribbling helps our hands get ready for writing. We can use many colours. We talk about what we drew with our friends. We can draw a big sun or a small house. Our pictures do not need to look perfect. Every drawing is a happy picture.
units.worked_example: Take a crayon and draw a big round sun. Add lines around it for the bright rays.
units.activity: Draw anything you like on paper with three colours. Tell a friend what your picture shows.
units.check: What shapes can you draw with your crayon?

options: No, every drawing is a happy picture

units.title: Moulding with clay and dough
units.notes: Clay and dough are soft to touch. We press, roll and squeeze them with our hands. We can make balls, snakes and flat cakes. We can shape a small animal or a cup. Moulding makes our fingers strong. We wash our hands after we play. We roll the dough into a long snake. We join the two ends to make a ring. We keep the clay on the table.
units.worked_example: Roll the dough into a long snake. Join the two ends to make a round ring or bangle.
units.activity: Make a small ball with clay and flatten it into a little cake. Press your thumb in the middle.

units.title: Cutting, tearing and pasting
units.notes: We use safe scissors with round ends. We hold the paper with one hand and cut with the other. We can tear paper into small pieces too. We use glue to stick pieces on paper. Pasting makes bright pictures. We keep glue away from our mouths. We cut along a straight line first. Tearing paper is easy and safe for small hands. We clean the table when we finish.
units.worked_example: Tear small pieces of coloured paper. Paste them inside a drawn circle to make a flower.
units.activity: Cut or tear paper shapes and paste them on a card to make a picture for your family.
units.check: Where should the sharp ends of the scissors always point?

units.title: Moving to music and rhythm
units.notes: Music makes us want to move. We clap, stamp and sway to the beat. We can dance fast or slowly. A drum or a song keeps the rhythm. We copy the leader's moves. Moving to music is fun and makes us happy. We can use our hands and feet. We stop the music and freeze. We dance in our own space. A shaker or a bottle of beans makes a good sound. We listen with our ears before we move.
units.worked_example: Clap a slow beat and ask children to stamp their feet to it. Speed up and let them clap faster.
units.activity: Play a short song and dance freely. When the music stops, stand still like a statue.

Religious Education.overview: A gentle guide for young learners about love, kindness and good behaviour at home, at school and in the community, shared through simple stories, songs and everyday examples.

units.title: My family loves me
units.notes: A family cares for each other. My mother and father love me. My brothers and sisters play with me. My grandparents tell me stories. We eat and share together. Love makes our home a happy place. We help each other at home. We greet our family with a smile. We say thank you for the good things we get. A family can be big or small. Every family is special.
units.worked_example: Talk about your family. Name one person in your family and say why you love them.
units.activity: Sing a short family song with the class. Then draw your family on paper.
units.check: Who takes care of you at home?

units.title: Being kind to others
units.notes: Kindness means being good to people. We share our things with friends. We help someone who is sad. We speak with soft and gentle words. We do not push or hurt others. Kind people make others happy. We give a seat to an older person. We say a kind word to a crying friend. Small acts of kindness are very big. Kindness makes God happy too.
units.worked_example: Tell a story about a girl who shared her snack with a hungry friend. Ask how the friend felt.
units.activity: Find one kind thing to do today, like helping a friend carry a bag.

units.title: Sharing with my friends
units.notes: Sharing means letting others use what we have. We can share toys, food and books. When we share, everyone feels happy. We take turns and wait patiently. We do not grab things from others. Sharing shows we care. We can share a ball at play time. We ask politely before we take a turn. Sharing makes play fun for all. When we share, we have more friends.

units.activity: Share your crayons with a friend and draw one picture together.

units.title: Saying thank you
units.notes: We say thank you when someone helps us. We thank our parents for food and clothes. We thank our teachers for teaching us. We thank friends who share with us. Thanking shows good manners. It also shows we are grateful. We can thank God for our food. We can thank our family with a smile. We say thank you in a kind voice. Good manners make people happy.
units.worked_example: Practise a short rhyme: Thank you, thank you, kind and true. Say it together softly.
units.activity: Thank one person today who helped you, like your mother or your teacher.

units.title: Saying sorry and forgiving
units.notes: Sometimes we do wrong things. We may push a friend or take a toy. When we do wrong, we say sorry. We say sorry with a kind and soft voice. We try not to do it again. When someone says sorry, we forgive them. Forgiving means we do not stay angry. We shake hands and play again. God is happy when we say sorry. A sorry heart is a clean heart.

units.title: Talking to God in prayer
units.notes: Prayer is talking to God. We can pray in the morning and at night. We close our eyes and fold our hands. We thank God and ask for help. We can pray alone or with our family. God always listens to us. We can also say a short prayer before we eat. We pray quietly with a calm heart. Praying makes us feel safe and loved.
units.worked_example: Fold your hands and say a simple prayer: Thank you, God, for this day. Please help us to be good.

units.notes: We sing to show love and joy. Praise songs thank God for good things. We can clap and sway as we sing. We sing with our family and friends. We can sing in church, mosque or at home. Singing makes our hearts glad. We can sing a short song with actions. We can learn a new song each week. Singing together makes us happy.

units.title: Stories of good people
units.notes: Stories tell us about good people. Good people help and love others. We hear stories at home and in class. We can act out a story with our friends. We learn what is right from stories. units.title: Caring for animals and plants
units.notes: Animals and plants are living things. We give our pets food and water. We do not beat or hurt animals. We water the plants in our home. We keep our environment clean. Caring for living things shows love. We can plant a small seed and watch it grow. We can feed the birds with small grains. God made all living things for us to care for.

units.title: Telling the truth
units.notes: Honesty means telling the truth. We tell the truth even when we are afraid. We do not take things that are not ours. When we do wrong, we say the truth. People trust a truthful child. Telling the truth makes us feel good. We can be honest at home and in class. A friend who tells the truth is a good friend. God loves truthful children.

units.notes: We obey our parents and teachers. They guide us and keep us safe. We listen when they speak to us. We follow the rules at home and school. Obeying shows respect. units.title: Celebrating special days
units.notes: We celebrate special days with our family. We have days for praying and giving thanks. We share food and joy together. We wear good clothes and sing. We also celebrate our birthdays. Special days bring people together. We greet our friends on their special days. We can give a small gift or a kind word. We say thank you to God for these days.
