English.overview: This guide builds listening, speaking, reading and writing skills for learners in Grades Four to Six. It moves from everyday greetings and clear speech to grammar, punctuation, comprehension and confident composition writing.

units.title: Greetings and polite introductions
units.notes: Every conversation begins with good listening and speaking habits. When you greet someone, look at them, use a clear voice and choose words that fit the time of day. Introductions tell the other person your name, your class or your home area. Polite requests use words like please, kindly and thank you. Practising these skills at school and at home helps you speak with confidence and respect.
units.worked_example: At the school gate you meet a new teacher and say, Good morning, Madam. My name is Amina and I am in Grade Five.
units.activity: With a partner, act out greeting a visitor at your school gate and introduce yourselves politely.
units.check: Which polite words would you use when asking a friend to lend you a pencil?

quiz.prompt: Which word shows politeness when you ask for something?
True or false: You should look at someone and use a clear voice when you greet them?
What do introductions usually tell the other person?
options: your name, class or home area

quiz.prompt: Which word would you use to thank someone?
True or false: Greetings should change depending on the time of day?

units.title: Listening for details and following instructions
units.notes: Good listening means hearing not just words but also the details. When someone gives instructions, listen to the whole message before you start. Notice the order of the steps, the names and the numbers mentioned. You can repeat the message quietly in your mind or write short notes. In class, sitting quietly and facing the speaker shows that you are ready to listen. Careful listening helps you answer questions correctly and avoid mistakes.
units.worked_example: The teacher says, Open your book at page twenty, then write the date and underline the title. A good listener follows these three steps in order.
units.activity: Ask a friend to give you four short instructions and carry them out in the correct order.
units.check: Why is it important to listen to all the instructions before starting a task?

quiz.prompt: What should you do before starting a task when instructions are given?
True or false: Sitting quietly and facing the speaker shows that you are ready to listen?
Besides the words, what details should a good listener notice?
options: the order of steps, names and numbers

quiz.prompt: How can you help yourself remember instructions?
options: write short notes or repeat them in your mind

quiz.prompt: True or false: Careful listening helps you answer questions correctly and avoid mistakes?

units.title: Sounding out new words
units.notes: When you meet a long word, you can break it into smaller sound parts called syllables. Say each part slowly, then join them together to read the whole word. Looking at the letters at the beginning, middle and end helps you guess how to say the word. After you say it, check whether it makes sense in the sentence. This habit makes reading new words easier and more accurate.
units.worked_example: The word 'en-vi-ron-ment' has four syllables; join them slowly to read 'environment'.
units.activity: Choose five long words from your reading book, clap their syllables and read them aloud to a partner.
units.check: How many syllables can you hear in the word 'butterfly'?

quiz.prompt: What are the small sound parts that make up a word called?
True or false: Joining the sound parts together helps you read the whole word?
When you meet a long word, what should you do first?
options: break it into smaller sound parts
always ask someone to read it for you

quiz.prompt: How many syllables are in the word 'butterfly'?
True or false: After saying a new word, you should check whether it makes sense in the sentence?

units.title: Reading aloud with expression
units.notes: Reading aloud is not only about saying words correctly; it is also about meaning. Pausing at commas and stopping at full stops helps listeners understand. Changing your voice for questions and exclamations brings the story to life. Looking up now and then lets you share the words with your audience. Practice makes your reading smooth, clear and enjoyable for everyone listening.
units.worked_example: A question ends with a rising voice, so 'Are you coming home?' is read with a lift at the end.
units.activity: Read a short paragraph from a story to your group, pausing at the right places and changing your voice for questions.
units.check: How does your voice change when you read a sentence that ends with a question mark?

quiz.prompt: What should your voice do at a full stop?
True or false: Pausing at commas helps listeners understand the reading?
How does your voice change when you read a question?
Why should you look up now and then while reading aloud?
options: to share the words with your audience

quiz.prompt: True or false: Reading aloud is only about saying words correctly?

units.title: Building vocabulary from context
units.notes: You can learn the meaning of new words without a dictionary by looking at the words around them. This is called using context clues. Sometimes a sentence gives an example, a contrast or a reason that explains the new word. Comparing the word to one you already know also helps. Keeping a small vocabulary book and writing new words with their meanings builds your word bank.
units.worked_example: In the sentence, The arid land had no rain for months, the words 'no rain' tell you that 'arid' means very dry.
units.activity: Find six new words in a newspaper or story book and write what you think each one means from the sentence.
units.check: What clues in a sentence can help you guess the meaning of a new word?

quiz.prompt: What is the name for using nearby words to find the meaning of a new word?
True or false: You can learn a new word's meaning without a dictionary by looking at nearby words?
Which of these can a sentence give to explain a new word?
options: an example, a contrast or a reason

quiz.prompt: What helps build your word bank?
True or false: Comparing a new word to one you already know does not help at all?

units.title: Nouns, pronouns and their uses
units.notes: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea, such as teacher, Kisumu, river or kindness. Nouns can be common or proper, countable or uncountable. A pronoun replaces a noun so that we do not repeat it, for example he, she, it, they and we. Using pronouns well makes your writing shorter and clearer. You must match the pronoun with the noun it stands for.
units.worked_example: Instead of saying 'Amina went to the shop because Amina needed salt', we write 'Amina went to the shop because she needed salt'.
units.activity: Write five sentences about your family and then rewrite them using pronouns in place of repeated nouns.
units.check: Which pronoun would you use to replace the noun 'the pupils' in a sentence?

quiz.prompt: Which word is a noun?
True or false: A pronoun can replace a noun so that we do not repeat it?
Which pronoun would replace 'the pupils'?
What does a noun name?
options: a person, place, thing or idea

quiz.prompt: True or false: You must match a pronoun with the noun it stands for?

units.title: Verbs and simple tenses
units.notes: A verb tells us what someone or something does, like run, eat, write or sing. The tense of a verb shows when the action happens. The simple present tells about habits and facts, the simple past tells about things already done, and the simple future tells about things yet to come. Most verbs add '-ed' in the past, but some change completely. Matching the verb to the correct time makes sentences clear.
units.worked_example: Today I walk to school; yesterday I walked to school; tomorrow I will walk to school.
units.activity: Write three sentences about your day using one verb in the present, one in the past and one in the future.
units.check: What is the past tense of the verb 'go'?

quiz.prompt: Which word is a verb?
True or false: The tense of a verb shows when the action happens?
What is the past tense of the verb 'go'?
Which tense tells about habits and facts?
True or false: Most verbs add '-ed' in the past, but some change completely?

units.title: Adjectives, adverbs and describing words
units.notes: Adjectives describe nouns and tell us more about them, such as a tall tree, a red dress or two goats. Adverbs describe verbs and tell us how, when or where an action happens, such as quickly, yesterday or outside. Choosing exact describing words makes your writing interesting and clear. Too many describing words can confuse the reader, so use only the best ones. Notice whether the word describes a naming word or an action word.
units.worked_example: In 'The hungry lion ran quickly', 'hungry' describes the lion and 'quickly' tells how the lion ran.
units.activity: Describe a market scene in five sentences using at least four adjectives and two adverbs.
units.check: In the sentence 'She sings beautifully', which word is the adverb?

quiz.prompt: Which word is an adjective?
True or false: An adverb can tell us how, when or where an action happens?
In the sentence 'She sings beautifully', which word is the adverb?
What does an adjective describe?
True or false: Using too many describing words can confuse the reader?

units.title: Constructing clear sentences
units.notes: A sentence is a group of words that gives a complete thought. A simple sentence needs a subject, which tells who or what, and a predicate, which tells what happens. The subject and verb must agree in number, so we say the boy runs and the boys run. Joining short sentences with words like and, but and because makes your writing flow. Reading your sentence aloud helps you check whether it sounds complete.
units.worked_example: 'The girls are sweeping the classroom' has 'the girls' as subject and 'are sweeping the classroom' as predicate.
units.activity: Rearrange jumbled words to form five correct sentences, then underline the subject in each one.
units.check: What two parts must every simple sentence have?

quiz.prompt: What two parts must every simple sentence have?
True or false: In a sentence, the subject and verb must agree in number?
Which word joins short sentences in the notes?
What does the predicate tell us?
options: who or what the sentence is about

quiz.prompt: True or false: Reading your sentence aloud helps you check whether it sounds complete?

units.title: Punctuation and capital letters
units.notes: Punctuation marks are signs that help readers understand writing. A full stop ends a statement, a question mark ends a question and an exclamation mark shows strong feeling. Commas separate items in a list and show short pauses. Capital letters begin sentences, names of people, places, days and months. Correct punctuation makes your meaning clear and your work easy to read.
units.worked_example: On Monday, Amina bought maize, beans and rice. This sentence begins with a capital letter, uses commas in the list and ends with a full stop.

units.title: Reading comprehension skills
units.notes: Comprehension means understanding what you read. First skim the passage quickly to get the general idea, then read it again slowly for details. Look for the main idea, which is what the passage is mostly about. Supporting details explain or prove the main idea. When you answer questions, go back to the passage to find the exact words or ideas that support your answer.
units.worked_example: If a passage is mostly about how bees make honey, the main idea is the honey-making process, and details about nectar support it.
units.activity: Read a short passage, write its main idea in one sentence and list three supporting details.

units.title: Writing a short narrative composition
units.notes: A narrative tells a story about events that happened. A good story has a beginning that introduces the characters and setting, a middle where a problem happens, and an end where the problem is solved. Choose one clear order of events so the story is easy to follow. Use describing words to make characters and places come alive. Always plan your story briefly before you write it.
units.worked_example: A story beginning 'One Saturday morning, Kato set off to the river with his fishing line' introduces a character, a time and a place.
units.activity: Plan and write a short story about a day you will never forget, using a clear beginning, middle and end.

units.title: Writing friendly letters and filling forms
units.notes: A friendly letter is written to someone you know, such as a friend or a relative. It has an address, a greeting, the body, a closing and your name. The body carries your message and should be arranged in clear paragraphs. Filling forms needs neat handwriting and care. You write your full name, date of birth, class and other details exactly in the spaces given, without mistakes.
units.worked_example: A friendly letter starts with 'Dear Aunt Wanjiku', ends with 'Your loving nephew, Otieno' and gives news in between.
units.activity: Write a short friendly letter to a cousin inviting them to your school's sports day.

Kiswahili.overview: Mwongozo huu unamsaidia mwanafunzi wa darasa la nne hadi la sita kukuza stadi nne za lugha: kusikiliza, kuzungumza, kusoma na kuandika kwa Kiswahili sanifu. Kila kipengele kina mifano halisi na mazoezi yanayotumia mazingira ya shule, nyumbani na jamii.

units.title: Salamu na maamkizi ya heshima
units.notes: Salamu ni maneno ya heshima tunayotumia tunapokutana au kuagana na watu. Katika Kiswahili, salamu hubadilika kulingana na wakati wa siku, kama asubuhi, mchana au jioni. Tunaposema salamu, tunatazama mtu, tunatumia sauti ya upole na tabasamu. Salamu nzuri hujenga uhusiano mzuri kati ya watu. Kwa mfano, tunamwambia mzee shikamoo na kumjibu marahaba. Kuagana pia ni sehemu ya salamu, kama kwaheri au tutaonana.
units.worked_example: Unakutana na mwalimu wako asubuhi na kusema, Shikamoo mwalimu, naye akajibu, Marahaba. Kisha unauliza, Habari za asubuhi?
units.activity: Kwa wenzako wawili, fanyeni mazungumzo mafupi ya salamu na kuagana kwa heshima.
units.check: Salamu gani unapaswa kumtumia mzee unapomkuta jioni?

quiz.prompt: Salamu gani unamwambia mzee unapomkuta?
True or false: Tunaposema salamu tunatazama mtu na kutumia sauti ya upole?
Mzee humjibu nini anaposaliwa shikamoo?
Salamu hubadilika kulingana na kitu gani?
True or false: Salamu nzuri hujenga uhusiano mzuri kati ya watu?

units.title: Kusikiliza na kufuata maelekezo
units.notes: Kusikiliza vizuri ni zaidi ya kusikia maneno; ni kuelewa maana yake. Unapopewa maelekezo, sikiliza hadi mwisho kabla ya kuanza kutekeleza. Zingatia mpangilio wa hatua, majina na namba zinazotajwa. Unaweza kurudia maelekezo kwa sauti ya chini akilini au kuandika vidokezo vifupi. Kukaa kimya na kumtazama mzungumzaji huonyesha kuwa uko tayari kusikiliza. Ukiwa hukuelewa, uliza kwa upole ili mzungumzaji arudie maelekezo. Kusikiliza kwa makini huzuia makosa darasani.
units.worked_example: Mwalimu anasema, Fungua kitabu ukurasa wa ishirini, andika tarehe kisha upige mstari chini ya kichwa. Mwanafunzi mzuri hufuata hatua hizi tatu kwa mpangilio.
units.activity: Mwambie mwenzio atoe maelekezo manne mafupi, kisha uyatekeleze kwa mpangilio sahihi.
units.check: Kwa nini ni muhimu kusikiliza maelekezo yote kabla ya kuanza?

quiz.prompt: Unapaswa kufanya nini kabla ya kuanza kutekeleza maelekezo?
True or false: Kukaa kimya na kumtazama mzungumzaji huonyesha uko tayari kusikiliza?
Mbali na maneno, mambo gani mwingine unapaswa kuzingatia?

quiz.prompt: Unaweza kujisaidiaje kukumbuka maelekezo?

units.title: Matamshi safi ya Kiswahili
units.notes: Matamshi safi humsaidia msikilizaji kukuelewa vyema. Sauti za Kiswahili hutamkwa wazi, kama vile a, e, i, o, u. Baadhi ya maneno hutofautiana kwa maana kutokana na matamshi, kwa mfano barabara na bara bara. Silabi ni vipande vya sauti vinavyounda neno. Tamka maneno kwa uangalifu ili usibadilishe maana yake. Kuzungumza polepole na kufungua mdomo vizuri huboresha matamshi yako. Maneno yenye silabi moja hutamkwa kwa haraka kidogo.
units.worked_example: Neno 'shule' lina silabi mbili, shu-le, na hutamkwa wazi bila kuchanganya sauti.
units.activity: Soma orodha ya maneno matano kwa sauti, ukigonga meza mara moja kwa kila silabi.
units.check: Neno 'mwalimu' lina silabi ngapi?

quiz.prompt: Silabi ni nini?
True or false: Kuzungumza polepole na kufungua mdomo vizuri huboresha matamshi?

units.title: Kusoma kwa ufasaha
units.notes: Kusoma kwa ufasaha humaanisha kusoma kwa sauti safi, kasi inayofaa na kueleweka. Kusimama kwenye koma na kuacha kwenye nukta husaidia msikilizaji kufuatilia. Kubadilisha sauti kwa maswali na mshangao huleta uhai kwenye kisa. Kuitazama hadhira mara kwa mara huonyesha ujasiri. Mazoezi ya mara kwa mara hufanya kusoma kuwa laini na kupendeza. Kufuatilia alama za uakifishaji wakati wa kusoma huongeza uelewa wa maana. Soma kwa kasi inayofaa ili msikilizaji akufuatilie.
units.worked_example: Sentensi ya swali ina sauti inayopanda mwishoni, kwa hivyo 'Unakuja nyumbani?' husomwa kwa kupandisha sauti.
units.activity: Soma aya fupi kutoka kitabu cha hadithi mbele ya kikundi chako, ukisimama mahali panapofaa.
units.check: Sauti yako hubadilikaje unaposoma sentensi inayoishia kwa alama ya kuuliza?

quiz.prompt: Sauti yako hufanya nini mwisho wa sentensi ya kuuliza?

Ni nini hufanya kusoma kuwa laini na kupendeza?

units.title: Msamiati na maana ya maneno
units.notes: Unaweza kujifunza maana ya neno jipya bila kamusi kwa kutazama maneno yanayoizunguka. Mbinu hii huitwa kutumia vidokezo vya muktadha. Wakati mwingine sentensi hutoa mfano, kinyume au sababu inayoeleza neno jipya. Kulinganisha neno jipya na lile unaolijua husaidia pia. Kuweka daftari dogo la msamiati na kuandika maneno mapya na maana yake hukuza hazina yako ya maneno. Kutumia neno jipya katika sentensi yako huhakikisha umelielewa.
units.worked_example: Katika sentensi, Eneo kame halikupata mvua kwa miezi, maneno 'halikupata mvua' yanatuonyesha kuwa 'kame' humaanisha kavu sana.
units.activity: Tafuta maneno sita mapya kwenye gazeti au kitabu cha hadithi na uandike maana unayodhani yanayo.
units.check: Vidokezo gani katika sentensi vinaweza kukusaidia kubashiri maana ya neno jipya?

quiz.prompt: Mbinu ya kutazama maneno yanayozunguka neno jipya huitwa nini?
True or false: Unaweza kujifunza maana ya neno jipya bila kamusi kwa vidokezo vya muktadha?
Sentensi huweza kutoa nini kueleza neno jipya?

options: kuandika maneno mapya na maana yake

quiz.prompt: True or false: Kutumia neno jipya katika sentensi yako huhakikisha umelielewa?

units.title: Nomino na viwakilishi
units.notes: Nomino ni neno linalotaja mtu, mahali, kitu au wazo, kama mwalimu, Kisumu, mto au wema. Nomino za Kiswahili hugawanywa katika makundi yenye ngeli mbalimbali. Kiwakilishi huchukua mahali pa nomino ili tusirudie neno mara kwa mara, kama yeye, sisi na wao. Kutumia viwakilishi vizuri hufanya sentensi kuwa fupi na wazi. Ni muhimu kuhakikisha kiwakilishi kinalingana na nomino inayowakilishwa. Nomino huweza kuwa za kawaida au za jina maalum.
units.worked_example: Badala ya kusema 'Amina alienda dukani kwa sababu Amina alihitaji chumvi', tunasema 'Amina alienda dukani kwa sababu yeye alihitaji chumvi'.
units.activity: Andika sentensi tano kuhusu familia yako, kisha uzibadilishe kwa kutumia viwakilishi badala ya kurudia nomino.
units.check: Kiwakilishi kipi utakitumia kuchukua mahali pa nomino 'wanafunzi'?

quiz.prompt: Neno lipi ni nomino?
True or false: Kiwakilishi huchukua mahali pa nomino ili tusirudie neno?
Kiwakilishi kipi huchukua mahali pa nomino 'wanafunzi'?
Nomino hutaja nini?
True or false: Kiwakilishi hakiwezi kuchukua mahali pa nomino yoyote?

units.title: Vitenzi na nyakati
units.notes: Kitenzi hueleza kile mtu au kitu hufanya, kama kukimbia, kula, kuandika au kuimba. Wakati wa kitenzi huonyesha lini tendo hutendeka. Wakati uliopo hueleza mazoea na ukweli, wakati uliopita hueleza yaliyokwisha tendeka, na wakati ujao hueleza yatakayotendeka. Vitenzi vingi huongeza kiambishi cha wakati. Kulinganisha kitenzi na wakati sahihi hufanya sentensi kuwa wazi. Kitenzi hubadilika kulingana na idadi ya kiima, kama nilikula na walikula. Kuandika sentensi zenye nyakati mbalimbali huimarisha uandishi wako.
units.worked_example: Leo ninatembea shuleni; jana nilitembea shuleni; kesho nitatembea shuleni.
units.activity: Andika sentensi tatu kuhusu siku yako ukitumia kitenzi kimoja katika wakati uliopo, uliopita na ujao.
units.check: Kitenzi 'kula' huandikwaje katika wakati uliopita?

quiz.prompt: Neno lipi ni kitenzi?
True or false: Wakati wa kitenzi huonyesha lini tendo hutendeka?
Kitenzi 'kula' huandikwaje katika wakati uliopita?
Wakati uliopo hueleza nini?
True or false: Kitenzi hubadilika kulingana na idadi ya kiima?

units.title: Vivumishi na vielezi
units.notes: Kivumishi hufafanua nomino na kutupa maelezo zaidi, kama mti mrefu, gauni jekundu au mbuzi wawili. Kielezi hufafanua kitenzi na hueleza jinsi, lini au wapi tendo hutendeka, kama haraka, jana au nje. Kuchagua maneno sahihi ya kufafanua hufanya maandishi yako kuwa ya kuvutia. Maneno mengi mno ya kufafanua yanaweza kumchanganya msomaji. Zingatia kama neno hufafanua nomino au kitenzi. Vivumishi huweza kuja kabla au baada ya nomino.
units.worked_example: Katika 'Simba mwenye njaa alikimbia haraka', 'mwenye njaa' hufafanua simba na 'haraka' hueleza jinsi alivyokimbia.
units.activity: Eleza mandhari ya soko kwa sentensi tano ukitumia vivumishi vinne na vielezi viwili.
units.check: Katika sentensi 'Yeye huimba vizuri', neno lipi ni kielezi?

quiz.prompt: Neno lipi ni kivumishi?
True or false: Kielezi hufafanua kitenzi?
Katika sentensi 'Yeye huimba vizuri', neno lipi ni kielezi?
Kivumishi hufafanua nini?
True or false: Maneno mengi mno ya kufafanua yanaweza kumchanganya msomaji?

units.title: Kuunda sentensi sahihi
units.notes: Sentensi ni kundi la maneno linalotoa maana kamili. Sentensi sahihi huwa na kiima, kinachotaja mtu au kitu, na kiarifu, kinachoeleza kinachotendeka. Kiima na kitenzi hulingana kwa idadi, kwa hivyo tunasema mtoto anacheza na watoto wanacheza. Kuunganisha sentensi fupi kwa maneno kama na, lakini na kwa sababu hufanya maandishi kuwa laini. Kusoma sentensi yako kwa sauti hukusaidia kuona kama imekamilika. Kutaja kiarifu peke yake hakutoshi kuunda sentensi kamili.
units.worked_example: 'Wasichana wanafagia darasa' ina 'wasichana' kama kiima na 'wanafagia darasa' kama kiarifu.
units.activity: Panga maneno yaliyochanganywa kuunda sentensi tano sahihi, kisha upige mstari chini ya kiima.
units.check: Sentensi sahihi huwa na sehemu gani mbili muhimu?

quiz.prompt: Sentensi sahihi huwa na sehemu gani mbili muhimu?
True or false: Kiima na kitenzi hulingana kwa idadi?

Kiarifu hueleza nini?

units.title: Alama za uakifishaji
units.notes: Alama za uakifishaji ni ishara zinazomsaidia msomaji kuelewa maandishi. Nukta huisha sentensi ya taarifa, alama ya kuuliza huisha swali, na alama ya mshangao huonyesha hisia kali. Koma hutenganisha vitu katika orodha na kuonyesha mapumziko mafupi. Herufi kubwa huanza sentensi na majina ya watu, mahali, siku na miezi. Uakifishaji sahihi hufanya maana yako kuwa wazi. Alama za mshangao na alama ya kuuliza hazipaswi kuchanganywa kabisa.
units.worked_example: Jumatatu, Amina alinunua mahindi, maharage na mchele. Sentensi hii huanza kwa herufi kubwa, hutumia koma katika orodha na kuishia kwa nukta.
units.activity: Nakili aya fupi kutoka kitabuni na uangalie kila herufi kubwa na alama ya uakifishaji unayoiona.
units.check: Alama ipi ya uakifishaji huisha sentensi 'Saa ngapi basi linaondoka'?

quiz.prompt: Alama ipi huisha sentensi ya taarifa?

quiz.prompt: True or false: Alama ya mshangao na alama ya kuuliza zinaweza kuchanganywa bila shida?

units.title: Ufahamu wa kusoma
units.notes: Ufahamu humaanisha kuelewa unachokisoma. Kwanza soma kifungu kwa haraka kupata wazo kuu, kisha soma tena kwa makini kupata maelezo. Wazo kuu ni lile kifungu kinachozungumzia zaidi. Maelezo ya kusaidia hueleza au kuthibitisha wazo kuu. Unapojibu maswali, rudi kwenye kifungu kutafuta maneno au mawazo yanayounga mkono jibu lako. Kichwa cha kifungu mara nyingi huonyesha wazo kuu. Jibu maswali kwa sentensi kamili na maneno yako mwenyewe.
units.worked_example: Kama kifungu kinazungumzia jinsi nyuki hutengeneza asali, wazo kuu ni mchakato wa kutengeneza asali, na maelezo kuhusu nekta huunga mkono.
units.activity: Soma kifungu kifupi, uandike wazo kuu kwa sentensi moja na kuorodhesha maelezo matatu ya kusaidia.
units.check: Wapi unaweza kupata uthibitisho wa jibu lako katika kifungu cha ufahamu?

quiz.prompt: Wazo kuu ni nini?

Wapi unaweza kupata uthibitisho wa jibu lako?

units.title: Kuandika insha fupi
units.notes: Insha ya masimulizi husimulia matukio yaliyotendeka. Insha nzuri huwa na mwanzo unaotambulisha wahusika na mandhari, kati ambapo tatizo hutokea, na mwisho ambapo tatizo hutatuliwa. Chagua mpangilio mmoja wazi wa matukio ili kisa kifuatilike kwa urahisi. Tumia maneno ya kufafanua ili wahusika na mahali vipate uhai. Panda mpango wa insha yako kwa ufupi kabla ya kuandika. Kumbuka kuweka kichwa kinachovutia na sentensi fupi zenye maana.
units.worked_example: Insha inayoanza 'Asubuhi moja ya Jumamosi, Kato alielekea mtoni na ndoano yake ya kuvua' hutambulisha mhusika, wakati na mahali.
units.activity: Panga na uandike insha fupi kuhusu siku usiyoweza kuisahau, ukitumia mwanzo, kati na mwisho wazi.
units.check: Insha iliyopangwa vyema huwa na sehemu gani tatu?

quiz.prompt: Insha iliyopangwa vyema huwa na sehemu gani tatu?

ukurasa wa kwanza, wa pili na wa tatu

units.title: Barua na kujaza fomu
units.notes: Barua ya kirafiki huandikwa kwa mtu unayemjua, kama rafiki au ndugu. Huwa na anwani, salamu ya mwanzo, mwili wa barua, salamu ya mwisho na jina lako. Mwili wa barua hubeba ujumbe wako na hupangwa katika aya wazi. Kujaza fomu kunahitaji mwandiko nadhifu na uangalifu. Unaandika jina lako kamili, tarehe ya kuzaliwa, darasa na maelezo mengine kwa usahihi kwenye nafasi zilizotolewa.
units.worked_example: Barua ya kirafiki huanza kwa 'Ndugu yangu Wanjiku', huishia kwa 'Wako mpendwa, Otieno' na kutoa habari katikati.
units.activity: Andika barua fupi ya kirafiki kwa binamu yako ukimwalika kwenye siku ya michezo ya shule yako.
units.check: Nini huja mwishoni kabisa mwa barua ya kirafiki?

quiz.prompt: Barua ya kirafiki huandikwa kwa nani?
options: mtu unayemjua, kama rafiki au ndugu

Mathematics.overview: This guide builds number sense and problem-solving skills for learners in Grades Four to Six. It moves from place value and the four operations to fractions, measurement, geometry and handling data, using everyday Kenyan examples such as shopping in shillings and measuring school fields.

units.title: Place value of whole numbers
units.notes: Place value tells us the worth of a digit based on its position in a number. In the number 4 372, the digit 4 is in the thousands place, so it stands for four thousand. Moving from right to left, the places are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and so on. Each place is ten times the value of the place on its right. Understanding place value helps you read, compare and calculate with large numbers correctly.
units.worked_example: In 5 608, the 5 is worth 5 000, the 6 is worth 600, the 0 is worth 0 and the 8 is worth 8.
units.activity: Write any four-digit number, then say the value of each digit in it to a partner.
units.check: What is the value of the digit 7 in the number 2 743?

quiz.prompt: In the number 4 372, what does the digit 4 stand for?
True or false: In the number 4 372, the digit 7 is in the hundreds place?
What is the value of the digit 7 in the number 2 743?
Moving from right to left, in what order do the places come?
True or false: Each place is ten times the value of the place on its right?

units.title: Reading, writing and ordering numbers
units.notes: Numbers can be written in figures or in words. We write 3 250 in figures and three thousand, two hundred and fifty in words. To compare numbers, start with the digit in the highest place value. The number with the larger digit in that place is greater, and if they are equal you compare the next place. Ordering means arranging numbers from smallest to largest, or the other way round.
units.worked_example: To order 4 512, 4 521 and 4 125, compare the hundreds: 4 125 is smallest, then 4 512, then 4 521.
units.activity: Write the populations of five Kenyan towns in figures and arrange them from smallest to largest.
units.check: Which is greater, 6 089 or 6 098?

quiz.prompt: How do we write 3 250 in words?
options: three thousand, two hundred and fifty

quiz.prompt: True or false: When comparing numbers, you start with the digit in the highest place value?
Which is greater, 6 089 or 6 098?
What does ordering numbers mean?
options: arranging them from smallest to largest or the other way round

quiz.prompt: True or false: Numbers can be written in figures or in words?

units.title: Addition and subtraction of whole numbers
units.notes: Addition means putting numbers together to find a total, and subtraction means taking one number away from another. When adding or subtracting, line up the digits by place value, starting with the ones. If adding gives more than nine in a place, carry to the next place on the left. If subtracting is not possible in a place, borrow from the next place on the left. Always check your answer using the opposite operation.
units.worked_example: To work out 1 456 plus 2 378, add the ones, tens, hundreds and thousands to get 3 834.
units.activity: Add the cost of three items from a shop receipt, then subtract to find the change from one thousand shillings.
units.check: What is 5 000 minus 2 675?

quiz.prompt: What is 5 000 minus 2 675?
True or false: When subtracting is not possible in a place, you borrow from the next place on the left?
When adding numbers, which place do you start with?
How can you check your answer to a calculation?
True or false: Addition means taking one number away from another?

units.title: Multiplication and division
units.notes: Multiplication is repeated addition, and division is sharing or grouping into equal parts. Knowing multiplication tables up to twelve makes both operations quicker. For long multiplication, multiply by each digit by place value and add the results. For division, work from the largest place and record any remainder. Multiplication and division are opposites, so you can use one to check the other.
units.worked_example: To share 96 mangoes equally among 8 baskets, divide 96 by 8 to get 12 mangoes per basket.
units.activity: Work out the total cost of 24 exercise books if each book costs 15 shillings, then check using repeated addition.
units.check: What is 45 multiplied by 6?

quiz.prompt: What is 45 multiplied by 6?
True or false: Division is the same as sharing or grouping into equal parts?
Multiplication is also known as what?
Which table knowledge makes multiplication and division quicker?
True or false: Multiplication and division are opposites, so one can check the other?

units.title: Factors, multiples and number patterns
units.notes: A factor is a number that divides another number exactly without a remainder. A multiple is what you get when you multiply a number by a whole number. For example, the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Number patterns are sequences that follow a rule, such as adding 3 each time. Finding the rule helps you predict the next terms in a pattern.
units.worked_example: In the pattern 5, 10, 15, 20, the rule is add 5, so the next two terms are 25 and 30.
units.activity: List all the factors of 24 and write the first five multiples of 7.
units.check: What is the next number in the pattern 2, 4, 8, 16?

quiz.prompt: Which list shows all the factors of 12?
True or false: A factor divides a number exactly without a remainder?
What is the next number in the pattern 2, 4, 8, 16?
A multiple is what you get when you do what?
options: multiply a number by a whole number

quiz.prompt: True or false: Number patterns are sequences that follow a rule?

units.title: Fractions and equivalent fractions
units.notes: A fraction shows equal parts of a whole. The denominator tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into, and the numerator tells how many parts we take. Equivalent fractions look different but have the same value, such as one half and two quarters. You make equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number. Comparing fractions is easier when they share the same denominator.
units.worked_example: One half equals two quarters because multiplying the numerator and denominator of one half by two gives two quarters.
units.activity: Fold a strip of paper into halves, quarters and eighths, then write the fractions you create.
units.check: Which fraction is equal to one third, two sixths or three sixths?

quiz.prompt: In a fraction, what does the denominator tell you?
options: how many equal parts the whole is divided into

quiz.prompt: True or false: One half and two quarters are equivalent fractions?
Which fraction is equal to one third?
How do you make equivalent fractions?
options: multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same number

quiz.prompt: True or false: The numerator tells how many parts we take?

units.title: Decimals and money
units.notes: Decimals use a point to show parts of a whole that are smaller than one. The digits after the point stand for tenths, hundredths and thousandths. In Kenya, money is written in shillings and cents using decimals, for example one hundred fifty shillings and fifty cents is Ksh 150.50. Adding and subtracting money follows the same rules as ordinary decimals. Always keep the decimal points lined up when calculating.
units.worked_example: If a pen costs Ksh 25.50 and a ruler costs Ksh 14.50, together they cost Ksh 40.00.
units.activity: Make a shopping list of four items with prices in decimals and work out the total cost.
units.check: How would you write seven shillings and five cents using a decimal point?

quiz.prompt: How would you write seven shillings and five cents using a decimal point?
True or false: In Kenya, money is written in shillings and cents using decimals?
What do the digits after the decimal point stand for?
What must you always do when calculating with decimals?
True or false: One hundred fifty shillings and fifty cents can be written as Ksh 150.50?

units.title: Length, mass and capacity
units.notes: Measurement tells us how long, how heavy or how much a thing holds. Length is measured in millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres. Mass is measured in grams and kilograms, and capacity in millilitres and litres. Each larger unit is made of a fixed number of smaller units, such as one metre equals one hundred centimetres. Choosing the right unit and tool gives accurate results.
units.worked_example: A bag of maize flour of 2 kilograms equals 2 000 grams, since one kilogram is one thousand grams.
units.activity: Measure the length of your desk in centimetres and the mass of your school bag in kilograms.
units.check: How many millilitres are there in three litres?

quiz.prompt: How many millilitres are there in three litres?
True or false: Mass is measured in grams and kilograms?
Which unit is used to measure length?
One metre equals how many centimetres?
True or false: Capacity is measured in millilitres and litres?

units.title: Perimeter and area
units.notes: Perimeter is the distance all the way round a shape, found by adding the lengths of all its sides. Area is the amount of surface a shape covers, measured in square units. For a rectangle, area equals length multiplied by width. For a square, area equals side multiplied by side. The same shape can have the same perimeter but different areas, so always check what the question asks.
units.worked_example: A rectangle of length 8 metres and width 5 metres has an area of 8 times 5, which is 40 square metres.
units.activity: Measure the length and width of your classroom floor and work out its area and perimeter.
units.check: What is the perimeter of a square whose side is 6 centimetres?

quiz.prompt: What is the perimeter of a square whose side is 6 centimetres?
True or false: Perimeter is found by adding the lengths of all the sides of a shape?
How do you find the area of a rectangle?
What is the area of a square whose side is 5 centimetres?
True or false: Two shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas?

units.title: Time and the calendar
units.notes: Time is measured in seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years. One hour has sixty minutes, one minute has sixty seconds, and one day has twenty-four hours. The calendar shows days, weeks and months, and helps us plan events and know dates. To find how long something lasts, subtract the starting time from the finishing time. Reading both analogue and digital clocks accurately is an important life skill.
units.worked_example: If a lesson starts at 8:20 and ends at 9:00, it lasts 40 minutes.
units.activity: Read the starting and ending times of three lessons on your timetable and work out how long each one lasts.
units.check: How many minutes are there in two and a half hours?

quiz.prompt: How many minutes are there in two and a half hours?
True or false: One hour has sixty minutes?
How many hours are there in one day?
To find how long something lasts, what do you do?
options: subtract the starting time from the finishing time

quiz.prompt: True or false: One minute has sixty seconds?

units.title: Angles and plane shapes
units.notes: An angle is formed when two lines meet at a point, and it is measured in degrees. A right angle is ninety degrees, like the corner of a book. An acute angle is smaller than a right angle, and an obtuse angle is larger but less than a straight line. Plane shapes such as triangles, rectangles and circles have different numbers of sides and angles. A protractor helps you measure and draw angles accurately.
units.worked_example: The four corners of a rectangle are all right angles, each measuring ninety degrees.
units.activity: Look around your classroom and list five objects that show right angles.
units.check: What kind of angle is smaller than a right angle?

quiz.prompt: What kind of angle is smaller than a right angle?
True or false: A right angle is ninety degrees?
Which instrument helps you measure angles accurately?
An angle is formed when two lines do what?
True or false: An obtuse angle is larger than a right angle but less than a straight line?

units.title: Collecting and presenting data
units.notes: Data is information we gather by counting, measuring or asking questions. We collect data using lists, tallies or tables. After collecting it, we present it using pictographs, bar graphs or tables so it is easy to understand. A bar graph uses bars of different heights to show amounts. Interpreting data means answering questions such as which item is the most or least common.
units.worked_example: A tally of fruits eaten by a class might show mangoes first, then bananas, then oranges, and a bar graph displays these clearly.
units.activity: Ask ten classmates their favourite game, record the answers as tallies and draw a bar graph.
units.check: Which graph uses bars of different heights to show data?

quiz.prompt: Which graph uses bars of different heights to show data?
True or false: Data is information we gather by counting, measuring or asking questions?
Which of these is a way to collect data?
What does interpreting data mean?
options: answering questions such as which item is most or least common

quiz.prompt: True or false: A pictograph uses bars of different heights to show amounts?

units.title: Solving word problems
units.notes: Word problems describe real situations using words instead of numbers alone. To solve one, read it carefully, find what is asked and identify the numbers given. Decide which operation or operations are needed, such as addition for a total or division for equal sharing. Write a number sentence and work it out step by step. Finally, check whether your answer makes sense in the situation.
units.worked_example: A trader had 240 eggs and sold 85 in the morning and 60 in the afternoon; 240 minus 145 leaves 95 eggs.
units.activity: Write two word problems about buying and sharing food, then exchange them with a partner to solve.
units.check: Which operation would you use to share 72 sweets equally among 9 children?

quiz.prompt: Which operation would you use to share 72 sweets equally among 9 children?
True or false: In a word problem, you first read it carefully to find what is asked?
Which operation is used for finding a total?
After working out a word problem, what should you do?
options: check whether the answer makes sense

quiz.prompt: True or false: A number sentence helps you work out a word problem step by step?

Science and Technology.overview: This guide introduces learners in Grades Four to Six to the living and non-living world around them and to simple technology. It develops observation, classification, recording and investigation skills using familiar plants, animals, materials and machines found in Kenyan homes, farms and schools.

units.title: Living and non-living things
units.notes: Living things grow, feed, breathe, move and reproduce, while non-living things do not. A mango tree, a goat and a pupil are living, while a stone, a chair and water are non-living. Some non-living things were once part of living things, such as a wooden desk made from a tree. Scientists group things by observing their features carefully. This grouping is called classification and it is the first step in studying nature.
units.worked_example: A young seedling grows taller each week, so it is living; a metal nail keeps the same size, so it is non-living.
units.activity: Walk around your school compound and list ten things, then group them as living or non-living.
units.check: Which features show that a plant is a living thing?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a living thing?
True or false: Living things grow, feed, breathe, move and reproduce?
What is the grouping of things by their features called?
Which non-living thing was once part of a living thing?
True or false: Non-living things can grow and reproduce on their own?

units.title: Classification of plants
units.notes: Plants can be grouped by their size, leaves, flowers and the way they grow. Trees are large and woody with a single stem, while shrubs are shorter and branch near the ground. Herbs are small and soft-stemmed, often used as food or medicine. Some plants are flowering and others are non-flowering, such as ferns and mosses. Classifying plants helps us learn their uses and how to care for them.
units.worked_example: A maize plant is a herb with a soft stem, while a eucalyptus is a tree with a thick woody trunk.
units.activity: Collect and press five different leaves, then sort them by shape, size and edge type.
units.check: What makes a shrub different from a tree?

quiz.prompt: What makes a shrub different from a tree?
options: it is shorter and branches near the ground
it has no leaves at all
it grows taller than a tree

quiz.prompt: True or false: Trees are large and woody with a single stem?
Which plants are small and soft-stemmed?
Which of these is a non-flowering plant?
True or false: Classifying plants helps us learn their uses and how to care for them?

units.title: Classification of animals
units.notes: Animals are grouped according to features such as their body covering, how they move and what they eat. Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk. Birds have feathers and beaks, fish have scales and fins, and reptiles have dry scaly skin. Animals are also grouped as herbivores, carnivores or omnivores depending on their food. Careful observation of these features makes classification easier.
units.worked_example: A cow has fur and feeds its calf on milk, so it is a mammal; a chicken has feathers, so it is a bird.
units.activity: List ten animals found in your area and group them by body covering and by the food they eat.
units.check: Which word describes an animal that eats both plants and meat?

quiz.prompt: Which word describes an animal that eats both plants and meat?
True or false: Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk?
Which animals have feathers and beaks?
Which animals have scales and fins?
True or false: Reptiles have dry scaly skin?

units.title: The human body: teeth and digestion
units.notes: Teeth help us bite and chew food, and digestion begins in the mouth. Children have twenty milk teeth that later fall out, and adults have thirty-two permanent teeth. There are four kinds of teeth: incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, and premolars and molars for grinding. Saliva in the mouth softens food as chewing continues. Cleaning teeth twice a day prevents tooth decay and keeps the mouth healthy.
units.worked_example: The front incisors cut a piece of sugarcane, while the back molars grind it into small pieces.
units.activity: Use a mirror and a small clean spoon to count and identify the types of teeth in your own mouth with a partner.
units.check: Which type of teeth is used for grinding food?

quiz.prompt: Which type of teeth is used for grinding food?
True or false: Children have twenty milk teeth that later fall out?
How many permanent teeth do adults have?
Where does digestion begin?
True or false: Cleaning teeth twice a day prevents tooth decay?

units.title: Health and hygiene in the community
units.notes: Good health comes from clean habits practised every day. Washing hands with soap and clean water before eating and after using the toilet stops germs from spreading. Keeping the home, classroom and latrine clean reduces diseases such as diarrhoea and typhoid. Handling food carefully and covering it protects it from flies and dust. Immunisation and treating common illnesses early also keep people healthy.
units.worked_example: Washing hands with soap for at least twenty seconds removes many of the germs that cause diarrhoea.
units.activity: In groups, make a poster showing five times when everyone should wash their hands.
units.check: Why should you wash your hands after visiting the latrine?

quiz.prompt: Why should you wash your hands after visiting the latrine?
True or false: Washing hands with soap and clean water before eating stops germs from spreading?
Which diseases can be reduced by keeping places clean?
Why should food be covered?
options: to protect it from flies and dust

quiz.prompt: True or false: Immunisation and treating common illnesses early help keep people healthy?

units.title: Nutrition and a balanced diet
units.notes: Food gives the body energy and materials to grow and stay healthy. A balanced diet has carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fats and water in the right amounts. Carbohydrates from ugali, rice and potatoes give energy, while proteins from beans, fish and eggs help the body grow. Fruits and vegetables supply vitamins and minerals that protect us from sickness. Drinking enough clean water is also part of a healthy diet.
units.worked_example: A meal of ugali, sukuma wiki, beans and a mango gives energy, vitamins and proteins in one plate.
units.activity: Draw a plate showing a balanced meal using foods that grow or are sold in your county.
units.check: Which food group helps the body to grow and repair itself?

quiz.prompt: Which food group helps the body to grow and repair itself?
True or false: A balanced diet has carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fats and water in the right amounts?
Which foods give the body energy?
Which foods supply vitamins and minerals?
True or false: Drinking enough clean water is part of a healthy diet?

units.title: Water and its uses
units.notes: Water is needed by people, animals and plants to stay alive. We use it for drinking, cooking, washing and watering crops, and it also turns machines in factories that make electricity. Water exists in three states: solid ice, liquid water and water vapour. It changes from one state to another when heated or cooled during the water cycle. Keeping water sources clean protects health and life.
units.worked_example: When water is heated it turns into vapour, and when the vapour cools it forms liquid drops again.
units.activity: Investigate how long a small wet cloth takes to dry in the sun and in the shade, and compare the results.
units.check: What are the three states of water?

quiz.prompt: What are the three states of water?
options: solid ice, liquid water and water vapour

quiz.prompt: True or false: Water is needed by people, animals and plants to stay alive?
Water changes from one state to another when what happens?
Which of these is a use of water in factories?
options: to grow crops in the field

quiz.prompt: True or false: Water can only exist as a liquid?

units.title: Air and weather
units.notes: Air is a mixture of gases that surrounds us and is needed for breathing and burning. Though we cannot see air, we feel it moving as wind, and we can trap it in a balloon. Weather is the condition of the air around us at a given time, and it includes sunshine, rain, wind and clouds. Weather changes from day to day and season to season. Simple instruments such as a rain gauge and wind vane help us observe and record it.
units.worked_example: A rain gauge placed in the open collects rainwater, and the amount collected over a day shows how much it rained.
units.activity: Keep a weather chart for one week, recording each day whether it is sunny, cloudy, rainy or windy.
units.check: Which instrument can you use to show the direction of the wind?

quiz.prompt: Which instrument shows the direction of the wind?
True or false: Air is a mixture of gases that surrounds us and is needed for breathing and burning?
What is weather?
options: the condition of the air around us at a given time
the usual weather over many years

quiz.prompt: What can we use to trap and show that air exists?
True or false: Weather stays the same every day and never changes?

units.title: Soil and rocks
units.notes: Soil is the loose top layer of the ground in which plants grow. It is made of tiny rock particles, dead plant and animal remains called humus, water and air. There are different types of soil such as sandy, clay and loamy soil. Loamy soil holds water and air well, so it is best for growing most crops. Rocks are solid natural materials made of minerals, and they slowly break down to form soil.
units.worked_example: Sandy soil lets water drain quickly, while clay soil holds water and becomes sticky when wet.
units.activity: Collect three soil samples from around your school and compare how well each one holds water.
units.check: Which type of soil is best for growing most crops?

quiz.prompt: Which type of soil is best for growing most crops?
True or false: Soil is the loose top layer of the ground in which plants grow?
What is the dead plant and animal material in soil called?
How does soil form from rocks?
True or false: Loamy soil holds water and air well?

units.title: Simple machines
units.notes: Simple machines help us do work with less effort or in an easier way. Common examples are the lever, inclined plane, wheel and axle, pulley, wedge and screw. A wheelbarrow uses a lever and a wheel to move heavy loads easily. A ramp is an inclined plane that helps push a load upward with less force. Machines do not reduce the work done, but they make it easier to perform.
units.worked_example: Using a wheelbarrow to carry stones for a school garden needs less effort than carrying them by hand.
units.activity: Identify three simple machines used in your home or school and explain the work each one makes easier.
units.check: Which simple machine is formed by a sloping surface, such as a ramp?

quiz.prompt: Which simple machine is formed by a sloping surface, such as a ramp?
True or false: Simple machines help us do work with less effort or in an easier way?
Which simple machines are found in a wheelbarrow?
What do machines do to the work done?
options: they make it easier but do not reduce the work
they always reduce the work to zero

quiz.prompt: True or false: A pulley is a simple machine?

units.title: Force and energy
units.notes: A force is a push or a pull that can start, stop or change the movement of an object. Forces act when we kick a ball, pull a cart or squeeze a sponge. Energy is the ability to do work, and it exists in forms such as movement, heat, light and sound. Energy can change from one form to another but cannot be created or destroyed. Friction, a force between surfaces, slows moving objects and produces heat.
units.worked_example: Rubbing your hands together uses movement energy and produces heat energy through friction.
units.activity: Push a toy car on smooth and rough surfaces and describe how the surface affects how far it moves.
units.check: What type of force slows down an object moving on a rough surface?

quiz.prompt: What type of force slows down an object moving on a rough surface?
True or false: A force is a push or a pull that can start, stop or change movement?
What is energy?
Which of these is a form of energy?
True or false: Energy can be created and destroyed freely?

units.title: Light and shadows
units.notes: Light is a form of energy that helps us see objects. It travels in straight lines and comes from sources such as the sun, a torch or a lamp. When light is blocked by an opaque object, a dark area called a shadow forms behind it. Transparent materials let most light pass through, while translucent materials let only some light through. Shadows change in size and position when the light source or the object moves.
units.worked_example: Standing in the sun in the morning makes a long shadow, but at noon the shadow becomes short.
units.activity: Use a torch and small objects to make shadows on a wall and record how the shadow changes as you move the torch.
units.check: Why does a shadow form behind an opaque object?

quiz.prompt: Why does a shadow form behind an opaque object?
options: because light is blocked by the object

quiz.prompt: True or false: Light travels in straight lines?
Which materials let most light pass through?
What happens to a shadow when the object or light source moves?
options: it changes in size and position

quiz.prompt: True or false: Opaque objects let all light pass through them?

units.title: Electricity and simple circuits
units.notes: Electricity is a form of energy that can light lamps, run radios and power machines. A simple circuit is a complete path that lets electric current flow from a source through wires and a component, and back to the source. If the path is broken, the current stops and the bulb goes off. Materials that let current pass are conductors, such as metals, while insulators like rubber do not. Electricity is useful but must be handled safely.
units.worked_example: Connecting a dry cell, two wires and a torch bulb in a loop makes the bulb light when the circuit is complete.
units.activity: Build a simple circuit with a dry cell, wires and a bulb, then test which materials let the bulb light.
units.check: What happens to a bulb in a circuit when the path is broken?

quiz.prompt: What happens to a bulb in a circuit when the path is broken?
True or false: A simple circuit is a complete path that lets electric current flow?
Which materials let current pass through them?
Which of these is an insulator?
True or false: Electricity is useful but must be handled safely?

Social Studies.overview: This guide helps upper primary learners understand the people, places and systems around them, from their own school to the nation of Kenya. It builds skills in observing, mapping, discussing and recording information about communities and government.

units.title: Our school and its surroundings
units.notes: A school is found in a particular place with natural and built features around it. Learners can describe the direction of the gate, the market, the river or the road near the school. Knowing the surroundings helps us move safely and find help when we need it. We also learn the name of our county and sub-county, which makes it easier to talk about where we come from. Recording what we see around school is the first step in learning geography.
units.worked_example: When asked to describe the route home, Amina says she leaves the school gate, walks east past the health centre, then turns left at the market before reaching her estate.
units.activity: Walk around the school compound with a partner and list five things you can see, then say whether each one is natural or built by people.
units.check: Which direction does the main gate of your school face?

quiz.prompt: What helps you know where you come from when talking about your area?
options: the name of your county and sub-county

quiz.prompt: True or false: Knowing your school's surroundings helps you move safely and find help?
What should you record about the area around your school?
options: what you see, such as the gate, market, river or road

quiz.prompt: Recording what we see around school is the first step in learning which subject?
True or false: A school is found in a particular place with natural and built features around it?

units.title: Reading and making simple maps
units.notes: A map is a drawing of a place as seen from above. Maps use a key to explain symbols, a compass direction to show north, and a scale to show distance. We read maps to find roads, rivers, schools and markets without visiting the place. Making a simple map of the classroom or school helps us understand how real places are shown on paper. Always check the key before you begin reading a map.
units.worked_example: On a map of the school, a small blue line is labelled river in the key, so when Daniel sees the blue line behind the dormitory he knows there is a river there.
units.activity: Draw a map of your classroom showing the door, windows, teacher's desk and two rows of desks, and add a key for the symbols you use.
units.check: Why does every map need a key?

quiz.prompt: Why does every map need a key?
True or false: A map is a drawing of a place as seen from above?
What shows north on a map?
What does a scale on a map show?
True or false: You should check the key before you begin reading a map?

units.title: Physical features of Kenya
units.notes: Kenya has many natural features formed over a very long time. They include mountains such as Mount Kenya, the Rift Valley, highlands, plains, rivers, lakes and the coastline. Rivers like the Tana and the Athi flow from the highlands toward the sea. Lake Victoria, Lake Turkana and Lake Naivasha are some of the lakes found in the country. These features affect where people live, farm and build towns.
units.worked_example: Because the land around Mount Kenya is high and receives plenty of rain, farmers grow tea and coffee on the slopes, while people on the dry northern plains keep camels and goats.
units.activity: In groups, name two physical features found in your county and explain how each one affects the way people live there.
units.check: Name one mountain and one lake found in Kenya.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a physical feature of Kenya?
True or false: Lake Victoria, Lake Turkana and Lake Naivasha are lakes found in Kenya?
Where does the River Tana flow towards?
What is one effect of physical features?
options: they affect where people live, farm and build towns
they change the colour of the sky

quiz.prompt: True or false: Kenya has no mountains at all?

units.title: Weather and climate of Kenya
units.notes: Weather is the condition of the air at a particular time, such as sunny, cloudy, windy or rainy. Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. Kenya has seasons such as the long rains, the short rains and the dry season. Weather affects farming, dressing, transport and water supply. We can measure rainfall using a rain gauge and temperature using a thermometer, then record the readings in a table.
units.worked_example: A class recorded 20 millimetres of rain on Monday and 35 millimetres on Tuesday using a rain gauge, so they concluded that Tuesday was the wetter day.
units.activity: Keep a weather chart for one week, recording each day as sunny, cloudy, windy or rainy, and count how many days each type appeared.
units.check: What is the difference between weather and climate?

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between weather and climate?
options: weather is the condition at a particular time, while climate is the usual weather over many years
weather is over many years, while climate is today
they mean exactly the same thing
weather is about water, climate about land

quiz.prompt: True or false: Weather affects farming, dressing, transport and water supply?
Which instrument measures rainfall?
Which instrument measures temperature?
True or false: Kenya has seasons such as the long rains, the short rains and the dry season?

units.title: Natural resources and their uses
units.notes: Natural resources are things found in nature that people use to meet their needs. Examples include soil, water, forests, minerals, wildlife and sunlight. Some resources such as trees can be replaced if we plant more, but minerals and oil take a very long time to form. In Kenya we use soil for farming, rivers for water and fishing, and forests for timber and honey. We must use resources carefully so that they last for the future.
units.worked_example: Kevin explains that the sand and stones used to build his school came from a river nearby, while the timber for the desks came from trees grown on a farm.
units.activity: List five natural resources you can see on your way to school and write one use for each.
units.check: Why should we use natural resources carefully?

quiz.prompt: Why should we use natural resources carefully?
options: so that they last for the future
so that we use them all today

quiz.prompt: True or false: Some resources such as trees can be replaced if we plant more?
Which resources take a very long time to form?
In Kenya, what do we use forests for?
True or false: Natural resources are things found in nature that people use to meet their needs?

units.title: Communities and cultural heritage in Kenya
units.notes: Kenya is home to many communities such as the Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya, Kalenjin, Kamba, Kisii, Maasai, Somali, Swahili and many others. Each community has its own language, foods, dress, songs, dances and festivals. Cultural heritage also includes crafts, stories, riddles and proverbs passed down from grandparents. Learning about other communities helps us respect one another and live together in peace. Kenya's unity comes from sharing and appreciating these different traditions.
units.worked_example: During a school cultural day, pupils displayed ugali with sukuma wiki, pilau and mukimo, and explained which community prepares each food.
units.activity: Ask an elder at home for one proverb or story from your community, then share it with your class in your own words.
units.check: Name two communities found in Kenya and one tradition of each.

quiz.prompt: Which of these are communities found in Kenya?
options: Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya, Kalenjin and Kamba

units.title: Family, clans and social groups
units.notes: A family is the smallest group of people related by blood, marriage or adoption. Families may be nuclear, with parents and children, or extended, including grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins. Many Kenyan communities are organised into clans, which are groups of families sharing a common ancestor. Social groups such as age sets, churches, mosques and welfare groups also bring people together. Each group has rules, roles and responsibilities that help members live well.
units.worked_example: When Grace's uncle lost his job, the extended family and the clan welfare group contributed money and food until he found new work.
units.activity: Draw a simple family tree showing your grandparents, parents and yourself, and mark the people who live in your home.

units.title: Early people and settlement in Kenya
units.notes: Long ago, people moved from place to place looking for water, pasture and food, and this movement is called migration. Some groups settled near rivers and lakes where fish and water were available, while others settled in the highlands to farm. As people settled, they built homes, learned to keep animals and grew crops. Over time these settlements grew into villages, towns and cities. Studying the past helps us understand how Kenya's present communities came to live where they do.
units.worked_example: A class visited Olorgesailie and saw stone tools made by early people, then discussed why those people chose to live near the old lake bed.
units.activity: Discuss with a partner three reasons why early people would choose to settle near a river.

units.title: Economic activities in Kenya
units.notes: Economic activities are the ways people earn a living. Farming, fishing, livestock keeping, mining, tourism, trade and manufacturing are all important in Kenya. Some activities such as farming take place in rural areas, while trade, banking and offices are common in towns. People choose activities according to the resources and climate of where they live. These activities produce goods and services that families need and also earn the country money.
units.worked_example: Wanjiru sells vegetables at the local market, while her brother works in a hotel in Mombasa serving tourists, and both earn money for the family.
units.activity: Interview one adult at home about how they earn a living, and present your findings to the class in two or three sentences.

units.title: County government and leadership
units.notes: Kenya is divided into forty-seven counties, and each county has its own government. The county government is led by a governor, assisted by a deputy governor and a county assembly. Counties are responsible for services such as health centres, local roads, markets, water and waste collection. Citizens pay taxes and rates that help fund these services. Leaders are chosen through elections, and voters should choose wisely and peacefully.
units.worked_example: When the market road in Kisumu County became muddy, residents reported it to their ward representative, and the county later repaired the road.
units.activity: With your class, list three services the county government provides in your area and say which one your community needs most.

units.title: National government and the Constitution
units.notes: The national government of Kenya makes laws and manages the whole country. It has three arms: the legislature which makes laws, the executive which implements them, and the judiciary which interprets them. Parliament is made up of the National Assembly and the Senate. The Constitution is the supreme law that guides how the country is governed and protects the rights of all people. The President leads the executive and is elected by citizens.
units.worked_example: When a new law on school safety was debated, members of Parliament discussed it, and after it passed the executive published rules for all schools to follow.
units.activity: In small groups, name the three arms of government and write one duty of each on a chart.
units.check: Why is the Constitution called the supreme law of the land?

options: the supreme law that guides how the country is governed

units.title: Citizenship, rights and responsibilities
units.notes: A citizen is a person who legally belongs to a country. Kenyan citizens are entitled to rights such as education, health care, freedom of expression and protection by the law. Alongside rights come responsibilities, including obeying the law, paying taxes, caring for the environment and respecting other people. Good citizens take part in activities that improve their school and community. Rights and responsibilities work together to build a fair and peaceful society.
units.worked_example: Mary knows she has the right to attend school, so she also does her duty by arriving on time, keeping the classroom clean and helping new pupils settle in.
units.activity: Make a list of three rights you enjoy at school and three responsibilities you have as a pupil, then compare with a partner.

units.title: Kenya and her neighbours in East Africa
units.notes: Kenya shares borders with Uganda, Tanzania, South Sudan, Ethiopia and Somalia, and the Indian Ocean lies to the south-east. Together with some of these countries, Kenya belongs to the East African Community, which promotes trade, travel and cooperation. Neighbours buy and sell goods, share roads and ports, and work together on security and conservation. Good relations with neighbours bring peace and business opportunities. Learners should know the names, capitals and main products of neighbouring countries.
units.worked_example: Trucks carry Kenyan tea to Uganda and bring back sugar, showing how trade between neighbouring countries benefits people on both sides.

Agriculture.overview: This guide introduces upper primary learners to farming in Kenya, covering soil, crops, livestock and the simple tools used on a farm. Learners investigate, record observations and practise safe, practical methods in the school garden.

units.title: Agriculture around us and its importance
units.notes: Agriculture is the practice of growing crops and keeping animals for food, income and other needs. It provides food such as maize, vegetables, milk and eggs, and it employs many people in Kenya. Farming can be done on a small piece of land for a family or on a large farm for business. Agriculture also supplies raw materials like cotton and sugarcane to factories. Learning agriculture helps us produce food and care for the land properly.
units.worked_example: A family in Kiambu grows maize and beans on a half-acre plot, keeps three dairy cows, and sells the surplus milk to buy school books.
units.activity: Walk around your school and list five plants or animals you can see, then say whether each is used for food, income or both.
units.check: Give two reasons why agriculture is important in Kenya.

options: Growing crops and keeping animals for food and income

units.title: Soil and how it forms
units.notes: Soil is the loose upper layer of the ground in which plants grow. It forms very slowly when rocks are broken down by heat, rain, wind and living things over many years. Soil contains minerals, water, air and humus, which is the dark part made from dead plants and animals. Humus makes the soil fertile and helps it hold water. Without soil, farmers would have nothing in which to plant their crops.
units.worked_example: Peter noticed that the soil under the trees was darker than the soil on the open path, and his teacher explained that fallen leaves had rotted to form humus.
units.activity: Dig a small hole in the school garden and describe the colour, feel and any small living things you find in the soil.

options: The hard rock deep under the ground

units.title: Types of soil and simple soil tests
units.notes: There are three main types of soil: sandy, clay and loamy. Sandy soil has large particles, drains water quickly and feels rough. Clay soil has tiny particles, holds water and feels smooth and sticky when wet. Loamy soil is a mixture of sand, clay and humus, and it is the best for most crops. We can test soil by feeling it, shaking it in a bottle of water, or seeing how fast water drains through it.
units.worked_example: A group put equal amounts of three soils in funnels; water passed quickly through the sandy soil, slowly through clay and at a medium rate through loam.
units.activity: Collect a handful of soil from the school compound, add water and roll it in your hands, then describe whether it feels sandy, sticky or in between.

units.title: Water in the soil and drainage
units.notes: Plants take in water and dissolved minerals through their roots, so soil must hold enough water. If the soil holds too much water and cannot drain, plant roots may rot because they get no air. Farmers add manure or compost to improve how soil holds water, and they make drains to remove excess water from gardens. Over-watering young plants is just as harmful as letting them dry out. Testing how fast water sinks tells us whether a soil drains well.
units.worked_example: After heavy rain, Juma saw water standing in a part of the garden, so he dug a shallow drain and the water flowed away, saving the bean seedlings.
units.activity: Pour half a cup of water on dry soil in the school garden and time how long it takes to disappear, then record the time.

units.title: Simple farm tools and their care
units.notes: Farmers use simple tools such as the jembe, panga, rake, watering can, wheelbarrow and slasher. Each tool has a particular job: the jembe is used for digging, the panga for cutting, the rake for levelling, and the watering can for giving plants water. Tools should be cleaned after use, dried well and stored in a dry place to avoid rust. Sharp edges make work easy and safe, so a blunt jembe should be sharpened. Using the right tool for a job protects both the farmer and the tool.
units.worked_example: After weeding, Mwangi washed the jembe, dried it in the sun and hung it in the store so that it would not rust before the next planting season.

units.title: Land preparation and planting
units.notes: Before planting, the land must be cleared of weeds and bushes, then dug to loosen the soil. Digging lets air and water enter the soil and makes it easy for roots to grow. Large clods are broken and the surface is levelled with a rake. Seeds are then planted at the right depth and spacing so that each plant gets enough light, water and nutrients. Good spacing also makes weeding and harvesting easier.
units.worked_example: A class dug a bed, removed weeds, raked it flat, then planted maize seeds three centimetres deep and twenty-five centimetres apart along a string line.
units.activity: Prepare a small seedbed in the school garden, mark rows with a string, and plant bean or maize seeds at the spacing your teacher gives.

units.title: Growing cereals and legumes
units.notes: Cereals are crops grown for their grain, and in Kenya they include maize, millet, sorghum and wheat. Legumes are crops that produce pods with seeds, such as beans, cowpeas, groundnuts and green grams. Legumes are special because their roots work with tiny living things to add nutrients to the soil. Cereals and legumes are often grown together so that the soil stays fertile. These crops are important food and can also be sold for money.
units.worked_example: Kagure planted maize and beans in the same field; the beans ripened first and were eaten while the maize was still growing, so the family had food over a longer period.
units.activity: In a small plot, plant a few maize and bean seeds together, then record how many days each takes to germinate.

units.title: Growing vegetables at school
units.notes: Vegetables such as kale, spinach, tomatoes, onions and carrots supply vitamins and minerals that keep our bodies healthy. They grow well in loamy soil with plenty of sunshine and regular watering. Vegetables need weeding, thinning and top dressing with manure to grow strong. Some are harvested by picking leaves and others by pulling up the whole plant. Growing vegetables at school teaches responsibility and gives fresh food for the school feeding programme.
units.worked_example: The class watered its kale bed every morning, removed weeds weekly, and after six weeks harvested enough leaves for the school kitchen.

units.title: Fruit trees and agroforestry
units.notes: Fruit trees such as mango, orange, avocado and pawpaw provide food, shade and income. Trees are planted in holes filled with a mixture of topsoil and manure, and they need watering until their roots are established. Agroforestry means growing trees together with crops on the same land. This practice improves the soil, provides firewood and timber, and protects the land from strong winds and erosion. Trees planted today will benefit the family for many years.
units.worked_example: The pupils planted grevillea trees along the school fence and mango seedlings behind the classrooms, and they watered them twice a week during the dry season.

units.title: Soil erosion and its control
units.notes: Soil erosion is the carrying away of the top layer of soil by water or wind. It removes the fertile part of the soil and leaves land poor and rocky. Erosion is worse on bare slopes, on land without plants and where people have cut down all the trees. We can control it by planting cover crops, digging terraces and contour lines, mulching, and planting trees and grass strips. Controlling erosion keeps the soil fertile and protects crops and roads.
units.worked_example: After a steep school plot was washed by heavy rain, pupils dug contour lines and planted grass along them, and the next rain carried much less soil away.
units.activity: In groups, pour water gently on a bare soil slope and on a grassy slope, then compare how muddy the water that runs off is.

units.title: Keeping poultry
units.notes: Poultry keeping means rearing birds such as chickens, ducks and turkeys for eggs and meat. Birds need a clean, dry house with enough space, feeders and drinkers, and protection from predators at night. They are fed on grains, greens and special feeds, and they must always have clean water. Hens that are well fed and cared for lay more eggs. A simple record of eggs collected each day helps the farmer know whether the flock is doing well.
units.worked_example: Njeri keeps eight hens; after she improved their house and started giving them balanced feed, her daily collection rose from three eggs to six.

units.title: Keeping rabbits and goats
units.notes: Rabbits and goats are small animals that are easy and cheap to keep in many parts of Kenya. Rabbits eat greens, hay and pellets and are kept in hutches that must be cleaned often, while goats browse on shrubs and need a shed or boma at night. Both animals provide meat, and dairy goats give milk, while rabbit droppings make good manure. They need clean water, protection from disease and shelter from strong sun and rain. Regular cleaning stops bad smells and disease.
units.worked_example: Ali keeps two dairy goats and sells four litres of milk each day; the money pays for his sister's school needs and for goat feed.

units.title: Dairy animals and marketing farm produce
units.notes: Dairy animals such as cows and goats are kept for milk, which is a valuable food and a source of income. They need plenty of clean water, good pasture, mineral salts and a clean shed, and cows should be milked at the same times each day. Milk must be handled cleanly, kept in clean containers and delivered quickly so that it does not go bad. Farmers sell their produce at markets, to cooperatives or to hotels. Keeping simple records of milk and money helps the farmer plan well.
