Creative Arts.overview: This guide develops upper primary learners' skills in drawing, craft, music and performance. Learners explore ideas from their surroundings and practise creating, performing and appreciating original work.

units.title: What creative arts are and where ideas come from
units.notes: Creative arts are the many ways people express ideas and feelings through making, singing, moving and acting. They include drawing, painting, craft, music, dance and drama. Ideas for creative work come from what we see, hear and imagine around us, such as markets, animals, rivers and family life. Artists plan by choosing a subject and the materials they will use. Everyone can be creative with practice, patience and observation.
units.worked_example: After watching hens scratch in the school compound, Wendo decided to draw them and chose a pencil for fine feathers and crayons for the red combs.

units.title: Drawing lines, shapes and forms
units.notes: Every drawing is built from lines, shapes and forms. A line is a mark made by a moving tool, and it can be straight, curved, thick, thin, long or short. Shapes are flat areas such as circles, triangles and rectangles, while forms are shapes that look solid, like a ball or a box. Artists use light lines to plan and dark lines to show importance. Practising different lines and shapes makes our drawing more controlled and expressive.
units.worked_example: To draw a jembe, Rose first sketched a thin rectangle for the handle, added a curved shape for the blade, then darkened the outline to make the tool clear.

units.title: Drawing from observation
units.notes: Drawing from observation means looking carefully at a real object or scene and drawing what you actually see, not what you remember. Artists first study the shape, size, texture and where light falls on the object. They begin with light guide lines and correct the proportions before adding details and shading. Shading with a pencil or crayon shows light and dark areas and makes objects look solid. Good observation takes time and quiet looking.
units.worked_example: A pupil placed a cup on the desk, noticed the light came from the window on the left, and shaded the right side of the cup darker to show shadow.

units.title: Colour and painting
units.notes: Colour makes artwork lively and can show mood, light and distance. The primary colours are red, blue and yellow, and mixing them gives secondary colours such as green, orange and purple. Mixing a colour with white makes it lighter, and with black it becomes darker. Artists choose colours that match the subject, such as green for leaves and blue for water. Paint should be applied carefully, cleaning the brush before changing colours.
units.worked_example: To paint a sunset, Brian mixed red and yellow for the orange sky, then used a little blue to make the far hills look distant.

units.title: Printmaking
units.notes: Printmaking is a way of making pictures by transferring ink or paint from a raised surface onto paper. The surface may be a potato, a leaf, a bottle top, a piece of card or a carved block. The raised parts are coated with colour and pressed onto paper, while the lower parts stay blank. Repeating a print in a pattern creates interesting designs for cards, cloth and wall art. Printmaking teaches careful planning because the design appears the opposite way round when printed.
units.worked_example: A group cut a leaf shape into a potato, dipped it in green paint and printed a row of leaves to make a border for a class poster.
units.activity: Collect safe objects such as bottle tops, leaves and cut potatoes, dip them in paint and print a repeating pattern on a sheet of paper.

units.title: Modelling with clay
units.notes: Modelling is shaping a soft material such as clay, plasticine or dough into a form. Clay must be wedged, or kneaded, to remove air bubbles before shaping, otherwise the model may crack. Artists use methods such as pinching, coiling and slab building to make pots, animals and figures. Models must be dried slowly in the shade and then fired if they are to be strong. Small details are added with sticks or fingers before drying.
units.worked_example: Using the coiling method, pupils rolled long clay ropes, stacked them in circles to build a pot and smoothed the inside with a wet finger.

units.title: Weaving and basketry
units.notes: Weaving is the interlacing of threads or strips to make cloth or baskets. One set of strands runs lengthwise and another set is woven over and under it in a pattern. Baskets can be made from sisal, papyrus, palm leaves or strips of plastic and are used for carrying food and storing grain. In Kenya, weaving is an important craft that also earns income for families. Neat, even tension makes the finished work strong and attractive.
units.worked_example: A pupil cut banana fibre into thin strips, soaked them, then wove them over and under to make a small mat with alternating colours.
units.activity: Make a simple paper mat by weaving strips of two different coloured papers over and under each other.

units.title: Paper craft and collage
units.notes: Craft work uses simple materials to make useful and beautiful things. In paper craft, learners fold, cut, tear and join paper to make cards, flowers, masks and models. A collage is a picture made by gluing pieces of paper, cloth or other materials onto a surface. Careful cutting along a drawn line and neat gluing make the work tidy. Craft teaches planning, patience and the reuse of materials that would otherwise be thrown away.
units.worked_example: Patrick tore old magazines into small pieces, arranged them to form the shape of a fish and glued them onto card to create a colourful collage.

units.title: Traditional Kenyan musical instruments
units.notes: Traditional Kenyan instruments are grouped into drums, strings and wind instruments, as well as rattles. Drums such as the isukuti are played by hitting with the hand or a stick. String instruments include the nyatiti and the orutu, while wind instruments include the flute and the horn. Rattles and shakers add rhythm to songs and dances. These instruments are used in ceremonies, storytelling and celebrations, and they carry the history of a community.
units.worked_example: During a music lesson, a group used an empty tin filled with dry beans as a shaker, keeping time with a drum made from a bucket covered with a tight skin.
units.activity: Make a simple shaker from a closed tin or bottle filled with dry seeds, then play a steady beat with two other classmates.

units.title: Singing and Kenyan folk songs
units.notes: Singing is the use of the voice to produce musical sounds, usually with words. Folk songs are songs passed down from older generations and are sung in local languages for work, play, worship and ceremonies. Singers must breathe properly, open their mouths well and listen to each other to stay together. Songs can be sung in unison, where everyone sings the same part, or in parts and rounds. Singing together builds confidence and a sense of belonging.
units.worked_example: The class learned a Luo lullaby in two parts, with one group singing the melody and another adding a soft lower part.
units.activity: In groups, choose one folk song from your community, practise it with actions and present it to the class.

units.title: Rhythm, beat and percussion
units.notes: The beat is the steady pulse you feel in music, like the ticking of a clock, while rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences played over that beat. Percussion instruments such as drums, shakers and clapping produce sound when they are struck or shaken. Different note values, such as long and short sounds, can be clapped as patterns. Keeping a steady beat helps singers and dancers perform together. Practice improves our sense of timing.
units.worked_example: A class clapped a four-count beat, then added short-short-long patterns on shakers so that the rhythm played against the steady beat.
units.activity: With a partner, clap a steady beat while the other claps a short rhythm on top, then swap roles.

units.title: Drama and storytelling
units.notes: Drama is the acting out of a story or situation in front of others. Storytelling and drama use voice, facial expression, gestures and movement to make characters come alive. A short play has characters, a setting and a simple plot with a beginning, middle and end. Actors must speak clearly, project their voices and face the audience. Performing builds confidence, teamwork and the ability to express ideas.
units.worked_example: Three pupils acted a short play about a pupil who wasted water at the tap, using loud clear voices and sad faces to show the character's regret.
units.activity: In groups of four, prepare and perform a two-minute play about keeping your school clean, then discuss what the audience learned.

units.title: Dance, movement and performance
units.notes: Dance is moving the body in time to music to express feelings and tell stories. Dancers need good posture, balance, coordination and a sense of rhythm. Kenyan dances use steps, jumps, hand movements and body shakes that reflect community life and celebrations. Performers should warm up first and observe safety so that no one gets hurt. A good performance combines careful practice, confidence and respect for the audience.
units.worked_example: A group practised a circular dance, first warming up their legs and arms, then moving in step with the drum beat and clapping in time.
units.activity: In groups, create a one-minute dance to a drum beat using three different movements, then perform it for the class.

Physical and Health Education.overview: This guide helps learners in Grade 4 to Grade 6 build healthy habits, move skilfully and play safely. It covers movement, games, athletics, hygiene and safety in everyday Kenyan settings.

units.title: Understanding my growing body
units.notes: During upper primary your body changes quickly as you grow taller and stronger. Bones lengthen, muscles develop and you need more energy from food and more rest. Good posture while sitting, standing and carrying your bag protects your spine. Getting enough sleep, drinking clean water and eating balanced meals help your body grow well. Know that every learner grows at a different speed, and that is normal.
units.worked_example: If a learner sleeps only five hours each night, they may feel tired in class and perform poorly in games. Sleeping nine to ten hours and drinking water during break can improve both mood and performance.
units.activity: Keep a one-week chart of your sleep hours and glasses of water each day, then discuss with a partner which day you felt most energetic.

units.title: Warming up and cooling down
units.notes: Before any game or athletics you must warm up so your muscles are ready and less likely to tear. A warm-up starts with light jogging, then slow stretching of arms, legs and back, and simple joint rolls. Warming up raises your heartbeat and body temperature gradually. After activity, cool down with slow walking and gentle stretches to let your heart rate return to normal. Skipping these steps can cause cramps or injuries.
units.worked_example: Before a football match at school, a team jogs two laps, stretches for five minutes, then plays. Afterwards they walk one lap and stretch again to cool down.
units.activity: Design a five-minute warm-up and a three-minute cool-down routine with a partner and lead the class through it.

units.title: Locomotor and non-locomotor movements
units.notes: Movement skills are grouped into two types. Locomotor movements move the body from one place to another, such as walking, running, jumping, hopping and skipping. Non-locomotor movements happen in one place, such as bending, twisting, stretching, pushing and turning. Combining both kinds makes your movement smooth and controlled. Practising these skills helps you in games, dance and daily activities. Practise each skill slowly at first, then faster, to improve control.
units.worked_example: In a relay, a learner skips forward (locomotor), stops and twists to pass a baton (non-locomotor), then runs again. The two types work together.
units.activity: In small groups, call out movements like hop, twist or skip and let classmates show whether each is locomotor or non-locomotor.

units.title: Throwing, catching and aiming
units.notes: Throwing and catching are basic manipulative skills used in many games. To throw well, stand side-on, step forward and release the ball towards the target while following through with your arm. To catch, watch the ball, make a cup with your hands and pull it gently towards your chest. Aiming improves when you focus on the target and control your strength. These skills need regular practice to become accurate and reliable.
units.worked_example: When throwing a small ball at a target, a learner stands side-on, steps with the opposite foot and follows through. Aiming at the centre of the target usually scores more points than aiming anywhere.
units.activity: Set up three targets at different distances and throw five balls at each, recording how many times you hit them.

units.title: Ball games and teamwork
units.notes: Ball games like football, netball, volleyball and handball teach both skill and teamwork. Each game has simple rules that keep it fair and safe. Passing, dribbling, marking and shooting are common skills you should practise. Teamwork means listening, sharing the ball and encouraging others, not just trying to score yourself. Respecting the referee and opponents shows good sportsmanship. Team spirit is often as important as winning the match.
units.worked_example: In a netball match the ball is passed, not dribbled. A player who breaks this rule gives away a free pass, which shows why rules must be followed.

units.title: Simple athletics events
units.notes: Athletics includes running, jumping and throwing events. Sprints are short fast races, while long-distance races need steady speed and pacing. In the long jump you run, take off from one foot and land with both feet in the pit. In throws such as the ball throw, you use a side-on stance and release with power. Athletics builds speed, strength and endurance.
units.worked_example: In a 100 m sprint a learner starts low in the crouch, drives hard for the first steps, then runs tall through the finish line to keep speed.

units.title: Traditional games and dances
units.notes: Kenya has many traditional games and dances that keep learners active and teach culture. Games like kati, rope skipping, and dances from different communities use running, jumping and rhythm. They can be played with little or no equipment, making them easy to enjoy at school or home. These activities build fitness, coordination and social bonds. They also help us appreciate the cultures of other communities.
units.worked_example: A class learns a dance from a local community by watching, then copying the steps, clapping rhythm and singing together until the group moves in time.

units.title: Personal hygiene and cleanliness
units.notes: Good hygiene keeps you healthy and confident. You should bathe daily, brush your teeth twice a day, wash your hands with soap and clean your nails and hair. Wearing clean, ironed uniform protects your skin and shows respect for yourself and others. Dirty habits can cause skin diseases, germs and bad odour. Keeping clean also prevents the spread of disease in crowded classrooms.
units.worked_example: A learner who washes hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating reduces the chance of getting diarrhoea and stomach worms.

units.title: First aid basics
units.notes: First aid is the simple help given to an injured person before proper medical care. You can clean small cuts with clean water, press gently on a minor wound to stop bleeding, and cover it with a clean cloth or plaster. For a bruise you may apply a cool compress. Always tell a teacher or adult if someone is hurt. Never give medicine or move a badly injured person by yourself.
units.worked_example: If a classmate falls and gets a small cut on the knee, you wash the wound with clean water, cover it with a plaster and inform the teacher.

units.title: Safety at home and school
units.notes: Many accidents can be prevented with simple care. At home, keep away from fire, sharp tools and exposed wires, and never play near a cooking fire. At school, walk in corridors, keep the playground tidy and follow rules on the field. Wear shoes on rough ground and use play equipment properly. Reporting broken or dangerous items to an adult prevents injury.
units.worked_example: Playground stones left near a running track can cause a fall. Clearing them before a game shows how keeping the area safe prevents injuries.
units.activity: Walk around your school compound with a partner and list three possible dangers and how each could be removed.

units.title: Nutrition and healthy eating
units.notes: A balanced diet gives your body energy, growth and protection. It includes energy foods such as ugali, rice and bananas, body-building foods such as beans, eggs and fish, and protective foods such as greens, mangoes and tomatoes. Eating a variety of local foods at meals helps you stay strong. Drink plenty of clean water and limit sugary drinks and snacks. Eating well improves learning and concentration.
units.worked_example: A lunch of ugali, sukuma wiki, beans and a mango gives energy, body-building foods and vitamins, making a well-balanced meal.

units.title: Communicable and non-communicable diseases
units.notes: Communicable diseases spread from one person to another, such as common colds, influenza and diarrhoea. They spread through the air, dirty water, food and touch, and can be reduced by washing hands, covering the mouth when coughing and keeping food covered. Non-communicable diseases like diabetes and some heart problems are not spread between people and are linked to diet and lifestyle. Both types are managed by healthy habits.
units.worked_example: Covering your mouth with a hand or handkerchief when coughing stops droplets from spreading a cold to classmates seated nearby.
units.activity: In groups, sort a list of diseases into communicable and non-communicable groups and state one way to prevent each.

units.title: Fitness, rest and recreation
units.notes: Physical fitness means your body can carry out daily activities without getting too tired. Regular exercise makes the heart, lungs and muscles strong. Rest and sleep let the body repair and grow, while recreation such as games, music and reading refreshes the mind. Balancing exercise with rest helps you feel and perform better. A fit learner is more alert in class and calmer in daily life.
units.worked_example: A learner who plays actively for an hour, sleeps well and reads for pleasure is more alert in lessons than one who only watches television all evening.

Religious Education.overview: This guide helps learners in Grade 4 to Grade 6 explore values, beliefs and moral choices in a broad and inclusive way. It uses stories, examples and reflection to support good character and respect for others.

units.title: Living together with respect
units.notes: People live together in families, schools and communities where everyone has a place. Respect means treating others kindly even when they differ from you in age, religion or background. We show respect by listening, greeting, sharing and following rules. When everyone respects one another, there is peace and cooperation. Respect begins with how we speak and behave each day. Small acts of politeness build a peaceful and happy community.
units.worked_example: When two classmates disagree during a game, one listens first and answers politely. This respect prevents a quarrel and lets the game continue.

units.title: Honesty and telling the truth
units.notes: Honesty means always speaking and acting truthfully. It builds trust between friends, family and teachers. A dishonest act may seem to help for a moment but it usually brings trouble and lost trust. Being truthful even when it is hard shows strong character. Honest people are trusted with duties and responsibilities. Speaking the truth may feel difficult at first, but it earns lasting respect. A truthful learner is a reliable learner.

units.title: Kindness and sharing
units.notes: Kindness is caring for others and helping them without expecting a reward. Sharing what we have, such as food, books or time, eases the burden of those in need. Simple acts like carrying a bag for an elderly person or helping a new learner feel welcome show kindness. Kind communities are happier and stronger. Every learner can practise kindness daily.

units.title: Courage and doing what is right
units.notes: Courage is being brave enough to do the right thing even when it is difficult or unpopular. It may mean refusing to join in cheating, standing up against bullying or admitting a mistake. Courage is not about being fearless but about acting well despite fear. Brave choices often encourage others to act rightly too. Everyone can build courage step by step.

units.title: Responsibility and duty
units.notes: Responsibility is being dependable and doing the tasks you are trusted with. Learners have duties such as doing homework, keeping classrooms clean and caring for their property. Responsible people keep promises and admit when they fail. Family members, teachers and leaders all have responsibilities. Practising responsibility now prepares you for adult life. Even small duties matter, such as returning borrowed items on time.

units.title: Forgiveness and reconciliation
units.notes: Forgiveness is choosing to let go of anger after someone wrongs you. Reconciliation is making peace and restoring the relationship. Both need honesty, regret from the one who did wrong and willingness from the one hurt. Refusing to forgive can keep sadness and conflict alive. Forgiving does not always mean forgetting, but it frees us to move forward. Choosing to forgive also protects our own peace of mind.

units.title: Stories of faith and good people
units.notes: Many religions and communities tell stories about good people who followed their beliefs and served others. These stories often teach patience, faith, charity and sacrifice. Learners can learn lessons from stories of kindness, courage and honesty told across different faiths. Listening respectfully to others' stories teaches tolerance. The values in such stories guide our daily choices. Learners should listen to stories from other faiths with an open and respectful mind.

units.title: Worship, prayer and reflection
units.notes: Believers worship and pray in different ways in churches, mosques, temples and at home. Prayer can include thanks, requests for help and quiet reflection. Reflection means thinking calmly about our words and actions and how to improve. Quiet time helps learners handle difficult feelings and make good choices. Respecting how others worship is part of living together well. However people pray, sincerity and respect matter most.
units.worked_example: A learner sets aside a few quiet minutes each evening to think about the day, give thanks and plan to do better tomorrow.
units.activity: Write or draw a short personal reflection about something you are grateful for and one good change you hope to make.
units.check: Why can quiet reflection help you make better choices?

quiz.prompt: Why can quiet reflection help you make better choices?
options: It helps you think calmly about your actions and how to improve

quiz.prompt: What is reflection?
options: Thinking calmly about our words and actions

quiz.prompt: Do believers worship and pray in different ways?
Which of these is a place of worship?
Is respecting how others worship part of living together well?

units.title: Respecting different beliefs
units.notes: Kenya has people of many religions and cultures living side by side. Respecting different beliefs means not mocking, teasing or forcing your views on others. We can learn about one another's traditions while keeping our own faith. Peace grows when communities live together without fear or conflict. Respectful curiosity and kind words build harmony. A peaceful nation depends on people who accept one another.
units.worked_example: During a national holiday, learners of different faiths wish one another well and explain their own customs politely, showing tolerance.
units.activity: In groups, share one tradition from your family and listen respectfully to traditions of classmates from other beliefs.
units.check: How can you show respect to a classmate whose religion is different from yours?

quiz.prompt: How can you show respect to a classmate whose religion is different from yours?
options: Not teasing them and learning about their traditions kindly

quiz.prompt: What does respecting different beliefs mean?
options: Not mocking, teasing or forcing your views on others

quiz.prompt: Does Kenya have people of many religions and cultures living side by side?
What builds harmony in a community?
Does a peaceful nation depend on people who accept one another?

units.title: Caring for the environment as a value
units.notes: Many faiths teach that the earth is a gift that should be cared for. Learners can show this value by planting trees, cleaning their surroundings, saving water and not littering. Caring for animals and plants protects the balance of nature. These acts of stewardship are a way of showing gratitude and responsibility. Small daily habits make a big difference. This caring attitude shows gratitude for the world we share.
units.worked_example: A class plants a tree in the school compound and waters it weekly, showing care for creation and responsibility to the community.
units.activity: Start a tree or flower in a container or school garden and care for it for a month, recording its growth.
units.check: Why is caring for the environment considered a good moral value?

quiz.prompt: Why is caring for the environment considered a good moral value?
options: Because it is a rule only
Because the earth is a gift that should be cared for

quiz.prompt: Which of these shows caring for the environment?
Does caring for animals and plants protect the balance of nature?
What do many faiths teach about the earth?
options: That it belongs to no one
That it is a gift that should be cared for

quiz.prompt: Do small daily habits of caring for nature make no difference?

units.title: Marriage, family and community
units.notes: The family is the first place where people learn values, love and cooperation. In many communities marriage joins two families and is celebrated with respect and tradition. Grandparents and elders pass on wisdom and stories to the young. Healthy families support one another in good and hard times. Strong families help build strong communities. Learning about family life helps learners value their own relatives.
units.worked_example: At a family gathering, an elder explains how relatives help one another during planting and harvest, showing the value of cooperation.
units.activity: Draw your family tree with help from a parent or guardian and share one lesson older relatives teach in your family.
units.check: Why are elders important in a family and community?

quiz.prompt: Why are elders important in a family and community?
options: They pass on wisdom and stories to the young

quiz.prompt: Where is the first place people learn values, love and cooperation?
In many communities, does marriage join two families?
What do strong families help build?
Do healthy families support one another in good and hard times?

units.title: Fairness and justice
units.notes: Fairness means giving each person what is right and treating everyone equally. Justice calls for doing the right thing when someone is treated unfairly. In school, fairness means sharing equipment, marking work honestly and giving everyone a turn. Standing up for a bullied learner shows justice. Fairness protects the weak and keeps communities peaceful. Fairness begins with small decisions we make every day.
units.worked_example: When choosing a team, a learner ensures everyone gets a turn to play, including the quieter ones, which shows fairness and justice.
units.activity: Discuss a situation where someone was treated unfairly at school and suggest what a fair solution would look like.
units.check: What would you do if you saw a classmate being treated unfairly?

quiz.prompt: What would you do if you saw a classmate being treated unfairly?
options: Stand up for them and report to an adult

quiz.prompt: What is fairness?
options: Giving each person what is right and treating everyone equally

quiz.prompt: Does fairness mean sharing equipment and giving everyone a turn?
What does justice call for when someone is treated unfairly?
Does fairness protect the weak and keep communities peaceful?

units.title: Good character and making choices
units.notes: Good character is the habit of making wise, kind and honest choices even when no one is watching. It grows from the values you have learnt, such as respect, honesty, courage and responsibility. Every day brings choices about words, actions and friends. Thinking about consequences before acting helps you choose well. Good character builds trust and a bright future. Your choices today shape the person you become tomorrow.
units.worked_example: Faced with the choice to join friends in cheating or to study honestly, a learner remembers the value of honesty and chooses to work hard instead.
units.activity: Write down a daily choice you face and list the good and bad consequences of each option before deciding.
units.check: How can thinking about consequences help you make a good choice?

quiz.prompt: How can thinking about consequences help you make a good choice?
options: It helps you choose well by considering what may happen

quiz.prompt: What is good character?
options: The habit of making wise, kind and honest choices even when no one is watching

quiz.prompt: Does good character grow from values such as respect, honesty, courage and responsibility?
What shapes the person you become tomorrow?
Does thinking about consequences before acting help you choose well?

Indigenous Language.overview: This guide supports Grade 4 to Grade 6 learners in listening, speaking, reading and writing in a Kenyan indigenous language. It also builds appreciation of culture through songs, stories and proverbs.

units.title: Listening carefully and following instructions
units.notes: Good listening is the first step in learning any language. You should sit still, look at the speaker and try to understand each word. Listening to stories, songs and instructions in the indigenous language helps you learn new words and sounds. Repeating what you hear improves your memory and pronunciation. Listening respectfully also shows good manners. When you listen well, you can answer and follow directions correctly.
units.worked_example: After the teacher gives three instructions in the indigenous language, a learner repeats them in order and carries them out correctly, showing good listening.
units.activity: Listen to a short story told in your indigenous language and retell the main events to a partner in your own words.
units.check: What should you do with your body and eyes to listen well?

quiz.prompt: What should you do with your body and eyes to listen well?
options: Sit still and look at the speaker

quiz.prompt: Why is good listening important when learning a language?
options: It helps you ignore the speaker
It is the first step in learning any language

quiz.prompt: Does repeating what you hear improve your memory and pronunciation?
Listening respectfully to a speaker shows what?
When you listen well, can you answer and follow directions correctly?

units.title: Greetings and polite words
units.notes: Greetings open every conversation and show respect. Each indigenous language has different greetings for morning, afternoon and evening, and polite words for please, thank you and sorry. Greetings may differ by age or relationship, such as greeting an elder respectfully. Using the right greeting at the right time pleases listeners. Learners should practise greetings daily. Using the correct greeting shows respect for the person you meet.
units.worked_example: Greeting an elder in the morning with the correct respectful phrase, and answering politely when greeted, shows good manners in the language.
units.activity: Practise greeting different people in your language, such as a friend, a teacher and an elder, and note how the words change.
units.check: Why do greetings change depending on who you are speaking to?

quiz.prompt: Why do greetings change depending on who you are speaking to?
options: Because greetings show respect and may differ by age or relationship

quiz.prompt: What do greetings do at the start of a conversation?
Does each indigenous language have different greetings for morning, afternoon and evening?
Which of these is a polite word?
Does using the correct greeting show respect for the person you meet?

units.title: Sounds and pronunciation
units.notes: Every indigenous language has its own sounds, some of which may not exist in English or Kiswahili. Paying attention to vowels, consonants and tones helps you pronounce words correctly. Some languages use tone, where the pitch of your voice changes the meaning of a word. Listening to elders and repeating carefully improves your speech. Clear pronunciation helps others understand you.
units.worked_example: A learner notices that changing the tone of a short word changes its meaning and practises saying both forms until listeners hear the difference.
units.activity: With a partner, practise saying pairs of words that sound similar and check whether the meaning changes with pronunciation.
units.check: Why is it important to listen for tones when learning your language?

quiz.prompt: Why is it important to listen for tones when learning your language?
options: Because the pitch of your voice can change the meaning of a word

quiz.prompt: What helps you pronounce words correctly?
options: Paying attention to vowels, consonants and tones

quiz.prompt: Do some languages use tone, where the pitch of your voice changes the meaning of a word?
Who should you listen to and repeat carefully to improve your speech?
Does clear pronunciation help others understand you?

units.title: Everyday vocabulary and naming things
units.notes: Building vocabulary means learning the names of things around you. You can name body parts, family members, foods, animals, tools and places in your indigenous language. Grouping words into sets, such as foods or animals, helps you remember them. Using new words often keeps them in your memory. A rich vocabulary helps you speak and write clearly. Review new words often so you do not forget them.
units.worked_example: A learner lists ten animals found in their area, writes their names in the indigenous language and uses three of them in sentences.
units.activity: Draw and label five objects in your home in your indigenous language and show the labels to a classmate.
units.check: How can grouping words into sets help you remember them?

quiz.prompt: How can grouping words into sets help you remember them?
options: By sorting them, such as foods or animals, so they are easier to recall

quiz.prompt: What does building vocabulary mean?
options: Learning the names of things around you

quiz.prompt: Does using new words often keep them in your memory?
Which of these is a group of things you can name in your language?
options: Body parts, family members and foods

quiz.prompt: Does a rich vocabulary help you speak and write clearly?

units.title: Simple sentences and word order
units.notes: A sentence expresses a complete thought. In the indigenous language, words follow a particular order that may differ from English or Kiswahili. Most simple sentences have a subject and a verb, and some add an object. Building short sentences first makes longer ones easier later. Practising sentence patterns helps you speak and write correctly. Read your sentences aloud to check that they sound right.
units.worked_example: Using a pattern like subject plus verb, a learner builds short sentences such as naming who is doing what, then adds an object to extend them.
units.activity: Write five simple sentences in your indigenous language describing what your family did today.
units.check: What two main parts does a simple sentence usually have?

quiz.prompt: What two main parts does a simple sentence usually have?
options: A comma and a full stop

quiz.prompt: What does a sentence express?
In the indigenous language, do words follow a particular order that may differ from English or Kiswahili?
Why should you read your sentences aloud?
options: To check that they sound right

quiz.prompt: Does practising sentence patterns help you speak and write correctly?

units.title: Songs, rhymes and rhythm
units.notes: Songs and rhymes are fun ways to learn a language. They carry words, sounds and culture from one generation to the next. Singing helps you remember new words and correct pronunciation. Children's songs often repeat words, which makes learning easier. Songs also mark important events like harvests, births and ceremonies. Singing together also brings people closer and keeps culture alive, and it makes language practice enjoyable.
units.worked_example: A group learns a children's song in the indigenous language, sings it together with clapping, and explains what the words mean.
units.activity: Learn one song or rhyme in your indigenous language and perform it in class, explaining its meaning.
units.check: How can singing a song help you remember new words?

quiz.prompt: How can singing a song help you remember new words?
options: Songs repeat words, which makes learning easier

quiz.prompt: What do songs and rhymes carry from one generation to the next?
Do songs mark important events like harvests, births and ceremonies?
Why does singing together help people?
options: It brings people closer and keeps culture alive

quiz.prompt: Does singing make language practice enjoyable?

units.title: Reading short texts aloud
units.notes: Reading aloud connects written words with their sounds and meaning. Begin with short, familiar texts such as captions and simple stories. Point to each word, sound it out and read at a steady pace. Reading aloud helps you notice punctuation and improve fluency. Sharing reading with a partner builds confidence. If you meet a hard word, sound it out slowly and ask for help, since regular reading makes you faster and smoother.
units.worked_example: A learner reads a short paragraph in the indigenous language aloud, pausing at full stops and changing voice at question marks.
units.activity: Choose a short passage in your indigenous language and read it aloud to a partner, who notes any words you found hard.
units.check: Why should you pause at a full stop when reading aloud?

quiz.prompt: Why should you pause at a full stop when reading aloud?
options: To show a pause between sentences

quiz.prompt: What should you do if you meet a hard word when reading aloud?
options: Sound it out slowly and ask for help

quiz.prompt: Does reading aloud connect written words with their sounds and meaning?
What does sharing reading with a partner do?
Does regular reading make you faster and smoother?

units.title: Writing short paragraphs
units.notes: Writing lets you record your thoughts in the indigenous language. A short paragraph has a main idea and supporting sentences that follow in order. Start with a clear opening sentence, add details, and end with a closing thought. Neat handwriting and correct spelling make your work easy to read. Writing regularly improves your skill. Read over your work to correct any spelling and word order.
units.worked_example: A learner writes a short paragraph about their school day with an opening sentence, three details and a closing sentence.
units.activity: Write a short paragraph of four to six sentences about your best friend in your indigenous language.
units.check: What does the opening sentence of a paragraph usually do?

quiz.prompt: What does the opening sentence of a paragraph usually do?
What does a short paragraph contain?
options: A main idea and supporting sentences

quiz.prompt: Do neat handwriting and correct spelling make your work easy to read?
What should you do after writing to improve your work?
options: Read over it to correct spelling and word order

quiz.prompt: Does writing regularly improve your skill?

units.title: Proverbs and wise sayings
units.notes: Proverbs are short wise sayings that carry lessons about life. They are passed down by elders and are used to advise, warn or encourage. Each proverb has a deeper meaning beyond its literal words. Learning proverbs helps you understand the culture and use the language well. Using a proverb at the right time shows wisdom. Proverbs also keep the wisdom of past generations alive for us.
units.worked_example: When a friend gives up easily, an elder quotes a proverb about patience and hard work, then explains the lesson of persistence.
units.activity: Collect three proverbs from an elder, write them down and explain the meaning of each in your own words.
units.check: Why do proverbs carry deeper meaning than their literal words?

quiz.prompt: Why do proverbs carry deeper meaning than their literal words?
options: They carry lessons about life beyond the literal words

quiz.prompt: Who passes down proverbs?
Are proverbs used to advise, warn or encourage?
What does using a proverb at the right time show?
Do proverbs keep the wisdom of past generations alive?

units.title: Stories and storytelling
units.notes: Storytelling is an important part of indigenous culture. Stories teach values, history and entertainment, and often include animals, ancestors or clever characters. A good storyteller uses expression, gestures and changes of voice. Listeners often join in with songs or responses. Retelling a story helps you practise speaking and remember details. Stories also teach values and history, so listen carefully and retell them well.
units.worked_example: A learner tells a folk tale with different voices for each character and pauses dramatically to keep listeners interested.
units.activity: In small groups, choose a folk tale and present it to the class with sound effects and expressive voices.
units.check: How can a storyteller keep listeners interested in a story?

quiz.prompt: How can a storyteller keep listeners interested in a story?
options: By speaking in a flat voice
By using expression, gestures and changes of voice

quiz.prompt: What do stories often include?
Does retelling a story help you practise speaking and remember details?
What do listeners often do during storytelling?
options: Join in with songs or responses

quiz.prompt: Do stories teach values and history?

units.title: Conversation and discussion
units.notes: Conversation means taking turns to speak and listen. In a discussion, learners share ideas, agree or disagree politely and ask questions. Using the indigenous language in everyday talk builds fluency and confidence. Respecting others' turn to speak keeps the discussion orderly. Good conversation is a skill that improves with practice. Listening closely to your partner helps you reply well, and speaking often makes you more confident.
units.worked_example: In a class discussion about school rules, learners take turns, listen to one another and respond politely in the indigenous language.
units.activity: Hold a small group discussion on a familiar topic such as favourite local foods, making sure everyone speaks.
units.check: Why must we take turns when having a conversation?

quiz.prompt: Why must we take turns when having a conversation?
options: To keep the discussion orderly and respect others

quiz.prompt: What does conversation mean?
options: Taking turns to speak and listen

quiz.prompt: Does using the indigenous language in everyday talk build fluency and confidence?
What does listening closely to your partner help you do?
Is good conversation a skill that improves with practice?

units.title: Culture, food and traditional dress
units.notes: Language is tied closely to culture. Food such as ugali, sukuma wiki, beans and traditional dishes, and clothing worn for ceremonies, carry the identity of a community. Learning their names in the indigenous language helps you understand your heritage. Taking part in cultural events strengthens belonging and pride. Describing these things in the language builds vocabulary. Learning about our culture gives learners pride and a sense of belonging.
units.worked_example: A learner describes a traditional meal and the clothes worn at a family ceremony, naming each item in the indigenous language.
units.activity: Describe in writing or speech one cultural event you have attended, naming the foods and clothes involved.
units.check: Why is learning the names of traditional foods and clothes important?

quiz.prompt: Why is learning the names of traditional foods and clothes important?
options: To help you understand your heritage and build vocabulary

quiz.prompt: What do traditional foods and clothing carry?
Does taking part in cultural events strengthen belonging and pride?
Which of these is a traditional food mentioned in the notes?
Does learning about our culture give learners pride and a sense of belonging?

units.title: Composing and performing short pieces
units.notes: Composing lets you create your own words, such as a short poem, song or speech in the indigenous language. Start with a topic, plan your main points and choose words that fit. Performing your piece helps you practise speaking clearly and with expression. Revising your work improves both meaning and style. Creating original work shows your language skills. Practise your piece several times before performing it for others.
units.worked_example: A learner writes a short speech thanking parents for their care, practises it aloud and delivers it confidently at a school event.
units.activity: Compose a short poem or speech in your indigenous language and perform it for your class.
units.check: What steps can you follow to prepare and perform a short speech well?

quiz.prompt: What steps can you follow to prepare and perform a short speech well?
options: Choose a topic, plan your points and practise

quiz.prompt: What should you do before performing your piece for others?
Does composing let you create your own words, such as a short poem, song or speech?
What does revising your work improve?
Does performing your piece help you practise speaking clearly and with expression?

English.overview: This guide builds English listening, speaking, reading and writing skills for junior secondary learners, moving from basic grammar to confident communication. Each unit offers short notes, a guided example, a practical activity and a self-check question.

units.title: Listening and speaking: polite requests
units.notes: Polite language helps us get help without offending others. In English we often use please, could you, would you mind, or excuse me when asking for something. The tone of your voice matters as much as the words, so speak calmly and clearly. In a Kenyan classroom, a learner may say, Could you please lend me a ruler, instead of the blunt Give me your ruler. Listen carefully to the answer and thank the person whether they agree or not.
units.worked_example: If you need a dictionary from the library, a polite request would be: Excuse me, could I please borrow a dictionary for ten minutes?
units.activity: Work with a partner and take turns making three polite requests for items in your classroom, then change each rude request into a polite one.
units.check: How would you politely ask a classmate to lower their voice during a group discussion?

quiz.prompt: Which phrase is a polite way to ask a classmate to lower their voice during a group discussion?
options: Could you please speak more softly?

quiz.prompt: Using please and a calm tone helps you get help without offending others?
Which of these is mentioned as a polite word used when asking for something?
According to the notes, what should you do after someone answers your polite request?
options: Thank the person whether they agree or not

quiz.prompt: A blunt command like Give me your ruler is the politest way to ask for something?

units.title: Pronunciation and word stress
units.notes: English words are made of syllables, and one syllable usually sounds stronger than the others. Saying a word with the wrong stress can confuse a listener, for example the noun RE-cord and the verb re-CORD. Vowel sounds, consonant sounds and silent letters also affect pronunciation, such as the silent k in knee. Practise by clapping the beats of words and by reading aloud with a partner who corrects you kindly. Good pronunciation makes you easier to understand in class and beyond.
units.worked_example: For the word important, say im-POR-tant, stressing the middle syllable, and for the word photograph, say PHO-to-graph, stressing the first syllable.
units.activity: Choose ten words from your science or Kiswahili lesson, clap their syllables and mark the stressed syllable before reading them aloud to your group.
units.check: Which syllable do you stress when you say the word begin?

quiz.prompt: In the noun RE-cord, which syllable is stressed?
Which word is given as an example of a silent letter?
Saying a word with the wrong stress can confuse a listener?
According to the notes, how can you practise word stress?
options: By writing the word many times
By clapping the beats of words
By copying from a dictionary only

quiz.prompt: The verb re-CORD and the noun RE-cord are pronounced exactly the same way?

units.title: Reading for comprehension: finding the main idea
units.notes: The main idea is the most important point a passage makes about its topic, while supporting details explain or prove it. To find it, ask yourself what the whole paragraph is mainly about, not just what one sentence says. The main idea is often in the first or last sentence, but sometimes you must build it from the details yourself. Skimming the passage quickly first helps you see the general shape before reading closely. With practice you can summarise a whole page in one clear sentence.
units.worked_example: In a passage describing how a farmer in Nakuru plants, waters and harvests maize, the main idea is that the farmer carefully follows steps to grow maize successfully.
units.activity: Read a short newspaper article with a partner, underline the details and write one sentence stating the main idea of the whole article.
units.check: Why is a main idea different from a supporting detail?

quiz.prompt: What is the main idea of a passage?
options: A small detail that proves a point
The most important point the passage makes about its topic
The first word of the passage

quiz.prompt: Supporting details explain or prove the main idea?
According to the notes, where is the main idea often found?
options: In the first or last sentence

quiz.prompt: Why does skimming help before reading closely?
options: It helps you memorise every word
It helps you see the general shape of the passage

quiz.prompt: A supporting detail is the most important point of the whole passage?

units.title: Building vocabulary with context clues
units.notes: You meet new words every day, and you do not always have a dictionary nearby. Context clues are the words and ideas around an unknown word that hint at its meaning. A writer may give a definition, an example, a contrast or a cause-and-effect relationship to help you. For instance, in the river was so shallow, not deep enough for a boat, the word shallow is explained by what follows. Building a personal word bank of new words and using them in your own sentences helps them stick.
units.worked_example: In the sentence Amina was reluctant, or unwilling, to leave the market, the word unwilling tells you that reluctant means not eager.
units.activity: While reading any story, list five unfamiliar words and write the clues from the same paragraph that helped you guess each meaning.
units.check: What does the context tell you when a writer gives an example after a new word?

quiz.prompt: What are context clues?
options: The words and ideas around an unknown word that hint at its meaning

quiz.prompt: In the sentence the river was so shallow, not deep enough for a boat, what explains the word shallow?
A writer may use a definition, an example, a contrast or cause-and-effect to hint at a word's meaning?
According to the notes, what helps new words stick?
options: Keeping a word bank and using the words in your sentences

quiz.prompt: You always have a dictionary nearby when you meet new words?

units.title: Grammar: nouns and pronouns
units.notes: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea, such as teacher, Kisumu, jembe or honesty. Nouns can be common or proper, countable or uncountable, singular or plural. A pronoun replaces a noun so that we do not repeat it, as in Wanjiku lost her pen and she looked for it. Pronouns must agree with the noun they replace in number and gender. Choosing the right pronoun keeps your writing clear and smooth rather than clumsy and repetitive.
units.worked_example: In Musa and Halima went to the shop because they needed sugar, the pronoun they correctly replaces the two names.
units.activity: Write a short paragraph about your family, then underline every noun and replace one repeated noun with a suitable pronoun.
units.check: Which pronoun would you use to replace the noun the girls in a sentence?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a proper noun?
A pronoun replaces a noun so that we do not repeat it?
In Wanjiku lost her pen and she looked for it, what does the pronoun it replace?
Which pronoun would best replace the noun the girls?
Pronouns do not need to agree with the noun they replace?

units.title: Grammar: verbs and verb tenses
units.notes: A verb shows an action, a state or an event, such as run, is or happen. Tense tells when the action happens: past, present or future. The simple past often adds ed for regular verbs, as in walked, but many verbs are irregular, as in go and went. The present tense changes with the subject, so we say she writes but they write. Using tenses consistently makes a story easy to follow, while sudden changes confuse the reader.
units.worked_example: Change I eat ugali every day into the past: I ate ugali yesterday, and into the future: I will eat ugali tomorrow.
units.activity: Write five sentences about what you did last weekend, then rewrite each one in the present and future tense.
units.check: What is the past tense of the verb to buy?

quiz.prompt: What is the past tense of the verb to buy?
Tense tells when an action happens: past, present or future?
Which sentence uses the present tense correctly?
The notes say many verbs are irregular, for example what?
Using tenses consistently makes a story hard to follow?

units.title: Adjectives, adverbs and comparison
units.notes: Adjectives describe nouns and tell us which one, what kind or how many, as in a tall acacia tree. Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives or other adverbs and often tell us how, when or where, as in she ran quickly. Many adverbs are formed by adding ly to an adjective. To compare, short words add er and est, while longer words use more and most. Watch out for irregular forms such as good, better and best.
units.worked_example: Change the adjective fast into comparisons: this matatu is fast, that one is faster, and the third one is the fastest.
units.activity: Describe a favourite meal using at least four adjectives and four adverbs, then underline each one and label it.
units.check: Would you say more beautiful or beautifuler, and why?

quiz.prompt: In a tall acacia tree, which word is the adjective?
How are many adverbs formed?
options: By adding ly to an adjective
By adding ing to a noun
By adding ed to a verb
By adding s to a pronoun

quiz.prompt: Short words usually compare by adding er and est?
Which is the correct way to compare the word beautiful?
The words good, better and best are irregular forms?

units.title: Prepositions, conjunctions and interjections
units.notes: Prepositions show the relationship between a noun and another word, telling us place or time, such as in, on, under, before and after. Conjunctions join words, phrases or clauses, for example and, but, because and although. Interjections express sudden feeling, like Oh, Wow or Alas, and are usually followed by an exclamation mark. Together these small words hold sentences together and show clear relationships between ideas. Using them correctly turns short, choppy sentences into smooth ones.
units.worked_example: Join two ideas: I was tired and I finished my homework become Although I was tired, I finished my homework.
units.activity: Take five separate short sentences from a textbook and join pairs using different conjunctions, reading the results aloud.
units.check: Which conjunction would you use to show a reason instead of a contrast?

quiz.prompt: Which word is an interjection?
Prepositions show the relationship between a noun and another word?
Which conjunction would you use to show a reason?
Which of these words tells us place or time?
Interjections are usually followed by an exclamation mark?

units.title: Sentence structure and punctuation
units.notes: A sentence expresses a complete thought and usually has a subject and a predicate. The subject tells who or what the sentence is about, and the predicate says something about the subject. Sentences may be simple, compound or complex, depending on how many clauses they contain. Punctuation marks such as full stops, commas, question marks and apostrophes guide the reader. A capital letter begins every sentence and every proper noun, so careful punctuation makes your meaning clear.
units.worked_example: Fix the run-on the bell rang we went to class as the bell rang, so we went to class.

units.title: Composition writing: writing a good narrative
units.notes: A narrative tells a story with a beginning, a middle and an end, and usually answers who, what, where, when and why. A strong opening hooks the reader, and the events follow in clear order. Use direct speech, descriptive words and linking words such as then, later and finally to move the story along. Plan your ideas before writing, then check your spelling, punctuation and tenses afterwards. Edit your first draft so your final story is clear and interesting.
units.worked_example: An opening like the rain started just as I stepped out of the school gate instantly makes the reader want to know what happened next.
units.activity: Write a two-paragraph story about a day you helped someone in your community, then read it aloud to a partner for feedback.

units.title: Functional writing: letters, notices and messages
units.notes: Functional writing passes on information for a real purpose, such as letters, notices, messages, invitations and reports. Each form follows a layout, for example a formal letter has your address, the date, the receiver address, a salutation, the body and a closing. A notice is short, clear and read quickly, so it states what, where and when. Always match your language to your audience and purpose. Correct format and neat presentation make your message easy to follow.
units.worked_example: A school notice could read: all Grade Eight learners should report to the hall at 8 a.m. on Friday for a science club meeting, and should bring their notebooks.

units.title: Reading for pleasure: poetry and oral literature
units.notes: Poems and oral literature such as riddles, proverbs and folk tales are meant to be enjoyed and shared. A poem uses lines and stanzas, and often has rhythm and rhyme, plus imagery that helps you picture things. Folk tales carry lessons and values from a community, like the clever hare in many African stories. When reading, notice the sounds of the words, the pictures they create and the message hidden in the story. Enjoying this literature builds your imagination and your language.
units.worked_example: In the proverb a single stick is easily broken but a bundle is strong, the image teaches the value of unity and teamwork.
units.activity: Recite a short poem or tell a folk tale you know to your group, then explain in two sentences the lesson it carries.

units.title: Study skills: note taking and summary writing
units.notes: Good study skills help you learn faster and remember longer. Notes should be short, using your own words, headings and bullet points rather than whole sentences copied from a book. A summary reduces a longer text to its most important ideas, usually in about one third of the original length. Read carefully, pick out key points, then write them briefly and clearly. Reviewing your notes often, and testing yourself, keeps knowledge fresh for examinations and everyday use.
units.worked_example: A page describing the water cycle can be summarised as: water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain and flows back to rivers and the sea.
units.activity: Take a two-page text from any subject, list five key points as notes and then write a summary in no more than four sentences.

Kiswahili.overview: Mwongozo huu hujenga ujuzi wa Kiswahili wa mwanafunzi wa shule ya msingi ya juu katika kusikiliza, kuzungumza, kusoma na kuandika, kutoka misingi hadi ufasaha. Kila somo huwa na notisi fupi, mfano uliofafanuliwa, shughuli ya vitendo na swali la kujipima.

units.title: Kusikiliza na kuzungumza: maamkizi na heshima
units.notes: Maamkizi ni sehemu muhimu ya mazungumzo ya Kiswahili na huonyesha heshima na utu. Tunatumia maneno kama habari yako, shikamoo kwa wakubwa na salama kwa wenzetu. Mtu aliyemsalimia kwa shikamoo hujibiwa marahaba, na aliyemsalimia kwa habari yako hujibiwa salama. Lugha ya heshima pia hutumia tafadhali wakati wa kuomba na asante baada ya kupokea msaada. Kujua lini na jinsi ya kutumia maamkizi huhakikisha mazungumzo yanaenda vizuri.
units.worked_example: Mwanafunzi anapokutana na mwalimu asubuhi, anasema shikamoo mwalimu, na mwalimu hujibu marahaba.
units.activity: Kwa wenzio wawili, fanyeni mazungumzo mafupi ya kuigiza hali ya kumkaribisha mgeni nyumbani kwenu kwa kutumia maamkizi ya heshima.
units.check: Ni neno gani la heshima unalotumia kumwamkua mtu mzima asubuhi?

quiz.prompt: Ni neno gani la heshima unalotumia kumwamkua mtu mzima asubuhi?
Mtu aliyemsalimia kwa shikamoo hujibiwa marahaba?
Mtu anayemsalimia kwa habari yako hujibiwa nini?

units.title: Matamshi na silabi za maneno
units.notes: Silabi ni kipande cha neno kinachotamkwa kwa mpigo mmoja wa sauti, kama vile ma-ji au ki-ta-bu. Kiswahili hufuata muundo wa silabi rahisi, mara nyingi ukikwisha kwa irabu. Matamshi sahihi hutegemea kutamka irabu wazi na kufunga konsonanti ipasavyo, kwa mfano kuna tofauti kati ya mbuzi na mbushi. Mkazo wa sauti huwa kawaida kwenye silabi ya pili kutoka mwisho. Kuzingatia kanuni hizi hufanya usemaji wako uwe wazi na rahisi kueleweka.
units.worked_example: Neno shule lina silabi mbili, shu-le, na mkazo huwa kwenye silabi ya kwanza wakati wa kufundisha matamshi.
units.activity: Andika maneno matano kutoka somo lako, yagawanye katika silabi na kuyasoma kwa sauti mbele ya wenzako.

options: Kipande cha neno kinachotamkwa kwa mpigo mmoja wa sauti

quiz.prompt: Muundo wa silabi za Kiswahili mara nyingi hukwisha kwa nini?

units.title: Kusoma kwa ufahamu: wazo kuu
units.notes: Wazo kuu ni jambo la muhimu zaidi linalozungumzwa katika aya au kifungu. Mazungumzo mengine hutoa maelezo yanayounga mkono wazo hilo kuu. Ili kulipata, jiulize kifungu kizima kinazungumzia nini, si sentensi moja tu. Mara nyingi wazo kuu hupatikana mwanzoni au mwishoni mwa aya, lakini wakati mwingine hulazimu kulijenga kutokana na maelezo. Kusoma kwa haraka kwanza hukusaidia kuona muundo wa kifungu kabla ya kusoma kwa makini.
units.worked_example: Katika kifungu kinachoeleza jinsi mkulima wa Kitale anapanda, anamwagilia na kuvuna mahindi, wazo kuu ni kwamba mkulima hufuata hatua za kukuza mahindi kwa mafanikio.
units.activity: Someni kifungu kifupi kwenye gazeti, tambueni maelezo muhimu kisha andikeni sentensi moja inayotoa wazo kuu.
units.check: Kwa nini wazo kuu hutofautiana na maelezo yanayounga mkono?

units.title: Msamiati, methali na nahau
units.notes: Msamiati ni jumla ya maneno unayoyajua na kuyatumia katika lugha. Methali ni sentensi fupi zenye maana ya kina, kama haraka haraka haina baraka, ambayo hufundisha kuwa na subira. Nahau ni maneno yanayotumiwa kwa maana isiyo ya moja kwa moja, kwa mfano kula chumvi humaanisha kuishi pamoja kwa muda mrefu. Kujua maana na matumizi ya misemo hii hukuza ufasaha wa lugha yako. Tumia methali na nahau ipasavyo kwa muktadha unaofaa.
units.worked_example: Methali umoja ni nguvu, utengano ni udhaifu hutumika kuhimiza ushirikiano katika kazi ya kikundi shuleni.
units.activity: Chagua methali tano unazozijua, andika maana yake na mfano wa sentensi inayoonyesha matumizi yake sahihi.

units.title: Sarufi: nomino na viwakilishi
units.notes: Nomino ni neno linalotaja mtu, mahali, kitu au wazo, kama vile mwalimu, Nakuru, kitabu na upendo. Nomino za Kiswahili hupangwa katika ngeli mbalimbali, na ngeli huamua upatanisho wa sentensi. Kiwakilishi ni neno linalochukua nafasi ya nomino ili kuepuka kurudia jina mara kwa mara, kwa mfano yeye, wao na hilo. Kiwakilishi hupaswa kuafikiana na nomino inayowakilishwa kwa ngeli na idadi. Kutumia nomino na viwakilishi ipasavyo hufanya sentensi zako ziwe safi na wazi.
units.worked_example: Katika sentensi Juma alisoma kitabu kisha akakirudisha, kiwakilishi ki katika akakirudisha kinawakilisha nomino kitabu.
units.activity: Andika aya fupi kuhusu familia yako, kisha tambua nomino zote na kiwakilishi kimoja kilichotumika.

units.title: Sarufi: vitenzi na nyakati
units.notes: Kitenzi ni neno linaloonyesha tendo, hali au tukio, kama vile kusoma, kuwa na kufika. Nyakati huonyesha wakati tendo lilipofanyika: wakati uliopita, uliopo na ujao. Kwa mfano, nilikula ni wakati uliopita, nakula ni wakati uliopo na nitakula ni wakati ujao. Kitenzi hubadilika kwa kuongeza kiambishi cha wakati, na pia huafikiana na mtendaji wa sentensi. Kutumia nyakati ipasavyo hufanya simulizi lako lieleweke bila kuchanganya msomaji.
units.worked_example: Badilisha sentensi ninasoma kitabu kuwa wakati uliopita nilisoma kitabu, na wakati ujao nitasoma kitabu.
units.activity: Andika sentensi tano kuhusu kile ulichofanya jana, kisha uzibadilishe katika wakati uliopo na ujao.

units.title: Vivumishi na vihusishi
units.notes: Kivumishi ni neno linaloeleza nomino kwa kuonyesha hali, rangi, ukubwa au idadi, kama vile nyumba kubwa au mti mrefu. Vivumishi vya Kiswahili mara nyingi huambatana na nomino kwa upatanisho wa ngeli. Kihusishi ni neno linaloonyesha uhusiano kati ya nomino na sehemu nyingine ya sentensi, kama vile katika, juu ya, chini ya na karibu na. Kivumishi husaidia msomaji kuona picha waziwazi, na kihusishi hueleza mahali au wakati. Kutumia vyote viwili ipasavyo huongeza uwazi wa maelezo yako.
units.worked_example: Katika sentensi kitabu kizuri kiko juu ya meza, kizuri ni kivumishi kinachoeleza kitabu, na juu ya ni kihusishi kinachoonyesha mahali.
units.activity: Eleza chumba chako kwa kutumia vivumishi vinne na vihusishi vinne, kisha viweke alama ya aina yake.

units.title: Vielezi na viunganishi
units.notes: Kielezi ni neno linaloeleza kitenzi, kivumishi au kielezi kingine, kama vile haraka, polepole na vizuri. Vielezi hutuambia jinsi, wakati au mahali tendo lilifanyika. Kiunganishi ni neno linalounganisha maneno, vishazi au sentensi, kama vile na, lakini, kwa sababu na ingawa. Viunganishi hutusaidia kuonyesha uhusiano kati ya mawazo, iwe ni nyongeza, upinzani au sababu. Kutumia vielezi na viunganishi vizuri hufanya lugha yako itiririke kwa utondoti na mpangilio mzuri.
units.worked_example: Unganisha mawazo mawili, nilikuwa nimechoka na nilimaliza kazi yangu, kuwa ingawa nilikuwa nimechoka, nilimaliza kazi yangu.
units.activity: Chukua sentensi tano fupi na uzichanganye kwa kutumia viunganishi mbalimbali, kisha uzisome kwa wenzako.

units.title: Mpangilio wa sentensi na alama za uakifishaji
units.notes: Sentensi ni kundi la maneno yanayotoa maana kamili, na mara nyingi huwa na mtendaji na kiarifu. Sentensi inaweza kuwa rahisi, ambatani au changamani kutegemea idadi ya vishazi. Alama za uakifishaji kama kikomo, koma, alama ya kuuliza na alama ya mshangao huelekeza msomaji jinsi ya kusoma. Herufi kubwa hutumika mwanzoni mwa sentensi na kwa majina ya pekee. Uakifishaji sahihi huweka maana wazi na huepusha mkanganyiko katika maandishi yako.
units.worked_example: Rekebisha sentensi isiyo na kikomo kengele ililia twende darasani kuwa kengele ililia, kwa hivyo twende darasani.
units.activity: Nakili aya moja kutoka kitabu chako cha Kiswahili na uongeze herufi kubwa na alama za uakifishaji zinazostahili.

units.title: Insha ya masimulizi
units.notes: Insha ya masimulizi husimulia tukio au kisa kwa mfululizo wa mwanzo, kati na mwisho. Insha nzuri hujibu maswali ya nani, nini, wapi, lini na kwa nini. Mwanzo mzuri huvutia msomaji, na matukio hufuata kwa mpangilio unaoeleweka. Tumia usemi wa moja kwa moja, maneno ya kueleza na viunganishi kama kisha, baadaye na mwishowe kusukuma simulizi mbele. Panga mawazo yako kabla ya kuandika, kisha hakiki tahajia, uakifishaji na nyakati baada ya kuandika rasimu yako.
units.worked_example: Mwanzo kama mvua ilianza kunyesha nilipokuwa nikitoka shuleni humfanya msomaji atake kujua kilichofuata.
units.activity: Andika insha ya masimulizi ya aya mbili kuhusu siku ulipomsaidia mtu mmoja jamii yako, kisha uisome kwa mwenzako.

units.title: Uandishi wa kazi: barua, tangazo na ujumbe
units.notes: Uandishi wa kazi huwasilisha taarifa kwa madhumuni halisi, kama barua, tangazo, ujumbe, mwaliko na ripoti. Kila aina ina mpangilio wake; kwa mfano barua rasmi huwa na anwani yako, tarehe, anwani ya mpokeaji, salamu, mwili wa barua na kumalizia. Tangazo huwa fupi, wazi na hueleweka haraka, hivyo hutaja nini, wapi na lini. Lugha yako hupaswa kuendana na msomaji na kusudi lako. Mpangilio sahihi na uandishi nadhifu hufanya ujumbe wako ueleweke kwa urahisi.
units.worked_example: Tangazo la shule linaweza kusema: wanafunzi wote wa Gredi ya Nane wakutane katika ukumbi saa mbili asubuhi Ijumaa kwa mkutano wa klabu ya sayansi, na walete madaftari yao.
units.activity: Andika barua rasmi fupi kwa mwalimu wako mkuu ukiomba ruhusa ya kujiunga na klabu mpya, kwa kutumia mpangilio sahihi.

units.title: Fasihi: hadithi na mashairi
units.notes: Fasihi ni sanaa ya kutumia lugha kusimulia, kuimbia na kufundisha. Hadithi za wazee na ngano hubeba maadili na malezi ya jamii, kama vile ujanja wa sungura katika hadithi nyingi za Kiafrika. Shairi hupangwa kwa mistari na beti, na mara nyingi huwa na mizani pamoja na urari unaoleta mdundo mzuri. Unaposoma, angalia sauti za maneno, picha zinazojitokeza na ujumbe uliofichika. Kupenda na kufurahia fasihi hukuza ubunifu wako na utajiri wa lugha yako.

units.title: Ufupisho na stadi za kujifunza
units.notes: Stadi nzuri za kujifunza hukusaidia kujifunza haraka na kukumbuka kwa muda mrefu. Notisi zako zipaswe kuwa fupi, zikitumia maneno yako mwenyewe, vichwa vya habari na alama za vitone badala ya kunakili sentensi zote. Ufupisho hupunguza maandishi marefu kwa kuweka mawazo ya muhimu zaidi, kwa kawaida katika theluthi moja ya ukubwa wa awali. Soma kwa makini, chagua hoja muhimu, kisha ziandike kwa ufupi na wazi. Kurudia notisi zako mara kwa mara na kujipima hukuweka maarifa kuwa mapya kwa mitihani na maishani.
