Mathematics.overview: This guide develops number, algebra, measurement, geometry and statistics skills for junior secondary learners, building from careful number work towards problem solving. Each unit gives short notes, a worked example, a practical activity and a self-check question.

units.title: Whole numbers and place value
units.notes: Whole numbers are the counting numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on, with no fractions or decimals. The value of a digit depends on its place, such as ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. In 47 382, the 4 is worth 40 000 because it is in the ten-thousands place. Numbers can be written in words, in figures or in expanded form, for example 6 000 plus 400 plus 50 plus 7. We also round numbers to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand to make estimates easier and quicker.
units.worked_example: In the number 58 406, the digit 8 stands for 8 000, and the number in expanded form is 50 000 plus 8 000 plus 400 plus 0 plus 6.
units.activity: Find five large numbers from a newspaper, write each in words and in expanded form, then round each to the nearest thousand.
units.check: What is the place value of the digit 7 in the number 372 509?

quiz.prompt: What is the place value of the digit 7 in the number 372 509?
In the number 47 382, the 4 is worth 40 000?
Whole numbers are what?
options: the counting numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on

quiz.prompt: Which is the expanded form of 6 457?
We round numbers to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand to make estimates easier?

units.title: Factors, multiples and divisibility
units.notes: A factor divides a number exactly without leaving a remainder, while a multiple is the result of multiplying a number by a whole number. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, while the multiples of 12 include 12, 24 and 36. The highest common factor is the largest factor shared by two or more numbers, and the lowest common multiple is the smallest multiple they share. Divisibility rules help us test quickly whether one number divides another, for example a number ending in 0 or 5 is divisible by 5.
units.worked_example: For 18 and 24, the common factors give a highest common factor of 6, and the multiples give a lowest common multiple of 72.
units.activity: List the factors of 24 and 36, find their highest common factor and lowest common multiple, then test whether 1 245 is divisible by 3 and 5.
units.check: How can you tell quickly whether a large number is divisible by 10?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a factor of 12?
A number ending in 0 or 5 is divisible by 5?
The highest common factor is what?
options: the largest factor shared by two or more numbers

quiz.prompt: Which list shows multiples of 12?
A factor divides a number exactly without leaving a remainder?

units.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
units.notes: A fraction shows parts of a whole, written as a numerator over a denominator, such as three quarters. A decimal uses place value after the point, for instance 0.75, and a percentage is a fraction out of one hundred, like 75 per cent. These three forms can describe the same amount, so you can change one into another. To change a fraction to a percentage, multiply by one hundred; to change a decimal to a percentage, multiply by one hundred also. Recognising equal values helps in shopping and in sharing things fairly.
units.worked_example: Three quarters equals 0.75, which equals 75 per cent, so a shop selling at three quarters of the price charges 75 per cent of the original amount.
units.activity: Take a sheet of paper, fold it into equal parts, shade some parts, and write the shaded amount as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
units.check: What is 0.4 written as a fraction in its simplest form?

quiz.prompt: What is 0.4 written as a fraction in its simplest form?
A percentage is a fraction out of one hundred?
To change a fraction to a percentage, you do what?
Three quarters, 0.75 and 75 per cent all describe what?
Recognising equal values helps in shopping and sharing things fairly?

units.title: Operations on fractions and decimals
units.notes: To add or subtract fractions, first change them to have the same denominator, then work with the numerators. Multiplication of fractions is simpler because you multiply numerators together and denominators together. In division, you multiply by the reciprocal, that is, turn the second fraction upside down. For decimals, line up the decimal points when adding or subtracting, and count the decimal places when multiplying. Always simplify your final answer and check whether it is reasonable.
units.worked_example: To add one half and one third, use sixths: three sixths plus two sixths equals five sixths, and to divide one half by one quarter, multiply one half by four, giving two.
units.activity: Work out five problems mixing fractions and decimals, such as adding 2.5 to three quarters, and compare your answers with a partner.
units.check: When adding 0.7 and 0.25, where should you place the decimal point in the answer?

quiz.prompt: When adding fractions with different denominators, you first do what?
options: change them to have the same denominator

quiz.prompt: To divide by a fraction you multiply by its reciprocal?
Multiplication of fractions is done by what?
options: multiplying numerators together and denominators together

quiz.prompt: When adding decimals like 0.7 and 0.25, you should do what?
After working with fractions you should always simplify your answer?

units.title: Integers and the number line
units.notes: Integers include positive numbers, negative numbers and zero, and are shown on the number line with zero in the middle. Negative numbers are used in real life to show temperatures below zero, debts and positions below sea level, such as an account showing minus 500 shillings. Adding a positive integer moves you to the right, while adding a negative integer moves you to the left. Subtracting a negative is the same as adding its positive. The number line makes these rules easy to see and apply.
units.worked_example: Starting at negative three on the number line and adding positive five lands on positive two, so minus three plus five equals two.
units.activity: Draw a number line from minus ten to ten and use it to work out five sums involving negative numbers, such as minus four plus seven.
units.check: What do you get when you subtract negative six from positive two?

quiz.prompt: What do you get when you subtract negative six from positive two?
Adding a negative integer moves you to the left on the number line?
Subtracting a negative is the same as doing what?
Integers include which numbers?
options: positive numbers, negative numbers and zero

quiz.prompt: Negative numbers can show temperatures below zero and debts?

units.title: Ratio, proportion and rates
units.notes: A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind, such as 3 boys to 5 girls, which we write as three to five. When two ratios are equal they form a proportion, and we can find a missing value by solving. A rate compares quantities of different kinds, like kilometres per hour or shillings per kilogram. Dividing a quantity in a given ratio means sharing it fairly according to the parts. These ideas help in cooking, mixing, scaling maps and sharing money or harvests fairly.
units.worked_example: To share 600 shillings between two friends in the ratio two to three, the parts total five, so each part is 120 shillings, giving 240 shillings and 360 shillings.
units.activity: Share 900 shillings among three learners in the ratio one to two to three, then explain how you checked that your answer was correct.
units.check: If a car travels 240 kilometres in 4 hours, what is its average speed per hour?

quiz.prompt: If a car travels 240 kilometres in 4 hours, what is its average speed?
A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind?
A rate compares quantities of what?
When two ratios are equal they form what?
Dividing a quantity in a given ratio means sharing it fairly according to the parts?

units.title: Algebraic expressions and simplification
units.notes: Algebra uses letters to stand for unknown or changing numbers, so a letter like x can represent any number. An expression such as 3x plus 5 combines terms, and like terms have the same letter part and can be collected together. We simplify by adding or subtracting like terms, for example 4a plus 2a becomes 6a. Substitution means replacing a letter with a given number and working out the value. Remember that 3x means 3 multiplied by x, not 3 plus x.
units.worked_example: Simplify 5p plus 3q plus 2p minus q to get 7p plus 2q, then find its value when p is 2 and q is 1, which equals 16.
units.activity: Write expressions for real situations, such as the cost of x exercise books at 50 shillings each, and simplify three mixed expressions.
units.check: What is the value of 4y plus 3 when y equals 5?

quiz.prompt: What is the value of 4y plus 3 when y equals 5?
3x means 3 multiplied by x?
Which of these is the correct simplification of 4a plus 2a?
Substitution means what?
options: replacing a letter with a given number and working out the value

quiz.prompt: Like terms have the same letter part and can be collected together?

units.title: Linear equations and inequalities
units.notes: An equation says that two expressions are equal, and solving it means finding the value of the unknown that makes it true. We keep the equation balanced by doing the same operation to both sides, for example adding, subtracting, multiplying or dividing. In 2x plus 3 equals 11, first subtract 3 to get 2x equals 8, then divide by 2 to get x equals 4. An inequality uses signs like greater than or less than instead of an equals sign and gives a range of answers. Always check your solution by putting it back into the original statement.
units.worked_example: Solve 3x minus 4 equals 14 by adding 4 to both sides to get 3x equals 18, then dividing by 3 to get x equals 6.
units.activity: Form and solve three simple equations from word problems, then check each answer by substituting it back into the equation.
units.check: What is the value of x if 5x equals 45?

quiz.prompt: What is the value of x if 5x equals 45?
An inequality gives a range of answers?
To solve an equation you must keep it what?
options: balanced by doing the same operation to both sides

quiz.prompt: In 2x plus 3 equals 11, what is the first step?
You should check your solution by putting it back into the original statement?

units.title: Measurement of length, area and perimeter
units.notes: Perimeter is the distance around a shape, found by adding the lengths of all its sides, while area is the space it covers, measured in square units. Common units of length are millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres, and we convert between them by multiplying or dividing by ten, one hundred or one thousand. The area of a rectangle is length times width, and the area of a triangle is half the base times the height. Units must be consistent before calculating, or your answer will be wrong.
units.worked_example: A rectangular shamba 8 metres long and 5 metres wide has an area of 8 times 5, which is 40 square metres, and a perimeter of 26 metres.
units.activity: Measure the length and width of your classroom with a tape measure and calculate its perimeter and area in metres and square metres.
units.check: What is the area of a triangle with a base of 10 centimetres and a height of 6 centimetres?

quiz.prompt: What is the area of a triangle with a base of 10 centimetres and a height of 6 centimetres?
Perimeter is the distance around a shape?
The area of a rectangle is what?
The area of a triangle is what?
options: half the base times the height

quiz.prompt: Units must be consistent before calculating?

units.title: Volume and surface area of solids
units.notes: Volume is the amount of space a solid occupies, measured in cubic units, while surface area is the total area of all its faces. A cuboid with length, width and height has volume equal to length times width times height. A cube has all edges equal, so its volume is the cube of one edge and its surface area is six times the square of the edge. A cylinder volume is the area of its circular base times its height, using pi as approximately three point one four. These ideas are used when filling tanks, buying boxes and painting walls.
units.worked_example: A water tank shaped as a cuboid 2 metres long, 1 metre wide and 1.5 metres high has a volume of 3 cubic metres, which is 3 000 litres.
units.activity: Find a rectangular tin or box at home, measure its dimensions in centimetres and calculate its volume and surface area.
units.check: What is the volume of a cube whose edge is 4 centimetres long?

quiz.prompt: What is the volume of a cube whose edge is 4 centimetres long?
The volume of a cuboid is length times width times height?
Surface area is what?
options: the total area of all the faces of a solid
the amount of space inside a solid

quiz.prompt: The surface area of a cube is what?
options: six times the square of the edge

quiz.prompt: The volume of a cylinder is the area of its circular base times its height?

units.title: Geometry: angles, lines and polygons
units.notes: An angle is formed where two lines meet and is measured in degrees. Angles can be acute, right, obtuse, straight or reflex, and two angles adding to 90 degrees are complementary while those adding to 180 degrees are supplementary. Parallel lines never meet, and a transversal creates equal and co-interior angles that help us find unknown values. A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides, and the angles inside a triangle always add up to 180 degrees. These rules help in construction, drawing and design.
units.worked_example: In a triangle with angles of 65 degrees and 55 degrees, the third angle is 180 minus 120, which equals 60 degrees.
units.activity: Draw five different angles with a protractor, measure them and label each as acute, right, obtuse or reflex.
units.check: What do the three interior angles of any triangle add up to?

quiz.prompt: What do the three interior angles of any triangle add up to?
Two angles adding to 90 degrees are complementary?
Angles that add to 180 degrees are called what?
An angle that is greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees is what?
Parallel lines never meet?

units.title: Statistics: collecting and presenting data
units.notes: Statistics is the study of collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting data to answer questions. Data may be collected by counting, measuring, asking questions or observing, such as recording the number of learners who walk to school. We organise data in frequency tables and display it using bar graphs, pictograms, line graphs and pie charts. The mean, or average, is found by adding all values and dividing by how many there are, while the mode is the most common value and the median is the middle one. Choosing a clear graph helps others see the story in the numbers.
units.worked_example: For the scores 4, 6, 6, 8 and 10, the mean is 34 divided by 5, which is 6.8, the mode is 6 and the median is also 6.
units.activity: Collect data from your class on favourite foods, make a frequency table and draw a neat bar graph, then find the mode.
units.check: How do you calculate the mean of five given numbers?

quiz.prompt: How do you calculate the mean of five given numbers?
options: Add all values and divide by five

quiz.prompt: The mode is the most common value?
The median is what?
Which of these is a way of displaying data mentioned in the notes?
Statistics is the study of collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting data?

units.title: Money, profit, loss and simple interest
units.notes: Money in Kenya is the shilling, written as KSh, and business uses buying price, selling price, profit and loss. Profit is the selling price minus the buying price when you sell for more, while loss is the buying price minus the selling price when you sell for less. Percentage profit or loss compares the profit or loss to the buying price. Simple interest is calculated as principal times rate times time, divided by one hundred, and is paid on savings or loans. These ideas help you budget and make wise decisions with money.
units.worked_example: A trader buys a bag of maize for 3 000 shillings and sells it for 3 450 shillings, making a profit of 450 shillings, which is 15 per cent of the buying price.
units.activity: Visit a nearby shop and record the buying and selling prices of three items, then calculate the profit or loss on each and its percentage.
units.check: How much simple interest do you earn on 5 000 shillings at 10 per cent per year for 2 years?

quiz.prompt: How much simple interest do you earn on 5 000 shillings at 10 per cent per year for 2 years?
Profit is the selling price minus the buying price when you sell for more?
Loss happens when what?
options: you sell for more than the buying price
you sell for less than the buying price

quiz.prompt: Money in Kenya is the shilling, written as what?
Simple interest is calculated as principal times rate times time, divided by one hundred?

Integrated Science.overview: This guide introduces junior secondary learners to integrated science, bringing together basic biology, chemistry and physics through practical investigations. Each unit provides short notes, a worked example, a hands-on activity and a self-check question.

units.title: Introduction to integrated science and laboratory safety
units.notes: Integrated science studies living things, matter and energy, showing how biology, chemistry and physics connect. Scientists work by observing, asking questions, forming hypotheses, experimenting, recording results and drawing conclusions. A school laboratory holds apparatus such as beakers, test tubes and burners, which must be handled carefully. Safety rules include tying back long hair, never tasting chemicals, wearing goggles, and reporting spills to the teacher at once. Working carefully protects both you and your classmates during investigations.
units.worked_example: To test whether a plant needs light, a learner places one bean seedling in a cupboard and another on a windowsill, waters both equally and compares their growth after a week.
units.activity: In groups, list ten safety rules for your science room, make a poster of them and show where the first aid kit and fire blanket are kept.
units.check: What should you do first if you break a glass beaker during an experiment?

quiz.prompt: What should you do first if you break a glass beaker during an experiment?
options: Pick it up with bare hands
Report the spill to the teacher at once

quiz.prompt: Integrated science shows how biology, chemistry and physics connect?
Which of these is a safety rule in the laboratory?
The steps scientists use include observing, asking questions, forming hypotheses and what else?
You may taste chemicals in the laboratory if they look harmless?

units.title: Living things and their classification
units.notes: Living things grow, feed, respire, excrete, move, reproduce and respond to their surroundings. To study the millions of species, scientists group them by shared features into large groups called kingdoms. Plants make their own food using sunlight, while animals feed on other organisms. Animals are further grouped into vertebrates with backbones, such as fish, birds and mammals, and invertebrates without backbones, such as insects and worms. Classifying makes it easier to identify organisms and to understand how they are related.
units.worked_example: A cow, a tilapia and a dove are all vertebrates, but the cow belongs to mammals, the tilapia to fish, and the dove to birds because of its feathers.
units.activity: Collect or draw ten organisms from your school compound, then sort them into groups using observable features and explain your groupings.
units.check: Which feature separates invertebrates from vertebrates?

quiz.prompt: Which feature separates invertebrates from vertebrates?
Living things grow, feed, respire, excrete, move, reproduce and respond to their surroundings?
Which of these groups has a backbone?
Animals without a backbone are called what?
Plants make their own food using sunlight?

units.title: Cells as the basic unit of life
units.notes: The cell is the smallest unit of a living thing and can carry out all life processes. Most cells can only be seen under a microscope, and a group of similar cells forms a tissue, tissues form organs, and organs form systems. A plant cell has a cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts, which an animal cell lacks. Both types have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus that controls activities. Understanding cells explains how living things grow and repair themselves.
units.worked_example: Looking at an onion skin under a microscope, you can see brick-like plant cells with clear cell walls, while a cheek smear shows rounded animal cells without walls.
units.activity: Draw and label a plant cell and an animal cell side by side, then list three differences between them.
units.check: Which part of a plant cell traps sunlight for making food?

quiz.prompt: Which part of a plant cell traps sunlight for making food?
A group of similar cells forms a tissue?
Which of these is found in a plant cell but NOT an animal cell?
The part that controls the activities of the cell is what?
The cell is the smallest unit of a living thing?

units.title: Human body systems and their functions
units.notes: The human body is organised into systems that work together to keep us alive and healthy. The digestive system breaks food into nutrients that the body absorbs, the circulatory system carries blood, oxygen and nutrients, and the respiratory system takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. The excretory system removes waste such as urine, and the nervous system carries messages and controls responses. Exercise, a balanced diet and enough water keep these systems working well. Each organ has a special job that supports the whole body.
units.worked_example: When you run, your breathing and heart rate increase so that the respiratory and circulatory systems deliver more oxygen to your muscles.
units.activity: Measure your pulse rate while resting and again after one minute of star jumps, then explain the difference using body systems.
units.check: Which body system is mainly responsible for taking in oxygen?

quiz.prompt: Which body system is mainly responsible for taking in oxygen?
The digestive system breaks food into nutrients the body absorbs?
Which system removes waste such as urine?
The system that carries blood, oxygen and nutrients is the what?
Each organ has a special job that supports the whole body?

units.title: Nutrition and a balanced diet
units.notes: A balanced diet contains carbohydrates for energy, proteins for growth and repair, fats for warmth and storage, vitamins and minerals for health, water and roughage for digestion. Common Kenyan foods include ugali, rice, ndengu, sukuma wiki, eggs, fish and fruits such as mangoes and bananas. Deficiency diseases result from missing nutrients, for example kwashiorkor from lack of protein and scurvy from lack of vitamin C. Eating a variety of foods in the right amounts prevents these problems and keeps the body strong. Safe handling and cooking of food also prevent illness.
units.worked_example: A balanced lunch might be ugali, sukuma wiki, ndengu and a banana, which together provide energy, vitamins, protein and roughage.
units.activity: Plan a one-day balanced menu for a Kenyan family using local foods, and label each food with the nutrient it mainly provides.
units.check: Which nutrient prevents the deficiency disease scurvy?

quiz.prompt: Which nutrient prevents the deficiency disease scurvy?
Kwashiorkor results from a lack of protein?
Carbohydrates are needed mainly for what?
Which of these is a common Kenyan food mentioned in the notes?
Roughage and water help in digestion?

units.title: Health, hygiene and common diseases
units.notes: Good health is more than the absence of disease; it includes physical, mental and social well-being. Many diseases spread through dirty water, poor food handling, coughing and contact with germs, so handwashing with soap, safe drinking water and clean surroundings reduce risk. Common illnesses include malaria, spread by the anopheles mosquito, and typhoid, spread by contaminated food. Vaccination and sleeping under treated mosquito nets protect families from some infections. Knowing how diseases spread helps us prevent them before they start.
units.worked_example: Because malaria is spread by mosquitoes that breed in stagnant water, clearing old tins and draining puddles around the home reduces malaria cases.
units.activity: Draw and label the stages of the malaria parasite life cycle, then list four ways your family can prevent mosquito bites.
units.check: Which two simple habits best prevent the spread of germs through food?

quiz.prompt: Malaria is spread by what?
Handwashing with soap reduces the risk of disease?
Which two habits best prevent the spread of germs through food?
options: Handwashing with soap and clean surroundings

quiz.prompt: Typhoid is spread by what?
Good health includes physical, mental and social well-being?

units.title: Matter, its states and changes
units.notes: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space, and it exists as solids, liquids and gases. In a solid the particles are packed closely and only vibrate, in a liquid they are close but can slide, and in a gas they move freely and far apart. Matter changes state when heated or cooled: melting, boiling, evaporation, freezing, condensation and sublimation. These changes in state are physical changes because no new substance forms. Heating and cooling therefore explain many everyday events such as drying clothes and making ice.
units.worked_example: When water is heated to 100 degrees Celsius it boils and turns to steam, and when the steam cools it condenses back to liquid water on a cold surface.
units.activity: Place an ice cube in a covered glass and observe it over ten minutes, drawing and labelling the changes of state you notice.
units.check: What is the change of state called when a gas turns into a liquid?

quiz.prompt: What is the change of state called when a gas turns into a liquid?
In a solid the particles are packed closely and only vibrate?
Melting, boiling, freezing and condensation are examples of what?
In a gas, particles do what?
Changes in state form new substances?

units.title: Mixtures, solutions and separation techniques
units.notes: A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined, such as sand and water or salt and water. A solution forms when a solute dissolves in a solvent, for example salt in water, and if no more will dissolve the solution is saturated. Mixtures can be separated using physical methods, including filtration, evaporation, decantation, sieving and magnetism. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, and evaporation recovers a dissolved solid. These techniques are used in treating water, mining and preparing food.
units.worked_example: To obtain clean salt from salty water, filter the mixture first, then evaporate the water slowly, leaving white salt crystals behind.
units.activity: Mix salt with water and sand, then use filtration and evaporation to separate all three components and explain each step.
units.check: Which separation method would you use to remove iron filings from sand?

quiz.prompt: Which separation method would you use to remove iron filings from sand?
A solution forms when a solute dissolves in a solvent?
Filtration separates what?
options: a dissolved solid from a liquid
an insoluble solid from a liquid

quiz.prompt: Which method recovers a dissolved solid from its solution?
A mixture contains substances that are chemically joined?

units.title: Acids, bases and indicators
units.notes: Acids have a sour taste and turn blue litmus paper red, while bases have a bitter taste, feel slippery and turn red litmus paper blue. Common acids include lemon juice, vinegar and car battery acid, and common bases include soap, baking soda and wood ash. An indicator such as litmus, methyl orange or red cabbage water is used to test whether a substance is acidic or basic. When an acid reacts with a base, neutralisation occurs and a salt and water are formed. Understanding this helps us handle household chemicals safely.
units.worked_example: When red litmus paper is dipped into soap solution it turns blue, showing the soap is a base, but in lemon juice it stays red, showing the juice is an acid.
units.activity: Test samples such as lemon juice, soap water, milk and soda with red cabbage indicator and record whether each is acidic, basic or neutral.
units.check: What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acid?

quiz.prompt: What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acid?
Bases have a bitter taste and feel slippery?
Which of these is a common base?
When an acid reacts with a base, the reaction is called what?
Acids turn red litmus paper blue?

units.title: Force, pressure and simple machines
units.notes: A force is a push or a pull that can change an object shape, speed or direction, and it is measured in newtons. Common forces include gravity, friction, magnetic force and upthrust, and gravity pulls objects towards the earth. Pressure is force acting on a given area, and it is greater when the same force acts on a smaller area. Simple machines such as the lever, pulley, inclined plane and wheel make work easier by increasing force or changing its direction. Friction can be reduced using oil or rollers.
units.worked_example: Sharpening a jembe reduces the area of its edge, so the same push produces greater pressure and cuts the soil more easily.
units.activity: Use a ruler and a pencil as a lever to lift a book, then compare the effort needed when you move the pivot closer to or further from the book.
units.check: Why does a wide flat shoe sink less in soft mud than a narrow heel?

quiz.prompt: Why does a wide flat shoe sink less in soft mud than a narrow heel?
options: It spreads the force over a larger area

quiz.prompt: Force is measured in newtons?
Pressure is greater when the same force acts on what?
Which of these is a simple machine?
Friction can be reduced using oil or rollers?

units.title: Energy, work and its transformations
units.notes: Energy is the ability to do work, and it exists in forms such as chemical, heat, light, sound, electrical, kinetic and potential energy. Energy can change from one form to another but cannot be created or destroyed, which is called the law of conservation of energy. In a torch, chemical energy from the cell changes to electrical energy, then to light and heat energy. Work is done when a force moves an object over a distance, and it is measured in joules. Using energy wisely helps conserve resources and reduce costs.
units.worked_example: In a charcoal jiko, chemical energy stored in the charcoal changes to heat energy, which cooks food, showing a useful energy transformation.
units.activity: Trace the energy changes in three devices such as a torch, a radio and a bicycle, drawing arrows to show each transformation.
units.check: What energy change happens in a solar cell when sunlight shines on it?

quiz.prompt: What energy change happens in a solar cell when sunlight shines on it?
Energy can be changed from one form to another but cannot be created or destroyed?
In a torch, chemical energy from the cell changes to electrical energy, then to what?
Work is done when what happens?
options: a force moves an object over a distance

quiz.prompt: Work is measured in joules?

units.title: Electricity and magnetism
units.notes: Electricity is a form of energy carried by electric charges and is useful in lighting, heating and running machines. A simple circuit needs a source such as a dry cell, connecting wires, and a component like a bulb, all joined in a complete loop. A switch controls the circuit by opening or closing it, and conductors such as copper allow current to pass while insulators such as rubber do not. Magnets attract iron and steel and have two poles, north and south, that attract or repel each other. Electromagnets are made by passing current through a coil around an iron core.
units.worked_example: When a wire carrying current is coiled around an iron nail, the nail becomes an electromagnet that can pick up small pins, and the magnetism stops when the current is switched off.
units.activity: Build a simple circuit with a cell, a bulb and a switch, then test which materials around you conduct electricity and which do not.
units.check: Why does a bulb fail to light when the switch is open?

quiz.prompt: Why does a bulb fail to light when the switch is open?
options: The circuit is broken so current cannot flow

quiz.prompt: Conductors such as copper allow current to pass?
Which of these is an insulator?
A magnet has how many poles?
A simple circuit needs a source, connecting wires and a component joined in a complete loop?

units.title: Environment, ecosystems and conservation
units.notes: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings such as soil, water and air. Energy flows through an ecosystem from the sun to plants, then to herbivores and finally to carnivores, forming food chains and food webs. Human activities such as deforestation, pollution, overgrazing and poor waste disposal damage these systems. Conservation measures include planting trees, protecting water sources, recycling and using energy efficiently. Keeping the environment healthy protects the air, water and soil that all life depends on.
units.worked_example: In a grassland food chain, grass is eaten by a zebra, which is eaten by a lion, so if the grass is overgrazed, both the zebra and lion populations fall.
units.activity: Draw a food web with at least six organisms from your local area, then suggest three ways people can conserve that ecosystem.
units.check: What happens to the energy stored in dead plants and animals when decomposers act on them?

quiz.prompt: What happens to the energy stored in dead plants and animals when decomposers act on them?
options: It is released and recycled in the ecosystem

quiz.prompt: Energy flows through an ecosystem from the sun to plants, then to herbivores and finally to carnivores?
Which human activity damages ecosystems?
Conservation measures include what?
An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with their non-living surroundings?

Health Education.overview: This guide covers personal health, nutrition, disease prevention, first aid and mental wellbeing for junior secondary learners. Each unit gives clear notes, a worked example, a practical activity and a self-check question.

units.title: Personal hygiene and cleanliness
units.notes: Personal hygiene means keeping your body, clothes and surroundings clean every day to stay healthy. Bathing regularly, brushing teeth twice a day and washing hands with soap remove dirt and germs. Clean fingernails, well-combed hair and fresh uniforms help you feel confident at school. Hygiene also protects people around you because germs spread easily in crowded places. Good habits started now prevent skin infections, tooth decay and stomach illnesses later in life.
units.worked_example: If you play football at break and then eat lunch, wash your hands with soap and running water for at least twenty seconds before touching food because sweat and soil carry germs.

units.title: Nutrition and a balanced diet
units.notes: A balanced diet gives the body the right amounts of carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fats and water. Carbohydrates such as ugali, rice and ndengu give energy, while proteins like beans, eggs and fish build and repair the body. Fruits and vegetables supply vitamins that protect against disease. Eating many different foods each day, rather than one favourite dish, keeps the body strong. Too much sugar and fried food can lead to weight gain and poor health.
units.worked_example: A plate with ugali, sukuma wiki, beans and a banana gives energy, vitamins and protein, making it a better lunch than chips alone.

units.title: Meal planning with local foods
units.notes: Meal planning means choosing what to eat for each meal in advance so that the family eats well and spends wisely. A good plan uses foods that are in season and available in the local market, such as maize, sweet potatoes, kales and avocado. Planning saves money, reduces waste and saves the time used to decide at the last minute. It also helps include all food groups across the day. Families can grow some vegetables in a kitchen garden to lower costs further.
units.worked_example: For a family of four, a Monday plan could be ugali and managu for lunch, then rice, ndengu and fruit for supper, using vegetables bought at the weekly market.

units.title: Safe water and food handling
units.notes: Safe water is free from germs and harmful chemicals, and it is needed for drinking, cooking and washing. Water from rivers, wells and taps should be boiled, filtered or treated before drinking. Food must be handled with clean hands, stored covered and kept away from flies and dust. Raw and cooked foods should be separated to stop germs spreading. Proper handwashing and clean utensils prevent diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
units.worked_example: If your home stores drinking water in a jerrican, boil the water first, let it cool, then pour it into a clean covered container with a tap or ladle.

units.title: Communicable disease prevention
units.notes: Communicable diseases spread from one person to another through air, water, food, insects or direct contact. Common examples in Kenya include malaria, tuberculosis, cholera, flu and HIV. Simple habits such as covering the mouth when coughing, sleeping under a treated net and washing hands break the chain of infection. Keeping the environment clean removes breeding places for mosquitoes and flies. Vaccination, early treatment and staying home when sick also protect the community.
units.worked_example: If a classmate has flu and keeps coughing, ask them to cover the cough with an elbow, open windows for fresh air and avoid sharing cups.
units.activity: Draw a chart showing three ways diseases spread and one preventive action for each, then display it in class.

units.title: Immunisation and health services
units.notes: Immunisation protects a person from serious diseases by giving a vaccine that helps the body build defences. In Kenya, children receive free vaccines at health centres and during immunisation campaigns. Vaccines prevent illnesses such as measles, polio, tetanus and whooping cough. A complete immunisation schedule keeps the whole community safe from outbreaks. Health services, including clinics and community health workers, support families with advice, treatment and referrals.
units.worked_example: A baby taken to the clinic at six weeks receives the first dose of polio drops on the schedule, and the mother is given a card recording the next visit.

units.title: Non-communicable diseases and lifestyle
units.notes: Non-communicable diseases are long-term conditions that do not spread from person to person. They include diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, asthma and some cancers. Unhealthy habits such as eating too much sugar, smoking, drinking alcohol and sitting for long hours raise the risk. Regular exercise, a balanced diet, enough sleep and avoiding tobacco keep the body healthy. Many of these diseases can be prevented or controlled through good daily choices.
units.worked_example: A person who walks for thirty minutes daily and swaps sugary sodas for water lowers their risk of diabetes and high blood pressure.
units.activity: Track your physical activity for three days and suggest one change that would make it healthier.

units.title: First aid basics
units.notes: First aid is the immediate help given to a sick or injured person before professional treatment. It aims to save life, prevent the condition getting worse and promote recovery. A first aid kit should contain clean gloves, bandages, cotton wool, antiseptic, scissors and a list of emergency numbers. Before helping, check that the scene is safe and call for an adult or emergency services. Do not move a seriously injured person unless there is danger.
units.worked_example: For a small cut, put on clean gloves, rinse the wound with clean water, press with a clean pad to stop bleeding, then cover it with a plaster.

units.title: Common accidents and injuries at school
units.notes: Accidents at school happen during play, in the laboratory, on stairs or in the kitchen. Common injuries include cuts, bruises, sprains, burns and fractures. Most can be prevented by following rules, walking instead of running and using equipment correctly. A sprain is treated with rest, ice, compression and elevation. Any serious injury should be reported to a teacher immediately. Keeping calm helps you think clearly and help others safely.
units.worked_example: If a learner twists an ankle at the field, help them sit down, apply a cold cloth, keep the foot raised and send word to the teacher on duty.

units.title: Substance use and abuse prevention
units.notes: Substances such as alcohol, tobacco, miraa and drugs harm the body and mind, especially in young people. They damage the brain, lungs and liver, reduce concentration and can lead to addiction and school drop-out. Peer pressure and stress sometimes push learners to try them, so it helps to know how to say no firmly. Choosing positive friends, doing sports and seeking support from trusted adults protect you. Possessing or selling illegal drugs is against the law in Kenya.
units.worked_example: If a friend offers you a cigarette behind the classroom, a firm reply such as 'No thanks, I do not smoke' followed by walking away is a clear refusal.
units.activity: Role-play with a partner two ways to refuse a harmful substance and discuss which felt easier to use.

units.title: Mental health and emotional wellbeing
units.notes: Mental health is about how we think, feel and cope with daily life. Good mental wellbeing helps learners concentrate, build friendships and handle stress. Feelings like sadness, worry and anger are normal, but they should not be ignored for long. Talking to a trusted adult, resting well, exercising and doing hobbies support emotional health. Seeking help for persistent low mood is a sign of strength, not weakness.
units.worked_example: A learner who feels anxious before exams can write down worries, take slow deep breaths and speak to the class teacher or school counsellor.
units.activity: Keep a feelings journal for one week, noting one thing that went well each day.

units.title: Puberty and adolescent health
units.notes: Puberty is the stage when the body changes from that of a child to that of an adult. It usually begins between ages nine and fourteen and brings growth spurts, new feelings and changes in body shape. Boys may notice a deeper voice and growth of body hair, while girls may begin menstruation. These changes are normal and happen at different times for different people. Good hygiene, correct information and respect for others help learners cope with this stage confidently.
units.worked_example: A girl who has her first period at school can use sanitary pads, change them regularly and speak to the matron if she needs help.

units.title: Environmental health and sanitation
units.notes: Environmental health is about keeping our surroundings clean and safe for everyone. Poor sanitation, open defecation and stagnant water allow diseases such as cholera, typhoid and malaria to spread. Proper disposal of rubbish, use of latrines and drainage of stagnant water reduce these risks. Planting trees, keeping rivers clean and avoiding litter protect the land, air and water. Every person plays a part in caring for the environment at home, school and in the community.
units.worked_example: A class that clears stagnant water around the school compound and empties old tins removes mosquito breeding sites and lowers malaria risk.
units.activity: Organise a cleanup of one area in your school and record the types of waste collected.

Pre-technical Studies.overview: This guide introduces basic technical, material and workshop skills and the design process for junior secondary learners. It covers safety, tools, materials, drawing, simple machines, electricity and enterprise skills.

units.title: Safety in the workshop
units.notes: A workshop contains tools and machines that can cause injury if used carelessly. Before starting work, learners should wear protective clothing such as overalls, goggles and closed shoes. Sharp tools must be carried with the point down and away from the body. The floor should stay dry and free of offcuts to prevent slips. Knowing where the first aid box and fire extinguisher are kept prepares you for emergencies.
units.worked_example: Before using a tenon saw, check that the wood is clamped, wear goggles and keep your fingers clear of the marked line.

units.title: Hand tools and their uses
units.notes: Hand tools are simple tools worked by hand rather than by power. Common examples include the hammer, screwdriver, hacksaw, chisel, file, plane and spanner. Each tool has a special job, so a tenon saw cuts wood, a cold chisel cuts metal and a screwdriver drives screws. Using the right tool for the job gives neat work and prevents damage. Tools should be kept sharp, dry and stored on a tool rack after use.
units.worked_example: To loosen a tight bolt on a bicycle, use a spanner of the correct size rather than pliers, which would round off the nut.

units.title: Materials: wood, metal and plastic
units.notes: Materials used in technical work come from different sources and have different properties. Wood is obtained from trees and is easy to cut, shape and join, but it swells when wet. Metals such as steel and aluminium are strong and conduct heat and electricity, so they are used for structures and wires. Plastics are man-made, light and waterproof, and are used for containers and electrical insulation. Choosing the right material depends on strength, cost, durability and the job at hand.
units.worked_example: A cooking stick is best made of wood because it does not conduct heat, while a nail is made of steel because it must be strong and hard.

units.title: Measuring and marking out
units.notes: Measuring and marking out means transferring the correct sizes onto a material before cutting or joining. Accurate work depends on using tools such as the steel rule, tape measure, try square, marking gauge and pencil. Always measure twice and cut once to avoid wasting material. Lines should be thin and clear, and the try square is used to check that corners are exactly ninety degrees. Careful marking produces neat joints and saves time and materials.
units.worked_example: To mark a 300 millimetre length on a piece of timber, place the steel rule along the edge, measure from the end twice, then draw a thin line across with a pencil and try square.
units.activity: Measure the top of your desk in centimetres and record its length and width to the nearest millimetre.

units.title: Fastening and joining techniques
units.notes: Joining methods hold two or more pieces of material together permanently or temporarily. Permanent joints include nailing, screwing, riveting, welding and gluing. Temporary fasteners such as bolts, nuts and wing nuts allow parts to be taken apart later. Wood can be joined with nails, screws or glue, while metal is often joined by welding or rivets. The choice of joint depends on the material, the strength needed and whether the item must be opened again.
units.worked_example: To fix two pieces of timber for a stool that must stay firm, drill pilot holes and drive in screws rather than using short nails.

units.title: Basic drawing and technical sketches
units.notes: Technical drawing uses clear lines, shapes and symbols to show what an object looks like and how it is made. A sketch is a quick freehand drawing, while a working drawing is neat and drawn to scale. Important parts include the outline, hidden lines, centre lines and dimension lines. Drawing in orthographic projection shows the front, top and side views. Good drawings help a maker build an item accurately without guessing.
units.worked_example: To draw a table, first sketch the front view as a rectangle, then add the top view showing the table surface and mark the height in millimetres.

units.title: The design process
units.notes: The design process is a step-by-step way of solving a practical problem and creating a useful product. It begins by identifying the need, then researching, generating ideas and choosing the best one. A sketch or model is made and tested, then improved before the final product is produced. Each stage is recorded so that decisions can be explained. Following the process helps avoid waste and produces items that really meet a user's needs.
units.worked_example: A learner whose brother struggles to carry books designs a simple trolley, identifying the need of carrying, sketching ideas, testing a cardboard model and then improving the best design.

units.title: Simple electrical circuits
units.notes: An electric circuit is a complete path through which electric current flows. A simple circuit needs a source such as a cell or battery, conductors like copper wires, and a device such as a bulb or buzzer. A switch controls the circuit by opening or closing the path. Materials that allow current to flow are conductors, while insulators such as rubber and plastic block it. Never experiment with mains electricity, as simple cells are safe for learning.
units.worked_example: Connecting one cell, two wires, a switch and a bulb in a loop makes the bulb light when the switch is closed and go off when it is opened.

units.title: Energy sources and conservation
units.notes: Energy is the ability to do work, and it exists in forms such as light, heat, sound, electrical and mechanical energy. Common sources include the sun, wind, flowing water, firewood and fossil fuels such as petrol and kerosene. Kenya also uses geothermal and solar energy, which are renewable and cleaner. Energy can be changed from one form to another, as when electrical energy becomes light in a bulb. Saving energy by switching off lights and using efficient stoves protects resources.
units.worked_example: In a torch, chemical energy stored in the cells changes into electrical energy, which then changes into light energy in the bulb.

units.title: Simple machines and mechanisms
units.notes: Simple machines make work easier by increasing force, changing its direction or increasing speed. The main types are the lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge and screw. Levers have a fulcrum, effort and load, and they are grouped into three classes. A pulley helps lift heavy loads upward, while gears and cams change the speed or direction of motion. Machines such as wheelbarrows and bicycles use several simple machines together.
units.worked_example: A wheelbarrow is a class two lever in which the wheel acts as the fulcrum and the load sits between the fulcrum and the handles where the effort is applied.

units.title: Maintenance and repair of tools
units.notes: Maintenance means keeping tools and equipment in good working condition so they are safe and last long. It includes cleaning off dust and rust, sharpening blades, oiling moving parts and tightening loose handles. Tools should be stored in a dry place on a rack rather than left on the floor. Regular checks help spot damage early before it causes injury. Simple repairs such as replacing a broken handle save money and build practical skills.
units.worked_example: After using a hoe, scrape off the soil, dry it, rub the blade with oil to prevent rust and store it hanging in a dry shed.

units.title: Entrepreneurship and small-scale production
units.notes: Entrepreneurship is the process of turning an idea into a product or service that people need and are willing to pay for. A small business, such as making and selling items in a school project, needs planning, costing and record keeping. Knowing the cost of materials, transport and labour helps set a fair price that gives a profit. Good customer care and quality products attract repeat buyers. Skills learned in technical work can become a source of income in the community.
units.worked_example: If a table mat costs thirty shillings in materials and labour, selling it at fifty shillings gives a profit of twenty shillings for each mat sold.

units.title: ICT and digital skills in technical work
units.notes: Information and communication technology helps people design, make and sell products more efficiently. Computers, tablets and phones can be used for research, drawing, measuring and keeping records. Simple design software allows a learner to draw a plan and change it quickly without using paper. Digital tools also help advertise products and communicate with customers. Using devices safely, protecting your data and sharing information responsibly are important digital skills.
units.worked_example: A learner uses a drawing app to sketch a stool, adjusts the height on the screen and prints the plan before cutting any wood.

Social Studies.overview: This guide covers Kenyan and East African geography, history, governance and citizenship for junior secondary learners. It moves from the local community to national and regional understanding.

units.title: Our school and local community
units.notes: A community is a group of people living in the same area and sharing services such as schools, markets and health centres. Our school is at the centre of learning and brings together learners from different families. Members of a community depend on one another for food, security, transport and support. Knowing your location, village and county helps you describe where you belong. Good citizens care for shared facilities and respect neighbours.
units.worked_example: A learner in Nakuru County can describe their school as being in a particular ward, mentioning nearby landmarks like the market and the local church.
units.activity: Draw a simple map of your school and mark the classrooms, office, playing field and water point.
units.check: Name three services that members of your community share?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a service that members of a community share?

options: a group of people living in the same area and sharing services

quiz.prompt: Knowing your location, village and county helps you do what?

units.title: Maps and map reading
units.notes: A map is a drawing of an area seen from above and drawn to scale. Maps use keys, scales, titles, compass directions and grid lines to give information. The scale shows the relationship between distance on the map and real distance on the ground. Directions are given using the four cardinal points and their subdivisions. Reading maps helps us locate places, plan journeys and understand the layout of our county and country.
units.worked_example: If the scale is one centimetre to one kilometre and two towns are four centimetres apart on the map, the real distance between them is about four kilometres.
units.activity: Using a map of your county, locate your nearest town and measure the distance to a neighbouring town.
units.check: Why does every good map need a key?

options: To explain what the symbols on the map mean

quiz.prompt: Directions on a map are given using what?
options: the four cardinal points and their subdivisions

quiz.prompt: Reading maps helps us locate places and plan journeys?

units.title: Physical features of Kenya
units.notes: Kenya has a variety of physical features formed by earth movements and volcanic activity. These include mountains such as Mount Kenya, the Rift Valley, highlands, plateaus and coastal plains. Rivers, lakes and swamps are also important features. Mount Kenya is the highest mountain in the country and is capped with snow. The Great Rift Valley runs from north to south and contains lakes such as Nakuru and Naivasha.
units.worked_example: Most of Kenya's tea is grown in the highlands around Kericho because the area is cool and receives plenty of rainfall.
units.activity: On a sketch map of Kenya, mark and label Mount Kenya, the Rift Valley and the Indian Ocean coast.

units.title: Climate and vegetation of Kenya
units.notes: Climate is the average weather condition of a place over a long period. Kenya has a range of climates, from hot and dry in the north to cool and wet in the highlands. Rainfall comes mainly during the long rains and the short rains, and it influences farming. Vegetation depends on climate, so forests grow in wet highlands while scrub and grass grow in dry areas. Understanding climate helps people choose what crops and livestock to keep.
units.worked_example: Kiambu County, with cool temperatures and good rainfall, is suited to growing coffee and tea, unlike the dry lowlands of Turkana.
units.activity: Find out the average rainfall for your area and describe how it affects the crops grown nearby.

options: Crops that suit the rainfall and temperature do well

Vegetation depends on climate?

units.title: Water resources and rivers of Kenya
units.notes: Water resources include rivers, lakes, springs, swamps and underground water. Major rivers such as the Tana and the Athi flow from the highlands towards the coast. Lake Victoria, the largest lake in Africa, is a major source of fish and water. Water is used for drinking, irrigation, transport and generating hydro-electric power. Clean rivers support animal life, while pollution from waste harms fish and plants.
units.worked_example: The Tana River is dammed at the Seven Forks area, where flowing water is used to generate electricity that powers homes and industries.
units.activity: Locate the nearest river or water source to your school and list three ways the community uses it.
units.check: Name two uses of rivers to people living in Kenya?

quiz.prompt: Which is the largest lake in Africa?

Pollution from waste harms fish and plants?

units.title: Population and settlement in Kenya
units.notes: Population refers to the number of people living in an area, while settlement is where they live. Kenya's population grows quickly, and most people live in the highlands where farming is good. Settlements may be rural, with scattered homesteads and farms, or urban, with towns and cities such as Nairobi and Mombasa. Migration from villages to towns happens when people seek jobs and services. Dense settlement puts pressure on land, water and housing.
units.worked_example: Many young people move from villages in Kakamega to Nairobi in search of work, increasing the number of residents in the city.
units.activity: List five reasons why people move from rural areas to towns in Kenya.
units.check: What is the difference between a rural and an urban settlement?

A rural settlement has only skyscrapers

Population refers to what?

units.title: Kenyan communities and culture
units.notes: Kenya has many communities, each with its own language, foods, dress, music and beliefs. Communities such as the Agikuyu, Luo, Luhya, Kalenjin, Kisii, Mijikenda and several pastoral groups live together as one nation. Culture is passed from one generation to the next through stories, songs, ceremonies and family teaching. Sharing cultural practices builds understanding and national unity. Respecting the languages and customs of other communities is an important value of citizenship.
units.worked_example: During a school cultural day, learners may present a traditional dance, share a local dish such as ugali with fish, and explain its origin to classmates.
units.activity: Interview an elder about one cultural practice in your community and share what you learn with the class.

units.title: Early history and the Kenyan coast
units.notes: The Kenyan coast has a long history of trade across the Indian Ocean. Arab, Persian, Indian and later Portuguese traders came to ports such as Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu. They exchanged goods including ivory, spices, cloth and beads. This trade led to the growth of Swahili towns and of the Swahili language and culture. Fort Jesus in Mombasa was built by the Portuguese and remains an important historical site.
units.worked_example: A visit to Fort Jesus in Mombasa shows the thick stone walls and cannons that the Portuguese used to defend the port in the sixteenth century.
units.activity: Draw a timeline showing the order in which Arab, Portuguese and other traders reached the Kenyan coast.

units.title: Colonial rule and the struggle for independence
units.notes: British colonial rule in Kenya began in the late nineteenth century and changed land ownership, taxation and labour. Africans were pushed off fertile land and forced to work, which caused much suffering and resistance. Leaders and movements organised opposition, and the Mau Mau uprising fought against colonial rule. After years of struggle, Kenya gained independence on 12 December 1963. Remembering this history helps us value freedom and the sacrifices made for it.
units.worked_example: Jomo Kenyatta became Kenya's first Prime Minister in 1963 after leading the independence struggle, and he later became the first President.

units.title: Government and the constitution
units.notes: A government is the body that makes and carries out laws and provides services to citizens. Kenya's government has three arms, namely the legislature, the executive and the judiciary. The Constitution of Kenya 2010 is the supreme law and sets out the rights of citizens and the powers of each arm. Kenya is a devolved republic with a national government and forty-seven county governments. Citizens choose their leaders through elections held every five years.
units.worked_example: The county government of Kisumu is responsible for local services such as refuse collection and some health facilities within the county.
units.activity: List the three arms of government and name one duty of each.

units.title: Democracy and human rights
units.notes: Democracy is a system of government in which power belongs to the people, who choose leaders through free and fair elections. It includes participation, majority rule, accountability and respect for the rights of others. Human rights are the basic freedoms every person is entitled to, such as education, health, life, expression and fair treatment. In Kenya these rights are protected in the Bill of Rights in the Constitution. Rights go together with responsibilities, such as obeying the law and respecting others.
units.worked_example: If learners are denied a fair hearing before punishment, that goes against the right to fair administrative action protected in the Bill of Rights.
units.activity: Choose three rights from the Bill of Rights and state one responsibility that goes with each.
units.check: Why do rights come with responsibilities?

units.title: The East African Community and regional cooperation
units.notes: The East African Community is a regional organisation whose member states work together for mutual benefit. Its members include Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Cooperation covers trade, transport, security, education and health. Member states allow goods and people to move more easily across borders through a common market. Regional unity helps countries grow and solve shared problems.
units.worked_example: A Kenyan trader can sell maize flour in Uganda under East African Community trade agreements, and Kenyan students benefit from shared educational programmes.
units.activity: On a map of East Africa, shade and label the member countries of the East African Community.

units.title: Citizenship, values and social responsibility
units.notes: A citizen is a person who is a recognised member of a country, with rights and duties. Good citizenship means obeying the law, paying taxes, voting responsibly and treating others fairly. Values such as honesty, hard work, integrity, patriotism and respect guide our behaviour. Social responsibility means caring for those in need and protecting public property and the environment. Active citizens take part in community work and help solve local problems.
units.worked_example: Joining a school tree-planting day and clearing litter along a nearby river is an example of social responsibility in action.
units.activity: Describe one way you can be a responsible citizen in your school and one way in your community.

Business Studies.overview: This guide introduces learners to basic business ideas such as needs and wants, money, saving, entrepreneurship and simple book-keeping. It uses everyday Kenyan examples to help learners make wise choices about money and understand how small businesses work.

units.title: Human wants and needs
units.notes: Needs are the basic things people must have to live, such as food, water, shelter and clothing. Wants are things we desire for comfort and enjoyment but can live without, such as sweets, video games or a new bicycle. Needs are limited because they are few and basic, while wants are many and keep changing as people grow. Money is limited, so families must decide which items to buy first. Goods are physical things we can touch, while services are work done for others. Understanding the difference helps us spend the shilling wisely.
units.worked_example: A learner has fifty shillings. Buying a pen for school is a need because it helps learning, while buying sweets is a want. The learner should buy the pen first and save any remaining money.
units.activity: List five things you would like to buy and mark each one as a need or a want. Explain to a partner which two you would buy first and why.
units.check: Why should needs be satisfied before wants?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a basic need rather than a want?
Why should needs be satisfied before wants?

Needs are necessary for survival while wants are for comfort
Needs keep changing as people grow

quiz.prompt: Wants are few and basic while needs are many and keep changing?
Which statement best describes goods?
options: They are work done for others
They are physical items we can touch

quiz.prompt: A service is work done for others, such as teaching or hair cutting?

units.title: Goods and services
units.notes: Goods are tangible items that we can see and touch, such as maize flour, textbooks or a bicycle. Services are useful work done by people for others, such as teaching, hair cutting or transporting goods. Both goods and services satisfy human wants and are exchanged for money in the market. Some businesses sell goods, others offer services, and many do both at the same time. A shopkeeper sells goods, while a teacher sells a service through knowledge and skill. Consumers must choose carefully because money is limited.
units.worked_example: A barber cuts hair for a customer for one hundred shillings. The haircut is a service because the barber uses skill rather than selling a physical item.
units.activity: Walk around your school or home and list four goods and four services you can see. Share your list with the class and group each item correctly.

quiz.prompt: What is the main difference between a good and a service?

Goods are sold only in shops

Which of these is an example of a service?

A business can sell goods and offer services at the same time?

units.title: Money and its uses
units.notes: Money is anything generally accepted as payment for goods and services. In Kenya we use the Kenya shilling, which comes in coins and notes. Money is used as a medium of exchange, a measure of value, a store of wealth and a unit of account. Before money existed, people used barter, exchanging goods directly. Barter was difficult because both people had to want what the other had. Money solves this problem because everyone accepts it. Money earned should be spent wisely, saved for the future and used honestly.
units.worked_example: A trader sells two kilograms of maize for one hundred shillings and uses the money to buy salt and soap. Money makes this exchange simple because both items have a clear price.
units.activity: Name the coins and notes you know and arrange them from the smallest to the largest value. Discuss how each is used in daily shopping.
units.check: Why is money better than barter as a means of exchange?

quiz.prompt: What is money?
options: Anything generally accepted as payment for goods and services

quiz.prompt: Why is money better than barter as a means of exchange?
options: Barter requires both people to want what the other has
Barter is used only in banks

quiz.prompt: Barter means exchanging goods directly without using money?

units.title: Sources of money for the family
units.notes: Families get money from different sources. Parents may earn wages or salaries from formal jobs, or income from farming, trading or offering services. Other sources include rent from property, interest from savings and gifts or remittances from relatives. In many Kenyan homes, farming maize, tea or keeping dairy cattle brings regular income. Young people can also earn money by doing small chores, selling vegetables or making crafts. All family members should know the sources of their income so they can plan how to use it carefully.
units.worked_example: A family earns a salary, sells milk from two cows and receives money from a relative in the city. Adding these together shows the total income for the month.
units.activity: Interview a parent or guardian about the sources of income at home and write down three of them. Discuss how the money is used.

units.title: Personal budgeting and saving
units.notes: A budget is a plan showing how money will be earned and spent over a period. To make a simple budget, list your expected income, then list your needs and wants, and decide what to spend. Needs should come before wants. Saving means keeping part of your money for future use, perhaps in a bank, a sacco or a piggy bank. Saving helps us buy bigger items later, prepare for emergencies and avoid borrowing. Even a small amount saved each week grows over time and teaches discipline with money.
units.worked_example: A learner receives one hundred shillings pocket money each week, spends sixty and saves forty. After five weeks the savings total two hundred shillings, enough to buy a school item.
units.activity: Prepare a simple weekly budget for yourself using your real income from chores or gifts. Show how much you would spend and how much you would save.

units.title: Business and entrepreneurship
units.notes: A business is any activity carried out to produce or sell goods and services with the aim of making a profit. An entrepreneur is a person who starts and runs a business, takes risks and looks for opportunities. Good entrepreneurs are creative, hardworking, honest and able to plan. Small businesses in Kenya include shops, salons, food kiosks and vegetable stalls. Starting a business needs an idea, some capital, skills and customers. Entrepreneurs create jobs and help the country grow. Anyone, including young people, can practise simple entrepreneurship after learning the basic skills.
units.worked_example: A learner notices that classmates want snacks and sells groundnuts during break, earning a small profit. This shows simple entrepreneurship using a small amount of capital.
units.activity: Think of a simple business you could start at school or home with little money. Write down the idea, the items needed and how you would attract customers.

quiz.prompt: What is the main aim of a business?

options: A person who never takes risks
A person who starts and runs a business and takes risks
A person who only works for the government

quiz.prompt: Only adults can practise simple entrepreneurship?

units.title: Factors of production
units.notes: Four factors are needed to produce goods and services. Land provides natural resources such as soil, water and minerals. Labour is the human effort, both physical and mental, used in production. Capital refers to the man-made resources such as tools, machines and money used to produce goods. Entrepreneurship organises the other three factors and takes the risks. For example, a farmer uses land to grow maize, hires labour to weed, uses capital to buy a hoe, and applies entrepreneurship to decide what to plant. These factors work together in every productive activity.
units.worked_example: In a small bakery, the building and oven are capital, the baker provides labour, the wheat comes from land, and the owner shows entrepreneurship by planning and selling the bread.
units.activity: Choose a business in your area, such as a shop or a farm, and list how each of the four factors of production is used there.

units.title: Business records and simple book-keeping
units.notes: Book-keeping means keeping written records of the money that comes in and goes out of a business. Simple records include sales, purchases, expenses and receipts. Records help a business owner know whether the business is making a profit or a loss. They also help in planning prices, paying taxes and applying for loans. Small traders can use a simple cash book to record daily sales. Keeping accurate and honest records builds trust and prevents money from being lost or misused.
units.worked_example: A kiosk owner records total sales of two thousand shillings and expenses of one thousand two hundred shillings in a day, showing a profit of eight hundred shillings.
units.activity: Create a simple cash book with two columns for money in and money out. Record any five transactions from a small business you know.

units.title: Income and expenditure accounts
units.notes: An income and expenditure account shows total money received and total money spent over a period, such as a week or a month. Income is money received from sales, wages or gifts. Expenditure is money spent on buying goods, paying rent or meeting other costs. When income is greater than expenditure, the difference is a surplus. When expenditure is greater than income, the difference is a deficit. Calculating this simple account helps traders and families see whether they are living within their means and where they can reduce spending.
units.worked_example: A family receives eight thousand shillings in a month and spends seven thousand. The surplus of one thousand shillings can be saved or used for emergencies.
units.activity: Record your family income and common expenses for one week on paper and work out whether there is a surplus or a deficit.

units.title: Markets and customers
units.notes: A market is any place or way through which buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods and services. Markets can be physical, such as a village market or a shop, or can take place online. Customers are the people who buy goods or services from a business. A good business tries to know what customers want, offers quality goods at fair prices and treats customers politely. Kenyan markets for farm produce include local trading centres and town markets such as Wakulima in Nairobi. Satisfied customers return and bring others, increasing sales and profit.
units.worked_example: A trader selling tomatoes at a busy market keeps the produce fresh and prices it fairly, so customers return every week and recommend the stall to friends.
units.activity: Visit or imagine a nearby market and list three things that attract customers to a particular stall. Discuss how these things help the seller.

units.title: Advertising and sales promotion
units.notes: Advertising is the process of informing customers about goods and services to encourage them to buy. Advertisers use posters, radio, television, social media, exhibitions and word of mouth. Sales promotion includes special offers such as discounts, free samples, buy one get one free and prize draws. The aim of advertising is to attract new customers, increase sales and create awareness of a product. Honest advertising gives true information about the product. False or misleading advertising is wrong and can make customers lose trust in a business.
units.worked_example: A shop announces a discount of ten per cent on school shoes for one week, attracting many learners and increasing sales without telling lies about the product.
units.activity: Design a simple poster advertising a product made or sold in your area. Make sure your message is clear and truthful.

units.title: Business ethics and honesty
units.notes: Business ethics are the accepted rules of good behaviour in running a business. Honest traders give correct change, use accurate scales and tell customers the truth about their goods. They pay their workers fairly and pay taxes on time. Dishonest practices such as cheating, selling expired goods or inflating prices are wrong and can lead to punishment by the law. Good ethics build a good reputation, encourage trust and keep customers coming back. Even young people can practise honesty by returning borrowed items and being truthful in class.
units.worked_example: A trader realises he gave a customer too little change and corrects the mistake at once. This honest act earns him the customer's trust and business.
units.activity: Role-play a market scene where a seller must decide whether to cheat a customer. Discuss which choice is right and why.

units.title: Government and business
units.notes: The government supports and controls business in many ways. It builds roads, markets and secure environments that help traders operate. It provides services such as health care, education and security, which are paid for through taxes collected from businesses and workers. Taxes in Kenya include value added tax, income tax and customs duty. The government also makes laws to protect consumers from harmful products and unfair prices. Businesses benefit from these services but must obey the law, register their activities and pay the required taxes honestly.
units.worked_example: A shopkeeper pays value added tax on goods sold, and in return benefits from good roads and security that bring customers to the area.
units.activity: List three government services in your area that help businesses to operate, and explain how they support traders.
units.check: How do taxes paid by businesses benefit the whole community?

quiz.prompt: How do taxes paid by businesses benefit the whole community?
