Agriculture.overview: This guide introduces learners to the basics of crop and livestock production, soil, farm tools and simple farm records. It uses Kenyan farming examples to help learners appreciate agriculture and manage farm resources wisely.

units.title: Introduction to agriculture
units.notes: Agriculture is the practice of growing crops and keeping animals for food and other useful products. It is the backbone of Kenya's economy and provides food, income and raw materials for industries. Agriculture is divided into crop farming and livestock keeping. Many Kenyan families depend on farming for their livelihood, growing crops such as maize, beans and tea. Farming also provides employment and earns the country foreign exchange through exports. Learning agriculture helps learners appreciate farming and use resources wisely to improve food security.
units.worked_example: A family in Kisii grows maize and beans for food and keeps a few dairy cows for milk and extra income, showing both crop farming and livestock keeping.
units.activity: Make a list of five crops grown and three animals kept in your county, and state one product from each.
units.check: Why is agriculture called the backbone of Kenya's economy?

quiz.prompt: Why is agriculture called the backbone of Kenya's economy?
options: It provides food, income, employment and raw materials
It has no effect on the economy
It is only done in cities

quiz.prompt: Agriculture is divided into which two main parts?

units.title: Soil formation and composition
units.notes: Soil is the loose top layer of the earth in which crops grow. It is formed slowly over many years when rocks are broken down by weather, water, wind and living organisms. Soil is made up of mineral particles, organic matter called humus, air, water and living things such as earthworms and bacteria. Humus makes soil dark and fertile. The mineral particles come in different sizes, and their mixture gives soil its texture. Good soil holds water and air, supplies nutrients and supports plant roots firmly.
units.worked_example: A learner digs a small pit and sees dark soil at the top and lighter, stony soil below, showing that the top layer is rich in humus and best for crops.
units.activity: Collect a handful of soil from a garden and examine it closely. Note its colour, feel and any living things you can see.

quiz.prompt: What makes the top layer of soil good for growing crops?
options: It contains minerals, humus, air and water
It is made of solid rock

quiz.prompt: What is humus?
options: Organic matter that makes soil dark and fertile

quiz.prompt: Soil is formed quickly in a single day?
Which of these helps to break down rocks into soil?
Good soil supports plant roots firmly?

units.title: Soil types and soil fertility
units.notes: Different soils have different sizes of mineral particles. Sandy soil has large particles, drains fast and dries quickly. Clay soil has tiny particles, holds water well but drains poorly and becomes sticky when wet. Loam soil mixes sand, clay and silt and is the best for most crops because it holds both water and air. Fertile soil contains enough nutrients, humus and water for healthy plant growth. Farmers improve fertility by adding manure or fertiliser, practising crop rotation and controlling erosion. Testing the soil texture helps a farmer choose suitable crops.
units.worked_example: A farmer with clay soil mixes in manure to improve drainage and fertility, allowing crops like maize to grow better than in the heavy soil alone.
units.activity: Collect samples of sandy, clay and loam soil and rub each between your fingers. Describe how each feels and which you think is best for farming.
units.check: Why is loam soil considered the best for most crops?

options: It holds both water and air

How can farmers improve soil fertility?
Testing soil texture helps a farmer choose suitable crops?

units.title: Soil erosion and conservation
units.notes: Soil erosion is the wearing away and removal of the top fertile layer of soil by wind, water or human activities. It is worse on bare, sloping or poorly covered land, and it reduces crop yields. Farmers control erosion using methods such as terracing on slopes, planting cover crops, mulching, contour ploughing and planting trees or grass strips. These methods slow down running water and hold soil particles in place. Keeping the soil covered and avoiding overgrazing protect the land. Conserving soil keeps farms productive for many years.
units.worked_example: A farmer on a steep slope digs terraces and plants napier grass along the edges, catching water and soil that would otherwise be washed downhill.
units.activity: Draw a simple picture of a farm on a slope and show two methods a farmer could use to control soil erosion.

options: The wearing away and removal of the top fertile layer of soil

quiz.prompt: Overgrazing helps protect the land from erosion?

units.title: Crop production: land preparation
units.notes: Land preparation means getting the field ready for planting. The farmer first clears bushes and weeds, then digs or ploughs the soil to loosen it. Loosening the soil allows air and water to enter and helps roots grow easily. The land is then levelled and broken into fine particles using a harrow or rake. Farmers may also make planting beds or ridges and add manure or fertiliser. Land should be prepared before the rains begin so that planting can start on time. Good preparation gives seedlings a strong and healthy beginning.
units.worked_example: Before the long rains, a farmer clears the field, ploughs it and makes raised beds. When the rains come, the crops are planted early and grow well.
units.activity: Watch or help with preparing a small garden plot. Describe, in order, the steps taken to make the land ready for planting.

quiz.prompt: Why should land be prepared before the rains begin?
options: So that planting can start on time

quiz.prompt: Why is soil loosened during land preparation?
options: To allow air and water to enter and help roots grow

units.title: Planting materials and planting
units.notes: Planting materials are the seeds, seedlings, cuttings, tubers or suckers used to grow new crops. The farmer should choose healthy, clean and high quality planting materials suitable for the local climate. Seeds can be planted directly, while crops such as tomatoes and cabbages may be raised in a nursery first. Correct spacing is important because plants need enough light, water and nutrients, and it makes weeding easy. The depth of planting must also be right. Planting at the right time, usually at the start of the rains, gives crops a good chance to grow well.
units.worked_example: A farmer plants maize seeds at a depth of about five centimetres and leaves space between rows. This spacing lets each plant get enough light and nutrients.
units.activity: Plant a few bean seeds in a pot or school garden at the correct depth and spacing, then record how many days they take to sprout.
units.check: Why is correct spacing important when planting crops?

quiz.prompt: Why is correct spacing important when planting crops?
options: Plants need enough light, water and nutrients and it makes weeding easy

options: At the start of the rains

units.title: Crop management practices
units.notes: After planting, crops need regular care until they are harvested. Common practices include weeding, watering, thinning, applying manure or fertiliser and controlling pests and diseases. Weeding removes unwanted plants that compete with crops for water, light and nutrients. Thinning removes crowded weak seedlings so the remaining plants grow strong. Top dressing adds nutrients when plants are growing actively. Mulching covers the soil to reduce water loss and control weeds. These practices together give healthy plants and better harvests, which increase the farmer's income and improve food supply.
units.worked_example: A farmer thins out weak maize seedlings and adds top dressing fertiliser when the plants are growing. The strong plants mature and produce a bigger harvest.
units.activity: Keep a small planted plot and carry out two management practices, such as weeding and watering, for two weeks. Note any changes in the plants.

units.title: Weeds, pests and diseases
units.notes: A weed is any plant growing where it is not wanted. Weeds compete with crops for water, nutrients, light and space, and some harbour pests. A pest is a living organism, such as insects, birds or rodents, that damages crops. Diseases are caused by germs, fungi or poor growing conditions and show as spots, wilting or rotting. Farmers control these problems by weeding, using clean planting materials, crop rotation, natural predators and approved chemicals used safely. Early detection and quick action prevent heavy losses. Healthy crops give a better harvest and more food for the family.
units.worked_example: A farmer spots black spots on tomato leaves and removes the affected plants quickly, preventing the disease from spreading to the whole crop.
units.activity: Examine a crop plant at home or school and identify any weeds, insects or signs of disease. Describe what you find and how it could be controlled.

units.title: Harvesting and post-harvest handling
units.notes: Harvesting is the gathering of mature crops from the farm when they are ready. The right harvesting time depends on the crop, and harvesting too early or too late reduces quality and quantity. After harvesting, crops must be handled carefully to avoid damage, rotting and loss. Practices include drying grains well before storage, sorting out spoiled produce, cleaning and packing in clean bags or containers. Proper storage keeps grain dry and safe from pests such as weevils. Good post-harvest handling reduces waste and allows farmers to sell quality produce at fair prices in the market.
units.worked_example: After harvesting maize, a farmer dries the grain in the sun, sorts out rotten cobs and stores the rest in a clean, dry granary to prevent weevils.

units.title: Common farm animals
units.notes: Farm animals are kept for food, income, transport and other products. Common animals in Kenya include cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits and poultry such as chickens and ducks. Cattle give milk and meat and can pull ox-ploughs. Goats and sheep provide meat, milk and wool, and thrive in dry areas. Poultry give eggs, meat and quick income, and need little space. Rabbits provide meat and manure and are easy to keep. Keeping the right animals for the local climate and available feeds helps farmers earn well.
units.worked_example: In a dry county, a family keeps goats and chickens because these animals survive well with little water and give quick returns from milk, meat and eggs.
units.activity: List the farm animals kept near your home and state one product from each. Explain which animal you would keep and why.

units.title: Livestock feeds and feeding
units.notes: Animals need the right food to grow and produce well. Feeds are grouped into roughages, concentrates and supplements. Roughages include grasses, hay, silage and crop residues, and they are bulky and rich in fibre. Concentrates such as maize meal, cotton seed cake and dairy meal are rich in energy and protein. Animals also need clean water all the time. Feeding should follow a regular timetable and match the animal's age and purpose. A dairy cow, for example, produces more milk when given enough good fodder and a balanced ration each day.
units.worked_example: A dairy farmer feeds a cow on fresh napier grass and adds dairy meal concentrate, and the cow gives more milk than when fed on grass alone.
units.activity: Find out what feeds are given to animals at home and group them into roughages and concentrates. Share your findings with the class.

units.title: Livestock health and housing
units.notes: Healthy animals grow faster, produce more and bring better income. A good animal house should be clean, well ventilated, dry and safe from predators and thieves. It should allow easy feeding and cleaning. Common animal health problems include worms, ticks, foot rot and diseases such as East Coast fever. Farmers prevent illness by vaccination, dipping or spraying against ticks, deworming, providing clean water and feeding well. Sick animals should be separated and treated by a qualified veterinary officer. Keeping daily records of treatment and production helps the farmer manage the herd well.
units.worked_example: A farmer dips cattle every week to control ticks and separates a sick cow from the rest. This prevents disease from spreading to the healthy animals.

units.title: Farm tools, equipment and farm records
units.notes: Farm tools make work easier and faster. Simple tools include the jembe, panga, rake, watering can, wheelbarrow and pruning saw. Equipment such as ox-ploughs, sprayers and water pumps are used for bigger jobs. Tools should be cleaned, sharpened and stored safely after use to last long and work well. Farm records are written details of what happens on the farm, such as planting dates, expenses, income and livestock numbers. Records help the farmer plan, know the profit and make good decisions. Every farmer should keep simple, honest records every day.
units.worked_example: A farmer records the date of planting, the cost of seeds and the money earned from selling the harvest, and uses these records to plan the next season.

Life Skills Education.overview: This guide helps learners understand themselves, make good decisions, build healthy relationships and cope with challenges. It covers values, communication, peer pressure, resilience and responsible citizenship using everyday Kenyan examples.

units.title: Self-awareness
units.notes: Self-awareness is knowing and understanding yourself, including your strengths, weaknesses, feelings, values and goals. A self-aware person recognises what they are good at and where they need to improve. This knowledge helps you make better choices, set realistic goals and relate well with others. You can build self-awareness by thinking about your actions, listening to honest feedback and reflecting on your day. Knowing yourself also helps you accept who you are and appreciate your unique abilities. It is the first step towards growing into a confident and responsible person.
units.worked_example: A learner notices that she understands science easily but finds mathematics hard, so she spends more time on mathematics and asks for help, improving her marks.
units.activity: Write down three of your strengths and two areas you would like to improve. Discuss with a partner how you can work on the areas that need improvement.

units.title: Self-esteem
units.notes: Self-esteem is how much you value and respect yourself. Learners with healthy self-esteem believe they can do well, try again after failure and accept their mistakes without giving up. Low self-esteem can make a person shy, fearful or easily discouraged. You can build self-esteem by setting small goals and achieving them, taking care of your body, dressing neatly and speaking positively about yourself. Praise for effort, not only for results, also helps. Everyone has value, and believing in yourself helps you face school work and life with courage and hope.
units.worked_example: A learner who fails a test decides to study harder, seeks help and passes the next test, which raises his confidence and self-esteem.
units.activity: Write three positive statements about yourself and read them aloud each morning for one week. Note how you feel by the end of the week.

units.title: Values and good behaviour
units.notes: Values are the beliefs and standards that guide how we behave. Important values include honesty, respect, responsibility, fairness, caring and hard work. Values shape our choices, relationships and character. A learner who values honesty will not cheat in examinations, and one who values respect will treat teachers, parents and classmates kindly. Values are learned from family, school, religion and community. When we practise good values every day, we earn trust and build a good reputation. Living by good values also helps create peace and unity in the community.
units.worked_example: A learner finds a lost wallet and returns it to its owner instead of keeping the money, showing the value of honesty.

units.title: Goal setting
units.notes: A goal is something you want to achieve in the future. Goals can be short term, such as finishing homework by evening, or long term, such as becoming an engineer. Good goals should be specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time bound. Writing goals down and breaking a big goal into small steps makes it easier to achieve. You should also review your progress and adjust your plans when necessary. Setting clear goals gives direction, builds discipline and helps you use your time well. With effort and patience, many goals can be reached.
units.worked_example: A learner sets a goal to improve her mathematics grade in three months by practising ten sums every evening, and reviews her progress each week.
units.activity: Write one short-term and one long-term goal for yourself. Break each into small steps and set a time by which you hope to achieve it.

units.title: Decision making
units.notes: Decision making is the process of choosing the best option among several alternatives. Good decisions are made after thinking carefully about the choices, the likely results and how they affect you and others. Steps include identifying the problem, listing possible options, considering the consequences of each, choosing the best option and acting on it. You then review whether the decision worked. Making decisions well helps you avoid trouble and reach your goals. Learners make many decisions daily, from choosing friends to managing study time, so this skill is very important.
units.worked_example: A learner is invited to join friends watching a film instead of revising for an exam. She thinks about the consequences and chooses to revise first, then rest afterwards.
units.activity: Think of a decision you must make this week and list three options. Write one advantage and one disadvantage of each, then choose the best option.

units.title: Problem solving
units.notes: Problem solving is finding ways to overcome difficulties or obstacles. When a problem arises, stay calm, identify exactly what the problem is and gather the facts. Then think of as many possible solutions as you can, weigh their advantages and disadvantages, and choose the best one. Carry out your chosen solution and check whether it worked. If it did not work, try another option. Good problem solvers are patient, creative and willing to ask for help when needed. This skill helps learners handle school work, family matters and relationships with confidence.
units.worked_example: A learner keeps arriving late to school. He identifies the cause as waking up late, decides to sleep earlier and set an alarm, and then arrives on time.
units.activity: Describe a real problem you have faced and list three ways you could solve it. Explain which solution you would choose and why.

units.title: Creative and critical thinking
units.notes: Creative thinking means coming up with new and useful ideas, while critical thinking means examining ideas carefully before accepting them. Both skills help us solve problems and make wise choices. A creative learner may invent a simple tool from local materials or find a new way to present a project. A critical thinker asks questions, looks for evidence and is not easily fooled by false information or rumours. Practising these skills through debate, puzzles, projects and group work makes the mind sharp and prepares learners for the challenges of daily life and future work.
units.worked_example: A learner makes a toy car from wire and bottle tops for a science project, while a critical thinker checks whether a rumour shared by friends is actually true before believing it.

units.title: Communication skills
units.notes: Communication is the sharing of information, ideas and feelings between people. It can be spoken, written or shown through gestures and body language. Good communication needs clear speech, careful listening and the right tone. Listening is the most important part, because it shows respect and helps you understand others before you reply. You should also consider other people's feelings and choose your words kindly. Barriers such as fear, noise or prejudice can block communication. Good communication improves friendship, teamwork and success at school, home and work.
units.worked_example: A learner listens carefully to a friend's problem without interrupting, then responds kindly. The friend feels understood and their friendship grows stronger.
units.activity: Practise a short conversation with a partner in which you must listen carefully and then repeat back what was said. Discuss how well you understood each other.

units.title: Interpersonal relationships
units.notes: Interpersonal relationships are the connections we have with other people, such as family, friends, teachers and neighbours. Healthy relationships are built on trust, respect, honesty, kindness and good communication. Friends should support each other, share ideas and solve disagreements peacefully. We should choose friends who influence us positively and avoid those who encourage bad behaviour. Good relationships make us feel loved, safe and confident. Disagreements are normal, and they can be settled by listening, apologising and forgiving. Building strong relationships helps us live happily with others.
units.worked_example: Two friends quarrel over a borrowed book. They talk calmly, one apologises for losing it, and they agree on how to replace it, keeping their friendship intact.

units.title: Peer pressure and resistance
units.notes: Peer pressure is the influence friends or classmates have on us to behave in a certain way. It can be positive, such as encouraging good study habits, or negative, such as pressuring someone to skip school, steal or use drugs. Learners should learn to resist negative pressure by saying no firmly, walking away, choosing good friends and seeking help from trusted adults. Having clear values and confidence in yourself makes it easier to stand firm. It is important to remember that true friends respect your choices and do not force you to do wrong.
units.worked_example: A learner is urged by friends to smoke, but she firmly refuses and walks away, choosing instead to join a study group with positive friends.
units.activity: Role-play a situation where friends pressure you to do something wrong. Practise saying no firmly and suggest a better choice.

units.title: Resilience and coping with challenges
units.notes: Resilience is the ability to recover and keep going after difficult experiences. Challenges such as failing an examination, losing a relative or facing family problems affect many learners. Resilient people accept the situation, stay hopeful and look for solutions instead of giving up. You can build resilience by staying positive, talking about your feelings with someone you trust, keeping healthy and setting small goals. Learning from mistakes makes you stronger. Remember that seeking help is a sign of courage, not weakness. Resilience helps us overcome hardships and grow.
units.worked_example: A learner who does poorly in an examination talks to a teacher, works on the weak topics and improves next term, showing resilience.
units.activity: Describe a challenge you once faced and how you coped with it. Share one thing that helped you keep going.

quiz.prompt: Why is seeking help a sign of strength rather than weakness?

quiz.prompt: What is resilience?
options: The ability to recover and keep going after difficult experiences

Which of these helps build resilience?
options: Staying positive and talking about your feelings

quiz.prompt: Learning from mistakes makes you stronger?

units.title: Managing emotions and stress
units.notes: Emotions are strong feelings such as joy, anger, fear, sadness and love. All emotions are normal, but how we express them matters. Stress is the tension we feel when we face pressure, such as examinations or family demands. Too much stress harms health and learning. You can manage emotions and stress by taking deep breaths, exercising, resting well, talking to a trusted person and planning your work. Anger should be controlled so that it does not harm others. Learning to understand and express feelings in healthy ways keeps the mind calm and helps us make good decisions.
units.worked_example: Before an examination, a learner feels nervous, so he takes slow deep breaths and plans his revision, which calms him and helps him focus.
units.activity: Practise a simple relaxation activity such as slow breathing for a few minutes and describe how your body and mind feel afterwards.

quiz.prompt: Which two are healthy ways of managing stress?
What is stress?
options: The tension we feel when we face pressure

quiz.prompt: All emotions are normal, but how we express them matters?

Too much stress harms health and learning?

units.title: Citizenship and responsibility
units.notes: A citizen is a member of a country who enjoys rights and has duties. Kenyan citizens have rights such as education, health care, protection and freedom of expression. They also have responsibilities such as obeying the law, respecting others, paying taxes, caring for public property and protecting the environment. Good citizens participate in community work, vote wisely and help those in need. As young learners, you can show good citizenship by keeping the school clean, following rules and helping classmates. Responsible citizens build a peaceful, united and developing nation for everyone.
units.worked_example: A class takes part in a cleanup of the local market and plants trees, showing responsibility towards their community and environment.
units.activity: List three rights and three responsibilities of a Kenyan citizen, then state one responsibility you can practise as a learner.
units.check: Name two responsibilities of a good citizen?

quiz.prompt: Which two are responsibilities of a good citizen?
options: Obeying the law and caring for public property

Physical Education.overview: Physical Education helps Junior Secondary learners build movement skills, fitness, teamwork and fair play through games, athletics and gymnastics. It uses simple equipment and local spaces so every learner can take part safely.

units.title: Locomotor movements and body awareness
units.notes: Locomotor movements carry the body from one place to another and include walking, running, jumping, hopping, skipping, galloping and sliding. Body awareness means knowing where your body parts are and how they move in space. In a Grade 7 lesson, learners practise each movement slowly first, then at speed, while keeping good posture. Space awareness helps you avoid bumping into others during games. These basic patterns are the foundation of every sport you will play.
units.worked_example: To teach a hop, a learner stands on one foot, bends the knee slightly and pushes off, landing on the same foot with arms swinging forward for balance. A gallop is a step followed by the same lead foot, done to a steady clap.
units.activity: Mark four stations on the school field for walking, running, hopping and skipping, and spend two minutes at each station practising with a partner.

quiz.prompt: Which locomotor movement keeps one foot leading and is often used in warm-up games?

units.title: Non-locomotor movements and balance
units.notes: Non-locomotor movements are done in place and include bending, stretching, twisting, turning, swinging, pushing and pulling. Balance is the ability to keep your body steady, either while standing still or while moving. Static balance happens when you hold a still position, such as standing on one leg, while dynamic balance happens while you move. Strong core muscles and focused eyes help you balance better. These skills improve control in gymnastics, dance and ball games.
units.worked_example: A learner practising a stork stand places hands on hips, lifts one foot to rest on the opposite knee and fixes the eyes on one point on the wall for ten seconds.
units.activity: With a partner, time how long each of you can hold three balances: a one-leg stand, a tiptoe stand and a wide straddle balance.

options: Static balance is holding a still position while dynamic balance happens while moving

units.title: Manipulative skills: throwing, catching and striking
units.notes: Manipulative skills involve controlling objects with the hands, feet or an implement. Throwing and catching build hand-eye coordination, while striking sends a ball or shuttle away with a bat, racket or the foot. In catching, learners should watch the ball into their hands and give with the ball to soften the impact. Throwing well uses a side-on stance, a step forward and a follow-through. These skills appear in netball, rounders, volleyball and football.
units.worked_example: For an overarm throw, stand sideways to the target, step forward with the opposite foot and release the ball as the arm passes the ear, finishing with the hand pointing at the target.
units.activity: Practise throwing a tennis ball against a wall and catching it with two hands, then one hand, counting successful catches in one minute.

units.title: Athletics: sprinting and relay basics
units.notes: Sprinting is running at maximum speed over short distances such as 100 metres or 200 metres. A good sprint start uses the crouch position with the strongest foot forward in the starting blocks. Runners drive hard for the first few steps, then relax the shoulders and run tall. In a relay, each runner carries a baton and passes it inside the exchange zone without breaking stride. Speed, safe technique and clean changeovers decide the race.
units.worked_example: On the command set, a sprinter raises the hips and holds still, then drives out low on the gun, taking short powerful steps for the first ten metres.
units.activity: Set out two cones twenty metres apart and practise three relay changeovers with a partner, walking through first and then jogging.
units.check: Where must the baton be passed in a relay race?

quiz.prompt: Where must the baton be passed in a relay race?
options: Inside the exchange zone without breaking stride

options: Running at maximum speed over short distances

units.title: Athletics: middle-distance running and pacing
units.notes: Middle-distance races such as 800 metres and 1500 metres need steady pacing rather than an all-out sprint. Pacing means choosing a speed you can hold to the finish instead of starting too fast and tiring early. Good runners breathe rhythmically, relax their arms and run behind a leader to save energy. A strong finish is built on even lap times set during training. Warm-ups and hydration matter because these races last several minutes.
units.worked_example: To run an 800 metres in about four minutes, aim for laps of about two minutes each; if you run the first lap in 1 minute 40 seconds, slow slightly so you still have energy for the last 200 metres.
units.activity: Run four laps of the school field and record the time for each lap, then compare whether your laps were even.

quiz.prompt: Why is even pacing usually better than sprinting the first lap of an 800 metres race?

options: Running as fast as possible from the start

units.title: Athletics: long jump and high jump basics
units.notes: The long jump has a run-up, a take-off from one foot, a flight phase and a landing. The run-up builds speed, and the take-off board must be hit without stepping over it. In flight, learners bring the knees up and reach forward with both heels before landing in the pit. The high jump uses a curved run-up and a scissor or Fosbury technique to clear the bar. Both events reward speed, timing and a safe landing.
units.worked_example: A learner counts eight strides back from the take-off board, marks that spot with a cone and uses the same run-up every attempt to jump consistently.
units.activity: Measure out a short run-up, place a marker and practise five long jumps, landing on both heels with knees bent for safety.

units.title: Gymnastics: rolls, balances and sequences
units.notes: Gymnastics develops strength, flexibility and control through movements such as forward rolls, backward rolls, cartwheels and balances. A safe forward roll starts from a crouch, tucks the chin to the chest and rolls over the rounded back, not the neck. Balances such as the shoulder stand should only be attempted with a mat and a spotter. Learners then join three or four movements into a smooth sequence. Always warm up and use correct mats.
units.worked_example: A simple sequence is a forward roll into a crouch, a two-second stork balance, then a cartwheel and a finishing pose held for three seconds.
units.activity: On a mat with a partner spotting, practise a forward roll and hold one balance, then link them into a short routine.

units.title: Ball games: football skills and small-sided play
units.notes: Football is one of Kenya's most popular sports and needs control of the ball with both feet. Key skills include passing with the inside of the foot, trapping a rolling ball, dribbling close to the body and shooting low and hard. Small-sided games such as five-a-side give every learner more touches and more decisions. Players must respect the referee and opponents. Being fit helps you keep pressing and supporting teammates for the whole match.
units.worked_example: To make an accurate pass, plant the non-kicking foot beside the ball, lock the ankle and push the ball with the inside of the foot toward a teammate's feet.
units.activity: In a group of five, play a ten-minute possession game where a team scores a point after five clean passes.

units.title: Ball games: netball and basketball basics
units.notes: Netball and basketball are fast games built on passing, footwork and scoring. In netball you may not run with the ball, so you must land, balance and pass within three seconds. Basketball allows dribbling and shooting at a hoop, with players using the chest pass and bounce pass to move the ball. Both games need marking, spatial awareness and quick decisions. Teamwork and discipline matter more than individual tricks.
units.worked_example: In netball, a player lands on one foot, pivots on that foot to face a teammate and releases a two-handed chest pass before the three-second limit.
units.activity: Practise chest and bounce passes against a wall for two minutes, then play a short netball game using only those two passes.

units.title: Net and wall games: volleyball and badminton
units.notes: Net and wall games require sending an object over a net or against a wall so the opponent cannot return it. Volleyball skills include the underarm serve, forearm pass, set and spike, with three touches allowed per side. Badminton uses a racket and shuttle, with overhead clears, drop shots and low serves. Footwork, ready position and watching the object are essential. These games reward patience, placement and quick recovery to the centre.
units.worked_example: For a volleyball underarm serve, hold the ball in the non-hitting hand, swing the other arm back and forward, and strike the ball with the heel of the hand to send it over the net.
units.activity: With a partner, rally a shuttle or ball over a low net or rope, aiming for five continuous returns without dropping.

units.title: Health-related fitness: warm-up, cool-down and flexibility
units.notes: A warm-up raises body temperature, loosens joints and prepares muscles for activity, reducing the risk of injury. It usually starts with light jogging followed by dynamic stretches such as arm circles and leg swings. A cool-down is slower activity plus static stretches held for about fifteen to thirty seconds. Flexibility is the range of movement at a joint and improves with regular stretching. Rest, water and good sleep also support fitness.
units.worked_example: Before a football session, jog two laps, then do ten arm circles, ten leg swings and ten hip rotations, and after play hold a hamstring stretch for twenty seconds on each leg.
units.activity: Design and lead a five-minute warm-up for your class, choosing four dynamic stretches and explaining why each helps.

units.title: Endurance, strength and circuit training
units.notes: Endurance is the ability to keep working for a long time, while strength is the ability to apply force against resistance. Circuit training combines several stations such as squats, press-ups, skipping and shuttle runs performed for a set time with short rests. Circuits build both fitness and discipline because you record your repetitions and try to improve. Body-weight exercises are safe for young learners when the technique is correct. Progress comes from consistent, gradual training, not from one hard session.
units.worked_example: A circuit of six stations done for forty seconds each with twenty seconds rest gives a full workout; a learner records press-ups and improves from eight to twelve over four weeks.
units.activity: Set up a six-station circuit in the school field and complete two rounds, writing down your score at each station.

units.title: Sportsmanship, rules and fair play in competition
units.notes: Sportsmanship means playing by the rules, respecting officials and treating opponents as partners, not enemies. Fair play includes shaking hands, accepting defeat without excuses and congratulating winners sincerely. Learners should learn the basic rules of each game so that competition is safe and enjoyable. Cheating, arguing and rough play spoil sport and can cause injury. Good sportsmanship builds character that helps in class and at home.
units.worked_example: After losing a house match, a captain gathers the team, thanks the referee and leads a handshake with the winning side before discussing what to improve.
units.activity: Before your next class game, agree on three fair-play rules as a group and appoint a learner to note examples of good sportsmanship.

Creative Arts and Sports.overview: Creative Arts and Sports gives learners a chance to create, perform and appreciate work in visual arts, craft, music, dance and drama. It builds confidence, teamwork and an understanding of Kenyan culture through practical making and performance.

units.title: Elements of visual arts: line, shape and form
units.notes: Visual arts rest on elements such as line, shape, form, texture, colour and space. Line can be thick or thin, straight or curved, and it guides the eye and shows movement. Shape is flat and two-dimensional, while form is three-dimensional with volume and depth. Texture describes how a surface looks or feels. Kenyan artists often use these elements to show landscapes, markets and wildlife.
units.worked_example: A learner sketches a market stall using thick lines for the frame, curved lines for the awning and cross-hatching to suggest texture on woven baskets.
units.activity: Draw three objects from your classroom using only lines, then repeat the drawing showing shape and texture.

units.title: Colour theory and mixing paints
units.notes: Colour theory explains how colours relate and mix. The primary colours are red, blue and yellow, and mixing two primaries gives a secondary colour such as green, orange or purple. Colours opposite each other on the wheel are complementary and create strong contrast. Warm colours like red and orange feel lively, while cool colours like blue and green feel calm. Learners should clean brushes between mixes to keep colours pure.
units.worked_example: Mixing blue and yellow paint gives green; adding more yellow makes a light yellow-green, while adding a little red dulls it toward olive.
units.activity: Paint a simple colour wheel showing three primaries and three secondaries, labelling each mix.

units.title: Drawing from observation and still life
units.notes: Drawing from observation means looking carefully at real objects and recording what you actually see. A still life is a group of objects such as fruits, bottles and cloth arranged for study. Artists begin with light outlines, compare proportions and then add shading to show light and shadow. Squinting at the objects helps you see the dark and light areas. Regular practice improves accuracy and confidence.
units.worked_example: When drawing a mango and a bottle, a learner first measures that the bottle is about twice as tall as the mango and marks those heights before drawing any detail.
units.activity: Arrange three objects on your desk, shine a torch from one side and draw the group, shading the dark side.

units.title: Craft: weaving and beadwork
units.notes: Weaving means interlacing threads, strips or fibres to make cloth, mats or baskets, and it is an old craft in many Kenyan communities. Common products include sisal mats, kiondo bags and beaded jewellery. Beadwork follows a pattern, so planning colours and counting beads keeps the design neat. These crafts strengthen patience and fine motor skills, and well-made items can be sold for income. African beadwork often uses colours that carry meaning about identity or occasion.
units.worked_example: To make a simple paper weave, a learner cuts a card loom with slits, threads vertical strips, then weaves horizontal strips over and under in a repeating pattern.
units.activity: Weave a small mat from paper strips or banana fibre, using at least two colours in a simple pattern.

units.title: Craft: clay modelling and pottery
units.notes: Clay is dug from the ground, kneaded to remove air bubbles and shaped by hand or on a wheel. Modelling techniques include pinching, coiling and slab building, all of which can make bowls, pots and figures. Once shaped, clay is dried slowly and then fired in a kiln to make it hard and durable. Smoothing joins and keeping the walls even prevents cracks. Kenyan potters produce water pots, cooking pots and decorative items.
units.worked_example: To make a coil pot, roll the clay into long equal coils, join them in circles, smooth the inside with a finger and blend each new coil to the one below.
units.activity: Model a small bowl using the pinch method, keeping the walls an even thickness, and leave it to dry slowly in the shade.

units.title: Music: rhythm, beat and note values
units.notes: Music has three main building blocks: melody, rhythm and harmony. The beat is the steady pulse you can clap or count, while rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds played over the beat. Note values show how long each sound lasts: a semibreve lasts four beats, a minim two, a crotchet one and a quaver half a beat. Kenyan drumming layers many rhythms together. Counting aloud helps learners keep time.
units.worked_example: A learner claps four steady beats, then claps a crotchet on each beat, and finally claps two quavers on the first beat to feel the difference.
units.activity: In small groups, clap a four-beat rhythm pattern while a partner keeps the steady beat, then swap roles.

units.title: Music: singing in parts and simple instruments
units.notes: Singing in parts means two or more groups sing different notes at the same time to create harmony. Singers must breathe from the diaphragm, listen to the other parts and keep a steady beat. Simple instruments such as drums, shakers, recorders and the thumb piano can accompany songs. Traditional Kenyan songs often use call and response, where a leader sings a line and the group answers. Practice builds confidence and good tuning.
units.worked_example: In a two-part song, group one holds a low drone note while group two sings the melody; when both are comfortable they swap lines.
units.activity: Form two groups and learn a short Kenyan call-and-response song, then add drums or shakers to keep the beat.

units.title: Dance: basic steps and traditional Kenyan dances
units.notes: Dance uses the body to express ideas, stories and feelings, usually with music or drumming. Warm-up and posture are important before practice to prevent injury. Basic dance elements include beat, rhythm, levels, direction and travelling steps. Kenya has many traditional dances, such as the Adumu jumping dance of the Maasai, isukuti of the Luhya and the chakacha and kiganda styles along the coast. Learners should respect the communities whose dances they study.
units.worked_example: In a Maasai-inspired jump, dancers keep the body upright, sink slightly into the knees to jump straight up on the beat and land softly on the balls of the feet.
units.activity: Learn a five-minute local dance from an elder or a video clip, practise the footwork slowly, then perform it for the class.

units.title: Dance: choreographing a short group piece
units.notes: Choreography is the art of creating and arranging dance movements into a whole piece. Choreographers choose a theme, select music, then build a sequence of steps that match the rhythm and mood. They use formations, levels, unison and cannon to make the dance interesting. Rehearsing with counts and reviewing a recording helps the group stay together. A good dance has a clear beginning, middle and ending.
units.worked_example: A group chooses the theme harvest, opens in a wide circle, performs a stamping step in unison, splits into two lines and finishes in a still pose.
units.activity: In a group of four, plan eight counts of movement on a chosen theme, rehearse to a song and show your sequence to another group.

units.title: Drama: improvisation and role play
units.notes: Improvisation is acting without a written script, creating characters and dialogue on the spot. It builds quick thinking, listening and confidence. Role play asks learners to act out a real or imagined situation, such as buying goods at a market or welcoming a new pupil. Actors should stay in character, speak clearly and respond to their partner. A short pause to think is fine; there is no single correct answer.
units.worked_example: Given the situation of losing school fees money on the way to school, two learners improvise a conversation with the head teacher, staying in character and showing the emotions involved.
units.activity: In pairs, improvise a one-minute scene about returning a lost phone, then discuss what felt realistic.

units.title: Drama: script writing and staging a short play
units.notes: A script is a written plan for a play and includes dialogue, stage directions and character names. Most plays follow a structure with a beginning that sets the scene, a middle that builds conflict and an ending that resolves it. Staging involves choosing costumes, props, background and blocking, which is where actors stand and move. Directors guide the actors and keep the story clear. Rehearsing in the performance space helps the group adjust voice and movement.
units.worked_example: A learner writes a short scene in which a dishonest pupil finally confesses; the script lists the setting, three characters and a stage direction such as Wanjiku enters slowly, looking at the ground.
units.activity: Write a one-page script for three characters on a theme like honesty, then read it aloud in a staged reading.

units.title: Performance skills: voice, movement and stage presence
units.notes: Performers use the voice and body to communicate meaning to an audience. Voice skills include projection, clear articulation, pace and expression; projecting does not mean shouting but supporting the voice with breath. Movement skills include gesture, facial expression and using the stage space. Stage presence is the confidence and focus that hold the audience's attention. Eye contact and facing the audience make every performance stronger.
units.worked_example: To make a line sound angry, a performer slows the pace slightly, increases the volume, frowns and steps toward the other character instead of turning away.
units.activity: Say the same sentence to the class in three different ways, showing happiness, fear and surprise with your voice and body.

options: The confidence and focus that hold the audience's attention

Which skill helps a performer communicate meaning?
Eye contact and facing the audience make every performance stronger?

units.title: Presenting and appreciating creative work
units.notes: Presenting art means showing finished work to others in a class exhibition, concert or performance. A display should be neat, well labelled and arranged so viewers can see each item. Appreciation means looking closely and giving honest, helpful comments about what works and what could improve. Feedback should be specific and polite, such as suggesting more contrast in shading or louder projection. Exhibitions and concerts build confidence and celebrate effort.
units.worked_example: In a gallery walk, learners move quietly around displayed drawings, leave a sticky note with one strength and one suggestion, and the artist reads the notes later.
units.activity: Organise a class exhibition of your artwork or a short concert, then write two kind comments about a classmate's piece.
units.check: What makes feedback helpful rather than hurtful to another learner?

quiz.prompt: What makes feedback helpful rather than hurtful to another learner?
options: It is specific and polite, suggesting what could improve

quiz.prompt: What does appreciation mean in creative work?
options: Looking closely and giving honest, helpful comments

quiz.prompt: A display should be neat, well labelled and arranged so viewers can see each item?
Where can learners present finished creative work?
options: In a class exhibition, concert or performance

quiz.prompt: Exhibitions and concerts build confidence and celebrate effort?

Religious Education.overview: Religious Education explores values, moral choices, sacred stories and the beliefs and practices of different faiths in Kenya. It encourages learners to think carefully, live respectfully with others and act with integrity.

units.title: Values that build good character
units.notes: Values are the beliefs that guide how we behave and make decisions. Honesty, kindness, respect, responsibility and patience are values taught in many faith traditions and in Kenyan schools. Values are seen in actions, such as sharing food, doing chores without being told and telling the truth. Character grows when good behaviour is practised daily, not just talked about. Learners should choose values that help them live well with others.
units.worked_example: If you find a fifty-shilling coin in the classroom, honesty means handing it to the teacher instead of keeping it, even if nobody saw you pick it up.
units.activity: List five values you admire in a person you respect, then write one small action you can practise this week for each value.
units.check: How can you tell that a person really values honesty?

quiz.prompt: How can you tell that a person really values honesty?
options: They tell the truth and act honestly every day

quiz.prompt: What are values?
options: The beliefs that guide how we behave and make decisions

quiz.prompt: Character grows when good behaviour is practised daily, not just talked about?
Which of these is a value taught in many faith traditions and Kenyan schools?
Values are seen in actions such as sharing food and doing chores without being told?

units.title: Honesty, integrity and trustworthiness
units.notes: Integrity means doing the right thing even when no one is watching. An honest person tells the truth, keeps promises and corrects mistakes instead of hiding them. Trust is built slowly through consistent honesty but can be broken in a moment. In a school, honesty shows in examinations, in reporting what happened and in returning borrowed items. Religious teachings across faiths encourage truthfulness and warn against deceit.
units.worked_example: A learner whose friend copied in a test decides to tell the teacher the truth about the group's plan, understanding that honesty may be hard but protects everyone.
units.activity: In groups, list three situations at school where honesty is tested and suggest the right action in each case.
units.check: Why is it harder to keep integrity when no one is watching?

quiz.prompt: Why is it harder to keep integrity when no one is watching?
options: Integrity means doing the right thing even when no one is watching

quiz.prompt: What is integrity?
options: Doing the right thing even when no one is watching

quiz.prompt: Trust is built slowly through consistent honesty but can be broken in a moment?
At school, honesty shows in which of these?
options: Examinations, reporting what happened and returning borrowed items

quiz.prompt: Religious teachings across faiths encourage truthfulness and warn against deceit?

units.title: Respect and living together across faiths
units.notes: Kenya is home to Christians, Muslims, Hindus, African traditional believers and others. Respect means treating people of other faiths with dignity, even when their beliefs differ from yours. Good neighbours share markets, schools and hospitals, so daily cooperation matters more than making everyone agree. You show respect by learning about others, avoiding insults and not forcing your beliefs on anyone. Freedom of worship is protected, and it comes with a duty to live peacefully.
units.worked_example: During a school festival, a Christian learner attends a Muslim classmate's Eid celebration as a guest, listens respectfully and wishes her well without mocking her prayers.
units.activity: Interview a classmate of a different faith about one celebration their family keeps, and share what you learned respectfully with the class.
units.check: What is one respectful action you can take when a friend observes a different religious festival?

quiz.prompt: What is one respectful action you can take when a friend observes a different religious festival?
options: Learn about it and wish them well without insulting their beliefs

quiz.prompt: What does respect mean in living together across faiths?
options: Treating people of other faiths with dignity, even when their beliefs differ

quiz.prompt: Kenya is home to Christians, Muslims, Hindus and African traditional believers, among others?
What comes with freedom of worship?
options: A duty to live peacefully with others

quiz.prompt: Good neighbours share markets, schools and hospitals, so daily cooperation matters?

units.title: Responsibility and service to the community
units.notes: Responsibility means doing what is expected of you and accepting the results of your actions. At home you care for siblings and clean your space; at school you complete tasks and help classmates; in the community you may join clean-up or tree-planting. Many religions teach that service to others is a duty, not an option. Service builds leadership and empathy. Small acts done consistently build a better Kenya.
units.worked_example: A class agrees to clean the school compound every Friday and to plant ten tree seedlings; each learner is assigned a duty and reports on progress monthly.
units.activity: Plan one service activity with your class, such as tidying a village stream or visiting a children's home, and agree on who does what.
units.check: How does serving your community also help you grow as a person?

quiz.prompt: How does serving your community also help you grow as a person?
What is responsibility?
options: Doing what is expected of you and accepting the results of your actions

quiz.prompt: Many religions teach that service to others is a duty, not an option?
Which of these is an act of service to the community?
options: Joining a clean-up or tree-planting exercise

quiz.prompt: At home, responsibility means caring for siblings and cleaning your space?

units.title: Sacred stories of compassion
units.notes: Sacred stories are treasured narratives that teach believers how to live. Many religions tell of figures who showed compassion to the poor, the sick and the stranger. The Christian parable of the Good Samaritan and Islamic teachings about mercy to orphans and travellers show this care. Such stories ask listeners to look beyond tribe, religion or family and help anyone in need. Values of generosity and kindness emerge from these narratives.
units.worked_example: In the parable of the Good Samaritan, a traveller is robbed and ignored by passers-by until a foreigner stops, treats his wounds and pays for his care.
units.activity: Retell a story of compassion from your faith or community and explain what lesson it holds for your class.
units.check: What makes an act of kindness truly generous, according to these stories?

quiz.prompt: What makes an act of kindness truly generous, according to these stories?
options: It helps anyone in need without expecting a reward
It is done to show off

quiz.prompt: Which story shows compassion to the poor, the sick and the stranger?
options: The parable of the Good Samaritan

quiz.prompt: Sacred stories ask listeners to look beyond tribe, religion or family and help anyone in need?
What values emerge from these compassionate stories?
Islamic teachings about mercy to orphans and travellers show care for others?

units.title: Sacred stories of courage and faith
units.notes: Many sacred stories show people facing danger while holding on to their beliefs. Believers remember them for courage, patience and trust in God during hardship. These stories are recited in places of worship and read at home to teach the young. Their examples encourage learners to stand for the truth and to endure difficulties without losing hope. The lesson is often that faith and courage go together.
units.worked_example: Learners discuss a story in which a believer refuses to act against their beliefs, and they explain how the person's courage affected the community.
units.activity: Choose a story of courage from a scripture or from an elder's account, and present its main lesson in a short class talk.
units.check: How can a story of courage help you when you face pressure to do wrong?

quiz.prompt: How can a story of courage help you when you face pressure to do wrong?
options: It encourages you to stand for the truth and not lose hope
It tells you to give in

quiz.prompt: What do sacred stories of courage often show?
options: People facing danger while holding on to their beliefs

quiz.prompt: These stories are recited in places of worship and read at home to teach the young?
What lesson is often drawn from stories of courage and faith?
options: That faith and courage go together
That hardship should never be faced

quiz.prompt: Believers remember such figures for courage, patience and trust in God during hardship?

units.title: Prayer, worship and sacred places
units.notes: Prayer is communication with God and takes many forms, including spoken prayers, silence, song and ritual. Places of worship such as churches, mosques and temples are treated with respect because believers gather there to worship. Different faiths pray at set times or on special days, and using water, mats or objects may form part of the practice. Sacred places also host charity and teaching. Visitors should dress modestly and follow the rules of the place.
units.worked_example: Before entering a mosque, a visitor removes shoes and enters quietly; in a church, a learner notices people bow for prayer and follows the same respectful conduct.
units.activity: Write a short paragraph describing how one place of worship in your area is treated with respect, then share it with the class.
units.check: What rules or habits show respect in a place of worship?

quiz.prompt: What rules or habits show respect in a place of worship?
options: Dressing modestly and following the rules of the place

quiz.prompt: What is prayer?
options: Communication with God, in forms such as words, silence, song or ritual

quiz.prompt: Places of worship such as churches, mosques and temples are treated with respect?
Besides worship, what else do sacred places host?
Different faiths may use water, mats or special objects as part of their worship?

units.title: Moral choices: right and wrong in daily life
units.notes: Moral choices are decisions about what is right and wrong, guided by values, conscience and religious teaching. Many decisions at school involve honesty, fairness, respect and self-control, such as whether to help clean up or leave early. Conscience helps people pause and think about consequences for themselves and others. Different faiths share teachings that protect life, property and dignity. Making good choices often means resisting pressure from friends.
units.worked_example: When friends suggest skipping class to watch a match, a learner weighs the consequences, chooses to attend the lesson and later watches highlights without breaking rules.
units.activity: In pairs, act out a moral dilemma such as finding unfair examination marks, and agree on the best solution.
units.check: What questions can you ask yourself before making a difficult moral choice?

quiz.prompt: What questions can you ask yourself before making a difficult moral choice?
options: Is it right, and how will it affect me and others?

quiz.prompt: What are moral choices?
options: Choices about what to eat only
Decisions about what is right and wrong, guided by values and conscience

quiz.prompt: Conscience helps people pause and think about consequences for themselves and others?
What does making good choices often mean?
Different faiths share teachings that protect life, property and dignity?

units.title: Family and relationships
units.notes: The family is the first place where love, discipline and values are learned. Families in Kenya come in different shapes, including nuclear, extended and single-parent households. Good relationships need respect, honest communication, shared work and forgiveness. Children have duties such as helping at home and supporting younger siblings, while elders guide and protect. Religious teaching honours parents and encourages care for the elderly and the vulnerable.
units.worked_example: A learner resolves a quarrel with a brother by listening to his side, apologising for shouting and agreeing to share the household chores fairly.
units.activity: Draw a simple family tree, then write one responsibility you carry toward each person in your home.
units.check: What are two ways respect is shown in a healthy family relationship?

quiz.prompt: What are two ways respect is shown in a healthy family relationship?
What is the family called in these notes?
options: The first place where love, discipline and values are learned

quiz.prompt: Families in Kenya come in different shapes, including nuclear, extended and single-parent households?
What duties do children have in a family?
options: Helping at home and supporting younger siblings

quiz.prompt: Religious teaching honours parents and encourages care for the elderly and the vulnerable?

units.title: Care for creation and stewardship
units.notes: Many faiths teach that the earth is a gift to be cared for and passed on to the next generation. Stewardship means using resources responsibly without wasting or destroying them. In Kenya this shows in planting trees, protecting rivers and water catchments, conserving wildlife and reducing waste. Pollution and careless cutting of forests harm people and animals, especially in dry areas. Small daily habits like saving water and recycling add up to real change.
units.worked_example: A class notices a nearby river filling with plastic; the learners organise a monthly clean-up and place labelled bins in the compound to reduce waste.
units.activity: Start a simple project in your school such as a tree nursery or a waste-separation corner, and track its progress each week.
units.check: Why do many religions describe humans as caretakers of the earth rather than owners?

quiz.prompt: Why do many religions describe humans as caretakers of the earth rather than owners?
options: The earth is a gift to be cared for and passed on to the next generation

quiz.prompt: What does stewardship mean?
options: Using resources responsibly without wasting or destroying them

quiz.prompt: In Kenya, stewardship shows in planting trees, protecting rivers and conserving wildlife?
Which daily habits help care for creation?
Pollution and careless cutting of forests harm people and animals?

units.title: Peace, forgiveness and conflict resolution
units.notes: Conflict is normal in human relationships, but it can be handled without violence. Forgiveness means letting go of anger and bitterness, even when it is difficult, and it often follows a sincere apology. Peace building requires listening to both sides, speaking calmly, negotiating and using elders or teachers as mediators. Many religious traditions teach that those who make peace are honoured. Lasting peace depends on justice as much as on apology.
units.worked_example: Two pupils who fought over a seat talk with the class teacher, each explains what happened, apologise to each other and agree on a fair seating arrangement.
units.activity: Practise a conflict-resolution role play using the steps listen, explain calmly, apologise and agree on a solution.
units.check: Why is forgiveness important even when the other person was clearly wrong?

quiz.prompt: Why is forgiveness important even when the other person was clearly wrong?
options: It lets go of anger and bitterness and brings peace

quiz.prompt: What is forgiveness?
options: Letting go of anger and bitterness, often after a sincere apology

quiz.prompt: Peace building requires listening to both sides and using elders or teachers as mediators?
Which of these can help resolve conflict peacefully?
Lasting peace depends on justice as much as on apology?

units.title: Justice, fairness and care for the needy
units.notes: Justice means giving each person what is fair and treating people equally, regardless of tribe, religion, gender or wealth. Care for the needy is a duty in many faiths, shown through alms, food drives and visiting the sick. Unfairness such as corruption, bullying or discrimination harms both victims and society. Learners can practise justice by sharing resources and speaking up for those who are treated badly. We should not be passive when wrong is happening around us.
units.worked_example: When a new learner from another county is teased about her accent, some classmates choose to sit with her, invite her to their group and report the bullying to the teacher.
units.activity: Identify one unfair practice in your school or village, then plan a simple fair action with your classmates.
units.check: How can you stand up for fairness in a situation where no adult is present?

quiz.prompt: How can you stand up for fairness in a situation where no adult is present?
options: Speak up calmly for the person being treated badly and refuse to join in

quiz.prompt: What is justice?
options: Giving each person what is fair and treating people equally

quiz.prompt: Care for the needy is a duty in many faiths, shown through alms, food drives and visiting the sick?
Which of these harms both victims and society?
We should not be passive when wrong is happening around us?

units.title: Festivals, celebrations and shared humanity
units.notes: Festivals mark important events in the life of a faith community and often include prayer, food, music, giving and family gathering. Examples include Christmas and Easter for Christians, Eid and the Prophet's birthday for Muslims, and Diwali and Holi for Hindus. Traditional harvest and initiation ceremonies are also observed in Kenyan communities. Celebrations teach generosity, gratitude and belonging. People of different faiths can share in one another's joy respectfully, and recognising these events promotes unity and understanding.
units.worked_example: At a school assembly, learners describe how their families celebrate different festivals, and the class discusses shared values of generosity, thanksgiving and family time.
units.activity: Prepare a short class presentation on one festival, showing its meaning, food, songs or dress and the values it teaches.
units.check: What values are shared by different religious festivals in Kenya?

quiz.prompt: What values are shared by different religious festivals in Kenya?
Which of these is a Muslim festival?
Festivals often include prayer, food, music, giving and family gathering?
Which festivals are celebrated by Hindus?
Recognising other people's festivals promotes unity and understanding?

English.overview: This guide develops senior secondary reading, writing, speaking and listening skills through analysis of texts, structured composition and oral communication. It builds the analytical and evidence-based literacy expected in Kenyan CBC Grade 10 to Grade 12.

units.title: Reading comprehension and inference
units.notes: Comprehension goes beyond locating facts on the page to interpreting what a writer implies. Skilled readers identify the main idea, separate supporting detail from illustration, and follow the logic of an argument. Inference means drawing a reasonable conclusion from evidence in the text rather than guessing. As you read passages about Kenyan life, markets or wildlife, ask what the writer assumes you already know. Track pronoun reference and cause and effect links carefully, because senior level questions reward precise textual evidence rather than general opinion.
units.worked_example: Given a passage about a farmer in Kitale losing a maize harvest to drought, a strong answer identifies the main idea as climate risk to smallholder income and cites the line about failed rains as evidence, rather than restating the whole paragraph.
units.activity: Read a newspaper editorial from a Kenyan daily and, in one paragraph, state its main claim and list two pieces of evidence the writer supplies.
units.check: What evidence in a passage lets you infer something the writer never states directly?

quiz.prompt: What does inference mean in reading comprehension?
options: Locating facts printed on the page
Guessing randomly at the writer's meaning
Drawing a reasonable conclusion from evidence in the text
Memorising every detail of a passage

quiz.prompt: At senior level, what should answers rely on most?
Which skill helps a reader follow links such as cause and effect in a passage?
options: Tracking pronoun reference and logical links

quiz.prompt: Is it true that inference means drawing a reasonable conclusion from evidence in the text rather than guessing?
When reading a passage, a skilled reader should separate the main idea from what?

units.title: Vocabulary development and word study
units.notes: A wide vocabulary is built deliberately, not accidentally. Study word roots, prefixes and suffixes to unlock unfamiliar words: knowing that bio means life helps you decode biology, biography and antibiotic. Distinguish denotation, the literal meaning, from connotation, the feeling a word carries, since a writer may call a settlement a village or a slum for very different effects. Record new words in context sentences, revise them weekly, and use them in your own writing so they become active rather than passive knowledge.
units.worked_example: If you meet the word sustainable in a geography text, the root sustain meaning to keep going plus the suffix able suggests something that can be maintained over time, as in sustainable farming.
units.activity: Collect ten new words from your textbook this week, write each in a sentence about school or home, and test a classmate on their meanings.
units.check: How does knowing the meaning of a prefix help you work out an unfamiliar word?

quiz.prompt: What does the prefix bio mean?
What is the difference between denotation and connotation?
options: Denotation is the feeling a word carries while connotation is its literal meaning
Denotation is the literal meaning while connotation is the feeling a word carries
They both mean exactly the same thing
Denotation applies only to spoken words

quiz.prompt: Why does the topic recommend recording new words in context sentences?
options: To make them active rather than passive knowledge
To increase the number of pages written
To avoid ever using a dictionary

quiz.prompt: Is it true that knowing bio means life helps you decode words such as biology and biography?
A writer may call a settlement a village or a slum mainly in order to do what?
options: Change the literal number of houses
Create very different effects through connotation
Improve the grammar of the sentence
Shorten the length of the text

units.title: Grammar: sentence structure and clauses
units.notes: A clause contains a subject and a verb; a phrase does not. An independent clause can stand alone as a sentence, while a dependent clause relies on a main clause to make complete sense. Recognise the three basic sentence types, simple, compound and complex, and notice how complex sentences let you show relationships of time, cause and condition with words like although, because and if. Varying sentence length and type is one of the fastest ways to improve the clarity and rhythm of senior writing.
units.worked_example: In Although the road was flooded, the students arrived on time, the first part is a dependent clause that sets a condition, and the second is the independent clause carrying the main message.
units.activity: Take a paragraph you have written and rewrite three of its simple sentences as complex sentences using subordinating conjunctions.
units.check: What is the difference between a phrase and a dependent clause?

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a phrase and a clause?
options: A clause contains a subject and a verb while a phrase does not
A phrase contains a subject and a verb while a clause does not
A phrase is always longer than a clause

quiz.prompt: Which clause can stand alone as a complete sentence?
Words such as although, because and if are used in complex sentences to show relationships of what?
Is it true that a dependent clause relies on a main clause to make complete sense?
Why does the topic suggest varying sentence length and type?
options: To improve the clarity and rhythm of writing

units.title: Punctuation and mechanics
units.notes: Punctuation is the traffic system of writing: it tells readers where to pause, what belongs together and where ideas end. Master the comma for lists and introductory phrases, the semicolon for joining closely related independent clauses, and the colon for introducing lists or explanations. Apostrophes show possession or contraction, and quotation marks frame direct speech accurately. Careless punctuation can reverse meaning, so proofread deliberately. In formal examination writing, correct mechanics signal control and protect the marks your content deserves.
units.worked_example: Compare Lets eat, grandma with Lets eat grandma: a single comma changes the meaning completely, showing why punctuation is not decoration but sense.
units.activity: Write six sentences using a semicolon, a colon, an apostrophe for possession and quotation marks for direct speech, then swap with a partner to check.
units.check: When should you use a semicolon instead of a full stop?

quiz.prompt: What does a semicolon do?
options: It joins closely related independent clauses

quiz.prompt: A colon is mainly used to do what?
options: Introduce a list or an explanation

quiz.prompt: Apostrophes are used to show what?
Is it true that punctuation matters less in formal examination writing than in casual writing?
Which mark is used to frame direct speech accurately?

units.title: Summary writing and note making
units.notes: Summary writing tests whether you can compress meaning without losing the essential points. Identify the topic sentence of each paragraph, decide what is central and what is merely illustrative, and then express the core ideas in your own words, keeping within the required word limit. Note making applies the same skill in a different form, using headings and short points rather than continuous prose. Both demand that you think about importance and hierarchy of ideas, which is a transferable skill in every senior subject.
units.worked_example: From a two hundred word article on the benefits of tree planting, a good fifty word summary states that trees conserve soil, regulate rainfall and provide income, without listing every example the writer gave.
units.activity: Summarise a one page passage from your history or biology textbook in no more than sixty words, keeping three main points.
units.check: What should you leave out of a summary, and why?

quiz.prompt: What is the key skill in summary writing?
options: Compressing meaning without losing essential points
Copying the passage word for word

quiz.prompt: What should you look for in each paragraph before summarising it?
Is it true that a summary should include every illustrative example from the original text?
How does note making differ from continuous prose?
options: It uses headings and short points
It must be more formal than an essay
It uses no words at all

quiz.prompt: Why are illustrative details usually left out of a summary?
options: They are central to the meaning
They are not central to the core ideas
They make the summary too short

units.title: Functional writing: letters and emails
units.notes: Functional writing has a purpose and an audience, and its format changes accordingly. A formal letter includes your address, the recipient address, the date, a salutation, a clear subject line, structured body paragraphs and a formal closing. An email mirrors this logic with a meaningful subject line and a courteous tone. The style is direct and impersonal, avoiding slang and casual abbreviations. Learning to write for a real audience, from a head teacher to a county officer, prepares you for civic and professional communication.
units.worked_example: A letter to the county director of education requesting permission to hold a school clean up would open with the reason, state the date and venue, and close by formally requesting approval.
units.activity: Draft a formal email to a local business inviting it to support your class community project, then review the subject line and tone.
units.check: Why does a formal letter avoid the abbreviations common in text messages?

quiz.prompt: Which of these belongs in a formal letter?
What is the tone of formal functional writing?
Is it true that an email should have a meaningful subject line and a courteous tone?
Why does a formal letter avoid the abbreviations common in text messages?
options: They suggest a casual style unsuitable for a formal audience

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate element of a formal letter?

units.title: Functional writing: reports and speeches
units.notes: Reports record what happened, while speeches persuade a live audience. A report usually opens with terms of reference, describes the activity, presents findings and ends with recommendations, all in neutral language. A speech uses a direct opening address, signposts the main points, builds rhythm with repetition and ends with a memorable call to action. Both demand careful structure because listeners and readers cannot easily re-read a muddled message. Keep the audience, occasion and purpose clear in your mind before you begin drafting.
units.worked_example: A speech for a school assembly on conserving water might open with Fellow students, imagine a week without taps, list three practical measures, and close by asking each class to appoint a water monitor.
units.activity: Write a short report on a class excursion, then present the same content as a two minute speech to your group.
