units.title: Sports leadership, ethics and first aid
units.notes: Sports leaders plan sessions, manage groups and promote fair play, respect and inclusion. Ethical issues include doping, cheating, match fixing and the treatment of young athletes. Leaders apply the RICE method for soft-tissue injuries and know how to manage bleeding, fainting and suspected fractures. Emergency action plans ensure rapid response when accidents occur. Good leadership communicates clearly, motivates others and keeps participants safe. These skills transfer to careers in coaching, officiating and sports administration.
units.worked_example: For a sprained ankle, the RICE method means rest, ice for about 20 minutes, compression and elevation to limit swelling.
units.activity: Plan and lead a ten-minute warm-up for a small group, then ask peers for one strength and one improvement.

Biology.overview: Senior school Biology explores living organisms from cells to ecosystems, developing the analytical and investigative skills needed to explain life processes, inheritance, human systems and the interactions that sustain Kenya's biodiversity.

units.title: Cell structure and organisation
units.notes: All living things are built from cells, the basic units of structure and function. Prokaryotic cells such as bacteria lack a membrane-bound nucleus, while eukaryotic cells in plants, animals and fungi have one. Organelles perform specialised roles: mitochondria release energy, ribosomes build proteins and chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis. Cells are organised into tissues, organs, systems and organisms. The microscope reveals structures too small for the naked eye. Understanding cells underpins nutrition, transport, genetics and health.
units.worked_example: A plant cell placed in pure water swells because its strong cellulose wall resists bursting, unlike an animal cell which would lyse.
units.activity: Prepare a wet mount of onion epidermis, stain it with iodine and draw the cells you observe under low and medium power.
units.check: Which organelle would be most abundant in a muscle cell that uses large amounts of energy?

units.title: Cell division and the cell cycle
units.notes: Cell division allows growth, repair and reproduction. Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells and is central to growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis halves the chromosome number to form gametes and creates genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment. The cell cycle includes interphase, where DNA replicates, and the mitotic phase, where chromosomes separate. Uncontrolled division can lead to tumours. Comparing the two divisions reveals their distinct purposes.
units.worked_example: A human body cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis to give two cells each with 46, while meiosis gives gametes with 23.
units.activity: Use a prepared slide of onion root tip to find and sketch cells at different stages of mitosis.

options: Gametes with half the chromosome number, creating variation

units.title: Nutrition in plants: photosynthesis
units.notes: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light, and carbon dioxide plus water are converted in the presence of light, releasing oxygen. The process has light-dependent and light-independent stages. Factors limiting the rate include light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. Plants are producers, forming the base of food chains. The stored energy supports nearly all life on Earth.
units.worked_example: A pondweed experiment counting oxygen bubbles shows the rate of photosynthesis rising as a lamp is moved closer, until another factor becomes limiting.
units.activity: Test a de-starched leaf for starch after exposing it to light, using iodine solution to confirm photosynthesis occurred.
units.check: Which three factors can limit the rate of photosynthesis in a green plant?

quiz.prompt: What does photosynthesis convert light energy into?

options: Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature

quiz.prompt: Is it true that photosynthesis releases oxygen?

options: They form the base of food chains by making their own food

units.title: Nutrition in animals and human digestion
units.notes: Animals need carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage. Digestion breaks large food molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. Mechanical digestion happens in the mouth and stomach, while enzymes such as amylase, pepsin and lipase act chemically. Absorption occurs mainly in the ileum, where villi increase surface area. Teeth and dental health matter for efficient chewing. A balanced diet prevents deficiency diseases such as kwashiorkor and scurvy.
units.worked_example: Starch begins digestion in the mouth by salivary amylase and is completed in the small intestine by pancreatic amylase into maltose and glucose.
units.activity: Test food samples such as ugali, milk and groundnut for starch, protein and lipids using iodine, Biuret and emulsion tests.

options: They increase the surface area for absorption

options: Small soluble ones that can be absorbed

units.title: Transport in plants
units.notes: Plants transport water and minerals through xylem and food through phloem. Water is absorbed by root hairs and moves up the stem by transpiration pull, cohesion and adhesion. Transpiration is the loss of water vapour through stomata and is affected by temperature, humidity, wind and light. It cools the plant and drives the upward flow of water. Wilting occurs when water loss exceeds uptake. Understanding transport helps explain irrigation and crop management.
units.worked_example: On a hot windy day a plant transpires faster than on a cool still day, so it may wilt unless watered promptly.
units.activity: Measure water loss by placing leafy shoots in graduated tubes under a fan and a still shelter, then compare results.
units.check: How does transpiration pull help water reach the leaves of a tall tree?

quiz.prompt: Through which tissue do water and minerals move in a plant?

options: The loss of water vapour through stomata

quiz.prompt: Is it true that transpiration pull, cohesion and adhesion help water move up the stem?
When does wilting occur?
options: When water uptake exceeds water loss

units.title: Transport in animals: the circulatory system
units.notes: Mammals use a double circulatory system in which blood passes through the heart twice per circuit. The heart's chambers and valves ensure one-way flow, while arteries, veins and capillaries suit different functions. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones and waste. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin that binds oxygen, and plasma transports dissolved substances. The heartbeat is controlled by the pacemaker and influenced by exercise and hormones. Regular activity strengthens the heart and improves circulation.
units.worked_example: During exercise, adrenaline raises heart rate and arterioles in muscles widen so more oxygen reaches working tissue.
units.activity: Measure your pulse before and after one minute of step-ups, then explain the change using the idea of demand for oxygen.
units.check: Why is the human circulatory system described as a double circulation?

quiz.prompt: Why is the human circulatory system described as a double circulation?
options: Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit

units.title: Respiration and gaseous exchange
units.notes: Respiration releases energy from food molecules in every living cell. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose into carbon dioxide and water, releasing much energy. Anaerobic respiration yields less energy and produces lactic acid in muscles or ethanol in yeast. Gaseous exchange in mammals occurs in alveoli, which have thin walls, rich blood supply and large surface area. Breathing brings air to the lungs, but respiration happens in cells. Oxygen debt explains continued heavy breathing after exercise.
units.worked_example: Yeast in warm sugar solution respires anaerobically, producing ethanol and carbon dioxide that makes bread dough rise.
units.activity: Investigate yeast respiration by trapping carbon dioxide in limewater at different temperatures and noting cloudiness.
units.check: Why does the body continue breathing heavily after vigorous exercise ends?

units.title: Excretion and homeostasis
units.notes: Excretion removes metabolic waste while homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable. The kidneys filter blood, reabsorb useful substances and excrete urea, excess salts and water as urine. The liver deaminates amino acids to form urea and breaks down toxins. Negative feedback controls body temperature, blood glucose and water balance. In hot Kenyan conditions, sweating and reduced urine output help conserve water. Failure of these systems causes serious illness.
units.worked_example: After drinking little water, antidiuretic hormone rises, so the kidney reabsorbs more water and urine becomes concentrated and dark.
units.activity: Compare the colour and volume of your urine after a hot game and after resting, then link this to water balance.

units.title: Support, movement and the skeleton
units.notes: The human skeleton supports the body, protects organs, allows movement and stores minerals. It is made of living bone, cartilage and connective tissue. Joints include hinge, ball-and-socket, pivot and fixed types, each allowing different movement. Muscles attach to bones by tendons and work in antagonistic pairs. The skeleton also produces blood cells in the marrow. Comparing human bones with those of other vertebrates reveals adaptation.
units.worked_example: The elbow is a hinge joint that allows bending in one plane, while the shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint allowing many directions.
units.activity: Label a diagram of the skeleton and mark three hinge joints, two ball-and-socket joints and one fixed joint.

units.title: Coordination: nervous and hormonal systems
units.notes: The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate body activities. The nervous system uses fast electrical impulses along neurones, with a synapse between cells. Reflex actions are rapid, automatic responses that protect the body. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. Hormones are slower chemical messengers carried in blood that control growth, reproduction and metabolism. The pituitary gland directs several other glands. Comparing both systems shows how speed and duration differ.
units.worked_example: Touching a hot sufuria triggers a reflex withdrawal of the hand before the brain consciously registers the pain.
units.activity: Draw and label a reflex arc from receptor to effector, marking where a synapse occurs.

options: A rapid automatic response that protects the body

units.title: Reproduction and growth
units.notes: Reproduction ensures continuity of species. In flowering plants, pollination transfers pollen to the stigma, followed by fertilisation, seed and fruit formation. In humans, gametes fuse to form a zygote that develops in the uterus. The placenta supplies nutrients and oxygen and removes waste. Growth occurs by cell division and cell enlargement and can be measured with height and mass charts. Knowledge of reproduction supports reproductive health and responsible decision-making.
units.worked_example: A bean flower pollinated by insects forms seeds inside a pod, and each seed can grow into a new plant under suitable conditions.
units.activity: Dissect a bean flower to identify the stigma, style, ovary, anther and filament, then draw a labelled diagram.

units.title: Genetics and inheritance
units.notes: Genetics explains how characteristics pass from parents to offspring. Genes on chromosomes carry instructions, with alleles as alternative forms of a gene. Dominant and recessive alleles determine phenotype, and the genotype is the allele combination. Mendel's laws describe segregation and independent assortment. Monohybrid crosses predict the ratios of offspring. Mutation, sex determination and genetic disorders illustrate further principles of inheritance. Careful reasoning about ratios links genotype to observable traits.
units.worked_example: A cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt x Tt) gives a phenotypic ratio of three tall to one short.
units.activity: Use a Punnett square to predict the offspring of a cross between two heterozygous parents for tongue rolling.

units.title: Ecology, conservation and human impact
units.notes: Ecology studies interactions among organisms and their environment. Energy flows through food chains and webs, while nutrients cycle through ecosystems. Populations are affected by competition, predation and disease. Human activities such as deforestation, pollution and poaching reduce biodiversity. Conservation measures include protected areas, reforestation and sustainable farming. Understanding ecology supports responsible management of Kenya's forests, lakes and wildlife. Learners can evaluate local issues using evidence.
units.worked_example: Removing a predator from a food web can cause herbivore numbers to rise and overgraze vegetation, upsetting the whole ecosystem.
units.activity: Survey a small area near your school, record the organisms present and construct a simple food web.
units.check: Why does energy decrease at each level of a food chain?

options: Interactions among organisms and their environment

Chemistry.overview: Senior school Chemistry builds a quantitative and structural understanding of matter, moving from atoms and bonding through the mole, acids, salts and electrochemistry to organic chemistry and analytical technique.

units.title: Atomic structure and the periodic table
units.notes: Atoms consist of protons and neutrons in the nucleus with electrons arranged in shells. Atomic number gives the number of protons and determines the element's identity. Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, showing periodic trends such as reactivity and atomic radius. Group properties help predict how elements react. Electron configuration explains these patterns clearly and predictably.
units.worked_example: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are isotopes with 17 protons each but 18 and 20 neutrons respectively; the average gives a relative atomic mass of about 35.5.
units.activity: Draw electron arrangements for the first twenty elements and identify which belong to the same group.

options: They have the same number of neutrons

units.title: Chemical bonding and structure
units.notes: Atoms bond to achieve stable electron arrangements. Ionic bonding involves transfer of electrons between metals and non-metals, forming charged ions in giant lattices. Covalent bonding involves sharing electrons, producing molecules or giant covalent structures. Metallic bonding involves delocalised electrons and explains conduction. Bond type strongly influences melting point, solubility and conductivity. Learners predict properties from structure and bonding rather than memorising facts, and they test predictions against evidence.
units.worked_example: Sodium chloride conducts electricity only when molten or dissolved because its ions must be free to move, whereas solid salt does not conduct.
units.activity: Compare the melting points of salt, sugar and candle wax, then explain the differences using bonding and structure.
units.check: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity while molten sodium chloride does?

quiz.prompt: Ionic bonding involves what?
options: Transfer of electrons between metals and non-metals

quiz.prompt: Covalent bonding involves what?
Metallic bonding involves what?
Is it true that solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity while molten sodium chloride does?
Bond type strongly influences what?

units.title: The mole concept and stoichiometry
units.notes: The mole is the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23. Molar mass links mass and moles, while concentration links moles and volume. Balanced equations give mole ratios that allow quantitative predictions of reactants and products. Stoichiometry is used to calculate masses, volumes and concentrations in reactions. Identifying the limiting reactant determines the actual yield. Percentage yield compares actual and theoretical results.
units.worked_example: How many moles are in 20 g of calcium carbonate? Moles equal 20 divided by 100, giving 0.20 mol.
units.activity: Calculate the mass of sodium chloride formed when 0.10 mol of sodium hydroxide reacts fully with hydrochloric acid.

Percentage yield compares what?

units.title: Gases and the gas laws
units.notes: Gases are described by pressure, volume, temperature and amount. Boyle's law states that pressure and volume are inversely proportional at constant temperature. Charles's law relates volume directly to absolute temperature at constant pressure. The combined and ideal gas equations link all variables. Absolute temperature must be in kelvin for these calculations. Molar gas volume allows volumes of gases in reactions to be calculated from balanced equations.
units.worked_example: A gas at 2.0 atm in 3.0 litres is expanded to 6.0 litres at constant temperature, so the new pressure is 1.0 atm.
units.activity: Use the ideal gas equation to find the volume occupied by 0.50 mol of gas at 273 K and 1.0 atm.

options: Volume directly to absolute temperature at constant pressure

Is it true that gases are described by pressure, volume, temperature and amount?
Molar gas volume allows you to calculate what?
options: Volumes of gases in reactions from balanced equations

units.title: Acids, bases and indicators
units.notes: Acids release hydrogen ions in solution and bases accept them; alkalis are soluble bases. The pH scale runs from 0 to 14, with values below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline. Strong acids ionise almost completely while weak acids ionise partially. Indicators and the pH meter measure acidity, and titration determines unknown concentrations. Neutralisation produces salt and water. Acidity affects soils, digestion and industry, so understanding it has wide relevance.
units.worked_example: A strong acid like hydrochloric acid has a very low pH because it ionises fully, while ethanoic acid of the same concentration has a higher pH as it ionises only partly.
units.activity: Test household substances such as lemon juice, soap and milk with universal indicator and record their approximate pH.
units.check: Why does a weak acid have a higher pH than a strong acid of the same concentration?

What is the range of the pH scale?

Is it true that neutralisation produces salt and water?
What is an alkali?

units.title: Salts: preparation and solubility
units.notes: Salts form when the hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. Soluble salts are prepared by reacting an acid with a metal, base or carbonate, followed by filtration, evaporation and crystallisation. Insoluble salts such as barium sulphate are made by precipitation. Solubility rules predict whether a salt will dissolve. Salt names combine the metal with the acid's anion. Purification and drying produce pure crystals suitable for analysis.
units.worked_example: To prepare copper(II) sulphate crystals, excess copper(II) oxide is added to warm dilute sulphuric acid, then filtered, and the filtrate is evaporated to crystallise.
units.activity: Prepare a sample of copper(II) sulphate crystals and record the mass of crystals obtained from a known volume of acid.
units.check: Which method would you use to prepare an insoluble salt such as barium sulphate?

units.title: Electrochemistry: electrolysis and cells
units.notes: Electrochemistry studies the relationship between electricity and chemical change. In electrolysis, electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous reaction, with oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Ions migrate toward oppositely charged electrodes. Electroplating and metal extraction use electrolysis industrially. Electrochemical cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy. Reactivity determines the direction of electron flow. Predicting products requires careful application of ion discharge rules.
units.worked_example: During electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, lead forms at the cathode and bromine is released at the anode.
units.activity: Electrolyse copper(II) sulphate solution with copper electrodes and observe the colour change and deposit at the cathode.

units.title: Energy changes in chemical reactions
units.notes: Chemical reactions either release energy (exothermic) or absorb it (endothermic). Energy changes arise from breaking and forming bonds. Bond breaking absorbs energy and bond forming releases it. Enthalpy change measures the heat exchanged at constant pressure. Energy level diagrams show reactants, products and activation energy. Catalysts lower activation energy without changing the overall enthalpy change. These ideas explain fuels, respiration and many industrial processes.
units.worked_example: Combustion of methane is exothermic because the energy released forming carbon dioxide and water bonds exceeds the energy needed to break the reactant bonds.
units.activity: Measure the temperature change when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid and classify the reaction.
units.check: Why does a catalyst speed up a reaction without changing the enthalpy change?

quiz.prompt: What is an exothermic reaction?
What happens to energy when bonds are broken?

options: Lowers activation energy without changing the enthalpy change

quiz.prompt: Is it true that bond forming releases energy?

units.title: Rates of reaction and equilibrium
units.notes: The rate of a reaction measures how quickly reactants are used or products formed. Factors affecting rate include concentration, temperature, surface area, pressure and catalysts. Collision theory explains these effects through frequency and energy of collisions. Reversible reactions may reach dynamic equilibrium where forward and reverse rates are equal. Le Chatelier's principle predicts how changes in conditions shift equilibrium. These ideas guide the optimisation of industrial processes such as ammonia manufacture.
units.worked_example: Powdered marble reacts faster with acid than a large chip because the greater surface area increases the frequency of collisions.
units.activity: React marble chips of different sizes with dilute acid and measure the volume of gas collected over time.
units.check: How does increasing temperature increase the rate of a chemical reaction?

options: The effects of conditions through the frequency and energy of collisions

quiz.prompt: How does increasing temperature increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: By increasing the frequency and energy of collisions

quiz.prompt: What may reversible reactions reach?
options: Dynamic equilibrium where forward and reverse rates are equal

quiz.prompt: Is it true that Le Chatelier's principle predicts how changes in conditions shift equilibrium?

options: Concentration, temperature, surface area, pressure and catalysts

units.title: Organic chemistry: hydrocarbons
units.notes: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, which are central to fuels, plastics and life. Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes are saturated with single bonds, while alkenes contain a carbon-carbon double bond. Homologous series share a general formula and show gradual changes in properties. Structural and molecular formulae represent compounds. Fractional distillation separates crude oil into useful fractions with different boiling points and uses.
units.worked_example: Ethene, C2H4, is an alkene that decolourises bromine water, whereas ethane, C2H6, an alkane, does not.

An alkene decolourises it while an alkane does not

quiz.prompt: Is it true that fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions with different boiling points?
What do members of a homologous series share?
options: A general formula with gradual changes in properties

units.title: Organic chemistry: functional groups
units.notes: Functional groups determine the chemical properties of organic compounds. Alcohols contain a hydroxyl group, carboxylic acids a carboxyl group, and esters form from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid. Aldehydes and ketones contain a carbonyl group. Functional group tests, such as oxidation of alcohols, identify compounds. Esters have pleasant smells used in flavourings and perfumes. Naming follows the parent chain plus the suffix for the group.
units.worked_example: Ethanol oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate turns the solution from orange to green, forming ethanoic acid.

units.title: Metals, extraction and reactivity
units.notes: The reactivity series ranks metals by their tendency to lose electrons. More reactive metals are extracted by electrolysis, while less reactive ones may be reduced by carbon. Iron is extracted in a blast furnace using coke and limestone. Metals react with oxygen, water and acids to varying degrees. Displacement reactions reveal relative reactivity. Alloys are mixtures of metals designed for strength or resistance, such as steel and bronze.
units.worked_example: Zinc displaces copper from copper(II) sulphate solution because zinc is higher in the reactivity series, forming zinc sulphate.
units.activity: Place strips of zinc, iron and copper in copper(II) sulphate solution and record which cause a colour change.

units.title: Quantitative analysis and laboratory technique
units.notes: Quantitative analysis determines how much of a substance is present. Titration, gravimetric analysis and colorimetry are common methods. Accurate measurement requires correct apparatus, calibration and technique. Concentration can be expressed in moles per cubic decimetre or grams per litre. Errors are classified as systematic or random, and precision differs from accuracy. Repeating measurements and averaging improve reliability. These skills support chemistry in industry, medicine and research.

Physics.overview: Senior school Physics develops a mathematical and experimental understanding of mechanics, waves, electricity, magnetism, thermal physics, optics and modern physics, with emphasis on calculation, measurement and evaluation.

units.title: Measurement and physical quantities
units.notes: Physics depends on accurate measurement of quantities such as length, mass, time and current. SI units provide a consistent system, with prefixes for very large and small values. Instruments have a least count that limits their precision. Errors may be systematic or random and should be reduced by careful technique and averaging. Derived quantities combine base units, as with speed in metres per second. Good measurement underpins every later experiment and calculation.
units.worked_example: A vernier caliper reading 2.46 cm is more precise than a metre rule reading 2.5 cm because its least count is 0.01 cm.
units.activity: Measure the thickness of a coin, the length of a desk and your heart rate, then state the SI unit and instrument used.
units.check: Why does repeating a measurement several times improve reliability?

quiz.prompt: What do SI units provide in physics?
What limits the precision of a measuring instrument?

options: It reduces the effect of random errors

units.title: Kinematics: motion in a straight line
units.notes: Kinematics describes motion using displacement, velocity and acceleration without considering causes. Average speed equals distance over time, while velocity includes direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Equations of motion relate initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time and displacement for uniform acceleration. Motion graphs show the relations among these quantities. Free fall is a common example near the Earth's surface.
units.worked_example: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.0 m/s2 for 5.0 s, reaching 10.0 m/s and covering 25.0 m.

units.title: Forces and Newton's laws of motion
units.notes: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's shape or motion. Newton's first law states that a body stays at rest or moves uniformly unless acted on by a resultant force. The second law relates resultant force to mass and acceleration. The third law states that action and reaction forces are equal and opposite. Free-body diagrams help analyse forces. Friction and weight are common forces affecting motion.
units.worked_example: A 5.0 kg mass pushed with a resultant force of 20 N accelerates at 4.0 m/s2, because acceleration equals force divided by mass.

units.title: Work, energy and power
units.notes: Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force. Energy exists in many forms and is measured in joules, and it is conserved but can transfer and transform. Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed, while gravitational potential energy depends on mass, height and gravity. Power is the rate of doing work. Efficiency compares useful output to total input. Simple machines trade force for distance.
units.worked_example: A 2.0 kg bag lifted 3.0 m gains 58.8 J of potential energy, using gravitational field strength of 9.8 N/kg.

units.title: Momentum and collisions
units.notes: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity and is a vector quantity. In a closed system, total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after it. Collisions may be elastic, conserving kinetic energy, or inelastic, where energy transforms to other forms. Impulse equals the change in momentum and depends on force and contact time. Safety features such as airbags extend contact time to reduce force. These principles explain many everyday events.
units.worked_example: A 4.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m/s collides with a stationary 2.0 kg trolley and they stick together, giving a common velocity of 2.0 m/s.

units.title: Circular motion and gravitation
units.notes: An object moving in a circle at constant speed still accelerates because its direction changes. This centripetal acceleration points toward the centre and requires a centripetal force. Common examples include a stone on a string and a car on a bend. Gravitational force provides the centripetal force for planets and satellites. Newton's law of gravitation states that force depends on masses and distance. Weight varies with gravitational field strength across bodies in the solar system.
units.worked_example: A satellite stays in orbit because gravity supplies the centripetal force that continually bends its path around the Earth.

units.title: Thermal physics and heat transfer
units.notes: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles, while heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference. Heat transfers by conduction, convection and radiation. Solids conduct mainly by particle vibration and free electrons, while fluids convect through density changes. Radiation travels without a medium and is affected by surface colour and texture. Specific heat capacity describes energy needed to raise temperature. These ideas explain cooking, insulation and climate.
units.worked_example: Heating 1.0 kg of water by 10 degrees Celsius needs 42000 J, using a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg per degree Celsius.

units.title: Waves and sound
units.notes: Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Transverse waves have vibrations perpendicular to travel, while longitudinal waves have vibrations along the direction of travel. Key features include wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed, related by speed equals frequency times wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave needing a medium. Reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference are common wave behaviours. Understanding waves explains communication and hearing.
units.worked_example: A wave of frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4.0 m travels at 200 m/s, since speed equals frequency times wavelength.

units.title: Light: reflection and refraction
units.notes: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium and can be reflected or refracted. The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Refraction occurs because light changes speed when entering a new medium. Snell's law relates the angles and refractive indices. Lenses and mirrors form real or virtual images, described by ray diagrams. These principles explain spectacles, cameras and the human eye.

units.title: Electrostatics and current electricity
units.notes: Electrostatics deals with charges at rest, produced by friction and stored on surfaces. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Current is the rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes. Ohm's law relates voltage, current and resistance for a conductor at constant temperature. Resistors may be arranged in series or parallel, changing total resistance. Electrical energy and power depend on current, voltage and time.

units.title: Magnetism and electromagnetic induction
units.notes: Magnets have north and south poles and produce magnetic fields. A current-carrying conductor creates a magnetic field, and a force acts on it within an external field, which is the motor effect. Electromagnetic induction occurs when a conductor moves in a magnetic field or when flux changes, generating an electromotive force. Faraday's and Lenz's laws explain the magnitude and direction of induced current. These principles underpin generators, transformers and motors.
units.worked_example: Moving a magnet quickly into a coil induces a larger current than moving it slowly, as the rate of change of magnetic flux is greater.

units.title: Electronics and modern physics
units.notes: Electronics uses components such as diodes, transistors and logic gates to control current. A diode allows current in one direction, enabling rectification of alternating current. Transistors amplify signals and act as switches. Modern physics includes the photoelectric effect, wave-particle duality and the structure of the atom. Photons carry energy proportional to frequency. These ideas led to solar cells, medical imaging and computers, connecting theory to real technology.

units.title: Practical physics and experimental method
units.notes: Practical physics develops skills in planning, measuring, recording and evaluating experiments. A good investigation states an aim, identifies variables and controls them fairly. Data are recorded in tables and displayed in graphs, with lines of best fit and error bars where appropriate. Conclusions must be supported by evidence, and sources of error discussed. Uncertainty analysis strengthens the reliability of results. These transferable skills support science and engineering pathways.

Geography.overview: Geography is the study of the Earth, its physical features, human activities and the relationships between them. This guide builds mapwork, physical, human, economic and regional understanding for senior secondary learners.

units.title: Introduction to geography and its branches
units.notes: Geography is the study of the Earth, its physical features and human activities, and the relationships between them. It is divided into physical geography, which examines landforms, climate, soils and vegetation, and human geography, which studies population, settlement and economic activity. In Kenya, geographers use observation, maps, statistics and fieldwork to explain patterns such as why farming dominates the highlands. Geography also trains learners to think spatially and to evaluate how people interact with their environment. It links closely with history, agriculture and business studies.
units.worked_example: A student comparing rainfall data for Kisumu and Garissa would find that Kisumu receives more rain, then conclude that lake proximity and altitude influence local climate.
units.activity: Sketch a simple map of your school compound and label five features, then list which branch of geography each feature relates to.

units.title: Mapwork: scale, direction and bearings
units.notes: Mapwork is the skill of reading and interpreting maps to describe locations and measure distances and areas. Scale shows the relationship between map distance and ground distance, and it may be stated, linear or a representative fraction. Direction is found using compass points, while a bearing is measured clockwise from north in degrees. Learners compute distance, gradient and area from maps and draw cross sections to show relief. These skills support fieldwork, planning and the location of resources and services.

Is it true that scale shows the relationship between distance on the map and distance on the ground?
Is it true that a bearing is measured anticlockwise from north?

units.title: The Earth's structure and plate tectonics
units.notes: The Earth has a crust, mantle and core, and the solid outer crust together with the upper mantle forms the lithosphere. This lithosphere is broken into large plates that move slowly over the plastic asthenosphere. Their movement causes earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and mountain building at plate boundaries. Convergent, divergent and transform boundaries each produce different landforms and hazards. Understanding tectonics explains why Kenya has features such as the Rift Valley and active geothermal areas.
units.worked_example: At a convergent boundary, an oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate, forming a deep trench and a chain of volcanoes such as those of the Andes.
units.activity: Draw a labelled diagram of the three plate boundary types and mark one real example of each from around the world.
units.check: What landforms are likely to form where two plates move apart?

quiz.prompt: The lithosphere is made up of which of the following?
options: The solid outer crust and the upper mantle

quiz.prompt: Over which layer do the Earth's plates move slowly?
Which type of plate boundary forms where two plates move apart?
Is it true that the Rift Valley in Kenya is associated with plate tectonic activity?
Is it true that earthquakes and volcanic eruptions happen only far away from plate boundaries?

units.title: Weather elements and their measurement
units.notes: Weather describes the short-term condition of the atmosphere, while climate is the average weather of a place over many years. Key elements include temperature, rainfall, humidity, pressure, wind and sunshine. Each is measured with specific instruments such as thermometers, rain gauges, barometers and anemometers. Weather stations record these elements at set times and the data is used for forecasting and farming decisions. Accurate records help farmers in Nyandarua time planting and help pilots plan safe flights.
units.worked_example: A school weather station records 24 mm of rain on Monday and 0 mm on Tuesday; the two-day total is 24 mm, suggesting a dry spell is setting in.
units.activity: Set up a simple rain gauge using a straight-sided tin and record daily rainfall for one week.
units.check: How does weather differ from climate?

quiz.prompt: Which instrument is used to measure rainfall?
Which statement correctly describes weather?

The short-term condition of the atmosphere

quiz.prompt: Which instrument measures wind speed?
Is it true that climate is the average weather of a place over many years?
Is it true that accurate weather records are of no use to farmers when timing planting?

units.title: Climate regions and the factors that control them
units.notes: The world has climate types ranging from equatorial to desert, Mediterranean, temperate and polar. Climate is controlled by latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, winds and relief. Latitude matters because the sun's rays strike the equator more directly than the poles. Kenya experiences equatorial, tropical, semi-arid and modified highland climates. Comparing these regions shows how one country can support very different farming and settlement patterns.
units.worked_example: Mombasa is hot and humid because it lies near the equator at low altitude, while Nairobi is cooler because it stands about 1 700 m above sea level.
units.activity: Use a rainfall and temperature table to classify three Kenyan towns into climate types and justify each choice.
units.check: Why are highland areas cooler than nearby lowland areas at the same latitude?

quiz.prompt: Why does latitude affect climate?
options: The sun's rays strike the equator more directly than the poles
The equator is farther from the sun than the poles
The poles receive more sunlight than the equator
Latitude has no effect on climate

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are factors that control climate?
options: Altitude and distance from the sea

quiz.prompt: Which climate type is found near the equator?
Is it true that highland areas are cooler than nearby lowland areas at the same latitude?
Is it true that distance from the sea has no effect on a place's climate?

units.title: Soils and natural vegetation
units.notes: Soil forms from weathered rock mixed with organic matter, water and air over long periods. Its properties include texture, structure, colour, depth and fertility, and these determine what can grow on it. Vegetation types such as forest, savanna, grassland and desert scrub reflect rainfall, temperature and soils. In Kenya, fertile volcanic soils support tea and coffee in the highlands. Human activities like deforestation, overgrazing and poor farming threaten soils and vegetation, so conservation matters.
units.worked_example: A soil that feels gritty and drains quickly is sandy; it warms fast but holds few nutrients, so it suits drought-tolerant crops such as sorghum.
units.activity: Collect soil samples from two sites, compare their colour and texture by feel, and record the differences.
units.check: How does soil texture influence the crops a farmer can grow?

quiz.prompt: Soil is formed from which of the following?
options: Weathered rock mixed with organic matter, water and air

quiz.prompt: Which soil property strongly influences drainage, aeration and nutrient availability?

Is it true that deforestation and overgrazing have no effect on soils and vegetation?

units.title: Rivers, drainage and water resources
units.notes: A river system begins at its source, gathers tributaries in a drainage basin and ends at its mouth. Rivers erode, transport and deposit material along their course, creating valleys, meanders, floodplains and deltas. Drainage patterns depend on rock type, relief and climate. Kenya's rivers, such as the Tana and the Athi, support irrigation, hydroelectric power and domestic supply. Managing rivers involves controlling pollution, floods and competing demands for scarce water.
units.worked_example: A river carrying a heavy load slows as it enters a lake, so it deposits sediment and gradually builds a delta, as at the mouth of the Tana.
units.activity: Trace the course of a nearby river on a map and mark its source, main tributaries and mouth.
units.check: Why does a river deposit material when it slows down?

quiz.prompt: What is a drainage basin?
options: The area drained by a river and its tributaries
The mouth of a river only

units.title: Denudation, landforms and landscape development
units.notes: Denudation is the wearing down of the land by weathering, erosion, transport and deposition. Weathering may be physical, chemical or biological, and it breaks rock in place without moving it. Running water, wind, ice and waves then transport the loosened material. Over time these processes create landforms such as hills, plains, escarpments and valleys. In Kenya, the Aberdare escarpment and the Chalbi desert record long periods of erosion and deposition.
units.worked_example: Repeated heating and cooling in a desert causes rock to expand and contract, producing block disintegration that splits the rock into angular fragments.
units.activity: Examine photographs of two landscapes, identify the landforms, and suggest which processes shaped each one.
units.check: How does weathering differ from erosion?

options: The wearing down of the land by weathering, erosion, transport and deposition
The building up of mountains only

options: Weathering breaks rock in place without moving it

quiz.prompt: Which of the following lists types of weathering?

units.title: Population geography
units.notes: Population geography studies the size, distribution, structure and movement of people. Birth rates, death rates and migration change population numbers and composition. A population pyramid shows age and sex structure and helps planners predict demand for schools, clinics and jobs. Kenya's population is young and unevenly distributed, with dense settlement in highland areas. Understanding these patterns helps explain pressure on land, urban growth and the use of resources.
units.worked_example: A country whose population pyramid has a wide base and narrow top has many children and few elderly people, indicating high birth and death rates.
units.activity: Survey ten households in your locality for family size and draw a simple bar graph of the results.
units.check: Why do population pyramids help governments plan services?

options: Birth rates, death rates and migration

units.title: Settlement patterns and urbanisation
units.notes: Settlements range from scattered homesteads to villages, towns and cities. Their location depends on water, fertile land, transport, defence and resources. Rural to urban migration drives urbanisation, which brings opportunities and also problems such as congestion, poor housing and strain on services. Nairobi and Kisumu illustrate rapid urban growth in Kenya. Planned settlement and land-use zoning aim to balance housing, industry, transport and green space.
units.worked_example: A town located at a crossroads grows faster than a nearby village because businesses and transport routes concentrate people and trade there.
units.activity: Map your local area and classify its settlement pattern as scattered, linear or nucleated, giving reasons.
units.check: What problems can rapid urbanisation create for a town's services?

options: The number of questions in a test

quiz.prompt: What problems can rapid urbanisation create?
options: Congestion, poor housing and strain on services

quiz.prompt: Which of the following Kenyan cities illustrate rapid urban growth?
Is it true that rural to urban migration drives urbanisation?
Is it true that rapid urbanisation places no strain on a town's services?

units.title: Agriculture, food security and land use
units.notes: Agriculture is the cultivation of crops and the rearing of livestock for food, income and raw materials. Systems differ by scale, purpose and intensity, from subsistence to commercial and from shifting to settled farming. Physical factors such as climate and soil combine with human factors like capital, labour and markets to determine what is produced. Kenya's exports of tea, coffee and flowers show the link between farming and trade. Food security depends on productivity, storage and fair distribution.
units.worked_example: A smallholder in Kiambu with fertile volcanic soil and reliable rainfall can grow intensive horticultural crops for urban markets, earning steady income.
units.activity: Visit or research a nearby farm and list its inputs, outputs and three problems it faces.
units.check: Why is food security about more than just producing enough food?

quiz.prompt: What is agriculture?
options: The cultivation of crops and rearing of livestock for food, income and raw materials

options: The link between farming and trade
That Kenya imports all its food

quiz.prompt: Is it true that food security depends only on producing enough food?
Is it true that subsistence and commercial farming differ in scale and purpose?

units.title: Industry and industrial location
units.notes: Industry transforms raw materials into finished goods and is classified as primary, secondary or tertiary. Manufacturing location depends on raw materials, power, labour, transport, markets and government policy. Industries range from cottage trades to processing plants and heavy manufacturing. Agro-processing is important in Kenya, turning tea, coffee, milk and sugar into value-added products. Industrial growth can raise incomes but also causes pollution, so sustainable planning is needed.
units.worked_example: A milk factory in Kiambu is sited near dairy farms and the Nairobi market because perishable raw materials and consumers must be close by.
units.activity: Choose one manufactured product and trace its raw material from farm to shop in a flow chart.
units.check: Why are some industries located close to their raw materials?

quiz.prompt: Agro-processing in Kenya turns tea, coffee, milk and sugar into what?

Is it true that manufacturing location is unaffected by markets and government policy?

units.title: Regional study and fieldwork
units.notes: A regional study examines the physical and human features of a chosen area to understand how people use their environment. Fieldwork gathers first-hand data using observation, interviews, measurements and maps, which is then analysed and presented. This method builds skills of planning, sampling, recording and report writing. Comparing regions reveals contrasts in climate, farming, settlement and development. Fieldwork evidence makes conclusions stronger than guesswork and links classroom learning to real places.
units.worked_example: A class studying a local market records trader numbers, goods sold and transport used, then concludes which factors attract trade to that site.
units.activity: Plan a short field study of a nearby market or river and prepare a simple data collection table.
units.check: Why should a field report present evidence rather than just opinions?

options: The physical and human features of a chosen area

quiz.prompt: Which methods does fieldwork use to gather first-hand data?

History and Citizenship.overview: History and Citizenship explores Kenya's and the world's past while building an understanding of governance, the constitution and active citizenship. Learners use evidence, evaluate change and connect historical roots to present-day civic life.

units.title: Sources of history and the historian's method
units.notes: History is the study of the human past based on evidence, not rumour. Sources are primary, such as artefacts, letters, oral accounts and photographs, or secondary, such as textbooks and later articles. Historians gather sources, check their authenticity and bias, then interpret them to build accounts. Oral traditions preserve community memory but must be cross-checked with other evidence. Careful use of sources helps explain events such as the building of the Kenya-Uganda railway.
units.worked_example: A historian studying Mombasa's past would compare old maps, travellers' diaries and oral accounts to test whether a claimed event actually occurred.
units.activity: Interview an older relative about an event in your community and compare their account with one written source.
units.check: Why must historians check the reliability of a source?

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is a primary source of history?
options: A textbook written many years later
An artefact or letter from the period

quiz.prompt: Why must historians check the reliability of a source?
options: Because all sources are always false
To check its authenticity and bias before interpreting it

quiz.prompt: Why must oral traditions be treated with care?
options: They preserve community memory but must be cross-checked with other evidence

quiz.prompt: Is it true that history is based on evidence rather than rumour?
Is it true that secondary sources like textbooks are the only evidence historians use?

units.title: Early human origins and prehistory
units.notes: Prehistory is the period before written records, studied mainly through fossils, tools and archaeology. Evidence from sites such as Lake Turkana and Olorgesailie shows that early human ancestors and their stone tools lived in East Africa. Human communities gradually moved from hunting and gathering to farming and herding, a change called the Neolithic revolution. This shift increased food supply and led to settled villages. Understanding prehistory explains how technology and society evolved over vast spans of time.
units.worked_example: Stone tools found beside animal bones at Olorgesailie suggest that early people butchered large game near reliable water sources.
units.activity: Draw a timeline of the stone age, bronze age and iron age, adding one key development to each period.
units.check: Why is the shift from hunting to farming considered a turning point in history?

options: The change from hunting and gathering to farming and herding

units.title: Early communities, trade and technology
units.notes: Early communities in East Africa organised themselves into clans and age sets and traded goods such as salt, iron and cloth. Long-distance trade linked the coast with the interior and the wider Indian Ocean world, spreading ideas, religions and languages. Iron working improved tools and farming, allowing larger populations to settle. The rise of towns like Kilwa and Mombasa shows how commerce builds urban life. These networks laid foundations for later states and for Kenya's cultural diversity.
units.worked_example: Coastal traders exchanged cloth and beads for ivory and gold from the interior, making Swahili towns wealthy centres of commerce.
units.activity: Make a simple trade-flow map showing goods that moved between the coast and one inland Kenyan community.
units.check: How did iron technology change early farming and trade?

units.title: Colonisation and African resistance
units.notes: European colonisation of Africa expanded in the late nineteenth century after the Berlin Conference set rules for partition. Colonial rule in Kenya was established through conquest, treaties and the building of the railway, which transformed land and labour systems. Africans resisted in many ways, from armed struggles like the Nandi and Giriama resistance to the Mau Mau uprising. Colonial policies on farming, taxation and land alienated communities. Studying resistance shows that colonisation was contested, not accepted passively.
units.worked_example: The Mau Mau fought against land alienation and colonial rule, and their struggle pressured Britain toward reform and eventually independence.
units.activity: Prepare a table listing two causes and two effects of African resistance to colonial rule in Kenya.

units.title: Nationalism and the road to independence
units.notes: Nationalism is the desire of a people to govern themselves. In Kenya, political parties and trade unions such as KANU, KADU and the Kenya African Workers' Union pressed for independence. Leaders mobilised support through rallies, petitions and international diplomacy. Britain responded with constitutional conferences and elections that widened African representation. Independence in 1963 came from years of organised pressure and negotiation. The story shows how collective action and leadership shape political change.
units.worked_example: The 1960 Lancaster House Conference set the stage for elections, and KANU's victory in 1963 led to internal self-rule and then to independence.
units.activity: Create a timeline of five key events between 1945 and 1963 that led to Kenya's independence.

units.title: Kenya after independence and nation building
units.notes: After independence Kenya faced the tasks of unifying diverse communities, expanding education and building an economy. The government adopted policies of Africanisation to increase local participation in jobs and business. Challenges included poverty, landlessness, disease and regional inequality. Institutions such as parliament, the courts and local government were strengthened. Nation building required balancing different interests while improving living standards. Understanding this period helps explain present-day debates about land, education and devolution.
units.worked_example: Free or subsidised primary education expanded literacy, but rapid enrolment also strained classrooms and teacher supply in many counties.
units.activity: Debate in groups whether education or land reform mattered more for Kenya's development after independence.

units.title: The world wars and the global order
units.notes: The First and Second World Wars reshaped politics, economies and borders across the world. Africans were drawn into both wars as soldiers and carriers, and their experiences fuelled demands for freedom. Post-war bodies such as the League of Nations and later the United Nations tried to keep peace and promote cooperation. War also accelerated technology and industry. Examining causes and consequences helps explain how the modern international system formed.
units.worked_example: The failure of the League of Nations to stop aggression in the 1930s revealed the weakness of collective security and contributed to the Second World War.
units.activity: List three causes and three consequences of the Second World War and share them with the class.

units.title: The Cold War and decolonisation
units.notes: After 1945 the world divided into rival blocs led by the United States and the Soviet Union, a period known as the Cold War. Superpowers competed for influence, and new African states had to navigate this rivalry. Decolonisation spread as colonies won independence, and some states chose non-alignment through groups like the Non-Aligned Movement. Kenya and its neighbours joined international organisations while guarding their sovereignty. This era shaped aid, trade and security policies that still affect Africa.
units.worked_example: A newly independent state that accepted aid from both blocs while joining the Non-Aligned Movement tried to avoid taking sides in the superpower rivalry.
units.activity: Draw a simple diagram showing the two Cold War blocs and list two countries aligned to each.

units.title: Governance and the separation of powers
units.notes: Governance is the way a state exercises authority and manages public affairs. A democratic system separates power among the legislature, executive and judiciary so that no single arm dominates. The legislature makes laws and oversees the executive, while the judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes. Checks and balances protect rights and promote accountability. In Kenya these arms operate under the Constitution, and citizens can hold them to account through elections and public participation.
units.worked_example: If a court finds that an official acted outside the law, it can declare the action invalid, demonstrating judicial checks on the executive.
units.activity: Role-play a short parliamentary session in which a committee questions a minister about a public project.

units.title: The constitution and the rule of law
units.notes: A constitution is the supreme law that sets out how a country is governed and limits state power. Kenya's 2010 Constitution expanded a bill of rights and created devolved government. The rule of law means everyone, including leaders, is subject to the law and is treated equally before it. Constitutional principles include the sovereignty of the people, transparency and accountability. A constitution that is respected protects citizens and guides public institutions, while disregard for it invites abuse.
units.worked_example: Because the Constitution guarantees free expression, a citizen can criticise government policy without fear, provided they do not break other laws.
units.activity: Read the bill of rights chapter and pick three rights, explaining how you can responsibly enjoy each one.

units.title: Citizenship, rights and responsibilities
units.notes: Citizenship is full membership of a state, giving people both rights and duties. In Kenya citizenship may be acquired by birth, registration or naturalisation. Rights such as education, health, expression and equality come with responsibilities like obeying laws, paying taxes and respecting the rights of others. Active citizens take part in public affairs, vote and volunteer. Responsible citizenship strengthens democracy and community development. Learning these duties prepares young people to participate constructively in national life.
units.worked_example: A citizen who pays taxes and votes at elections fulfils two duties that make government services and democratic choice possible.
units.activity: List four rights and match each with a corresponding responsibility, then discuss your list with a partner.

units.title: Democracy, elections and devolution
units.notes: Democracy is a system in which people choose their leaders and influence decisions, usually through free and fair elections. Elections require an independent body, voter registration, secret ballots and peaceful dispute resolution. Kenya's devolved system created county governments to bring services closer to citizens and to share resources. Devolution assigns specific functions to counties and others to the national government. Understanding these processes helps citizens monitor leadership and demand accountability in their own counties.
units.worked_example: Under devolution, a county assembly passes a budget for local clinics while the national government funds and runs national referral hospitals.
units.activity: Research one service provided by your county government and one by the national government, then present the difference.

units.title: Regional and international cooperation
units.notes: Countries cooperate in regional and international bodies to promote peace, trade and development. Kenya belongs to organisations such as the East African Community, the African Union and the United Nations. These bodies handle trade, security, health and humanitarian issues and give member states a shared voice. Cooperation brings benefits like bigger markets but also demands compromises over sovereignty. Studying them helps explain how nations solve problems that cross borders.
units.worked_example: Through the East African Community, member states reduce trade barriers, allowing Kenyan goods to reach Ugandan and Tanzanian markets more easily.
units.activity: Choose one international organisation and list two benefits and one challenge it poses for its member states.

Business Studies.overview: Business Studies introduces commerce, accounting, economic principles, entrepreneurship and finance. It prepares senior learners to understand how firms, markets and money work and to apply business skills confidently.

units.title: Introduction to business and commerce
units.notes: Business is any activity that produces or sells goods and services to satisfy needs at a profit. Commerce is the part of business concerned with trade and the aids to trade such as transport, banking and insurance. Studying business helps learners understand how goods move from producers to consumers. It also introduces the ideas of needs, wants, scarcity and choice. In Kenya, small retail shops, matatu services and large manufacturers all illustrate business activity in different forms.
units.worked_example: A farmer who grows maize and sells it to a miller illustrates production, while the lorry that transports the flour illustrates an aid to trade.
units.activity: List five businesses in your neighbourhood and classify each as goods or service and as small or large.
units.check: How does commerce differ from production?

quiz.prompt: What is business?
options: Any activity that produces or sells goods and services to satisfy needs at a profit

quiz.prompt: What is commerce?
options: The part of business concerned with trade and the aids to trade

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are aids to trade?
Is it true that studying business introduces ideas of needs, wants, scarcity and choice?
Is it true that commerce has nothing to do with moving goods from producers to consumers?

units.title: Forms of business ownership
units.notes: Businesses may be owned as sole proprietorships, partnerships, private or public companies, cooperatives or public corporations. Each form differs in ownership, liability, capital raising and control. A sole proprietor enjoys quick decisions but bears unlimited liability, while a limited company can raise large capital but faces more regulation. Choosing a form depends on capital, risk and size. In Kenya cooperatives are common in farming, allowing members to market produce jointly.
units.worked_example: Two dairy farmers who pool funds and share profits as partners gain more capital but must each accept liability for the firm's debts.
units.activity: Compare a sole proprietorship and a limited company in a table under capital, liability and control.
units.check: What is meant by limited liability?

quiz.prompt: What is meant by limited liability?
options: Owners are responsible for debts only up to the amount they invested
Owners must pay all business debts personally

units.title: The business environment
units.notes: The business environment includes internal factors a firm controls, such as staff and capital, and external factors it does not, such as laws, taxes, competition and technology. Political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental forces affect how a business operates. Firms scan this environment to spot opportunities and threats and to plan accordingly. In Kenya, mobile money and county licensing rules are examples of external forces shaping trade. Adapting to change helps businesses survive.
units.worked_example: When a government raises import duty on a good, a local trader may switch to a cheaper local supplier to keep prices competitive.

units.title: Entrepreneurship and business ideas
units.notes: An entrepreneur spots opportunities, organises resources and takes risks to start and run a business. Key qualities include creativity, initiative, persistence and a willingness to learn from failure. Business ideas can come from identifying a community need, improving an existing product or using local resources. A good idea is tested by assessing demand, cost and competition before investing. Entrepreneurship creates jobs and solves problems, which is vital for Kenya's growing workforce.
units.worked_example: A student notices that classmates struggle to buy affordable lunch and starts a small snack service, testing demand before buying stock in bulk.
units.activity: Write a one-paragraph business idea for your area and list the resources you would need to start it.

options: By assessing demand, cost and competition

units.title: Production and factors of production
units.notes: Production is the creation of goods and services to satisfy human wants. It uses four factors: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Land covers natural resources, labour is human effort, capital is man-made equipment and money, and the entrepreneur organises the others. Production may be direct or indirect and can be primary, secondary or tertiary. Improving the quality and combination of these factors raises output and efficiency in a firm or a farm.
units.worked_example: A bakery combines flour and oven capital, the baker's labour and the owner's management to produce bread for sale at a profit.
units.activity: Choose a local product and list the four factors of production used to make it.

units.title: Marketing and the marketing mix
units.notes: Marketing identifies customer needs and works to satisfy them profitably. The marketing mix combines product, price, place and promotion, sometimes called the four Ps. Pricing must cover costs and match customers' willingness to pay, while promotion informs and persuades buyers. Distribution ensures goods reach the right place at the right time. Effective marketing research reduces the risk of launching a product nobody wants, as new Kenyan brands often discover.
units.worked_example: A shop lowers its price and advertises through a WhatsApp status; sales rise, showing that price and promotion work together in the mix.
units.activity: Design a simple poster to promote a new snack and explain the four Ps you used.

units.title: Money, banking and financial services
units.notes: Money is anything generally accepted as a medium of exchange, a store of value and a unit of account. Banks accept deposits, lend money and safekeep valuables, while mobile money services extend these functions widely. Interest is the price of using borrowed money and can be paid on savings or charged on loans. Comparing services helps customers choose wisely and avoid high charges. In Kenya, banks and mobile platforms together support saving, payment and credit.
units.worked_example: A trader who saves 5 000 shillings in an account earning 6 per cent annual interest gains about 300 shillings in a year before tax.
units.activity: Compare the charges and interest of a bank account and a mobile money wallet using their published rates.

options: Accepting deposits, lending and enabling payments

units.title: Accounting: source documents and books of accounts
units.notes: Accounting records financial transactions so that a business can measure results and control its money. Transactions begin with source documents such as receipts, invoices and petty cash vouchers. These are entered into books of original entry like the cash book, sales day book and purchases day book, then posted to ledgers. The double-entry rule keeps debits equal to credits. Accurate records prevent theft, support tax compliance and guide business decisions.
units.worked_example: A business sells goods on credit for 20 000 shillings; the sales day book records this, and the ledger shows that the debtor owes 20 000 shillings.
units.activity: Collect three sample receipts or invoices and enter their details into a simple cash book.

units.title: Accounting: trial balance and financial statements
units.notes: After posting to the ledger, a trial balance lists debit and credit balances to check that totals agree. The trading account calculates gross profit from sales less cost of sales, while the profit and loss account deducts expenses to find net profit. A balance sheet then lists assets, liabilities and capital on a given date. These statements show profitability, liquidity and solvency. Interpreting them helps owners, lenders and investors judge a firm's health.
units.worked_example: If sales are 80 000 shillings and cost of sales is 50 000, gross profit is 30 000; after expenses of 12 000, net profit is 18 000.

units.title: Demand, supply and market equilibrium
units.notes: Demand is the quantity of a good buyers are willing and able to buy at a given price, while supply is what sellers offer. Normally, demand rises as price falls and supply rises as price increases. Where the two forces meet, the market sets an equilibrium price. Shifts in income, tastes, costs or technology move the whole curve and change the equilibrium. These ideas explain price changes in Kenyan markets for goods such as maize and vegetables.
units.worked_example: If a drought cuts the maize harvest, supply falls, and with demand unchanged, the equilibrium price of maize rises.
units.activity: Sketch demand and supply curves for a good and show what happens when supply falls.

units.title: Business finance and sources of capital
units.notes: Business finance is the money needed to start and run a firm. Capital may come from owners' savings, partners, loans, trade credit, hire purchase, leasing or the sale of shares. Each source has costs such as interest and conditions such as repayment dates and collateral. Short-term finance covers day-to-day needs, while long-term finance funds assets like buildings and machines. Choosing the right mix keeps the business liquid without excessive debt.
units.worked_example: A carpenter might lease a machine instead of buying it, saving the large cash outlay while still using the equipment to earn income.
units.activity: List four sources of business finance and state one advantage and one disadvantage of each.

units.title: Business communication and record keeping
units.notes: Effective communication moves clear, accurate messages between people so that tasks are done correctly. Business messages may be written, such as letters, memos and emails, or oral, such as meetings and telephone calls. Good records include letters, minutes, invoices and receipts that provide evidence of transactions and decisions. Barriers such as noise, poor wording and emotion can distort messages. Clear communication and tidy records improve teamwork, customer service and accountability in any firm.
units.worked_example: A firm that confirms orders in writing avoids disputes, because each party can refer to the recorded details of quantity, price and delivery date.

units.title: Government, taxation and business ethics
units.notes: Government influences business through taxation, licensing, regulation, subsidies and public spending. Taxes such as income tax, VAT and excise duty raise revenue for public services and may affect prices and profits. Regulation protects consumers, workers and the environment and promotes fair competition. Ethical business practice means honesty, fair dealing and social responsibility. Firms that act ethically build trust, while tax evasion and unfair practices attract penalties and damage reputation.
units.worked_example: A firm that charges VAT correctly, issues receipts and pays its taxes on time avoids penalties and gains customer trust.
units.activity: Interview a small trader about the taxes or licences they pay and present a short summary.

Agriculture.overview: Agriculture covers soil science, crop and livestock husbandry, farm management and agribusiness. Senior learners build the technical methods, records and business thinking needed for productive and sustainable farming.

units.title: Introduction to agriculture and farming systems
units.notes: Agriculture is the practice of growing crops and keeping livestock for food, income and raw materials. Farming systems include subsistence, commercial, mixed, pastoral and plantation farming, and they differ in scale and purpose. The choice of system depends on climate, soil, capital, labour, market and culture. In Kenya, smallholder mixed farming dominates while large plantations grow tea and sugarcane. Understanding systems helps farmers select practices suited to their land and goals.
units.worked_example: A farmer who grows maize and beans for family use while keeping two dairy cows for milk and income practises small-scale mixed farming.
units.activity: Survey three farmers near your home and record the type of farming system each uses and the reasons for it.
units.check: What factors determine the farming system a farmer chooses?

options: Growing crops and keeping livestock for food, income and raw materials

units.title: Soil: formation, profile and properties
units.notes: Soil forms when rock breaks down through weathering and mixes with organic matter, water and air. A mature soil profile has horizons: topsoil rich in humus, subsoil, parent material and bedrock. Soil properties include texture, structure, colour, porosity and pH, and these influence drainage, aeration and nutrient availability. Loam soils are usually best for crops because they hold water and air in balance. Testing soil guides liming, fertiliser use and crop choice.
units.worked_example: A soil sample that turns red litmus paper blue is alkaline, so a farmer might add acidic material or choose crops that tolerate a high pH.

units.title: Soil fertility and conservation
units.notes: Soil fertility is the ability of soil to supply the nutrients needed by plants. Fertilisers and manure add nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, while crop rotation and legumes enrich the soil naturally. Soil erosion, leaching, overgrazing and continuous cropping reduce fertility and, if unchecked, cause poor yields and desertification. Conservation methods include terracing, contour ploughing, mulching, cover crops and afforestation. Testing soil before applying fertiliser saves money and protects the environment.
units.worked_example: On steep land, cutting terraces across the slope slows runoff, traps water and reduces the loss of fertile topsoil to erosion.

units.title: Crop husbandry: land preparation and planting
units.notes: Crop husbandry is the skilled management of crop enterprises from land preparation to harvest. Land preparation involves clearing, ploughing, harrowing and levelling to create a suitable seedbed. Planting requires the right time, seed rate, spacing and depth, all of which influence competition, light and yield. Good spacing improves air movement and reduces disease. Choosing certified seed and planting at the onset of rains gives crops the best start. Records of dates and inputs guide later decisions.
units.worked_example: Maize planted at 75 cm by 25 cm rather than at random gives each plant room for nutrients, and one seed per hole reduces competition.

units.title: Crop management and harvesting
units.notes: After planting, crops need timely weeding, thinning, top-dressing, pest control and watering to grow well. Thinning removes weak plants so the remaining ones develop fully, while top-dressing supplies nutrients during growth. Harvesting at the correct maturity stage gives the best quality and quantity. Post-harvest handling such as drying, sorting and storage prevents losses. Good management from planting to storage raises the value a farmer finally earns from the crop.
units.worked_example: Maize harvested when grain moisture is still high may rot in storage, so drying it to about 13 per cent moisture before storage prevents spoilage.

units.title: Pests, diseases and weed control
units.notes: Pests, diseases and weeds reduce yields by damaging plants or competing for water, light and nutrients. Common pests include aphids, stem borers and armyworms, while fungal, bacterial and viral diseases cause spots, wilts and blights. Control combines cultural methods such as crop rotation and resistant varieties with biological and chemical methods. Chemical pesticides must be applied safely, at correct rates and with protective clothing. Integrated pest management minimises cost, damage and harm to the environment.
units.worked_example: Rotating maize with beans breaks the life cycle of a maize stem borer and adds nitrogen, reducing both pest damage and the need for fertiliser.

units.title: Livestock husbandry: cattle
units.notes: Cattle are kept for milk, meat, hides and manure, and their management requires shelter, feeding, watering, breeding and health care. Dairy breeds such as Friesian and Ayrshire give high milk yields, while beef breeds such as Boran are hardy for meat. Good hygiene and regular veterinary care prevent mastitis and other diseases. A proper milking routine and clean housing maintain yield and quality. Records of milk and feed help a farmer measure and improve profitability.
units.worked_example: A dairy cow giving 15 litres a day needs balanced feed and clean water; a consistent routine can raise the yield to 20 litres a day.
