units.title: Livestock husbandry: poultry, goats and sheep
units.notes: Poultry, goats and sheep are important for eggs, meat, milk and income, and they suit small farms with limited land. Poultry need clean housing, balanced feed, vaccination and protection from predators to lay well. Goats, especially dairy breeds, are hardy and give milk on poor pastures, while sheep provide meat and wool in suitable areas. Good hygiene prevents coccidiosis and other flock diseases. Records of eggs, milk and feed use show whether the enterprise is profitable.
units.worked_example: A small unit of 50 layers each laying five eggs a week produces 250 eggs weekly, so feed cost must be compared with egg sales.

units.title: Animal nutrition, health and breeding
units.notes: Animal nutrition supplies energy, protein, vitamins, minerals and water for growth, reproduction and production. Feeds may be roughages such as grass and silage or concentrates rich in protein and energy. Balanced rations and clean water improve growth and yield. Health care includes vaccination, deworming, dipping and isolating sick animals to prevent spread. Breeding selects parents with desired traits to improve herd quality. Together these practices determine a herd's productivity and a farm's profit.
units.worked_example: A ration mixing maize germ, cotton seed cake, minerals and fodder supplies energy, protein and minerals, raising milk yield above that from grass alone.

units.title: Water and irrigation management
units.notes: Water is essential for crop growth, livestock and farm operations, and its supply must be planned. Irrigation applies water to crops in dry periods using furrow, sprinkler or drip methods, with drip being the most water-efficient. Drainage removes excess water to prevent waterlogging and root disease. Water harvesting through tanks, pans and roofs conserves rain for dry spells. Efficient water use reduces cost and supports farming in Kenya's semi-arid counties. Careful scheduling matches water to crop needs.
units.worked_example: Drip irrigation delivers water slowly to plant roots, cutting evaporation losses so a farmer can irrigate more crops with the same amount of water.

units.title: Farm structures, tools and machinery
units.notes: Farm structures such as barns, stores, pens, silos and fences protect crops and livestock and improve working efficiency. Farm tools range from simple hand tools like jembes and hoes to machines such as tractors, ploughs and seed drills. Choosing the right tool or machine depends on the task, scale, terrain and cost. Proper maintenance, cleaning and safe operation lengthen the life of implements and prevent injury. Mechanisation raises output but requires capital and skilled handling.
units.worked_example: A well-ventilated grain store with raised pallets keeps maize dry and free of mould, preserving it for months without loss.

units.title: Farm records and agribusiness management
units.notes: Farm records such as inventory lists, production records, labour records and financial accounts guide decision making. They show costs, yields and profits so a farmer can judge which enterprises pay and which do not. Farm planning sets objectives, chooses enterprises and budgets resources of land, labour and capital. Simple records like a cash book and a daily milk sheet are easy to keep yet very useful. Good management uses records to reduce waste and increase returns.
units.worked_example: A farmer comparing a maize field's total cost of 40 000 shillings against sales of 55 000 shillings knows the enterprise made a 15 000 shilling profit.

units.title: Marketing of produce and value addition
units.notes: Marketing involves moving agricultural produce from the farm to consumers through grading, packaging, storage, transport and sale. Grading and standardisation improve prices because buyers trust quality. Value addition, such as processing milk into yoghurt or maize into flour, increases shelf life and price. Cooperatives help smallholders bargain, access markets and share costs. Understanding markets, prices and consumer demand lets farmers plan what to produce and when to sell. Quality and timing strongly affect income.
units.worked_example: A farmer who cleans, grades and packages tomatoes fetches a higher price than one who sells unsorted produce to a middleman.

Computer Studies.overview: Computer Studies builds the analytical and practical skills learners need to understand how digital systems work, from binary data to software development and safe use of networks. It prepares senior school learners for pathways in software engineering, data science, networking and information technology.

units.title: Data representation and number systems
units.notes: Digital devices store all information as binary digits, so number systems form the foundation of computing. Learners convert between denary, binary, octal and hexadecimal, and apply binary addition and simple subtraction. They also study how text, images and sound are encoded using standards such as ASCII, Unicode, pixels and sampling. This explains why file sizes differ and why data can appear corrupted. The knowledge supports later work in programming, networking and data analysis.
units.worked_example: To convert denary 45 to binary, divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders upwards: 45 gives 101101, which equals 32 plus 8 plus 4 plus 1. Check the answer by adding those place values.
units.activity: Work in pairs to encode both your names and school name in binary using ASCII, then compare the total number of bits used and explain the difference to the class.

options: Because each hexadecimal digit represents four binary bits
Because hexadecimal uses only two symbols

quiz.prompt: Is it true that file sizes differ because of how data is encoded?
Is it true that binary addition cannot be performed on digital data?

units.title: Computer hardware and system architecture
units.notes: A computer system combines input, processing, storage and output devices under the control of the processor. Learners examine the central processing unit, memory hierarchy and buses that move data between components. They compare primary memory such as random access memory with secondary storage like hard disks and solid state drives, weighing cost, speed and durability. Understanding the fetch decode execute cycle helps explain why processor speed, cache size and clock rate affect performance.
units.worked_example: When a learner opens a spreadsheet, the hard disk first loads the program into random access memory, the processor fetches and executes each instruction, and results are shown on the monitor while unsaved work risks being lost if power fails.
units.activity: Open a computer casing or use labelled diagrams to trace the path of data from a keyboard press to a file saved on the hard disk, drawing and labelling the flow.
units.check: Why does adding random access memory usually speed up a computer more than a larger hard disk?

quiz.prompt: Which cycle helps explain processor performance?
Which is an example of primary memory?
Why does adding random access memory usually speed up a computer more than a larger hard disk?
options: Because RAM is slower than storage
Because storage is faster than RAM
Because RAM gives the processor faster access to active data
Because it makes the CPU slower

quiz.prompt: Is it true that a computer system combines input, processing, storage and output devices?
Is it true that processor speed, cache size and clock rate have no effect on performance?

units.title: Operating systems and file management
units.notes: An operating system manages hardware, runs applications and provides the interface through which users work. Learners study functions such as process scheduling, memory allocation, device management and user authentication in systems like Windows, Linux and Android. They practise organising files into folders with clear, meaningful names and sensible extensions, and they examine backups and access permissions. Effective file management reduces data loss and makes projects easier to find, share and submit on time.
units.worked_example: A learner creates the folder structure Documents, SeniorSchool, ComputerStudies, Projects and names a saved file Project1_Arduino_2026.docx so that the file is self describing and easy to retrieve.
units.activity: Organise a messy folder on a school computer into a clear hierarchy, apply consistent naming rules, and prepare a two minute walkthrough explaining your decisions.
units.check: What problems arise when files are stored with vague names such as document1 and document2?

quiz.prompt: What does an operating system do?
options: Manages hardware, runs applications and provides the user interface

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are operating systems?
Why is vague file naming like document1 a problem?
options: It makes files easy to find
It makes projects harder to find, share and submit on time

quiz.prompt: Is it true that effective file management reduces data loss?
Is it true that an operating system does not manage memory allocation or device management?

units.title: Application software and digital documents
units.notes: Application software performs tasks for the user, from word processing and presentations to spreadsheets and design tools. Learners compare proprietary and open source options and judge which tool suits a given task. They apply good document design, including headings, alignment, tables and consistent fonts, to communicate clearly. They also consider file formats, compatibility and accessibility so that documents open correctly on other devices. This unit links everyday productivity with thoughtful, audience aware communication.
units.worked_example: For a school environmental club report, a learner uses a table for the budget, a chart for waste collected, and consistent heading styles so that the reader can scan the document quickly and see the key message.
units.activity: Redesign a poorly formatted one page school notice using clear headings, spacing and an appropriate font, then ask two classmates which version is easier to read and why.
units.check: How do you decide whether a table or a chart best presents a set of figures?

quiz.prompt: What does application software do?
options: Performs tasks for the user such as word processing and spreadsheets

quiz.prompt: Which are examples of good document design?
options: Headings, alignment, tables and consistent fonts

quiz.prompt: Why should you consider file formats, compatibility and accessibility?
options: So documents open correctly on other devices

quiz.prompt: Is it true that open source and proprietary options can both be compared to suit a task?
Is it true that document design has no effect on how clearly a message is communicated?

units.title: Spreadsheet modelling and data analysis
units.notes: Spreadsheets store data in cells and use formulas to calculate, summarise and analyse information. Learners build formulas with relative and absolute references, apply functions such as SUM, AVERAGE, IF, COUNTIF and VLOOKUP, and create charts. They learn to sort and filter data, and to test a model by changing inputs and checking outputs. Good spreadsheet practice includes clear labels, sensible formatting, error checking and protection of important formulas. These skills support budgeting, science investigations and business planning.
units.worked_example: To grade a class, enter marks in column B and use =IF(B2>=50,"Pass","Fail"). Then use =COUNTIF(C2:C41,"Pass") to count how many learners passed, and verify by manually tallying a few rows.
units.activity: Build a personal monthly budget with income, food, transport and savings, use formulas to total and find the savings rate, then test how the balance changes if transport rises by fifty shillings.
units.check: What is the difference between a relative and an absolute cell reference, and when is each useful?

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a relative and an absolute cell reference?
options: A relative reference changes when copied while an absolute reference stays fixed
An absolute reference changes when copied

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are spreadsheet functions?
options: SUM, AVERAGE, IF, COUNTIF and VLOOKUP

quiz.prompt: Why should a model be tested by changing inputs and checking outputs?
options: To check that the model works correctly

quiz.prompt: Is it true that good spreadsheet practice includes clear labels, error checking and protection of important formulas?
Is it true that spreadsheets cannot be used for budgeting or business planning?

units.title: Databases and information management
units.notes: A database organises related data so it can be stored once and retrieved many times. Learners study tables, records, fields, keys and data types, and they reduce duplication through sensible design. They create queries to select and filter records, and reports to present results. They also examine why validation rules, such as restricting a gender field or limiting marks to a range, protect data quality. Relational ideas show how a school might link learners, classes and subjects without repeating information.
units.worked_example: In a school library database, each borrower has one record with an admission number as the primary key, while a loans table stores the book, borrower and date so history is kept without repeating learner details.
units.activity: Design three linked tables for a small library or shop, enter five records in each, and write one query that lists items due or low in stock.
units.check: Why is it risky to store the same learner name in many records instead of using an admission number?

quiz.prompt: What does a database do?
options: Organises related data so it can be stored once and retrieved many times

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are database components?
options: Tables, records, fields, keys and data types

quiz.prompt: Why is it risky to store the same learner name in many records instead of using an admission number?
options: It causes duplication and inconsistency that a key would prevent

quiz.prompt: Is it true that validation rules help protect data quality?
Is it true that a database cannot link learners, classes and subjects without repeating information?

units.title: Algorithms and computational thinking
units.notes: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that solves a problem. Learners decompose problems into smaller parts, identify patterns, and express solutions using pseudocode and flowcharts with clear start and end points. They trace algorithms by hand to test correct and incorrect inputs, catching logic errors early. Efficiency matters, so learners compare simple approaches such as linear and binary search. This unit builds the discipline needed before any code is written in a programming language.
units.worked_example: A flowchart for finding the largest of three numbers compares A with B, keeps the larger, then compares that result with C and outputs the survivor, so the logic can be checked before coding.
units.activity: Write pseudocode and draw a flowchart for calculating a learner average from five subjects and stating Pass or Fail, then swap with a partner and trace each other's charts with sample marks.
units.check: Why should an algorithm be tested with unusual inputs such as zero or very large numbers?

quiz.prompt: What is an algorithm?
options: A finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that solves a problem

quiz.prompt: Which tools are used to express solutions in this unit?
Why should an algorithm be tested with unusual inputs such as zero or very large numbers?
Is it true that decomposition breaks a problem into smaller parts?
Is it true that efficiency never matters when choosing between approaches such as linear and binary search?

units.title: Programming fundamentals in Python
units.notes: Programming turns an algorithm into instructions a computer can run. Learners use Python to declare variables, apply arithmetic and string operations, accept input and display output with print. They learn about naming rules, comments and the importance of readable code, and they fix syntax errors by reading messages carefully. Tracing values line by line helps them link each statement to its effect. This practical foundation supports later control structures, functions and data handling.
units.worked_example: A program reading radius and printing area uses radius = float(input("Enter radius: ")) then area = 3.142 * radius * radius and print(area), tracing 7 to give about 153.96.
units.activity: Write a Python program that asks for a learner name and three subject marks, then prints the name and the total, testing it with your own data.
units.check: Why does a program fail when input is read as text but used as a number?

quiz.prompt: Which operation does the print statement perform in Python?
Which function is used to accept input in Python?
Why does a program fail when input is read as text but used as a number?
options: Because the text must be converted to a number before arithmetic

quiz.prompt: Is it true that naming rules, comments and readable code are important in Python?
Is it true that tracing values line by line cannot help link each statement to its effect?

units.title: Control structures and functions
units.notes: Control structures direct the flow of a program: selection chooses between paths and iteration repeats steps. Learners write if, elif and else statements, and use for and while loops, taking care to update loop variables so programs terminate. They define functions with parameters and return values to avoid repeating code. They also practise nesting and combining structures to solve richer problems, such as validating a password or finding prime numbers. Abstraction through functions makes larger programs easier to read, test and debug.
units.worked_example: A function def grade(mark): returns A for seventy and above, B for sixty, else C. Calling grade(64) returns B, and the same function can be reused for every learner without rewriting conditions.
units.activity: Write a Python program using a loop that asks for ten marks, rejects values outside zero to one hundred, and prints the average, testing invalid entries deliberately.
units.check: What goes wrong in a while loop if the condition never becomes false?

quiz.prompt: What do selection and iteration do in a program?
options: Selection chooses between paths and iteration repeats steps

quiz.prompt: What goes wrong in a while loop if the condition never becomes false?
Why are functions useful?
options: They avoid repeating code and make programs easier to test and debug

quiz.prompt: Is it true that loop variables must be updated so that programs terminate?
Is it true that if, elif and else are used for iteration rather than selection?

units.title: Computer networks and the internet
units.notes: A network connects devices so they can share resources and communicate. Learners compare local and wide area networks, and study topologies such as star and bus, transmission media including cables and wireless, and hardware such as routers and switches. They explore how data is divided into packets, addressed and reassembled, and why protocols and standards make communication reliable. They also weigh trade offs of speed, cost, security and coverage when designing a small network for a school computer laboratory.
units.worked_example: A school lab of twenty computers links each machine by cable to one switch, which connects to a router that shares the internet, so one printer and one connection serve all learners efficiently.
units.activity: Sketch a star topology for a ten computer cyber cafe, label the central device and media, and list two advantages and two disadvantages of your design compared with a bus.
units.check: Why is a star topology usually easier to fault find than a bus topology?

quiz.prompt: What does a network do?
options: Connects devices so they can share resources and communicate

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are network topologies?
Why is a star topology usually easier to fault find than a bus topology?
options: Because all devices share one cable
Because a fault brings down the whole network
Because a faulty device can be isolated without bringing down the whole network
Because it has no central device

quiz.prompt: Is it true that data is divided into packets, addressed and reassembled in a network?
Is it true that protocols and standards make communication unreliable?

units.title: Web development basics with HTML and CSS
units.notes: Web pages are built with structure and style separated into layers. Learners write HTML to create headings, paragraphs, lists, images and links, keeping tags correctly nested, and use CSS to control colour, fonts and layout. They plan a simple site with clear navigation and readable contrast, and they consider how pages behave on small screens. They also learn that links should carry meaning and images need alternative text for accessibility. These skills connect programming, design and responsible publishing.
units.worked_example: Using h1 for the page title, p for a description with an img that has an alt attribute, and a CSS rule p {color: teal;} gives a clean page where content stays separate from presentation.
units.activity: Create a two page site about an environmental issue in your county with a shared stylesheet, an image and working links, then test it by resizing the window to phone width.
units.check: Why is it better to control colours in a stylesheet than inside every HTML tag?

quiz.prompt: What does HTML provide in a web page?
options: Structure using headings, paragraphs, lists, images and links

quiz.prompt: Why is it better to control colours in a stylesheet than inside every HTML tag?
options: It keeps structure and style separated and easier to maintain

quiz.prompt: Why do images need alternative text?
options: To support accessibility for users who cannot see the image

quiz.prompt: Is it true that CSS controls colour, fonts and layout?
Is it true that tags in HTML do not need to be correctly nested?

units.title: Cyber safety, ethics and data protection
units.notes: Digital life carries risks that learners must manage and rights they must respect. This unit covers strong passwords, two factor authentication, recognising phishing and malware, and protecting personal data on shared devices. It examines copyright, plagiarism and respectful online conduct, and introduces Kenya's data protection law and principles such as lawfulness, minimisation and consent. Learners analyse real scenarios and propose practical safeguards. The aim is confident, ethical and responsible use of technology at school, at work and at home.
units.worked_example: A learner receives an email claiming a bank prize and asking for a password. Recognising the rushed tone, unfamiliar link and request for secrets, the learner reports and deletes it, and changes a reused password elsewhere.
units.activity: Review the privacy settings on one account, write a personal cyber safety checklist of five rules, and explain each rule to a family member.
units.check: Why is reusing one password across many accounts dangerous even if that password is strong?

quiz.prompt: Why is reusing one password across many accounts dangerous even if that password is strong?
options: Because one breach exposes all those accounts

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are good cyber safety practices?
options: Strong passwords, two factor authentication and recognising phishing

quiz.prompt: Which principles does Kenya's data protection law emphasise?
options: Principles such as lawfulness, minimisation and consent

quiz.prompt: Is it true that copyright, plagiarism and respectful online conduct are part of cyber ethics?
Is it true that personal data on shared devices needs no protection?

units.title: Emerging technologies and computing careers
units.notes: Computing keeps changing, and learners should evaluate new tools critically rather than simply accept the hype. This unit surveys artificial intelligence, cloud computing, the internet of things, blockchain and automation, examining benefits such as efficiency alongside concerns about jobs, bias, privacy and energy use. It also maps pathways in software development, data science, networking, cybersecurity and technical support, noting the qualifications and habits each needs. Structured argument and evidence help learners plan realistic next steps after senior school.
units.worked_example: A learner weighing a career in cybersecurity notes the growing demand and steady study path but also the responsibility and need for trust, then researches two local employers and lists the skills they require.
units.activity: Write a balanced one page argument for or against using artificial intelligence tools in school assessment, giving two benefits and two concerns with evidence, and present it briefly.
units.check: What evidence would convince you that a new technology would help rather than harm a local community?

quiz.prompt: How should learners approach new technologies?
options: Evaluate them critically rather than simply accept the hype

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are emerging technologies?
options: Artificial intelligence, cloud computing, the internet of things and blockchain

quiz.prompt: Which of the following are computing career pathways?
options: Software development, data science, networking and cybersecurity

quiz.prompt: Is it true that emerging technologies raise concerns about jobs, bias, privacy and energy use?
Is it true that learners should ignore qualifications and habits when planning computing careers?

Music and Dance.overview: Music and Dance develops performing, creating and listening skills while building understanding of musical elements, notation, instruments and dance across Kenyan and world traditions. It prepares learners for pathways in performance, composition, education, media and cultural work.

units.title: Elements of music: pitch, rhythm and dynamics
units.notes: All music can be described through its elements. Learners examine pitch as high or low sound, rhythm as patterns of long and short durations, and dynamics as loudness and softness. They also explore tempo, timbre, texture and form, using these terms to describe what they hear with precision. Recognising elements separately and together builds the vocabulary for performance, composition and analysis. Learners learn that careful listening, not just hearing, is the core musical skill.
units.worked_example: A drum pattern on a thirteenth birthday could be described as steady tempo, alternating strong and weak beats, mostly loud dynamics and a deep timbre, giving a precise account of the sound rather than a vague opinion.
units.activity: Listen to a Kenyan radio song and write down its tempo, main dynamics and most noticeable timbre, then compare your notes with a partner and discuss differences.
units.check: How does changing tempo alone change the mood of the same melody?

quiz.prompt: What does the element of pitch describe?
What does the element of dynamics describe?
True or false: careful listening, not just hearing, is the core musical skill?
Rhythm is best described as what?
options: Patterns of long and short durations

quiz.prompt: True or false: tempo and timbre are not considered elements of music?

units.title: Reading and writing staff notation
units.notes: Staff notation records pitch and duration so performers anywhere can read the same music. Learners study the five line stave, treble and bass clefs, the pitch names of lines and spaces, ledger lines and note values from semibreve to quaver. They practise writing notes correctly, including stems and stems direction, and reading short melodies aloud. Accuracy in notation matters because a misplaced note changes the pitch. Fluency here supports sight reading, transcription and composing notated music.
units.worked_example: In treble clef the lines spell E G B D F from bottom to top and the spaces spell F A C E, so a note sitting in the second space from the bottom is A and should be written with a stem going down.
units.activity: Draw a treble stave and notate the first eight notes of a familiar Kenyan song, then swap with a partner to check line and space positions.
units.check: Why must a clef be written at the start of every stave of music?

quiz.prompt: Why must a clef be written at the start of every stave?
options: To fix the pitch names of lines and spaces
To mark the end of the piece

quiz.prompt: How many lines does the standard stave have?
True or false: a misplaced note on the stave does not affect the pitch?
Which note values are studied in staff notation?
True or false: fluency in notation supports sight reading, transcription and composing?

units.title: Rhythm, metre and conducting
units.notes: Metre organises beats into recurring strong and weak patterns. Learners identify simple time signatures such as two four, three four and four four, clap rhythms in each, and count beats aloud. They study note grouping, rests, ties and dotted notes, and they practise basic conducting patterns with a clear preparatory beat, steady pulse and confident cut off. Conducting shows that music making involves leadership and communication. These skills underpin ensemble playing, singing and accurate performance from scores.
units.worked_example: For a waltz in three four, the conductor traces a downward beat then two outward beats in a triangle, keeping the pattern even so the choir stays together and accents the first beat of each bar.
units.activity: In groups of three, each learner conducts a short clapping pattern in a chosen time signature while the others follow, then swap roles and give feedback on clarity of beat.
units.check: What happens to a choir when the conductor's beat is uneven or lacks a clear starting gesture?

quiz.prompt: What does metre organise in music?
options: Beats into recurring strong and weak patterns

quiz.prompt: Which conducting elements are important?
options: A vague gesture and no pulse
A clear preparatory beat, steady pulse and confident cut off

quiz.prompt: True or false: an uneven beat without a clear starting gesture can confuse a choir?
Which are examples of simple time signatures?
options: Two four, three four and four four

quiz.prompt: True or false: conducting skills are unrelated to ensemble playing and singing?

units.title: Melody, scales and intervals
units.notes: Melody is a meaningful succession of pitches. Learners study major and minor scales, their tone and semitone patterns, and how key signatures indicate them. They identify intervals by number and quality, and recognise how steps and leaps give a melody shape, tension and release. They build simple melodies over given rhythms or chords. Understanding scale structure explains why some note combinations sound settled and others restless. This knowledge supports composing, improvising and accurate singing.
units.worked_example: In C major the pattern is tone tone semitone tone tone tone semitone, so the semitone between E and F, and between B and C, explains why a melody rests briefly on E before continuing upward.
units.activity: Compose an eight bar melody in C major using a given rhythm, including at least one leap and one stepwise passage, then sing it for a partner and note where it feels settled.
units.check: Why does a melody often sound unfinished if it ends on the seventh note of a major scale?

quiz.prompt: What is a melody?
How are intervals identified?
True or false: major and minor scales differ in their pattern of tones and semitones?
Why does a melody often sound unfinished if it ends on the seventh note of a major scale?
options: Because the seventh note creates tension that seeks resolution

quiz.prompt: True or false: understanding scale structure helps explain why some note combinations sound settled?

units.title: Harmony, chords and accompaniment
units.notes: Harmony combines pitches sounded together to support a melody. Learners build major and minor triads from scales, and use roman numeral labels to show how chords function within a key. They study common progressions such as one, five, six, four and how they generate movement and repose. They also practise simple accompaniment patterns, bass lines and broken chords. Hearing chords accurately and predicting likely progressions helps learners arrange songs and appreciate why certain music feels satisfying.
units.worked_example: A song in C major using chords C, G and A minor repeats the progression one, five, six while the melody is harmonised, and the move from G back to C at the end clearly signals the finish.
units.activity: Choose a well known Kenyan song and work out a simple three chord accompaniment, playing or singing it while a partner holds the melody, then discuss which chord felt like home.
units.check: Why does the fifth chord in a key create a strong pull back to the first chord?

quiz.prompt: What is harmony?
options: Pitches sounded together to support a melody

quiz.prompt: How are major and minor triads built?
True or false: the fifth chord in a key creates a strong pull back to the first chord?
Which is a common chord progression?
True or false: accompaniment never uses bass lines or broken chords?

units.title: Traditional Kenyan instruments and organology
units.notes: Kenya's traditional instruments reflect the environment, materials and social function of different communities. Learners classify instruments as idiophones, membranophones, chordophones and aerophones, giving local examples such as the nyatiti, orutu, valimba, various drums and horns. They study how instruments are made, tuned and performed, and the roles they play in ceremony, work and celebration. Comparing classification systems develops analytical listening and respect for diverse cultural knowledge passed down through generations.
units.worked_example: The nyatiti of western Kenya is a chordophone because its sound comes from plucked strings, while a drum is a membranophone because vibration of stretched skin produces the sound, showing classification by sound source.
units.activity: Research one traditional instrument from your community, describe its materials, classification and social use, and if possible demonstrate part of its sound or rhythm to the class.
units.check: How would you classify an instrument that is struck and has no stretched skin?

quiz.prompt: How would you classify an instrument that is struck and has no stretched skin?
Which family does a drum belong to?
True or false: the nyatiti and orutu are examples of Kenyan instruments?
Which four families are used to classify instruments?
True or false: traditional instruments have no social function in Kenyan communities?

units.title: Kenyan folk and contemporary music
units.notes: Kenyan music spans work songs, ceremonial songs, taarab, benga, gospel, genge and afro pop. Learners trace how folk materials such as call and response, polyrhythm and local languages shape present day styles. They examine the role of musicians and radio in national and community life, and how migration and technology spread music. Structured listening with attention to instruments, language, rhythm and audience helps learners assess originality and cultural meaning rather than dismiss unfamiliar styles.
units.worked_example: A benga recording can be analysed by noting its driving guitar patterns, Luo lyrics, bright tempo and layered rhythms, linking live performance traditions with modern recording and dance club audiences.
units.activity: Compare a traditional folk song from your community with a current Kenyan hit, listing three musical similarities and two differences with evidence from the recordings.
units.check: What does a musician's choice of language reveal about the audience being addressed?

quiz.prompt: Which styles belong to Kenyan music?
options: Taarab, benga, gospel, genge and afro pop

quiz.prompt: Which folk materials shape present day Kenyan styles?
options: Call and response, polyrhythm and local languages

quiz.prompt: True or false: migration and technology have helped spread Kenyan music?
What can a musician's choice of language reveal?
True or false: structured listening is useless for assessing cultural meaning?

units.title: Music of the world: traditions and styles
units.notes: World music study widens learners' ears beyond the familiar. They explore selected traditions such as West African drumming, Indian classical and film music, Latin American rhythms and Western art music, noting characteristic scales, instruments, textures and performance practice. They compare how these traditions organise time, melody and expression, and consider how musicians borrow and blend across cultures. Respectful, informed comparison supports global awareness and creative borrowing that acknowledges sources rather than simply copying them.
units.worked_example: Indian classical music may use a raga for melody and a tala cycle for rhythm, which can be compared with a Western scale and time signature, though the rules and expressive aims differ in important ways.
units.activity: Choose one world tradition, present its main instruments and rhythmic features in a short talk, and play a recorded excerpt while pointing out two features you identified.
units.check: Why is it misleading to judge an unfamiliar musical tradition by the standards of your own?

quiz.prompt: Which traditions are studied in world music?
options: West African drumming, Indian classical and Latin American rhythms

quiz.prompt: Why is it misleading to judge an unfamiliar tradition by your own standards?
options: Because each tradition organises time, melody and expression differently
Because unfamiliar music is always bad

quiz.prompt: True or false: respectful comparison supports global awareness and creative borrowing that acknowledges sources?
When musicians borrow across cultures, what should they do?
True or false: world music study is meant to narrow listening to the familiar?

units.title: Music composition techniques
units.notes: Composing means shaping musical ideas into a coherent whole. Learners develop motifs, repeat and vary them, and organise sections into simple forms such as binary, ternary and verse and chorus. They set words to music, matching stressed syllables to strong beats, and consider the mood the melody should convey. They revise drafts based on listening and feedback. Planning, drafting and editing are as important in music as in writing, and this unit develops both imagination and discipline.
units.worked_example: To set a two line poem to music, a learner repeats a two bar motif, changes its ending to suit the second line, and places a longer note on the final stressed word so the setting sounds complete.
units.activity: Compose and notate a short sixteen bar piece with at least one repeated and varied motif, then perform or play it and note one change you would make after hearing it.
units.check: Why does repetition alone, without any variation, weaken a composition?

quiz.prompt: What does composing mean?
options: Shaping musical ideas into a coherent whole

quiz.prompt: Which are simple musical forms used in composition?
options: Binary, ternary and verse and chorus

quiz.prompt: True or false: repetition with variation helps build interest in a composition?
When setting words to music, how should stressed syllables be matched?
True or false: planning, drafting and editing are unimportant in music?

units.title: Elements of dance: space, time, energy
units.notes: Dance communicates through the moving body. Learners analyse movement using space, time and energy, and describe actions such as travelling, turning, jumping, gesture and stillness. They study levels, pathways, directions and formations, and how timing, accent and dynamics shape the quality of movement. Safe warm up and cool down habits protect the body. This analytical vocabulary allows learners to describe, rehearse and improve dance as thoughtful art rather than mere imitation.
units.worked_example: A dance can be described as moving on a diagonal pathway at a low level with sudden, sharp energy on strong beats, then shifting to a smooth, sustained travelling step, giving a precise account of what the audience sees.
units.activity: Improvise a thirty second movement phrase exploring high, middle and low levels, then write down the space, time and energy choices you made and perform it for classmates.
units.check: How does changing the energy of a movement, without changing the steps, change its meaning?

quiz.prompt: Which three elements are used to analyse dance movement?
Which are dance actions?
options: Travelling, turning, jumping, gesture and stillness

quiz.prompt: True or false: levels, pathways, directions and formations are studied in dance?
How can changing the energy of a movement affect it?
options: It changes the quality and meaning of the movement

quiz.prompt: True or false: warm up and cool down are unnecessary in dance?

units.title: Kenyan traditional dance
units.notes: Traditional Kenyan dances carry history, identity and social meaning. Learners examine selected dances from different communities, their occasions, costumes, props, songs and community roles. They study formation, footwork, body posture and the relationship with drumming and singing, and they learn the value of accurate learning from knowledgeable practitioners. They also discuss how dances are adapted for stage and festival in ways that either honour or distort the original context. Informed practice builds cultural pride and critical awareness.
units.worked_example: A community's harvest dance can be studied by noting the circular formation, grounded footwork, call and response singing and the use of drums and shakers, showing how movement, music and social purpose are intertwined.
units.activity: With guidance, learn a short section of a dance from your community, note its occasion and music, and present it with a brief explanation of its meaning.
units.check: Why should performers understand a dance's original context before adapting it for a festival stage?

quiz.prompt: What do traditional Kenyan dances carry?
True or false: performers should understand a dance's original context before adapting it for a festival stage?
What should learners study in traditional dance?
options: Occasions, costumes, props, songs and community roles

quiz.prompt: How does informed practice help performers?
options: It builds cultural pride and critical awareness

quiz.prompt: True or false: accurate learning from knowledgeable practitioners is unimportant in traditional dance?

units.title: Choreography and performance
units.notes: Choreography is the deliberate arrangement of movement into a structured work. Learners select and order phrases, use repetition, contrast and transition, and plan spatial patterns and group relationships to build interest. They match movement to music or sound, rehearse for accuracy and safety, and refine timing, spacing and facial expression. They also consider audience viewpoint and staging at school level. Rehearsal discipline and constructive feedback turn good movement ideas into a confident, polished performance.
units.worked_example: For a three minute group piece, learners use unison to open, canon to create interest, a solo highlight in the middle, and a returning group phrase at the end, rehearsing entrances until transitions are seamless.
units.activity: As a group, choreograph and rehearse a two minute dance with at least three formations and one canon section, then perform it and collect two improvement notes from an audience member.
units.check: Why does careful planning of transitions improve a dance more than adding extra steps?

quiz.prompt: What is choreography?
options: The deliberate arrangement of movement into a structured work

quiz.prompt: Which devices build interest in choreography?
True or false: careful planning of transitions can improve a dance more than merely adding extra steps?
What should choreographers consider for the audience?
options: Audience viewpoint and staging at school level

quiz.prompt: True or false: constructive feedback and rehearsal discipline are unimportant for a polished performance?

units.title: Analysing and writing about music and dance
units.notes: Critical analysis moves learners from opinion to evidence based judgement. They describe what they hear and see using correct terminology, interpret meaning and cultural context, and evaluate effectiveness with reasons. They structure writing with an introduction, ordered observations and a justified conclusion, avoiding vague praise such as it was nice. They support claims with specific musical or movement evidence, and they remain fair to styles outside their preference. This builds confidence for exams, auditions, programme notes and media work.
units.worked_example: Instead of saying the dance was good, a learner writes that the sudden acceleration in the final section matched the sung climax and kept the audience engaged, giving specific, defensible evidence for the judgement.
units.activity: Watch a recorded Kenyan performance and write a structured review of three paragraphs with an introduction, evidence based observations and a justified conclusion.
units.check: Why is an evaluative judgement weak if it gives no specific supporting evidence?

quiz.prompt: What does critical analysis aim to produce?
Which structure is best for analytical writing about music and dance?
options: An introduction, ordered observations and a justified conclusion

quiz.prompt: True or false: an evaluative judgement is weak if it gives no specific supporting evidence?
Which phrase should be avoided in music and dance writing?
options: Vague praise such as it was nice

quiz.prompt: True or false: critical analysis should ignore styles outside your preference?

Visual Arts.overview: Visual Arts develops observation, technique and design thinking through drawing, colour, design, printmaking, sculpture and craft, alongside analysis of art in Kenyan and global contexts. It prepares learners for pathways in design, fine art, illustration, craft enterprise and creative industries.

units.title: Elements of art: line, shape, form and tone
units.notes: The elements of art are the basic ingredients artists use. Learners explore line for direction, contour and expression, shape as flat enclosed areas, form as three dimensional volume, and tone as light and dark. They practise varied line weights, positive and negative shapes, and simple shading to make objects look solid. They learn that combining elements deliberately conveys mood and emphasis. This vocabulary underpins every later technique, from drawing and painting to design and sculpture.
units.worked_example: A mug study uses an ellipse for the rim, curved contour lines for the body and graduated shading so the light side is pale and the shadow side dark, making a flat shape read as a rounded form.
units.activity: Draw three simple objects using line and tone only, showing a clear light source, then label where you used contour line and where you used shading.
units.check: How does varying line weight change the expressive effect of a drawing?

quiz.prompt: What is form in art?
How does varying line weight affect a drawing?
options: It can change the expressive effect

quiz.prompt: True or false: tone refers to light and dark in an artwork?
Which is a basic element of art?
True or false: combining elements has no effect on mood or emphasis?

units.title: Principles of design
units.notes: The principles of design organise elements into effective compositions. Learners apply balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, movement, pattern, unity and variety. They analyse how placement, size and colour create a focal point and guide the eye, and they compare symmetrical and asymmetrical balance. They test ideas by sketching alternatives and choosing the strongest. Understanding principles lets learners explain why a composition works or fails, and moves them beyond accidental arrangement to deliberate, purposeful image making.
units.worked_example: A poster places a single bright figure slightly off centre on a calm background, using contrast and rule of thirds to create emphasis, while repeated small shapes give rhythm and keep the design unified.
units.activity: Make three quick thumbnail compositions of the same subject using symmetrical, asymmetrical and radial balance, then choose the most effective and justify your choice.
units.check: Why can asymmetrical balance still feel stable to a viewer?

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a principle of design?
What creates a focal point in a composition?
True or false: asymmetrical balance can still feel stable to a viewer?
Why is understanding principles of design useful?
options: It removes the need to sketch
It lets learners explain why a composition works or fails

quiz.prompt: True or false: symmetrical and asymmetrical balance cannot be compared in art?

units.title: Observational drawing and perspective
units.notes: Observational drawing trains the eye to record what is actually seen. Learners measure proportions with a pencil, compare relative sizes, and use negative space to check edges. They study one point and two point perspective to create believable depth, including the horizon line, vanishing points and converging lines. They practise foreshortening and overlapping to show near and far objects. Regular observation from life, rather than memory, improves accuracy and confidence and grounds imaginative work in solid structure.
units.worked_example: To draw a school gate in two point perspective, learners place two vanishing points on the horizon, converge the side walls toward them and keep vertical edges upright, so the structure recedes convincingly.
units.activity: Draw a corner of your classroom from life using one point perspective, including at least five objects and checking proportions with a pencil held at arm's length.
units.check: Why do the vertical edges of a building stay vertical in two point perspective?

quiz.prompt: What does observational drawing train the eye to do?
What is a vanishing point?
options: A point where converging lines meet on the horizon

quiz.prompt: True or false: negative space can help check edges in observational drawing?
How do overlapping and foreshortening help a drawing?
options: They show near and far objects

quiz.prompt: True or false: in two point perspective, the vertical edges of a building converge?

units.title: Colour theory and painting
units.notes: Colour affects emotion, depth and focus in art and design. Learners study the colour wheel, primary, secondary and tertiary colours, and relationships such as complementary, analogous and triadic schemes. They mix tints with white, shades with black and tones with grey, and explore warm and cool contrast to suggest distance. They practise painting techniques including flat wash, blending and layering while keeping the medium controlled. Planned colour choices, not random selection, strengthen meaning and unity.
units.worked_example: For a sunset landscape, a learner places warm orange and red in the sky against cool blues in the distant hills, so the complementary colour contrast separates the layers and creates a sense of depth.
units.activity: Paint a small colour study of one subject using an analogous palette, then repeat it with a complementary accent and compare which version draws the eye more strongly.
units.check: Why do warm colours tend to appear closer than cool colours?

quiz.prompt: What do complementary colours do?
options: They are opposite on the colour wheel
They are always the same colour

quiz.prompt: How is a tint made?
True or false: warm colours tend to appear closer than cool colours?
What is a triadic colour scheme?
options: Colours next to each other on the wheel
Colours spaced evenly around the wheel

quiz.prompt: True or false: random colour selection strengthens unity better than planning?

units.title: Graphic design and typography
units.notes: Graphic design solves communication problems visually. Learners study layout, grid, hierarchy, alignment, spacing and contrast, and they learn that typography conveys tone as well as words. They compare serif and sans serif typefaces, choose type sizes for readability, and pair fonts carefully. They design posters, logos or book covers with a clear message aimed at a defined audience. They also consider colour, imagery and simplicity, removing clutter so the main message is understood at a glance.
units.worked_example: A school event poster uses one bold sans serif heading, a smaller body font, a clear grid and strong colour contrast so the date and venue can be read from a distance without clutter.
units.activity: Design a poster for a school event, include a short written rationale explaining your grid, typeface choice and colour decisions, and gather feedback from two viewers.
units.check: Why is limited use of font styles usually more effective than many different fonts on one poster?

quiz.prompt: What does graphic design aim to do?
Which typefaces are compared in typography?
True or false: limited use of font styles is usually more effective than many different fonts?
Why is a clear message important in design?
options: So it is understood at a glance

quiz.prompt: True or false: adding clutter helps the main message stand out?

units.title: Printmaking techniques
units.notes: Printmaking transfers an image from a prepared surface to paper, allowing multiple copies. Learners explore relief methods such as potato, cardboard and lino printing, learning about cutting tools, safety, inking and even pressure. They study positive and negative image, registration and the idea of an edition, and how each pull differs slightly. They design their image in reverse, since the print appears flipped. Printmaking rewards planning and repetition, and it links image making with pattern and reproduction.
units.worked_example: Before cutting a lino block, a learner reverses the design and removes the areas that should stay white, leaving raised shapes to take the ink, then rolls the block evenly for a clean, consistent print.
units.activity: Design a simple pattern, cut it safely into a printing block, and pull at least three prints, noting how inking and pressure affect the result.
units.check: Why does a relief print appear reversed from the original drawn design?

quiz.prompt: Why does a relief print appear reversed?
options: Because the image is transferred from a prepared surface, flipping it

quiz.prompt: Which are relief printmaking methods?
True or false: each pull from a printmaking block can differ slightly?
What is an edition in printmaking?
options: A set of prints from the same block

quiz.prompt: True or false: registration is unimportant when printing more than one colour?

units.title: Sculpture and three dimensional form
units.notes: Sculpture occupies real space and is viewed from several sides. Learners study additive methods in clay and assemblage, and subtractive methods such as carving softer materials, along with construction using wire, paper and found objects. They consider mass, volume, balance, texture and negative space, and compare relief with free standing work. They plan stability and safety, since a sculpture must stand and materials can be sharp. Working in three dimensions deepens understanding of structure and form.
units.worked_example: A clay animal sculpture is built solid but hollowed and reshaped, with the legs thickened and joined firmly to the body so the finished piece supports its own weight without cracking in the kiln.
units.activity: Create a small sculpture from clay, wire or recycled materials that stands on its own, and present it from three angles explaining your choices of material and balance.
units.check: Why must materials and joining methods be planned carefully when making an animal on slender legs?

quiz.prompt: Which is an additive sculpture method?
Which is a subtractive sculpture method?
True or false: sculpture is viewed from several sides because it occupies real space?
Why must materials and joining methods be planned for a slender legged animal sculpture?
options: To ensure it stands and stays stable

quiz.prompt: True or false: safety is not a concern when working with sharp sculpture tools?

units.title: Kenyan craft traditions
units.notes: Kenyan crafts such as basketry, pottery, beadwork, wood carving and weaving show skill and cultural meaning. Learners examine materials, tools, techniques and functions of selected crafts, and the symbolic or social roles they play in communities. They consider how craft supports livelihoods and tourism and how mass production and imitation affect makers. By making a simple craft item and studying its context, learners connect technique, tradition and enterprise rather than treating craft as a lesser art than drawing or painting.
units.worked_example: A sisal basket can be analysed by noting the twining technique, natural dyes, market use and the livelihood it supports, linking an everyday object to design, culture and economics.
units.activity: Study one local craft, collect images and information, and create a simple related item while recording each technique and its source.
units.check: Why is it important to credit the community that developed a craft pattern or technique?

quiz.prompt: Which are examples of Kenyan crafts?
options: Basketry, pottery, beadwork and wood carving

quiz.prompt: Why should the community that developed a craft pattern be credited?
options: To respect and acknowledge its cultural source
To claim the work as new

quiz.prompt: True or false: crafts can support livelihoods and tourism?
How does studying craft context help learners?
options: It connects technique, tradition and enterprise

quiz.prompt: True or false: craft should be treated as a lesser art than drawing or painting?

units.title: Textiles and fabric arts
units.notes: Textile art uses cloth, thread and fibre as a creative medium. Learners explore dyeing, batik, tie and dye, embroidery, applique and basic weaving patterns, along with pattern repetition and colour planning. They consider the source of materials, sustainability and the reuse of fabric. They also connect fabric design to Kenyan dress, fashion and enterprise. Practical control of the medium, careful planning of pattern and awareness of cultural meaning lift textile work from decoration to considered visual art.
units.worked_example: A tie and dye cloth is planned by binding the fabric tightly at chosen points before dyeing, so the folds resist colour and a clear repeat pattern appears when the cloth is opened.
units.activity: Produce a small tie and dye or batik sample using one or two colours, then use it to plan how the repeat pattern could cover a larger fabric.
units.check: How does the way fabric is tied or waxed determine the final pattern?

quiz.prompt: Which techniques belong to textile art?
options: Dyeing, batik, tie and dye and embroidery

quiz.prompt: How does the way fabric is tied or waxed affect it?
True or false: textile artists consider sustainability and reuse of fabric?
What lifts textile work from decoration to considered art?
options: Practical control, careful planning and awareness of cultural meaning

quiz.prompt: True or false: fabric design has no connection to Kenyan dress or enterprise?

units.title: Digital art and photography
units.notes: Digital tools extend visual art through photography, drawing tablets, image editing and graphic software. Learners study composition, the rule of thirds, lighting, framing and viewpoint in photography, and basic editing such as cropping, contrast and colour balance. They learn that editing should support the intended message rather than distort truth, and they respect consent and copyright. They also compare digital and traditional methods, noting strengths such as speed and repeatability against concerns about originality and authorship.
units.worked_example: A learner photographs a market scene with the sun to one side, placing the main stall on a third line, then crops and adjusts contrast to emphasise the vendor while leaving the image truthful.
units.activity: Take ten photographs on a chosen theme, select and lightly edit your best three, and explain how composition and editing support your message.
units.check: Why should editing a photograph for a news or documentary purpose be kept minimal?

quiz.prompt: Which composition rule is used in photography?
Why should editing a photograph for news be kept minimal?
options: Because editing should support the message rather than distort truth

quiz.prompt: True or false: digital art raises concerns about originality and authorship?
Which are basic photo editing actions?
True or false: consent and copyright are unimportant when taking and editing photographs?

units.title: Composition and visual storytelling
units.notes: Every image tells a story through what it includes, excludes and emphasises. Learners plan compositions using viewpoint, framing, scale, sequence and the relationship between figure and ground. They study how a single image can imply before and after, and how a series creates narrative over time, as in comics or storyboards. They sketch thumbnails before final work to test ideas. Deliberate composition controls what the viewer notices first, feels next and remembers, turning scenes into meaning.
units.worked_example: To show a learner's long walk to school, an artist frames a tiny figure against a large empty landscape from a high viewpoint, so scale and emptiness suggest distance and effort without any words.
units.activity: Plan a four panel storyboard on a school or community story, using varied viewpoints and scale, then draw the strongest panel as a finished image.
units.check: How can viewpoint alone change the meaning of the same scene?

quiz.prompt: How can viewpoint change meaning in an image?
options: It changes what the viewer notices and how a scene is read
It only changes the frame size

quiz.prompt: What do thumbnails help artists do?
True or false: a series of images can create a narrative over time, as in comics or storyboards?
What does deliberate composition control?
options: What the viewer notices first, feels next and remembers

quiz.prompt: True or false: every image communicates only through what it includes, never through what it excludes?

units.title: Appreciating and critiquing art
units.notes: Art criticism turns looking into reasoned judgement. Learners describe what they see objectively, analyse how elements and principles are used, interpret possible meaning and context, and evaluate success against the artist's intention. They study selected Kenyan and world artworks with attention to period, materials and audience. They practise structured critique that is specific, respectful and evidence based rather than simply liking or disliking a work. This skill supports exams, exhibitions, curating and confident discussion of visual culture.
units.worked_example: Using describe, analyse, interpret and evaluate, a learner notes a painting's warm palette and bold shapes, suggests the theme of harvest, and concludes that the composition successfully directs attention to the central figure, giving reasons throughout.
units.activity: Choose one artwork and write a four part critique using description, analysis, interpretation and evaluation, citing specific evidence for each judgement.
units.check: Why should an art critique separate description from personal opinion?

quiz.prompt: Why should a critique separate description from personal opinion?
options: To keep judgement reasoned and evidence based

quiz.prompt: Which steps form structured art criticism?
True or false: a strong critique is specific and evidence based rather than simply liking or disliking?
What should claims in a critique be supported by?
True or false: describing what you see objectively is unnecessary in art criticism?

units.title: Portfolio development and art careers
units.notes: A portfolio presents an artist's best and most varied work with clear thinking about process. Learners select, organise and annotate pieces, showing sketches, experiments and final outcomes, and reflect on strengths and next steps. They explore pathways such as fine art, graphic design, illustration, animation, craft enterprise, teaching and gallery work, noting required skills and training. Health, safety and professional habits matter too. A strong portfolio communicates capability and growth to selectors, clients or employers.
units.worked_example: A learner arranges a portfolio with an introduction, dated studies showing progress, three finished pieces and a short reflection, so a viewer understands both the journey and the result.
units.activity: Compile a portfolio of at least six labelled works including studies and finished pieces, write a short reflection, and present it to the class or a mentor.
units.check: Why is showing process and rough studies valuable in a portfolio, not only final finished pieces?

quiz.prompt: What does a portfolio present?
options: An artist's best and most varied work with clear thinking about process

quiz.prompt: Why is showing process and rough studies valuable in a portfolio?
options: It shows growth and thinking, not just the final outcome

quiz.prompt: True or false: a strong portfolio communicates capability and growth to selectors, clients or employers?
Which are art career pathways?
options: Fine art, graphic design, illustration and animation

quiz.prompt: True or false: health, safety and professional habits do not matter in art careers?

Theatre and Film.overview: Theatre and Film develops performance, writing, technical and critical skills across stage and screen, exploring Kenyan and world traditions alongside film language and production. It prepares learners for pathways in acting, directing, scriptwriting, media production and performance criticism.

units.title: Origins and forms of theatre
units.notes: Theatre is live performance before an audience, and its forms have deep roots in ritual, storytelling and celebration. Learners examine selected traditions such as Greek theatre, African oral performance, masquerade and modern stage drama, comparing purpose, space and audience role. They identify common elements of plot, character, dialogue, spectacle and audience participation. They also discuss how live theatre differs from recorded media. This grounding gives learners a frame for making and judging performance throughout the course.
units.worked_example: A community storytelling circle can be compared with a staged play by noting the shared live audience, but also the flexible space, direct address and audience response typical of the oral tradition.
units.activity: In groups, present a folktale as a short live performance and afterwards list which theatrical elements you used and how the audience responded.
units.check: What does a live audience add to a performance that a recorded film cannot?

quiz.prompt: What adds to live theatre that a recorded film cannot?
options: The live audience and its immediate presence

quiz.prompt: Which are common elements of theatre?
options: Plot, character, dialogue, spectacle and audience participation

quiz.prompt: True or false: theatre has roots in ritual, storytelling and celebration?
Which traditions are studied as forms of theatre?
options: Greek theatre, African oral performance and masquerade

quiz.prompt: True or false: live theatre and recorded media are exactly the same?

units.title: Acting: voice, movement and character
units.notes: Acting requires control of voice, body and imagination. Learners develop projection, articulation, pace and pause, and use posture, gesture and movement to express intention. They explore given circumstances and objectives, asking what a character wants in each scene and how that drives action. Warm ups and relaxation protect the voice and body. They learn that truthful action on the specifics of a moment is more convincing than generalised emotion, and they refine work through rehearsal and feedback.
units.worked_example: Playing a learner who has lost a bus fare, an actor uses a tightened posture, quickened speech and a repeated glance at the road to show desperation, focusing on a clear objective rather than simply announcing the feeling.
units.activity: Perform the same two line exchange three times with different objectives, such as to comfort and to accuse, then ask classmates which objective they read from your voice and body.
units.check: Why is a clear objective more useful to an actor than deciding to simply be sad?

quiz.prompt: Why is a clear objective more useful to an actor than deciding to simply be sad?
options: Because objectives are easier to remember
Because objectives drive action in the scene

quiz.prompt: Which vocal skills does acting require?
True or false: truthful action on the specifics of a moment is more convincing than generalised emotion?
What do given circumstances describe?
options: The situation and facts surrounding a character in a scene

quiz.prompt: True or false: warm ups and relaxation are unnecessary for actors?

units.title: Script writing and dramaturgy
units.notes: A script provides the blueprint for performance through dialogue, action and stage directions. Learners create believable characters, construct conflict and stakes, and structure scenes with clear beginnings, turning points and ends. They write dialogue that reveals character and advances action, and use subtext so meaning lies beneath the words. They read drafts aloud to hear rhythm and trimming needs. Dramaturgy, the study of how a play works, helps writers test whether the story is coherent, buildable and emotionally effective.
units.worked_example: In a short scene a parent asks whether school fees are paid; the child avoids the question and studies the floor. The subtext carries the bad news without stating it, making the exchange tense and dramatic.
units.activity: Write a two page scene with two characters who want opposing things, read it aloud with classmates, then revise one line to sharpen the conflict using subtext.
units.check: How can dialogue reveal a character's feelings without naming them directly?

quiz.prompt: What does a script provide for a performance?
options: A blueprint through dialogue, action and stage directions

quiz.prompt: What does subtext mean in dialogue?
options: Meaning that lies beneath the words

quiz.prompt: True or false: reading drafts aloud helps writers hear rhythm and trimming needs?
What does dramaturgy study?
True or false: conflict and stakes are unimportant in constructing scenes?

units.title: Stagecraft and technical theatre
units.notes: Technical theatre supports the performance through scenery, props, lighting, sound, costume and stage management. Learners examine set design and construction, the functions of stage lighting, cue sheets and sound effects, and the role of costume in character and period. They consider safety, including cables, ladders and fire rules, and the value of a prompt script and rehearsed cues. Technical choices should serve the story, not merely decorate it. Good backstage work is invisible to the audience yet essential to a smooth show.
units.worked_example: For a night scene, a lighting cue dims the stage to a deep blue wash while a sound cue plays distant rain, and the stage manager calls both cues precisely so mood and continuity are maintained.
units.activity: Plan the set, lighting and sound for one scene of a class play by drawing a ground plan and writing a cue list, then explain how each cue supports the mood.
units.check: Why should technical effects support the story rather than attract attention to themselves?

quiz.prompt: What does technical theatre support?
options: The performance through scenery, props, lighting, sound and costume

quiz.prompt: Why should technical effects support the story?
options: So they attract attention to themselves
So they serve the story rather than distract

quiz.prompt: True or false: a prompt script and rehearsed cues help a show run smoothly?
Which safety concerns matter in technical theatre?
True or false: backstage work is invisible to the audience and therefore unimportant?

units.title: Directing stage productions
units.notes: The director shapes a production's interpretation and unifies the work of the whole company. Learners study script analysis, casting, blocking, pace, focus and the rehearsal process, from read through to technical and dress rehearsals. They learn to give clear, specific notes and to shape stage pictures that guide the audience's eye. They also manage time, people and conflict with respect. A director's job is not to perform for the actors, but to enable the clearest, most truthful telling of the story.
units.worked_example: Directing a crowded scene, the director moves the gossiping group downstage left and isolates the lead upstage right so the audience naturally follows the conflict without any line explaining it.
units.activity: Direct a two minute scene from a class script, plan your blocking on paper, run two rehearsals, and give each actor one specific note aimed at clear storytelling.
units.check: Why is specific, doable feedback more useful to an actor than a general comment such as be better?

quiz.prompt: What is the main job of a director?
options: To shape the interpretation and unify the whole company

quiz.prompt: Why is specific, doable feedback more useful than a general comment?
options: Because it tells the actor exactly what to adjust

quiz.prompt: True or false: blocking, pace and focus are part of the work of a director?
What happens from read through to dress rehearsal?
True or false: a director should give vague notes so actors can guess?

units.title: Kenyan and African theatre traditions
units.notes: African theatre draws on oral narrative, music, dance, ritual and community participation alongside written drama. Learners study selected Kenyan plays, festival drama and community performance, examining theme, language, character and the use of song and dance. They consider social issues addressed, such as family, education, corruption and identity, and how theatre can educate and provoke thought. They compare traditional and contemporary forms. This unit builds cultural understanding and respect for performance as a living, socially engaged practice.
units.worked_example: A Kenyan play about land disputes may open with a sung lament, use a chorus to comment on events, and mix English with a local language, showing how traditional devices carry social criticism to a modern audience.
units.activity: Read one Kenyan play and present a short analysis of its theme, language and use of traditional performance elements, quoting a line of dialogue as evidence.
units.check: How can theatre raise awareness of a social issue without becoming a plain lecture?

quiz.prompt: On what does African theatre draw?
options: Oral narrative, music, dance, ritual and community participation

quiz.prompt: Which social issues are addressed in Kenyan theatre?
True or false: theatre can educate and provoke thought as well as entertain?
How can theatre raise awareness without becoming a plain lecture?
options: By using story, character and emotion

quiz.prompt: True or false: African theatre ignores community participation?

units.title: Introduction to film language
units.notes: Film communicates through a language of shots, movement, sound and editing. Learners study shot sizes from extreme close up to wide shot, camera angles, composition, camera movement, and the relation of shots through cutting. They examine how lighting and sound shape mood and meaning. They learn that a sequence is built from choices, not merely recorded events, and that the same scene cut differently creates a different feeling. This vocabulary is the foundation for analysing and making screen work.
units.worked_example: A tense meeting is built from a series of close ups of hands and eyes cut with a wide establishing shot, so the audience feels both the pressure on the faces and the distance of the room.
units.activity: Shoot the same short action using six different shot sizes, then view them and write which shots best conveyed the emotion and why.
units.check: How can two shots edited together create a meaning that neither shot carries alone?

quiz.prompt: How can two shots edited together create new meaning?
options: Because each shot is watched separately
Because the juxtaposition creates meaning neither shot carries alone

quiz.prompt: Which are shot sizes in film language?
options: Extreme close up to wide shot

quiz.prompt: True or false: the same scene cut differently can create a different feeling?
Which elements shape mood and meaning in film?
True or false: a film sequence is merely recorded events with no creative choices?

units.title: Cinematography and visual storytelling
units.notes: Cinematography controls how the camera captures light, colour, movement and space. Learners study exposure, focal length, depth of field, framing and camera movement such as pan, tilt, tracking and crane. They explore how lighting direction shapes mood and how colour palettes support theme. They plan shot lists and storyboards so a scene is covered efficiently. They also consider practical constraints such as location, time and available equipment. Deliberate visual choices turn a script into images with atmosphere and point of view.
units.worked_example: To show a character's isolation, a cinematographer uses a low angle wide shot with the figure small at the edge of the frame under cool lighting, so framing and colour carry the theme visually.
units.activity: Storyboard and shoot a sixty second silent scene using at least four camera movements and a planned lighting mood, then screen it and explain your visual choices.
units.check: Why does a shallow depth of field often suit emotional close up moments?

quiz.prompt: What does cinematography control?
options: How the camera captures light, colour, movement and space

quiz.prompt: Why does a shallow depth of field suit emotional close up moments?
options: It isolates the subject from the background

quiz.prompt: True or false: shot lists and storyboards help cover a scene efficiently?
Which are camera movements?
True or false: lighting direction and colour palettes have no effect on mood or theme?

units.title: Editing and sound design
units.notes: Editing assembles footage into a coherent rhythm that shapes pace and story. Learners study continuity, the cuts that make action flow, and contrast edits that jump time or place, plus transitions such as dissolves and fades. They learn how cutting pace controls tension and how rhythm matches or deliberately resists the action. Sound design adds dialogue, effects, music and silence, and learners examine how ambience and a well timed pause deepen meaning. Picture and sound are shaped together, not one after the other.
units.worked_example: A chase sequence uses rapid short cuts on the running feet, then a held wide shot before the impact, while the music stops suddenly just before the crash, so silence makes the moment land hard.
units.activity: Edit a one minute scene from given footage, choose deliberate cut points, then add at least three sound elements including one moment of silence and justify each choice.
