units.check: Why can silence have a stronger effect in a scene than continuous background music?

quiz.prompt: What does editing shape?
options: The rhythm, pace and story of footage

quiz.prompt: Why can silence have a stronger effect than continuous music?
options: Because a well timed pause deepens meaning

quiz.prompt: True or false: picture and sound are shaped together, not one after the other?
Which are transitional edits?
True or false: cutting pace cannot control tension in a film?

units.title: Screenwriting for film
units.notes: Screenwriting tells a story meant to be seen and heard rather than read. Learners use scene headings, action lines and dialogue in correct format, and write visually so images carry information. They develop a logline, structure acts, and control pacing through scene length and order. They show rather than explain, revealing character through behaviour and choice. They revise for clarity and economy. A strong screenplay provides everything a production team needs to plan a shoot.
units.worked_example: Rather than a line saying a character is poor, the script shows a boy counting coins at a kiosk and returning a sweet, letting the action reveal the situation visually.
units.activity: Write a one page screenplay in correct format for a silent opening, including a logline, then exchange with a classmate for focused feedback on clarity and visuals.
units.check: Why is it stronger to show a character's trait through action than to state it in dialogue?

quiz.prompt: Why is showing a trait through action stronger than stating it in dialogue?
options: Because action reveals character through behaviour and choice

quiz.prompt: What does a strong screenplay provide?
options: Everything a production team needs to plan a shoot

quiz.prompt: True or false: screenwriting uses scene headings, action lines and dialogue in correct format?
What is a logline?
options: A brief summary of the film story

quiz.prompt: True or false: pacing in a screenplay is unaffected by scene length and order?

units.title: Film production: planning to post
units.notes: Film production moves through pre production, production and post production. Learners plan with a script, storyboard, shot list, schedule and simple budget, casting and locations. During the shoot they manage equipment, health and safety, continuity and time. In post production they edit picture, mix sound and add titles. They also consider roles such as director, producer, camera operator and editor. Good planning and teamwork, not expensive gear, usually decide whether a local production succeeds.
units.worked_example: A three minute school short is planned with a shot list and two day schedule, filmed with a borrowed phone and tripod, then edited with titles and a mixed soundtrack, showing that organisation matters more than costly kit.
units.activity: As a small crew, plan and shoot a two minute short with a shot list and schedule, then edit and screen it, noting in a short report what went well and what to improve.
units.check: Why does poor pre production planning usually cause problems during the shoot?

quiz.prompt: What are the three stages of film production?
options: Pre production, production and post production

quiz.prompt: Why does poor pre production planning cause problems during the shoot?
options: Because the team arrives unprepared and loses time

quiz.prompt: True or false: good planning and teamwork usually matter more than expensive gear?
Which roles belong to film production?
options: Director, producer, camera operator and editor

quiz.prompt: True or false: health and safety, continuity and time do not matter during the shoot?

units.title: Documentary and non fiction film
units.notes: Documentary records and interprets real life. Learners study forms such as expository, observational and participatory documentary, and examine techniques including interview, narration, archive material and b roll. They consider ethics: informed consent, honesty, fairness and the effect on people filmed. They plan research questions and shoot interviews with attention to framing, sound and respectful questioning. They distinguish informing from persuading, and they evaluate how editing shapes the audience's view of reality, since every cut implies a judgement.
units.worked_example: A documentary on a local water project interviews residents and farmers, shows the pipes in use, and uses measured narration, letting different voices be heard rather than pushing only one conclusion.
units.activity: In a group, plan and shoot a ninety second documentary on a local issue, including one interview, then screen it and discuss which ethical decisions you made.
units.check: Why must a filmmaker consider how editing can influence how real people are perceived?

quiz.prompt: Which are documentary forms?
Which ethics matter in documentary filmmaking?
True or false: every cut can imply a judgement about the people filmed?
Which techniques are used in documentary?
options: Interview, narration, archive material and b roll

quiz.prompt: True or false: a filmmaker need not consider how editing influences how real people are perceived?

units.title: Critical review of theatre and film
units.notes: Critical review judges a production with evidence from the performance or film. Learners describe what is presented, analyse how elements such as acting, direction, design, camera, editing and sound create effects, interpret meaning and context, and evaluate overall success with reasons. They write structured reviews with a clear standpoint and supporting detail, and they avoid vague praise. They also consider the intended audience and the purpose of the work. This skill prepares learners for exams, media work and informed cultural discussion.
units.worked_example: A review argues that a production's slow opening is justified by the powerful final scene, supporting the claim with specific examples of acting and design, so the judgement is reasoned rather than a bare opinion.
units.activity: Watch a live or recorded performance and write a structured review of three paragraphs with a clear standpoint and specific evidence for each judgement.
units.check: What makes a reviewer's negative judgement fair rather than merely personal dislike?

quiz.prompt: What makes a reviewer's negative judgement fair?
options: It is based on personal dislike
It is supported with evidence from the production

quiz.prompt: Which elements are analysed in a review?
options: Acting, direction, design, camera, editing and sound

quiz.prompt: True or false: a structured review avoids vague praise and supports its standpoint with detail?
What should a reviewer consider besides the work itself?
options: The intended audience and purpose of the work

quiz.prompt: True or false: critical review judges a production without any evidence?
